Mr Smeaton undertook the work, and completed it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1759. Of this Mr Smeaton gives an ample <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> in the volume he published in 1791: that edition has been sold some time ago, and a second is now in the press, under the revival of his much esteemed friend Mr Aubert, F.R.S. and governor of the London assurance corporation. Though Mr Smeaton completed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the Eddystone lighthouse in 1759 (a work that does him so much <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>) yet it appears he did not soon get into full bufines as a civil engineer; but in 1764, while in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, he offered himself a candidate for one of the receivers of the Derwentwater estate, and on the 31st of December in that year, he was appointed at a full board of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, in a manner highly flattering to himself; when two other persons strongly recommended and powerfully supported were candidates for the employment. In this appointment he was very happy, by the affluence and abilities of his partner Mr Walton one of the receivers, who taking upon himself the management and accounts, left Mr Smeaton leisure and opportunity to exert his abilities on public works, as well as to make many improvements in the mills and in the estates of Greenwich hospital. By the year 1775 he had so much bufines as a civil engineer, that he wished to resign this appointment; and would have done it then, had not his friend the late Mr Stuart the hospital surveyor, and Mr Ibbetson their secretary, prevailed upon him to continue in the office about two years longer. Mr Smeaton having now got into full bufines as a civil engineer, performed many works of general utility. He made the river Calder navigable; a work that required <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill and judgement, owing to the very impetuous floods in that river: he planned and at- Smeaton tended the execution of the great canal in Scotland for conveying the trade of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> either to the Atlantic or German ocean; and having brought it to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> originally intended, he declined a handsome yearly salary, in order that he might attend to the multiplicity of his other business. On the opening of the great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> at London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, the excavation around and under the sterlings was so considerable, that the bridge was thought to be in great danger of falling. He was then in Yorkshire, and was sent for by express, and arrived with the utmost dispatch: "I think (says Mr Holmes, the author of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>) it was on a Saturday morning, when the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the bridge was so general that few would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over or under it. He applied himself immediately to examine it, and to find about the sterlings as minutely as he could; and the committee being called together, adopted his advice, which was to repurchase the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> that had been taken from the middle pier, then lying in Moorfields, and to throw them into the river to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the sterlings." Nothing shows the apprehensions concerning the falling of the bridge more than the alacrity with which this advice was pursued; the stones were repurchased that day, horses, carts, and barges were got ready, and they began the work on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> morning. Thus Mr Smeaton, in all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, saved London bridge from falling, and secured it till more effectual methods could be taken. The vast variety of mills which Mr Smeaton constructed, so greatly to the satisfaction and advantage of the owners, will show the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> which he made of his experiments in 1752 and 1753; for he never trifled to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> where he could have an opportunity to investigate it by experiment. He built a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> engine at Authurpe, and made experiments thereon, purposely to ascertain the power of Newcomen's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE">steam-engine</a>, which he improved and brought to a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, both in its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and powers, than it was before. Mr Smeaton during many years of his life was a frequent attendant on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> being continually called for; and here his strength of judgement and perspicuity of expression had its full display: it was his constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, when applied to, to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> or support any measure, to make himself fully acquainted with it, to see its merits before he would engage in it: by this caution, added to the clearness of his description and the integrity of his heart, he seldom failed to obtain for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> which he supported an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament. No one was heard with more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, nor had any one ever more confidence placed in his testimony. In the courts of law he had several compliments paid him from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANSFIELD">Mansfield</a> and others, for the new light which he threw on difficult subjects. About the year 1785 Mr Smeaton's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> began to decline; and he then took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to endeavour to avoid all the business he could, so that he might have leisure to publish an account of his inventions and works, which was certainly the first wish of his heart; for he has often been heard to say, that "he thought he could not render so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his country as by doing that." He got only his account of the Eddystone lighthouse completed, and some preparations to his intended Treatise on Mills; for he could not refuse the solicitations of his friends in various works: and Mr Aubert, whom he greatly loved and respected, being chosen chairman of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAMSGATE">Ramsgate</a> harbour, prevailed upon him to accept the place of engineer to that harbour; and to their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> efforts the public is chiefly indebted for the improvements that have been made there within these few years, which fully appears in a report that Mr Smeaton gave in to the board of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> in 1791, which they immediately published. Mr Smeaton being at Authurpe, walking in his garden on the 16th of September 1792, was struck with the palsy, and died the 28th of October. "In his illness (says Mr Holmes) I had several letters from him, signed with his name, but written and signed by another's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>; the dictation of them showed that the strength of his mind had not left him. In one written the 26th of September, after minutely describing his health and feelings, he says, 'in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the foregoing, I conclude myself <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>-tenths dead; and the greatest favour the Almighty can do me (as I think), will be to complete the other part; but as it is likely to be a lingering illness, it is only in His power to say when that is likely to happen.'" Mr Smeaton had a warmth of expression that might appear to those who did not know him well to border on harshness; but those more intimately acquainted with him, knew it arose from the intense application of his mind, which was always in the pursuit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, or engaged in investigating difficult subjects. He would sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out hastily, when any thing was said that did not tally with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; and he would not give up any thing he argued for, till his mind was convinced by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> reasoning. In all the social duties of life he was exemplary; he was a most affectionate husband, a good father, a warm, zealous, and sincere friend, always ready to assist those he respected, and often before it was pointed out to him in what way he could serve them. He was a lover and encourager of merit whatever he found it; and many men are in a great measure indebted to his assistance and advice for their present situation. As a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, he was always entertaining and instructive; and none could spend any time in his company without improvement. SMELL; this word has in most languages two meanings, signifying either that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> of mind of which we are conscious, in consequence of certain impressions made on the nostrils, and conveyed to the brain by the olfactory nerves; or that unknown virtue, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in bodies, which is the cause of our sensations of smell. SMELLING is the act by which we perceive smells, or become sensible of the presence of odorous bodies. The sensations of smell are excited by certain effluvia, which, in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, are always rising from the surfaces of most bodies, and striking on the extremities of the olfactory nerves, give them a peculiar sort of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, which is communicated to the brain. The particles which issue thus from bodies are extremely volatile, and produce sensation by a degree of contact, which, though insensible, is still more efficient than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and palpable. It is by a similar <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of insensible contact that the eyes and ears are affected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects; whilst, in the excitation of the sensations of touch and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, an actual and sensible contact of the object with the organ is necessary. Smelling. fary. The organs of smelling are the nostrils and olfactory nerves; the minute ramifications of the latter being distributed throughout the whole concavity of the former. For a description of these, see Anatomy. The effluvia from odoriferous bodies are constantly floating about in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and must of course be drawn into the nostrils along with the air in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; "so that there is," as Dr Reid observes, "a manifest appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in placing the organ of smell in the inside of that canal, through which the air is continually passing in inspiration and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a>." It has been affirmed by Boerhaave, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in animals, vegetables, fossils, &c., which chiefly affects the sense of smelling, is that attenuated substance, inherent in their oily parts, called spirits; because, when this is taken away from the most fragrant bodies, what remains has scarcely any smell at all; but this, he says, if poured on the most odoriferous bodies, gives them a fragrance*. We cannot, however, enter at present upon this inquiry. The sense of smell has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with that of taste; and it seems probable from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> in the situation of their organs in all animals, that both are principally intended to guide them in the choice of their food; so that from this close connection, they are better enabled to choose what is good for them, and to reject what would be injurious. This is the opinion of Dr Reid, as it was, in a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, that of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> and of Cicero (A). Dr Reid also remarks, that the sense of smell probably serves the same purpose in the natural state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; but it is not always a sure guide for this purpose. The organs of smell differ, like those of the other senses, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of the animals to which they belong; and we know, that this sense is in man much less acute, than it is in many other animals. We feel, that in the choice of their food, they are guided by the senses of smell and of taste, except when man has brought them into a sort of unnatural state by domestication. And this circumstance renders it probable, that both these senses were intended to serve the same purpose in the natural state of our species, although less calculated for this end than they are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, on account of the great superiority of their smelling organs. Besides, since it is probable that man, in the natural state, acts more by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> than when civilized in society, so also it is reasonable to think, that he may possess some of the senses, (this of smell for instance,) in greater acuteness than we do. This indeed, we are assured to be a fact; for we are told, in the Histoire des Antilles, that there are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> who, by the smell alone, can distinguish the footsteps of a Frenchman from those of a negro. The sense of smell is much more obtuse in man than in some of the lower animals. Dogs we know possess a power of smelling, of which we can scarcely form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, and which, it is happy for us we do not possess (B); and birds of prey are said to possess this sense in still greater acuteness. But although this be more perfect, still the sense of smelling in man, who has other means of judging of his food, &c., is such as to fit him for deriving enjoyment from a diversity of scents, particularly those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and perfumes, to which dogs and other animals seem perfectly insensible. It has been said, we are aware, that some animals, the elephant for instance, are capable of this enjoyment (C); but of this fact we cannot help being very doubtful. There is a very great sympathy between the organs of smell and of taste; for any defect or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> of one is generally attended with some corresponding defect or disease of the other. There is also a greater similarity between the sensations of both these, than between those of any other two senses; and hence it is, that we can sometimes tell the taste of an object from its smell, and vice versa. Hence also the reason why we apply the same epithets to the names of both these classes of sensations; as a sweet smell or taste, &c. It deserves also to be remarked, that both these senses seem subservient to the preservation of the animal existence, rather than to any other purpose. They accordingly constitute an object of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural history</a> of man, rather than of intellectual or of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a>. The other three senses, on the contrary, seem rather intended for (as they certainly are essential to) our intellectual improvement, and become, of course, a proper object of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> in the sciences of moral philosophy, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. The advantages derived by man and the other animals from the sense of smelling are not confined to the assistance which it affords them in the choice of their food. Most bodies in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, when exposed to the open air, are constantly sending forth emanations or effluvia of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> acuteness as to be perfectly invisible. These diffuse themselves through the air, and however noxious or salutary, would not be perceived without the sense of smelling, which if not vitiated by unnatural habits, is not only a faithful monitor when danger is at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, but conveys to us likewise the most exquisite pleasures. --- (A) "Ut gustus (says a learned physiologist) cibi itineri, sic olfactus ostio viarum, quas aer subire debet, custos preponitur, monituras ne quid noxi, via quae semper patet, in corpus admittatur. Porro, ut gustus, sic quoque olfactus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> salutarem cibum invitat, a noxio aut corrupto, putrido imprimis vel rancido, deterret." "When thou feelst the mouth, through which animals take in whatever they desire, always placed near the nose and eyes, thinkest thou not, says Socrates to Aristodemus, that this is the work of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>?" Xenophon's Memorables, book i, chap. 4. (B) "The excessive eagerness which dogs express on smelling their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, seems to be but little connected with the appetite for food, and wholly independent of any preconceived ideas of the objects of their pursuit being fit for it. Hence several kinds of them will not eat the game which they pursue with such wild impetuosity; and of which the scent seems to animate them to a degree of ecstasy far beyond what the desire of food can produce." Knight on Taste. (C) There is an animal to which, naturalists say, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> is so agreeable and so necessary, that nature has provided it with a little bag stored with an exquisite odour. "On pretend, (says Buffon,) que la mangouste ouvre <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CETTE">cette</a> poche, pour se refraîchir lorsqu'elle est trop chaud." Smelling pleasures. The fragrance of a rose, and of many other flowers, is not only pleasant, but gives a refreshing and delightful stimulus to the whole system, whilst the odours proceeding from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a>, or any noxious vegetable, or other substance, are highly offensive to our nostrils. Hence we are naturally led to seek the one class of sensations, and to avoid the other. In some species of animals the sense of smell seems to be connected with certain mental sympathies, as those of hearing and sight are in all that possess them in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree: for not only their sexual desires appear to be excited by means of it, but other instinctive passions, which, according to the usual system of nature, should be still more remote from its influence. Dogs, although wholly unacquainted with lions, will shudder at their roar; and an elephant that has never seen a tiger, will in the same manner show the strongest symptoms of horror and affright at the smell of it. "The late Lord Clive (says an ingenious writer), exhibited a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> between two of these animals at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>; but the scent of the tiger had such an effect upon the elephant, that nothing could either force or allure him to go along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, where the cage in which the tiger was inclosed, had passed, until a gallon of arack was given him. Upon this, his horror suddenly turning into fury, he broke down the paling to get at his enemy, and killed him without difficulty." If riding along a road, near which a dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, or part of its carcass, happens to be lying, we know, that our horse, although he sees it not, cannot be made to pass the place but with difficulty. Where blood has been shed, particularly that of their own species, oxen will assemble, and upon smelling it, roar and bellow, and show the most manifest signs of horror and distress. And yet these symptoms could not arise from any associated notions of danger or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, since they appear in such as never had any opportunities of acquiring them. They must therefore be instinctive, like other instinctive antipathies and propensities. But although in their mutual intercourse, animals make much use of the sense of smell, still it does not seem to be further concerned in exciting their sexual desires, than in indicating their object. Some of those spleenetic philosophers, who are ready upon all occasions to quarrel with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of nature, have taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of condemning their Maker, because it has pleased his unfathomable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> to bestow so many influences upon the brute senses and instincts more perfect than he has given to man, without reflecting that he has given to man an ample <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>; for it may be asked with the poet, "Is not his reason all these powers in one? "Is Heaven unkind to man and man alone? "Shall he alone, whom rational we call, "Be pleased with nothing if not blest with all." With respect to that unknown peculiarity of bodies, which is the cause of our sensations of smell, the opinions of philosophers have been very various. Until of late, the doctrine of Descartes and Locke on this subject was pretty generally received; but, since the publication of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Reid's works, his opinion, which we deem the most correct and satisfactory, has become very popular. We will endeavour to abridge his account of this matter. For this purpose, let us suppose a person, who has grown up without the sense of smell, to be immediately endowed with the use of this organ, and placed near some flowers of an exquisite flavour. When he examines what he feels in such a situation, he can find no resemblance between this new sensation and anything with which he is already acquainted. He finds himself unable to explain its nature, and cannot ascribe to it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, or any known <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of matter. It is a simple affection, or feeling, of mind, and, considered abstractedly, can have no necessary connection with the nerves, the nostrils, or effluvia, or with any thing material whatever. By the nature of his constitution he is, however, led to refer this peculiar sensation to the nostrils, as its organ; and when, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and by means of touch, he learns that external objects have the power of exciting this sensation, he concludes, that there must exist in bodies some unknown cause by which it is excited. In the first part of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> he considers the feeling, or sensation, abstractedly. As such it exists in the mind only; and cannot exist there but when the mind is conscious of it. His consciousness soon enables him to distinguish different sorts of smells, all of them very distinct from one another; but, conformably to the nature of all sensation, extremely simple. He concludes, that each of these must have a distinct cause; and finding, by experience, that this cause is an unknown something in bodies, he concludes, that it must be a property of matter, and, for want of another, gives it the name of smell. When he removes an odoriferous body from the organ, the sensation vanishes; when the body is again applied, the sensation is excited: and hence it is, that he is led naturally to connect the sensation with this unknown peculiarity of bodies by which it is produced. But since we see, that the sensation is, in a great degree, related to other objects besides its unknown cause, to the mind in which it exists, for instance, and to the organ which is its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, it may be asked why it becomes associated in the mind with its cause only? The reason seems pretty obvious. No single sensation or class of sensations, is more connected with the mind, than any others of which it is susceptible. Nor is the connection subsisting between the organ and any of the sensations peculiar to it greater than that which subsists between it and every other sensation of which it is the inlet. Hence the connection between the smell of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> and the mind, or between it and the nostrils, is very general, and cannot, in the former instance, distinguish it from any other sensation of whatever kind, nor, in the latter from any other particular smell. But the connexion between this sensation and the orange is peculiar and permanent; and we accordingly find them always associated in the mind, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as we associate the notion of fire with the sensation of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. The relation which a sensation of smell, or any sensation, bears to the mind, to an organ, or to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> and conception of itself, is common to all sensations. The relation which any sensation bears to its own cause, supposing the sensation of smell to a particular virtue or quality of bodies, is common to it with every other sensation, when considered with respect to its peculiar cause. And finally, a sensation of any kind bears the same sort of relation to the memory and conception of itself, that any other feeling or operation of mind bears to the conception and memory of that particular feeling or operation. Whatever then be the nature of the minute particles Smelling of bodies by which our sensations of smell are excited, we cannot help conferring their unknown cause as a virtue or quality of matter. Like all other modifications of material substance, it must be confessed, that this can have no resemblance to the sensations of mind. But we are not, therefore, to conclude with the followers of Descartes and Locke, that this secondary quality is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> sensation; especially as we can readily conceive it existing where it is not smelled, or even after supposing the annihilation of every sentient being throughout the universe. The existence of the sensation we know to be momentary and fugitive; but in the existence of its cause we can, without difficulty, or inconveniency, conceive a permanency independent of mind and of its sensations. The doctrine we have been illustrating has of late been called into question by a sceptical writer, who, it appears to us, has upon this occasion been entirely deficient in his accustomed acuteness. Dr Reid's account of this affair seems so full, so clear and convincing, that we are at a loss to conceive how his meaning can be misinterpreted; and yet the arguments and objections of the writer to whom we allude, derive all their plausibility from a misinterpretation of Dr Reid's meaning, and from a deviation from the established use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. "An eminent metaphysician" (says this author) has declared that he has not the least difficulty in conceiving the air perfumed with aromatic odours in the deserts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; and he has decided, that the man who maintains smells to exist only in the mind, must be mad, or must abuse language and disgrace philosophy. There are some authors, nevertheless, who differ widely on this subject from the learned metaphysician. Is it possible for a sensation to exist where there is no sentient? The authors to whom I allude think it impossible." And so, we may tell this learned author, does Dr Reid, if he will take his word for it. Of the sensation of smell he remarks: "It is indeed impossible, that it can be in any body: it is a sensation; and a sensation can be in a sentient thing only." Again, "I can think of the smell of a rose when I do not smell it; and it is possible that when I think of it there is no rose there existing; but, when I smell it, I am necessarily determined to believe that the sensation really exists. This is common to all sensations, that, as they cannot exist but in being perceived, so they cannot be perceived but they must exist." But, continues this acute metaphysician, "a smell is nothing else than a sensation. It is a feeling, which may be agreeable or disagreeable; which may, as some think, be excited by various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of elements; but which, since it is a feeling, cannot be those elements which are said to cause it, and cannot exist where there is no creature to perceive it. What is to be understood, in philosophical strictness, by the perfumes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>? We can excuse the poet when he makes the ocean smile, the winds dance, and the flowers respire; or even were he to perfume the desert. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> is no such magician, and had better not wander through the regions of fancy in search of sensations where there is no sentient." And is it then true that the word smell means only a sensation? A sensation is no more than an effect; it is a transient modification of the mind, which the mind itself can never produce. It must then have some cause which is external to the mind. Now, it is to this cause, and not to the sensation, that the name smell is most frequently applied in all languages; and it is this cause which Dr Reid supposes capable of existing in the deserts of Arabia, where there is no sentient being to perceive it. But let us hear himself: "We have considered smell as signifying a sensation, feeling, or impression upon the mind; and in this sense it can only be in a mind or sentient being; but it is evident that mankind give the name of smell much more frequently to something which they conceive to be external, and to be a quality of body; they understand by it something which does not at all infer a mind, and have not the least difficulty in conceiving the air perfumed with aromatic odours in the deserts of Arabia, or in some uninhabited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> where the human foot never trod." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of smelling is something very different from the actual sensation of smell. For the faculty may remain when we have no sensation. And the mind is no less different from the faculty, for it continues the same individual being when that faculty is lost. What is smell in the rose? It is a quality or virtue of the rose, or of something proceeding from it, which we perceive by the sense of smelling; and this is all we know of the matter. But what is smelling? It is an act of the mind, but is never imagined to be a quality of the mind. Again, the sensation of smelling is conceived to infer necessarily a mind or sentient being; but smell in the rose infers no such thing. We say, this body smells sweet and that stinks; but we do not say, this mind smells sweet and that stinks; therefore, smell in the rose, and the sensation which it causes, are not conceived, even by the vulgar, to be things of the same kind, although they have the same name." There are some other remarks on Dr Reid's opinion in the work upon which we have been commenting, which we shall pass by; we may, however, notice the author's concluding argument: after mentioning some examples, he observes, "Now in these instances we see men and animals that must have perception of smell, if I may be permitted to say so, altogether different from each other. Is not smell sensation when the spaniel finds sport in the field for his master; when the shark pursues through the ocean its expected victim; and when the camel conducts the thirsty wanderer to a fountain of fresh water across the burning sands of the Arabian desert?" If no animal had the sensation of smell, there would be no odour; for aroma and oils may be thought to be material compositions, but are neither agreeable nor disagreeable feelings." If men and animals differ in their perceptions of smell, (and no doubt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of organization will cause them to do so,) the conclusion should not be, we think, that smell is merely sensation, but that there is actually something external which is the cause of their sensations, and about which they differ. A rose put to the nostrils of a man and then to those of a dog, may excite very different sensations; but we cannot think that the peculiarity of the rose, which excites these different sensations, varies by thus changing the position of the rose. If at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> one person mistakes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a> for beef, and another thinks that it is venison, the conclusion may be, that it is neither venison nor beef; but no man in his senses can conclude that there is no meat at the table. But, "is not smell sensation when the spaniel finds sport for his master in the field?" There is sensation no doubt; but we may be permitted to ask, what would become of the spaniel's sensation of smell and of his master's sport, were there no game in Smelling the field? What of the shark's sensation of smell and purfuit, were there no victim in the ocean? and what of the camel and the thirsty wanderer, were there no fountain of fresh water in the Arabian deserts? "The smell of a rose signifies two things," says Dr Reid; "First, A sensation which can have no existence but when it is perceived, and can only be in a sentient being or mind. Secondly, It signifies some power, quality, or virtue in the rose, or in effluvia proceeding from it, which hath a permanent existence independent of the mind; and which, by the constitution of nature, produces the sensation in us. By the original constitution of our nature we are both led to believe that there is a permanent cause of the sensation, and prompted to seek after it; and experience determines us to place it in the rose. The names of all smells, tastes, sounds, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, have a like ambiguity in all languages; but it deserves our attention, that these names are but rarely, in common language, used to signify the sensations; for the most part, they signify the external qualities which are indicated by the sensations." We have been induced thus to discuss this topic at some length, because we regretted to see Dr Reid's opinion and reasoning misrepresented; and we shall now conclude, not as this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Berkeleyan does, "that, if no animal had the sensation of smell, there would be no odour;" but, that if there were no odour or external cause of smell, no animal would have this sensation. The sense of smell becomes sometimes too acute, either in consequence of some defect or disuse of the organ, or from too great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of the whole nervous system, such as we sometimes observe in fevers, in phrenitis, and in hysterical diseases. It is however more frequently blunted in consequence of affections of the brain and nerves, arising from blows on the head, or from internal causes; or this may happen on account of too great a dryness of the organ, owing to a suppression of the accustomed humours, or to their being conveyed off by some other channel; or it may arise from too great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of tears and of mucus choking up the nostrils. We have instances of both in cases of common cold, in which, at the beginning of the disease, the nostrils are dry, but as it advances, begin to discharge a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of humour, or become obstructed by a thick mucus. Whatever hinders the free entrance of the air into the nostrils or its passage through them, must also injure the sense of smell. It is also sometimes depraved as to perceive smells when there is no odoriferous body present, or to perceive smells different from those that are really present. Some of the particles of the odoriferous effluvia, after having remained for some time in the caverns of the nostrils, issuing forth again and affecting the organ, will sometimes cause this species of false perception, even in the most healthy persons. The sense of smelling may be diminished or destroyed by diseases; as by the moisture, dryness, inflammation, or suppuration of the olfactory membrane, the compression of the nerves which supply it, or some fault in the brain itself at their origin. A defect, or too great a degree of solidity of the small spongy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the upper jaw, the caverns of the forehead, &c. may likewise impair this sense; and it may be also injured by a collection of fetid matter in these caverns, which is continually exhaling from them, and also by immoderate use of snuff. When the nose abounds with moisture, after gentle evacuations, such things as tend to take off irritation and coagulate the thin sharp serum may be applied; as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of anise mixed with fine flour, camphor dissolved in oil of almonds, &c., the vapours of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, frankincense, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-mastic, and benjamin, may likewise be received into the nose and mouth. For moistening the mucus when it is too dry, some recommend snuff made of the leaves of marjoram, mixed with oil of amber, marjoram, and aniseed; or a tincture of calcined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> vitriol, twelve grains of which may be mixed with two ounces of marjoram water and filtrated. The steam of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> upon hot iron, and received up the nostrils, is also of use for softening the mucus, removing obstructions, &c. If there be an ulcer in the nose, it ought to be dressed with some emollient ointment, to which, if the pain be very great, a little laudanum may be added. If it be a venereal ulcer, 12 grains of corrosive sublimate may be dissolved in a pint and a half of brandy, a table spoonful of which may be taken twice a day. The ulcer ought likewise to be washed with it, and the fumes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> may be received up the nostrils. If there be reason to suspect that the nerves which supply the organs of smelling are inert, or want stimulating, volatile salts, or strong snuffs, and other things which occasion <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SNEEZING">sneezing</a>, may be applied to the nose; the forehead may likewise be anointed with balsam of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, to which may be added a little oil of amber. SMELT. See SALMO, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SMELTING

Pages 16-16

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, the fusion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> melting of the ores of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, in order to separate the metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> from the earthy, stony, and other parts. See ORES, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">Reduction</a> of. SMEW. See MERGUS, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SMILAX

Pages 16-16

rough bindweed, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of dicotyledonous plants; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 11th order, Sarmentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SMITH

Pages 16-19

Sir Thomas, was born at Walden in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in 1512. At 14 he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he distinguished himself so much, that he was made Henry VIII.'s scholar together with John Cheke. He was chosen a fellow of his college in 1531, and appointed two years after to read the public Greek lecture. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> Greek at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was very faulty; the same found being given to the letters and diphthongs, ι, η, υ, ει, οι, ω. Mr Smith and Mr Cheke had been for some time sensible that this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> was wrong; and after a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of consultation and research, they agreed to introduce that mode of reading which prevails at present. Mr Smith was lecturing on Arisotle de Republica in Greek. At first he dropped a word <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two at intervals in the new pronunciation, and sometimes he would stop as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had committed a mistake and correct himself. No notice was taken of this for two or three days; but as he repeated more frequently, his audience began to wonder at the unusual sounds, and at last some of his friends mentioned to him what they had remarked. He owned that something was in agitation, but that it was not yet sufficiently digested to be made public. They entreated him earnestly to discover his project: he did so; and in a short time <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers resorted to him for information. The new pronunciation was was adopted with enthusiasm, and soon became universal at Cambridge. It was afterwards opposed by Bishop Gardiner the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; but its superiority to the old mode was so visible, that in a few years it spread over all England. In 1539 he travelled into foreign countries, and studied for some time in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. On his return he was made regius professor of civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at Cambridge. About this time he published a treatise on the mode of pronouncing English. He was useful likewise in promoting the reformation. Having gone into the family of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Somerset, the protector during the minority of Edward VI, he was employed by that nobleman in public affairs; and in 1548 was made secretary of state, and received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. While that nobleman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in office, he was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, first to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> and afterwards to France. Upon <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s accession he lost all his places, but was fortunate enough to preserve the friendship of Gardiner and Bonner. He was exempted from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, and was allowed, probably by their influence, a pension of £100. During <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s reign he was employed in public affairs, and was sent three times by that princess as her ambassador to France. He died in 1577. His abilities were excellent, and his attainments uncommonly great: He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a physician, a chemist, mathematician, linguist, historian, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>. He wrote, 1. A treatise called the English Commonwealth. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> De Repta et Emendata Lingua Graecae Pronunciatione. 3. De Moribus Turcarum. 4. De Druidum Moribus. Smith, Edmund, an English poet, the only son of Mr Neale an eminent merchant, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Baron Lechmere, was born in 1668. By his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> he was left young to the care of Mr Smith, who had married his father's sister, and who treated him with so much tenderness, that at the death of his generous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> he assumed his name. His writings are not many, and those are scattered about in miscellanies and collections: his celebrated tragedy of Phaedra and Hippolitus was acted in 1707; and being introduced at a time when the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> so much engrossed the polite world, gave Mr Addison, who wrote the prologue, an opportunity to rally the vitiated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the public. However, notwithstanding the esteem it has always been held in, it is perhaps rather to be considered as a fine poem than as a good play. This tragedy, with a Poem to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Mr John Philips, three or four Odes, with a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> spoken at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in laudem Thomae Bodleii, were published as his works by his friend Mr Oldifworth. Mr Smith died in 1710, sunk into indolence and intemperance by poverty and disappointments; the hard fate of many a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius. Smith, John, an excellent mezzotinter, flourished about 1700; but neither the time of his birth nor death is accurately known. He united strength with fineness, and finished with freedom. He served his time with one Tillet a painter in Moorfields; and as soon as he became his own <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, learned from Becket the secret of mezzotinto, and being farther instructed by Van der Vaart, was taken to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in Sir Godfrey Kneller's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and as he was to be the publisher of that master's works, doubtless received considerable hints from him, which he amply repaid. "To posterity perhaps his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> (says Mr Walpole) <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> carry an idea of something <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a>; perukes of an enormous length flowing over suits of armour, compose wonderful habits. It is equally strange that fashion could introduce the vers, one, and establish the practice of representing the other when it was out of fashion." Smith excelled in exhibiting both, as he found them in the portraits of Kneller, who was less happy in what he substituted to armour. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KIT_CAT_CLUB"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-KIT">Kit</a>-cat club he has poured full bottoms chiefly over night gowns. If those streams of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> were incommode in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, I know nothing (he adds) they were adapted to that can be done in a night-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>. Smith composed two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> volumes, with proofs of his own plates, for which he asked £50. His finest works are Duke Schomberg on horseback; that duke's son and successor Morhard; the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, Dorset, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>; three plates with two figures in each, of young persons or children, in which he shows; William Cowper; Gibbons and his wife; Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>; the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, a whole length, with a flowerpot; a very curious one of Queen Mary, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> head, fan, and gloves; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Godolphin; the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, a whole length, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; Sir George Rooke, &c. There is a print by him of James II. with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, but no inscription; which not being finished when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> went away, is so scarce that it is sometimes sold for above a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a>. Smith also performed many historic pieces; as the loves of the gods, from Titian, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLENHEIM">Blenheim</a>, in ten plates; Venus standing in a shell, from a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> by Corregio, and many more, of which perhaps the most delicate is the holy family with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, after Carlo Maratti." Smith, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, the celebrated author of the Philosophical Inquiry into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, was the only son of Adam Smith comptroller of the customs at Kirkaldy, and of Margaret Douglas, daughter of Mr Douglas of Stratherny. He was born at Kirkaldy on the 5th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1723, a few months after vol iii. the death of his father. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> during his infancy was infirm and sickly, and required all the care of his surviving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. When only three years old he was carried by his mother to Stratherny on a visit to his uncle Mr Douglas; and happening one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to be amusing himself alone at the door of the house, he was stolen by a party of those vagrants who in Scotland are called tinkers. Luckily he was missed immediately, and the vagrants pursued and overtaken in Leslie wood; and thus Dr Smith was preserved to extend the bounds of science, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the commercial policy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the school of Kirkaldy under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Miller, a teacher of considerable eminence, and whose name deserves to be recorded on account of the great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eminent men which that seminary produced while under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Dr Smith, even while at school, attracted notice by his passionate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to books, and by the extraordinary powers of his memory; while his friendly and generous disposition gained and secured the affection of his schoolfellows. Even then he was remarkable for those habits which remained with him through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, of speaking to himself when alone and of absence in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. He was sent in 1737 to the university of Glasgow, where he remained till 1740, when he went to Balliol college Oxford, as an exhibitioner on Snell's foundation. His favourite pursuits while at the university were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. After his removal to England he frequently employed himself in translating, particularly from the French, with a view to the improvement of his own style: a practice which he often recommended to all who wished to cultivate the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. It was probably then also that he applied himself with the greatest care to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of languages, of which, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, his knowledge was uncommonly extensive and accurate. After <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years residence at Oxford he returned to Kirkaldy, and lived two years with his mother without any fixed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for his future life. He had been designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; but disliking the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> profession, he resolved to abandon it altogether, and to limit his ambition to the prospect of obtaining some of those preferments to which literary attainments <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in Scotland. In 1748 he fixed his residence in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and for three years read a course of lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and belles lettres under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames. In 1751 he was elected professor of logic in the university of Glasgow, and the year following was removed to the professorship of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a>, vacant by the death of Mr Thomas Craigie, the immediate successor of Dr Hutcheon. In this situation he remained 13 years, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he used frequently to look back to as the most useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life. His lectures on moral philosophy were divided into four parts: The first contained natural <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; in which he considered the proofs of the being and attributes of God, and those truths on which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is founded: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> comprehended ethics, strictly so called, and consisted chiefly of those doctrines which he afterwards published in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of moral sentiments: in the third part he treated more at length of that part of morality called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and which, being susceptible of precise and accurate rules, is for that reason capable of a full and accurate explanation: in the last part of his lectures he examined those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> regulations which are founded, not upon the principle of justice, but of expediency; and which are calculated to increase the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, the power, and the prosperity of a state. Under this view he considered the political institutions relating to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, to finances, to ecclesiastical and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> governments: this contained the substance of his Wealth of Nations. In delivering his lectures he trifled almost entirely to extemporary elocution: his manner was plain and unaffected, and he never failed to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> his hearers. His reputation soon rose very high, and many students found their way merely upon his account. When his acquaintance with Mr Hume first commenced is uncertain; but it had ripened into friendship before the year 1752. In 1759 he published his Theory of Moral Sentiments; a work which deservedly extended his reputation: for, though several of its conclusions be ill-founded, it must be allowed by all to be a singular effort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, ingenuity, and subtlety. Besides, it contains a great mixture of important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; and, though the author has sometimes been misled, he has had the merit of directing the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of philosophers to a view of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, which had formerly in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> escaped their notice. It abounds everywhere with the purest and most elevated maxims concerning the practical conduct of life; and when the subject of his work leads him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> the imagination and the heart, the variety and felicity of his illustrations, the richness and fluency of his eloquence, and the skill with which he wins the attention and commands the passions of his readers, leave him among our British moralists without a rival. Towards the end of 1763 Dr Smith received an invitation from Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Townend to accompany the duke of Buccleugh on his travels; and the liberal terms in which this proposal was made induced him to resign his office at Glasgow. He joined the duke of Buccleugh at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> early in the year 1764, and set out with him for the continent in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> following. After a stay of about ten days at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, they proceeded to Thoulouse, where they fixed their residence for about 18 months; thence they went by a pretty extensive route through the south of France to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, where they passed two months. About Christmas 1765 they returned to Paris, and remained there till October following. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in which Dr Smith passed these ten months may be conceived in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the recommendation of Mr Hume. Turgot, Quinai, Necker, d'Alembert, Helvetius, Montesquieu, Madame Riccoboni, were among the number of his acquaintances; and some of them he continued ever after to reckon among the number of his friends. In October 1766 the duke of Buccleugh returned to England. Dr Smith spent the next ten years of his life with his mother at Kirkaldy, occupied habitually in intense study, but unbending his mind at times in the company of some of his old schoolfellows, who still continued to reside near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their birth. In 1776 he published his Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations; a book so universally known, that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on it would be useless. The variety, importance, and (may we not add) <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, of the information which it contains; the skill and comprehensiveness of mind displayed in the arrangement; the admirable illustrations with which it abounds; together with a plainness and perspicuity which makes it intelligible to all—render it unquestionably the most perfect work which has yet appeared on the general principles of any branch of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a>. He spent the next two years of his life in London, where he enjoyed the society of some of the most eminent men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>: but he removed to Edinburgh in 1778, in consequence of having been appointed, at the request of the duke of Buccleugh, one of the commissioners of the customs in Scotland. Here he spent the last twelve years of his life in an affluence which was more than equal to all his wants. But his studies seemed entirely suspended till the infirmities of old age reminded him, when it was too late, of what he yet owed to the public and to his own fame. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> materials of the works which he had announced had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago been collected, and little probably was wanting but a few years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and retirement to complete them. The death of his mother, who had accompanied him to Edinburgh in 1781, together with that of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Miss Douglas in 1788, contributed to frustrate these projects. They had been the objects of his affection for for more than 60 years, and in their society he had enjoyed from his infancy all that he ever knew of the endearments of a family. He was now alone and helpless; and though he bore his loss with equanimity, and regained apparently his former cheerfulness, yet his health and strength gradually declined till the period of his death, which happened in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1790. Some days before his death he ordered all his papers to be burnt except a few essays, which have since been published. Of the originality and comprehensiveness of his views; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, the variety, and the correctness of his information; the inexhaustible fertility of his invention—he has left behind him lasting monuments. To his private worth, the most certain of all testimonies may be found in that confidence, respect, and attachment, which followed him through all the various relations of life. He was habitually absent in conversation, and was apt when he spoke to deliver his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> in the form of a lecture. He was rarely known to start a new topic himself, or to appear unprepared upon those topics that were introduced by others. In his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> form and appearance there was nothing uncommon. When perfectly at ease, and when warmed with conversation, his gestures were animated and not ungraceful; and in the society of those he loved, his features were often brightened by a smile of ineffable benignity. In the company of strangers, his tendency to silence, and perhaps still more his consciousness of that tendency, rendered his manners somewhat embarrassed; an effect which was probably not a little heightened by those <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> ideas of propriety which his recluse habits tended at once to perfect in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, and to diminish his power of realizing.

SMITING-LINE

Pages 19-19

in a ship, is a small rope fastened to the mizen-yard arm, below at the deck, and is always furled up with the mizen-sail, even to the upper end of the yard, and thence it comes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the poop. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to loofe the mizen-sail without striking down the yard, which is easily done, because the mizen-sail is furled up only with rope-yarns; and therefore when this rope is pulled hard, it breaks all the rope-yarns, and so the sail falls down of itself. The sailor's phrase is, "finita est misera" (whence this rope takes its name), that is, hale by this rope that the sail may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down.

SMOKE

Pages 19-29

a dense <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> vapour, arising from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> bodies. As this vapour is extremely disagreeable to the senses, and often prejudicial to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, mankind have fallen upon several contrivances to enjoy the benefit of fire, without being annoyed by smoke. The most universal of these contrivances is a tube leading from the chamber in which the fire is kindled to the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, through which the smoke ascends, and is dispersed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. These tubes are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>; which, when constructed in a proper manner, carry off the smoke entirely; but, when improperly constructed, they carry off the smoke imperfectly, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> annoyance of the inhabitants. As our mansions at present seem to have a very imperfect knowledge of the manner in which chimneys ought to be built, we can hardly perform a more acceptable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the public than to point out the manner in which they ought to be constructed, so as to carry off the smoke entirely; as well as to explain the causes from which the defects so often complained of generally proceed, and the method of removing them. Those who would be acquainted with this subject should begin by considering on what principle smoke ascends in any chimney. At first many are apt to think that smoke is in its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and of itself, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and rises in it for the same reason that cork rises in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. There is no cause why smoke should not rise in the chimney though the room be ever so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. Others think there is a power in chimneys to draw up the smoke, and that there are different forms of chimneys which afford more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less of this power. They amuse themselves with searching for the best form. The equal dimensions of a funnel in its whole length is not thought <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> enough, and it is made, for fancied reasons, sometimes tapering and narrowing from below upwards, and sometimes the contrary, &c., &c. A simple experiment or two may serve to give more correct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. Having lighted a pipe of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, plunge the stem to the bottom of a decanter half filled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water; then putting a rag over the bowl, blow through it, and make the smoke descend in the stem of the pipe, from the end of which it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> rise in bubbles through the water; and being thus cooled, will not afterwards rise to go out through the neck of the decanter, but remain spreading itself and resting on the surface of the water. This shows that smoke is really heavier than air, and that it is carried upwards only when attached to or acted upon by air that is heated, and thereby rarified and rendered specifically lighter than the air in its neighbourhood. Smoke being rarely seen but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with heated air, and its upward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> being visible, though that of the rarified air that drives it is not so, has naturally given rise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. It is now well known that air is a fluid which has <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> as well as others, though about 800 times lighter than water; that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> makes the particles of air recede from each other, and take up more space, so that the same weight of air heated will have more bulk than equal weights of cold air which may surround it, and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> must rise, being forced upwards by such colder and heavier air, which presses to get under it and take its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. That air is rarified or expanded by heat, may be proved to their comprehension by a flask blown bladder, which laid before a fire, will soon swell, grow tight, and burst. Another experiment may be to take a glass tube about an inch in diameter, and 12 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, open at both ends, and fixed upright on legs so that it need not be handled, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> might warm it. At the end of a quill fallen five or six inches of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> filament of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, so that it may be held either above the upper end of the tube or under the lower end, your warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> being at a distance by the length of the quill. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> there were any motion of air through the tube, it would manifest itself by its effect on the silk; but if the tube and the air in it are of the same temperature with the surrounding air, there will be no such motion, whatever may be the form of the tube, whether crooked or straight, narrow below and widening up- wards, or the contrary, the air in it will be quiescent. Warm the tube, and you will find as long as it continues warm, a constant current of air entering below and passing up through it till discharged at the top; because the warmth of the tube being communicated to the air it contains, rarefies that air, and makes it lighter than the air without; which therefore presses in below, forces it upwards, follows and takes its place, and is rarefied in its turn. And, without warming the tube, if you hold under it a knob of hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, the air thereby heated will rise and fill the tube, going out at its top; and this motion in the tube will continue as long as the knob remains hot, because the air entering the tube below, is heated and rarefied by passing near and over that knob. That this motion is produced merely by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of specific gravity between the fluid within and that without the tube, and not by any fancied form of the tube itself, may appear by plunging it into water contained in a glass jar a foot deep, through which such motion might be seen. The water within and without the tube being of the same specific gravity, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> each other, and both remain at rest. But take out the tube, stop its bottom with a finger, and fill it with olive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which is lighter than water; then stopping the top, place it as before, its lower end under water, its top a very little above. As long as you keep the bottom flopped the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> remain at rest; but the moment it is unlopped, the heavier enters below, forces up the lighter, and takes its place; and the motion then ceases, merely because the new fluid cannot be successively made lighter, as air may be by a warm tube. In fact, no form of the funnel of a chimney has any share in its operation or effect respecting smoke except its height. The longer the funnel, if erect, the greater its force when filled with heated and rarefied air to draw in below and drive up the smoke, if one may, in compliance with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> draw, when in fact it is the superior weight of the surrounding atmosphere that presses to enter the funnel below, and so drives up before it the smoke and warm air it meets with in its passage. What is it then which makes a smoky chimney, that is, a chimney which, instead of conveying up all the smoke, discharges a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it into the room, offending the eyes and damaging the furniture? The causes of this effect may be reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, differing from each other, and therefore requiring different remedies. 1. Smoky chimneys in a new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> are such frequently from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> want of air. The workmanship of the rooms being all good, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> out of the workman's hands, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the boards of the flooring, and of the panels of wainscoting, are all true and tight; the more so as the walls, perhaps not yet thoroughly dry, preserve a dampness in the air of the room which keeps the woodwork swelled and close. The doors and the sashes too, being worked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, shut with exactness, so that the room is as tight as a snuff-box, no passage being left open for air to enter except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>-hole, and even that is sometimes covered by a little dropping shutter. Now if smoke cannot rise but as connected with rarefied air, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of such air, suppose it filling the funnel, cannot rise unless other air be admitted to supply its place; and if therefore no current of air enter the opening of the chimney—there is nothing to prevent the smoke from coming out into the room. If the motion upwards of the air in a chimney that is freely supplied be observed by the rising of the smoke or a feather in it, and it be considered that in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> such feather takes in rising from the fire to the top of the chimney, a column of air equal to the content of the funnel must be discharged, and an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> supplied from the room below, it will appear absolutely impossible that this operation should go on if the tight room is kept shut; for were there any force capable of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> constantly so much air out of it, it must soon be exhausted like the receiver of an air-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>, and no animal could live in it. Those therefore who stop every crevice in a room to prevent the admission of fresh air, and yet would have their chimney carry up the smoke, require inconsistencies, and expect impossibilities. Yet under this situation it is not uncommon to see the owner of a new house in despair, and ready to sell it for much less than it cost; conceiving it uninhabitable because not a chimney in any one of its rooms will carry off the smoke unless a door or window be left open. Much expense has also been made to alter and amend new chimneys which had really no fault: in one house particularly which Dr Franklin knew that belonged to a nobleman in Westminster, that expense amounted to no less than £300. After his house had been, as he thought, finished and all charges paid. And after all, several of the alterations were ineffectual, for want of understanding the true principles. Remedies.
