Many laws have been made with this view. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any goods be shipped or landed without warrant and presence of an officer, the vessel shall be forfeited, and the wharfinger shall forfeit 100l. and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> or mariner of any ship inward bound shall forfeit the value of the goods; and any <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a>, porter, or other assailing, shall be committed to gaol, till he find surety of his good behaviour, or until he shall be discharged by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of exchequer (13 & 14 C. II. c. 11.) If goods be landed after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a>, the vessel and goods shall be forfeited; and every person concerned therein shall forfeit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the value of the drawback (8 An. c. 13.) Goods taken in at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shall be forfeited, and also the vessel into which they are taken; and every person concerned therein shall forfeit treble value (9 G. II. c. 35.) A vessel hovering near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> shall be forfeited, if under 50 tons burden; and the goods shall also be forfeited, or the value thereof (5 G. III. c. 43.) Persons receiving or buying run goods shall forfeit 20l. (8 G. c. 18.) A concealer of run goods shall forfeit treble value (8 G. c. 18.) Offering run goods to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, the same shall be forfeited, and the person to whom they are offered may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> them; and the person offering them to sale shall forfeit treble value (11 G. c. 39.) A porter or other person carrying run goods shall forfeit treble value (9 G. II. c. 35.) Persons armed or disguised carrying run goods shall be guilty of felony, and transported for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years (8 G. c. 18. 9 G. II. c. 35.) But the last statute, 19 G. II. c. 34. is for this purpose infaust omnium; for it makes all forcible acts of smuggling, carried on in defiance of the laws, or even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> to evade them, felony without benefit of clergy: enabling, that if three or more persons shall assemble, with fire-arms or other offensive weapons, to assist in the illegal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> or importation of goods, or in rescuing the same after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZURE">seizure</a>, or in rescuing offenders in custody for such offences: or shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> with such goods in disguise; or shall wound, shoot at, or assault, any officers of the revenue when in the execution of their duty; such persons shall be felons, without the benefit of clergy. When we consider the nature, and still more the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of mankind, we must allow that the enacting of severe penal laws is not the way to prevent crimes. It were indeed much to be wished that there were no such thing as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> crime; for the generality of men, but especially the lower orders, not discerning the propriety or utility of such laws, consider them as oppressive and tyrannical, and never hesitate to violate them when they can do it with impunity. Instead therefore of punishing smugglers, it would be much better to remove the temptation. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> duties which have been imposed upon the importation of many different sorts of foreign goods, in order to discourage their consumption in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, have in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> served only to encourage smuggling; and in all cases have reduced the revenue of the customs below what more moderate duties would have afforded. The saying of Dr Swift, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> of the customs two and two, instead of making four, make sometimes only one, holds perfectly true with regard to such heavy duties, which never could have been imposed, had not the mercantile system taught us, in many cases, to employ <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, not of revenue, but of monopoly. The bounties which are sometimes given upon the exportation of home produce and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and the drawbacks which are paid upon the re-exportation of the greater part of foreign goods, have given occasion to many frauds, and to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of smuggling more destructive of the public revenue than any other. In order to obtain the bounty or drawback, the goods, it is well known, are sometimes shipped and sent to sea, but soon Heavy duties being imposed upon almost all goods imported, our merchant importers smuggle as much, and make entry of as little as they can. Our merchant exporters, on the contrary, make entry of more than they export; sometimes out of vanity, and to pay for great dealers in goods which pay no duty; and sometimes to gain a bounty or a drawback. Our exports, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these different frauds, appear upon the customhouse books greatly to overbalance our imports; to the unspeakable comfort of those politicians who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the national prosperity by what they call the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of trade.

SMYRNA

Pages 33-33
or IMSIR, at present the largest and richest city of Asia Minor, is situated in north latitude 38° 28', and in E. Long. 27° 25' from Greenwich, and about 183 miles west by south of Constantinople. The town extends along the shore about half a mile on a gentle declivity. The houses of the English, French, and Dutch consuls are handsome structures; these, with most of those occupied by the Christian merchants, are washed on one side by the sea, forming a street named Frank-Street, from its being solely inhabited by European Christians. In the year 1763 the whole of this quarter was consumed by fire: the loss sustained by this calamity in merchandise was estimated at a million and a half of Turkish dollars, or near 200,000 sterling. The port is one of the finest of the Levant, it being able to contain the largest fleet; and indeed there are seldom in it fewer than 100 ships of different nations. A castle stands at its entrance, and commands all the shipping which fall in or out. There is likewise an old ruinous castle, near a mile in circumference, which stands in the upper part of the city, and, according to tradition, was built by the empress Helena; and near it is an ancient structure, said to be the remains of a palace where the Greek council was held when Smyrna was the metropolis of Asia Minor. They also show the ruins of an amphitheatre, where it is said St Polycarp, the first bishop, fought with lions. This city is about four miles in circumference, and nearly of a triangular form; but the side next the mountain is much longer than the other sides. The houses are low, and mostly built with clay walls, on account of the earthquakes to which the country is subject; but the caravanserais and some other of the public buildings have an air of magnificence. The streets are wide, and almost a continued bazaar, in which a great part of the merchandise of Europe and Asia is exposed to sale, with plenty of provisions; though these are not so cheap as in many other parts of Turkey, on account of the populousness of the place, and the great resort of foreigners. It is said to contain 15,000 Turks, 10,000 Greeks, 1,800 Jews, 200 Armenians, and 200 Franks; but the whole population is computed at 120,000. The Turks have 19 mosques; two churches belong to the Greeks; one to the Armenians; and the Jews have eight synagogues. The Romanists have three convents. There is also one of the fathers Della Terra Santa. Here resides an archbishop of the Greek church; a Latin bishop who has a salary from Rome, Smyrna with the title of bishop of Smyrna in partibus infidelium; and the English and Dutch factories have each their chaplain. The walks about the town are extremely pleasant, particularly on the west side of Frank Street, where there are several little groves of orange and lemon trees, which being always clothed with leaves, blossoms, and fruit, regale several of the fencibles at the same time. The vines which cover the little hills about Smyrna afford both a delightful prospect and plenty of grapes, of which good wine is made. These hills are agreeably interspersed with fertile plains, little forests of olives and other fruit-trees, and many pleasure-houses, to which the Franks usually retire during the summer. In the neighbourhood of Smyrna is great plenty of game and wild-fowl, and particularly deer and wild-hogs. The sea also abounds with a variety of good fish. The European Christians are here allowed all imaginable liberties, and usually clothe themselves after the European manner. The chief commerce of this city consists in raw silk, silk-stuffs, grogram, and cotton yarn. However, the unhealthfulness of the situation, and more especially the frequent earthquakes, from which, it is said, they are scarcely ever free for two years together, and which have been felt 49 days successively, are an abatement of the pleasure that might otherwise be enjoyed here. A very dreadful one happened in June 1688, which overthrew a great number of the houses; and the rock opening where the cattle flood, swallowed it up, and no less than 5000 persons perished on this occasion. In the year 1758, so desolating a plague raged here, that scarcely a sufficient number of the inhabitants survived to gather in the fruits of the earth. In the year 1772, three-fourths parts of the city were consumed by fire; and five years after it was visited by the most dreadful earthquakes, which continued from the 23rd of June to the 5th of July; by which successive calamities the city has been so much reduced, that its former consequence is never likely to be restored. The ladies here wear the oriental dress, consisting of large trousers or breeches, which reach to the ankle; long veils of rich silk or velvet, lined in winter with costly furs; and round their waist an embroidered zone with clasps of silver or gold. Their hair is plaited, and descends down the back often in great profusion. The girls have sometimes above twenty thick tresses, besides two or three encircling the head as a coronet, and set off with flowers and plumes of feathers, pearls, or other jewels. They commonly tinge it of a chestnut colour, which is the most desired. Their apparel and carriage are alike antique. It is remarkable that the trousers are mentioned in a fragment of Sappho as part of the female dress.

Alexanders; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of pentandria, and to the order of digynia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 45th order, Umbellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SNaffle, in the manege, is a very slender bit-mouth without any branches, much used in England; the true bridles being reserved for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

See Helix, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Limax, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> Index.

SNELLIUS FOUND

Pages 229-236

s found means to abridge greatly the labour of calculation by some very ingenious theorems; and although he did not go beyond Van Ceulen, yet he verified his result. His discoveries on this subject are contained in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> called *Willebrodi Snelli Cyclometricus de Circuli Dimensione*, &c., Lugd. Bat. 1621. Descartes found also a geometrical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, which being repeated continually, gave the circumference, and from which he might easily have deduced an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a>. Gregory of St Vincent distinguished himself also on this subject. It is true he committed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in supposing he had discovered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> of both the circle and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a>; but he had previously made so many beautiful geometrical discoveries, deduced with much elegance after the manner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that Squaring, it would be wrong to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> him with those absurd pretenders which we have already noticed. Gregory's mistake was the cause of a sharp controversy carried on between his disciples on the one side, and by Huygens, Mercenius and Leffaud on the other; and it was this that gave Huygens occasion to consider particularly the quadrature of the circle, and to investigate various new and curious theorems relating to it, which are contained in his *Theoremata de Quadratura Hyperboles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELLIPSIS">Ellipsis</a> et Circuli*, 1651; and in his work *De Circuli Magnitudine Inventa*, 1654. In particular he showed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> \(c\) denote the chord of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, and \(s\) its sine, then the arch itself <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be greater than \(c + \frac{s}{2} (c - s)\), but less than \(c + \frac{4c + s}{2c + 3s} \times \frac{1}{2} (c - s)\): he also showed that the arch is less than the sum of \(\frac{1}{2}\) of its sine and \(\frac{1}{2}\) of its tangent. These theorems greatly shorten the labour of approximating to the ratio of the diameter to the circumference, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> and circumscribed figures, insomuch that by the inscribed polygons of 6 and 12 sides, we may obtain it to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of accuracy as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> did by the inscribed and circumscribed polygons of 96 sides. James Gregory, in his *Vera Circuli et Hyperbolae Quadratura*, gave several curious theorems upon the relation of the circle to its inscribed and circumscribed polygons, and their ratios to one another; and by means of these he found with infinitely less trouble than by the ordinary methods, and even by those of Snellius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the circle as far as 20 places of figures. He gave also, after the example of Huygens, constructions for finding straight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> nearly equal to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of a circle, and of which the degree of accuracy was greater. For example, he found that if \(A\) be put for the chord of an arch of a circle, and \(B\) for twice the chord of half the arch, and \(C\) be taken such that \(A : B : B : 2B : C\), then the arch itself is nearly equal to \(\frac{8C + 8B - A}{15}\), but a little less, the error in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> being less than its \(\frac{1}{3800}\) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; and when the arch does not exceed 12°, it is less than its \(\frac{1}{4000}\) part; and finally, for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> the error is not greater than its \(\frac{1}{10000}\) part. And farther, that if \(D\) be such that \(A : B : B : D\), then the arch is nearly equal to \(\frac{12C + 4B - D}{15}\), but a little greater, the error in the semicircle being less than its \(\frac{1}{3800}\) part, and in a quadrant less than its \(\frac{1}{4000}\) part. The discoveries of Dr Wallis, delivered in his *Arithmetica Infinitorum* published in 1655, led him to a singular expression for the ratio of the circle to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of its diameter. He found that the former was to the latter as 1 to the product \[ \frac{3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 5 \times 7 \times 7 \times 9 \times 9 \times 11 \times 11}{2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 6 \times 6 \times 8 \times 8 \times 10 \times 10 \times 12} \] the fractions \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{5}, \frac{1}{7}, \frac{1}{9}, \frac{1}{11}, \frac{1}{13}, \ldots\) being supposed infinite in number. The products being supposed <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to infinity, we have the ratio exactly; but if we stop at any finite number of terms, as must necessarily be the case in its application, the result will be alternately too great and too small, according as we take an odd <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an even number of terms of the numerator and denominator. Squaring. Thus the fraction \( \frac{3}{4} \) is too great; on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, \[ \frac{3 \times 3}{2 \times 4} = \frac{9}{8} \text{ is too small, and } \frac{3 \times 3 \times 5}{2 \times 4 \times 4} = \frac{45}{32} \text{ too great,} \] and so on. But to approach as near as possible in each case, Wallis directs to multiply the product by the square root of a fraction formed by adding to unity the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> of the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> in either its numerator or denominator; then the result, although much nearer, will be too great if the number whose reciprocal is taken be the last in the numerator, but too small if it be the number in the denominator. Thus the following series of expressions will give approximate values of the infinite product \[ \frac{3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 5 \times 7 \times 7}{2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 6 \times 6 \times 8 \times 8} \text{ which are alternately too great and too small.} \] \[ \frac{3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 6} \sqrt{(1 + \frac{1}{5})}; \quad \frac{3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 6} \sqrt{(1 + \frac{1}{5})}; \] \[ \frac{3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 7}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 6 \cdot 8} \sqrt{(1 + \frac{1}{7})}; \quad \frac{3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 7}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 6 \cdot 8} \sqrt{(1 + \frac{1}{7})}; \text{ &c.} \] These values, alternately too great and too small, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> between the known limits. An expression of another kind for the ratio of the circle to the square of the diameter was found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Brouncker. He showed that the circle being unity, the square of the diameter is expressed by the continued fraction \[ 1 + \frac{1}{2 + \frac{9}{2 + \frac{25}{2 + \frac{49}{2 + \text{&c.}}}}} \] which is supposed to go on to infinity, the numerators 1, 9, 25, 49, &c. being the squares of the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, &c. By taking two, three, four, &c. terms of this fraction, we shall have a series of approximate values which are alternately greater and less than its accurate value. Such were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> discoveries relating to the quadrature of the circle made before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Newton: many others, however, were quickly added by that truly great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, as well as by his contemporaries. In particular, Newton himself showed that if \( s \) denote the sine, and \( v \) the versed sine of an arch, then the radius being unity, the arch is equal to either of the following series, \[ s + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 7} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 8 \cdot 9} + \text{&c.} \] \[ \sqrt{2v} \times \left(1 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 7} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 8 \cdot 9} + \text{&c.}\<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>) \] And James Gregory found that \( t \) being put for the tangent, the arch is expressed by the very simple series \[ t - \frac{t^3}{3} + \frac{t^5}{5} - \frac{t^7}{7} + \frac{t^9}{9} - \text{&c.} \] We have investigated the first of these series at § 140, and the third at § 137, of the article <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>: the Squaring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is easily obtained from the first by considering that since the sine of an arch is half the chord of twice the arch, that is, half of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> between the diameter and versed sine of twice the arch; we have therefore only to multiply the first series by 2, and to substitute \( \frac{\pi}{2} \sqrt{2v} \) instead of \( s \), and we get the second series. By taking \( s = \frac{\pi}{2} \), then, because in this case the arch contains 30°, we have half the circumference to the radius 1, or the whole circumference to the diameter 1, expressed by the infinite series \[ 3 \left(1 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot 2^4} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 7 \cdot 2^6} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 8 \cdot 9 \cdot 2^8} + \text{&c.}\right) \] And by supposing that in the third series \( t = 1 \), in which case the arch is one-eighth of the circumference, we have the same things expressed by the series \[ 4 \left(1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7} + \frac{1}{9} - \frac{1}{11} + \text{&c.}\right) \] which was given by Leibnitz as a quadrature of the circle in the Leipzig Acts in the year 1682; but was discovered by him 1673. Gregory, however, had found the series under its general form several years before. By the first of these two numerical series we can readily compute the circumference of the circle to a tolerable degree of accuracy; but the second is altogether inapplicable in its present form on account of the slowness of its convergency; for Newton has observed that to exhibit its value exact to twenty places of figures, there would be occasion for no less than five thousand millions of its terms, to compute which would take up above a thousand years. The slowness of the convergency has arisen from our supposing \( t = 1 \). If we had supposed \( t \) greater than 1, then the series would not have converged at all, but on the contrary diverged. But by giving to \( t \) a value less than 1, then the rate of convergency will be increased, and that so much the more, as \( t \) is smaller. If we suppose the arch of which \( t \) is the tangent to be 30°, then \( t \) will be \( \sqrt{3} = \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{3} \), and therefore half the circumference to radius unity, or the circumference to the diameter unity, which in this case is \( 6t \left(1 - \frac{t^2}{3} + \frac{t^4}{5} - \frac{t^6}{7} + \frac{t^8}{9} - \text{&c.}\right) \) will be \[ \sqrt{12} \left(1 - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 3^2} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 3^3} + \frac{1}{9 \cdot 3^4} - \text{&c.}\right). \] By means of this series, in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s time the circumference may be found to be nearly 3.141592653590, which is true to 11 decimal places, and is a very considerable degree of accuracy, considering the smallness of the labour. But Mr Machin, enticed by the easiness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, was induced, about the beginning of the last century, to continue the approximation as far as 100 places of figures, thus finding the diameter to be to the circumference as 1 to 3.141592653589793238462643383279502884197169399375105820974945923078164062862089986280348253421170680. After him, De Lagny continued it as far as Squaring. 128 figures. But he has also been outdone; for in Radcliffe's library at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, there is a manuscript in which it is carried as far as 150 figures! Although this last series, which was first proposed by Dr Halley, gives the ratio of the diameter to the circumference with wonderful facility when compared with the operose method employed by Van Ceulen, yet others have been since found which accomplish it with still greater ease. In Halley's series we have to compute the irrational <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> \( \sqrt{12} \), because of the irrational value which it is necessary to give to \( t \) in order to render it sufficiently small, and at the same time an exact part of the whole circumference; but Mr Machin contrived, by a very ingenious artifice, to reduce the computation of an arch of 45°, and consequently the length of the whole circumference, to two series which contain only rational quantities, and which at the same time converge with great rapidity. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this artifice, and the manner in which it occurred to its author, is explained by Dr Hutton in his very excellent treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">Mensuration</a>, as follows: "Since the chief advantage (in the application of Gregory's series to the rectification of the circle) consists in taking small arches, whose tangents shall be numbers easy to manage, Mr Machin very properly considered, that since the tangent of 45° is 1, and that the tangent of any arch being given, the tangent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of that arch can easily be had; if there be assumed some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> simple number as the tangent of an arch, and then the tangent of the double arch be continually taken, until a tangent be found nearly equal to 1, which is the tangent of 45°, by taking the tangent answering to the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of 45° and this multiple, there would be found two very small tangents, viz. the tangent first assumed, and the tangent of the difference between 45° and the multiple arch; and that therefore the lengths of the arches corresponding to these two tangents being calculated, and the arch belonging to the tangent first assumed being often doubled as the multiple directs, the result, increased or diminished by the other arch, according as the multiple should be below or above it, would be the arch of 45°. "Having thus thought of his method, by a few trials he was lucky enough to find a number (and perhaps the only one) proper for his purpose; viz. knowing that the tangent of \( \frac{1}{x} \) of 45° is nearly \( \frac{1}{3} \), he assumed \( \frac{1}{3} \) as the tangent of an arch. Then, since if \( t \) be the tangent of an arch, the tangent of the double arch will be \( \frac{2t}{1-t^2} \); the radius being 1; the tangent of the double arch to that of which \( \frac{1}{3} \) is the tangent will \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{9}} \), and the tangent of the double of this arch will be \( \frac{4}{\sqrt{9}} \), which being very nearly equal to 1, shews, that the arch which is equal to four times the first arch is very near 45°. Then, since the tangent of the difference between an arch of 45°, and an arch greater than 45°, whose tangent is \( T \), is \( \frac{T-1}{T+1} \), we shall have the tangent of the difference between 45°, and the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{9}} \) equal to \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{9}} \). Now, by calculating from the general series the arches whose tangents are \( \frac{1}{3} \) and \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{9}} \), (which may be quickly done by reason of the smallness and simplicity of the numbers), and taking the latter arch from four times the former, the remainder will be the arch of Squaring. 45°." If we substitute \( \frac{1}{x} \) instead of \( t \) in the general series, we shall have the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{1}{x} \) expressed by the series \( \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 5^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 5^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 5^7} + \ldots \), &c.; and, in like manner, by substituting \( \frac{1}{x^2} \) for \( t \), we get the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{1}{x^2} \) expressed by the series \( \frac{1}{239} + \frac{1}{3 \cdot 239^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 239^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 239^7} + \ldots \), &c. Now, since four times the arch to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a>. \( \frac{1}{x} \) diminished by the arch to tan. \( \frac{1}{x^2} \) is equal to the arch to tan. 1, that is, to the arch of 45°, or \( \frac{\pi}{4} \) of the semicircumference; therefore, half the circumference of a circle to rad. = 1, or the whole circumference, the diameter being 1, is equal to \[ 16 \left( \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 5^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 5^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 5^7} + \frac{1}{9 \cdot 5^9} - \ldots \right) \] \[ - 4 \left( \frac{1}{239} + \frac{1}{3 \cdot 239^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 239^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 239^7} + \frac{1}{9 \cdot 239^9} - \ldots \right) \] and this is Machin's series for the rectification of the circle. The happy idea which Machin had conceived of reducing the rectification of the arch whose tangent is unity to that of two arches whose tangents are small rational fractions, having each unity for a numerator, appears also to have occurred to Euler; and the same thought has, since his time, been pursued by other mathematicians, who have contrived to resolve an arch of 45° into three or more such arches. We shall show how this may be done, beginning with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the following problem. **Problem.** Supposing \( n \), \( x \), and \( y \), to denote three whole numbers, such, that the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{1}{n} \) is equal to the sum of two arches whose tangents are \( \frac{1}{x} \) and \( \frac{1}{y} \), radius being unity, it is required to determine all possible values of the numbers \( x \) and \( y \) in terms of the number \( n \). **Solution.** It is manifest from the formula for the tangent of the sum of two arches (<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, § 368.) that \[ \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y}; \text{ hence we have } \frac{1}{n} = \frac{x+y}{xy}, \text{ and } nx + ny = xy - 1, \text{ and } y(x-n) = nx + 1; \text{ and, lastly, } y = \frac{nx + 1}{x-n} = n + \frac{1}{x-n}. \] Now, as by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, \( y \) is a whole number, it is manifest that \( \frac{n^2 + 1}{x-n} \) must be a whole number; therefore, \( x-n \) must be a divisor of \( n^2 + 1 \). Let \( p \) be any divisor of \( n^2 + 1 \), and \( q \) the quotient, that is, let \( p \cdot q = n^2 + 1 \), then \( x-n = p \), and \( x = n + p \); And since \( \frac{n^2 + 1}{x-n} = \frac{p}{q} = g \), therefore \( y = n + g \); thus the values of \( x \) and \( y \) are determined in terms of \( n \) as required; and by giving to \( p \) and \( q \) all possible values, we shall have... have all the values of \( x \) and \( y \) that can exist. This solution affords us the following theorem. **Theorem.** Let \( n \) denote any whole number, and let \( n^2 + 1 \) be resolved into any two factors \( p \) and \( q \), (one of which may be unity), that is, let \( pq = n^2 + 1 \); the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{1}{n} \) is equal to the sum of the arches whose tangents are \( \frac{1}{n+p} \) and \( \frac{1}{n+q} \) respectively. For the sake of brevity, let \( A_1 = \frac{1}{n} \) be put to denote the arch, having for its tangent \( \frac{1}{n} \); then, according to this notation, our theorem will be expressed thus, \( A_1 = A_1 + A_1 \). Let us now suppose \( n = 1 \), then \( n^2 + 1 = 2 = 1 \times 2 \), therefore, the only values which we can give in this case to \( p \) and \( q \) are \( p = 1, q = 2 \), and these being substituted, we have \[ A_1 = A_1 + A_1. \] From which it appears, that the arch whose tangent is unity (that is, \( \frac{1}{2} \) of the circumference), is the sum of the arches whose tangents are \( \frac{1}{3} \) and \( \frac{1}{5} \). This is Euler's theorem, and by means of it, putting \( \frac{1}{3} \) and \( \frac{1}{5} \) for \( t \) in the general series \( t - \frac{1}{3}t^3 + \frac{1}{5}t^5 - \frac{1}{7}t^7 + \ldots \), &c., we get half the circumference to radius 1 equal to \[ \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 2^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 2^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 2^7} + \frac{1}{9 \cdot 2^9}, & \text{&c.} \\ +\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 3^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 3^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 3^7} + \frac{1}{9 \cdot 3^9}, & \text{&c.} \end{align*} \] Let us now suppose \( n = 2 \), then \( n^2 + 1 = 5 = 1 \times 5 \), hence the only values which \( p \) and \( q \) can have are 1 and 5; and in this case our general formula gives \( A_1 = A_1 + A_1 \). If now from the two equations \[ A_1 = A_1 + A_1; \quad A_1 = A_1 + A_1, \] we eliminate successively \( A_1 \) and \( A_1 \), we shall obtain the two following: \[ A_1 = 2A_1 + A_1; \quad A_1 = 2A_1 - A_1. \] From the first of these it appears that \( \frac{1}{2} \) of the circumference is equal to the sum of twice the arch to tan. \( \frac{1}{3} \), and once the arch to tan. \( \frac{1}{5} \); and from the second, that the same quantity is equal to the excess of twice the arch to tan. \( \frac{1}{3} \) above the arch to tan. \( \frac{1}{5} \); and from each of these, an expression for the whole circumference may be obtained analogous to that which we have found above from Euler's formula, but which will converge faster, and therefore is better. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of an arch of \( 45^\circ \) into three other arches, may be effected by means of our general formula, as follows: Put \( n = 3 \), then \( n^2 + 1 = 10 = 1 \times 10 = 2 \times 5 \), hence we have \( p = 1, q = 10 \), and also \( p = 2, q = 5 \); therefore, substituting, we get two different values of \( A_1 \), viz. \[ A_1 = A_1 + A_1; \quad A_1 = A_1 + A_1. \] From these, and the equation \( A_1 = 2A_1 + A_1 \), we get, by exterminating \( A_1 \), the two following expressions for \( A_1 \), an arch of \( 45^\circ \). \[ A_1 = 2A_1 + A_1 + 2A_1; \quad A_1 = 2A_1 + A_1 + 2A_1. \] These give each an expression for the circumference composed of three series. The labour, however, of computing by either of them, particularly the latter, will probably be less than by any of the formulas composed of two series, on account of the greater degree of quickness with which the series will converge. All the preceding formulas have been investigated in different ways by different mathematicians. That, however, which we are about to investigate, we believe is new. Let \( n \) in the general formula be taken equal to 5; then \( n^2 + 1 = 26 = 1 \times 26 = 2 \times 13 \), therefore \( p = 1, q = 26 \), also \( p = 2, q = 13 \), hence we find \( A_1 = A_1 + A_1 \), and also \( A_1 = A_1 + A_1 \). From this last equation, and the equation \( A_1 = 2A_1 + A_1 + 2A_1 \), let \( A_1 \) be eliminated, and the result is \[ A_1 = 3A_1 + 2A_1 + 2A_1. \] This appears to be the most convenient expression of any we have yet found, because the fractions are smaller, while at the same time two of the denominators consist of only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and the third, which consists of two, admits of being resolved into factors. By the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of reasoning we have found this expression \[ A_1 = 2A_1 + 3A_1 + 2A_1 + 3A_1, \] which consists of four terms; but for the sake of brevity we omit its investigation. We shall now apply the formula \( A_1 = 3A_1 + 2A_1 + 2A_1 \) to the actual calculation of the arch of \( 45^\circ \), the radius of the circle being unity. I. Calculation of the length of the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{1}{7} \). In this case, because \( t = \frac{1}{7} \), we have \[ A_1 = \frac{1}{7} - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 7^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 7^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 7^7} + \frac{1}{9 \cdot 7^9}, \text{&c.} \] \[ \begin{align*} \frac{1}{7} &= .1428571428571 \\ \frac{1}{5 \cdot 7^5} &= .0000118998037 \\ \frac{1}{9 \cdot 7^9} &= .0000000027534 \\ \frac{1}{13 \cdot 7^{13}} &= .0000000000008 \\ \end{align*} \] amount of positive terms. \[ \begin{align*} \frac{1}{3 \cdot 7^3} &= .0009718172983 \\ \frac{1}{7 \cdot 7^7} &= .0000001734665 \\ \frac{1}{11 \cdot 7^{11}} &= .000000000460 \\ \frac{1}{15 \cdot 7^{15}} &= .0009719908108 \\ \end{align*} \] amount of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> terms. \[ A_1 = .1418970540042 \] II. Calculation of the length of the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{1}{8} \). Here \( t = \frac{1}{8} \), therefore, \[ A_1 = \frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 8^3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 8^5} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 8^7}, \text{&c.} \] Squaring. \[ \begin{align*} \frac{1}{8} &= .12500000000 \\ \frac{1}{3.8^3} &= .0006510416667 \\ \frac{1}{5.8^3} &= .000061035156 \\ \frac{1}{7.8^3} &= .000000681196 \\ \frac{1}{9.8^3} &= .00000008278 \\ \frac{1}{11.8^3} &= .00000000106 \\ \frac{1}{13.8^3} &= .00000000001 \\ \end{align*} \] \[A_{\frac{1}{8}} = .1243549945466\] III. Calculation of the arch whose tangent is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Here \(t = \frac{1}{3}\), therefore, \[ \begin{align*} A_{\frac{1}{18}} &= \frac{1}{18} - \frac{1}{3.18^3} + \frac{1}{5.18^3} - \frac{1}{7.18^3} + \ldots \\ \frac{1}{18} &= .055555555556 \\ \frac{1}{3.18^3} &= .000571559214 \\ \frac{1}{5.18^3} &= .000001058443 \\ \frac{1}{7.18^3} &= .00000002333 \\ \frac{1}{9.18^3} &= .0000000006 \\ \end{align*} \] \[A_{\frac{1}{18}} = .0554985052458\] Thus by a very easy calculation we have obtained one-fourth of the circumference true to 12 decimal places; and indeed by this method we may find an approximate value of the ratio of the diameter to the circumference to 200 places of figures with, perhaps, as much ease as Vieta or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> found it to 10 or 15 figures. We have already observed that Van Ceulen desired that his quadrature, which extended only to 35 decimals, might be inscribed on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>; from which we may reasonably infer that the time and labour he had bestowed in the calculation must have been very great; but by an artifice of the kind we have been explaining, Euler in 18 hours verified Lagny's quadrature of 128 figures. In concluding this article we shall briefly notice some series for the indefinite rectification of the circle, which have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> appeared in the fifth volume of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> Philosophical Transactions. They are given by Mr W. Wallace of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> entitled, *New Series for the Quadrature of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">Conic Sections</a>, and the Computation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">Logarithms</a>*. These series do not give the arch directly, but only its reciprocal, or the powers of that reciprocal; it is however evident, that any one of these being known, the arch itself becomes immediately known. The first series is as follows. Let \(a\) denote any arch of a circle, and let its tangent, the tangents of its half, &c. be briefly denoted by tan. \(a\), tan. \(\frac{1}{2}a\), &c. Then shall \[ \frac{1}{a} = \tan. a + \frac{1}{2} \tan. \frac{1}{2}a + \frac{1}{3} \tan. \frac{1}{3}a + \ldots + T + T' + S. \] Here the arches \(a, \frac{1}{2}a, \frac{1}{3}a, \ldots\) constitute a geometrical progression, having the number of its terms infinite, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). The letters \(T\) and \(T'\) are put for any two adjoining terms (after the first) of the series, and \(S\) is put for the sum of all the terms following these; and this sum is always contained between two limits, one of which is \(\frac{1}{2}\) of the latter of the two terms \(T, T'\), and the other is a third proportional to their difference; and the last of the two being always less than the first of these limits, but greater than the second. As a specimen of the way of applying this series, we shall give the calculation of the length of an arch of 90° to six decimal places. In this case \[ \tan. a = \cotan. a = 1, \] the remaining quantities tan. \(\frac{1}{2}a\), tan. \(\frac{1}{3}a\), &c. are to be computed from tan. \(\frac{1}{2}a\) by this formula, tan. \(\frac{1}{2}A = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{\tan^2 A} + 1\right)} - \frac{1}{\tan. A}\). Accordingly we find \[ \begin{align*} \tan. \frac{1}{2}a &= 1. \\ \tan. \frac{1}{3}a &= .4142136 \\ \tan. \frac{1}{4}a &= .1989123 \\ \tan. \frac{1}{5}a &= .0984914 \\ \tan. \frac{1}{6}a &= .0491268 \\ \tan. \frac{1}{7}a &= .0245486 \\ \end{align*} \] \[ \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \tan. \frac{1}{2}a &= .500000 \\ \frac{1}{3} \tan. \frac{1}{3}a &= .1035534 \\ \frac{1}{4} \tan. \frac{1}{4}a &= .0248040 \\ \frac{1}{5} \tan. \frac{1}{5}a &= .0061557 \\ T &= \frac{1}{4} \tan. \frac{1}{4}a = .0015352 \\ T' &= \frac{1}{3} \tan. \frac{1}{3}a = .0003836 \\ S &= .0001278 \\ \end{align*} \] Hence \(S = .0001278\) \[ \frac{1}{a} = .6366197 \] Arch of 90° = \(a = 1.570796\). The second series given in this paper is expressed as follows. Let cof. \(a\), cof. \(\frac{1}{2}a\), &c. denote the cosine of the arch, the cosine of its half, &c. Then \[ \frac{1}{a^2} = \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{1}{1 - \text{cof. } \frac{1}{2}a} + \frac{1}{1 + \text{cof. } \frac{1}{2}a} \right) \] \[ = \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{1}{1 - \text{cof. } \frac{1}{2}a} + \frac{1}{1 + \text{cof. } \frac{1}{2}a} \right) \] \[ + \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{1}{1 - \text{cof. } \frac{1}{2}a} + \frac{1}{1 + \text{cof. } \frac{1}{2}a} \right) \] Here, as before, the letters \(T, T'\) denote any two adjacent terms of the series in the parenthesis, and \(S\) is put for the sum of all the following terms, which in this case is always less than \(\frac{1}{2}T'\), but greater than a third proportional to \(T - T'\) and \(T'\). This second series con- Squaring verges quicker than the first, and is besides better adapted to calculation, because the cosines of the series of arches \( \frac{1}{2}a, \frac{3}{4}a, \ldots \) are more easily deduced from the cosine of \( a \) and one another than the tangents. The formula in this case being \( \cos \frac{\pi}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1 + \cos A}{2}} \). There are various other series for the rectification of any arch of a circle given in the same paper, some of which converge faster than either of the two we have here specified, and all have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of being applicable to every possible case, and of having very simple limits, between which the sum of all their terms following any proposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> are always contained. It may also be observed that the principles from which they are deduced are of the most simple and elementary kind, inasmuch that the author has stated it as his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that their investigation might even be admitted into and form a part of the elements of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>. **Squatina.** See *Squalus*, *<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*. **Squill.** See *Scilla*, *<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>* and *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> Index*. **Squilla,** the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cancer. See *Cancer, Entomology Index*. **Squinting.** See *Medicine*, No. 383. **Squirrel.** See *Sciurus*, *<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index*. **Stabbing**, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>. The offence of mortally stabbing another, though done upon sudden provocation, is punished as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>; the benefit of clergy being taken away from it by statute. (See *Murder*.) For by Ja. I. c. 8. when one thrusts or stabs another, not then having a weapon drawn, or who hath not then first stricken the party stabbing, so that he dies thereof within six months after, the offender shall not have the benefit of clergy, though he did it not of malice aforethought. This statute was made on account of the frequent quarrels and stabbings with short daggers between the Scotch and the English, at the accession of James I.; and being therefore of a temporary nature, ought to have expired with the mischief which it meant to remedy. For, in point of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and substantial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, it cannot be said that the mode of killing, whether by stabbing, strangling, or floothing, can either extenuate or enhance the guilt; unless where, as in the case of poisoning, it carries with it internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of cool and deliberate malice. But the benignity of the law hath confirmed the statute to favourably in behalf of the subject, and so strictly when against him, that the offence of stabbing now stands almost upon the same footing as it did at the common law. Thus, (not to repeat the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> mentioned under *Manslaughter*, of stabbing an adulterer, &c., which are barely manslaughter, as at common law), in the construction of this statute it hath been doubted, whether, if the deceased had struck at all before the mortal blow given, this does not take it out of the statute, though in the preceding quarrel the stabber had given the first blow; and it seems to be the better opinion, that this is not within the statute. Also it hath been resolved, that the killing a man, by throwing a hammer or other weapon, is not within the statute; and whether a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> with a pistol be so or not is doubted. But if the party slain had a cudgel in his hand, or had thrown a pot or a bottle, or discharged a pistol at the party stabbing, this is a sufficient reason for having a weapon drawn on his side within the words of the statute. **Stachys**, Hedge-nettle, or All-heal, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of didynamia, and order of gymnospermia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 42d order, Verticillatae. See *Botany Index*. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">Stadium</a>,** an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> measure, containing 125 geometrical paces, or 625 Roman feet, corresponding to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURLONG">furlong</a>. The word is said to be formed from the Greek word στάδιον “a station,” or ἰστάμενος “to stand,” because it is reported that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> having run a stadium at one breath, stood still at the end of it. The Greeks usually measured distances by stadia, which they called στάδια. Stadium also signified the course on which their races were run. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">Stadtholder</a>,** formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> or governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> United Provinces. Although this office is now abolished by the usurped influence of France, our readers will probably not be ill pleased with a short account of the several powers and claims connected with it. To render that account the more intelligible, we shall trace the office of a stadtholder from its origin. The Seven Provinces of the Low Countries were long governed by princes invested with the sovereignty, though limited in their powers, and under various titles; as Counts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Dukes of Guelder, Bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, &c. When these countries fell to the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and afterwards to those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, who had many other dominions, the absence of the sovereign was supplied by a stadtholder or governor, vested with very ample powers. These stadtholders or lieutenants had the administration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and presided in the courts of justice, whose jurisdiction was not at that time confined merely to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of causes, but extended to affairs of state. The stadtholders swore <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the princes at their inauguration, jointly with the states of the provinces they governed. They likewise took an oath to the states, by which they promised to maintain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> laws and privileges. It was upon this footing that William the First, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, was made governor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general of Holland, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and Utrecht, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the Second, upon his leaving the Low Countries to go into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The troubles beginning soon after, this prince found means to bring about an union, in 1576, between Holland and Zealand; the states of which two provinces put into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, as far as was in their power, the sovereign authority (for so long time as they should remain in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and under arms), upon the same footing as Holland had intrusted him with it the year before. In 1581 the same authority was again renewed to him by Holland, as it was soon after by Zealand likewise; and in 1584, being already elected <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Holland, upon certain conditions he would have been formally invested with the sovereignty, had not a wretch hired and employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Spain, put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by a horrid assassination. In the preamble of the instruments by which the states in 1581 conferred the sovereign authority upon Prince William the First, we find there remarkable words, which are there set <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as fundamental rules: “That all republics and communities ought to preserve...” Stadthold serve, maintain, and fortify themselves by unanimity; which being impossible to be kept up always among so many members, often differing in inclinations and sentiments, it is consequently necessary that the government should be placed in the hands of one single chief magistrate." Many good politicians, and the greatest part of the inhabitants of these provinces, since the establishment of the republic, looked upon the stadtholderian government as an essential part of her <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; nor has she been without a stadtholder but twice, that is to say, from the end of 1650 to 1672, and again from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1702 till April 1747. The provinces of Friesland and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, with Ommeland, had always a stadtholder without interruption: their instructions may be seen in Aitzema; but formerly the powers of the stadtholder of these provinces were confined within narrower bounds, and till William the Fourth there was no stadtholder of the seven provinces together. The stadtholder could not declare war or make peace, but he had, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> general of the union, the command in chief of all the forces of the state (A); and military persons were obliged to obey him in every thing that concerned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He was not limited by instructions; but he had the important power of giving out orders for the march of troops, and the disposition of all matters relative to them. He not only directed their marches, but provided for the garrisons, and changed them at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. All military edicts and regulations came from him alone; he constituted and authorized the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of war of the United Provinces, and, as captain-general of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, disposed of all military offices, as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> inclusively. The higher posts, such as those of veld-marlials, generals, lieutenant-generals, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-generals, were given by the states-general, who chose the persons recommended by his highness. He made the governors, commandants, &c., of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and strong places of the republic, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>. The persons nominated presented their instruments of appointment to their high mightinesses, who provided them with commissions. The states-general had likewise great regard to the recommendation of the prince stadtholder in the disposition of those civil employments which were in their gift. The power of the stadtholder as high-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, extended to every thing that concerned the naval force of the republic, and to all the other affairs that were here within the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. He presided at these boards either in person or by his representatives; and as chief of them all in general, and of every one in particular, he had power to make their orders and instructions he observed by themselves and others. He bestowed the posts of lieutenant-admiral, vice-admiral, and rear-admiral, who commanded under him; and he made likewise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-captains. The stadtholder granted likewise letters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and abolition, as well for the crimes called Com-Stadtholmumia Delicta, as for military offences. In Holland and Zealand these letters were made out for crimes of the first sort, in the name of the states, with the advice of his highness. In military offences he consulted the high council of war; and upon the commonia delicta he took the advice of the courts of justice, of the counsellors, committees of the provinces, of the council of state, and the tribunals of justice in the respective towns, according to the nature of the case. In the provinces of Holland and Zealand, the stadtholder elected the magistrates of the towns annually, out of a double number that were returned to him by the towns themselves. When any of these offices became vacant, which, at the time there was no governor, were in the disposal of the states of Holland, or as formerly in that of the chamber of accounts, the stadtholder had his choice of two, or, in some cases, of three candidates, named by their noble and great mightinesses. He chose likewise the counsellors, inspectors of the dykes of Rynland, Delfland, and Scheeland, out of three persons presented to him by the boards of the counsellors inspectors; which boards were of very ancient establishment in Holland. His highness presided in the courts of Holland, and in the courts of justice of the other provinces; and his name was placed at the head of the proclamations and acts, called in Dutch Mandamenten, or Provisien van Justitie. In Overijssel and in the province of Utrecht the possessors of fees held of the prince stadtholder. He was supreme curator of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Guelder, Friesland, and Groningen; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> forester and grand veneer in Guelder, in Holland, and other places. In the province of Utrecht, his highness, by virtue of the regulation of 1674, disposed of the provostships and other benefices which remained to the chapters, as also of the canonical prebends that fell in the months which were formerly the papal months. By the first article of the council of state of the United Provinces, the stadtholder was the first member of it, and had a right of voting there, with an appointment of 25,000 guilders a-year. He assisted also, as often as he thought fit for the service of the state, at the deliberations of the states-general, to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> to them, and sometimes also at the conferences which the deputies of their high mightinesses held in their different committees, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their standing orders. He likewise assisted at the assemblies of the states of each particular province, and at that of the counsellors committees. In Guelder, Holland, and Utrecht, his highness had a share of the sovereignty, as chief or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>; and in Zeeland, where he possessed the marquisate of Veer and Flushing, as first noble, and representing the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. In his absence he had (A) In times of war, however, the states had always named deputies for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, to accompany the stadtholders in the field, and to serve them as counsellors in all their enterprises, particularly in the most important affairs, such as giving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, or undertaking a siege, &c. This was always practised till the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William the Third to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was continued with regard to the general-in-chief of the army of the republic. In 1747 and 1748 there were likewise deputies with the army, but with more limited power. Stadtholder had in Zealand his representatives, who had the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in all the councils, and the first of whom was always first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> from the province to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of their high mightinesses. In 1749 the prince stadtholder was created by the states-general, governor-general and supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the East and West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> companies; dignities which gave him a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of authority and power, and which had never been conferred upon any of his predecessors, nor had they hitherto been made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. He had his representatives in the several chambers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and chose their directors out of a nomination of three qualified persons. The prince enjoyed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> in Zealand from the time of his elevation to the stadtholderate. The revenues of the stadtholderate of the seven United Provinces were reckoned (including the 25,000 guilders which the prince enjoyed annually as the first member of the council of state, and what he had from the India company's dividends) to amount to 300,000 guilders a-year. As captain-general of the union, his serene highness had 120,000 guilders per annum; besides 24,000 from Friesland, and 12,000 from Groningen, in quality of captain-general of those provinces. In times of war the state allowed extraordinary sums to the captain-general for the expense of every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. All these powers and privileges were held by the prince of Orange previous to the revolutionary war of France. The influence of the usurper of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> has extended to the states of Holland, and attached them as a province to France under the name of a kingdom, at the head of which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Bonaparte. STÆHELINA, a genus of plants belonging to the class of syngenesia, and order of polygamy aquilis; and in the natural system arranged under the 49th order, Compositae. See Botany Index.

SOCIETIES

Pages 48-62

associations voluntarily formed by a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of individuals for promoting knowledge, industry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> virtue. They may therefore be divided into three classes; societies for promoting science and literature, societies for encouraging and promoting arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and societies for diffusing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and morality and relieving distress. Societies belonging to the first class extend their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to all the sciences and literature in general, or devote it to one particular science. The same observation may be applied to those which are instituted for improving arts and manufactures. Those of the third class are established, either with a view to prevent crimes, as the Philanthropic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the Christian religion among unenlightened nations, as the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts; or for introducing arts and civilization, along with a knowledge of the Christian religion, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIERRA_LEONE">Sierra Leone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of planning and instituting societies for those valuable purposes is due to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. A literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> is said to have been formed in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> (see Academy); but the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> seems to have been rude and defective. Several others were instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the 16th century; but from the accounts which we have seen of them, they seem to have been far inferior to those which are most flourishing at present. The most enlarged idea of literary societies seems to have originated with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, the father of modern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, who recommended to the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to institute societies of learned men, who should give to the world from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time a regular account of their researches and discoveries. It was the idea of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, that the learned world should be united, as it were, into one immense republic; which, though consisting of many detached states, should hold a strict union and preserve a mutual intelligence with each other, in every thing that regards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. The want of this union and intelligence he laments as one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> obstacles to the advancement of science; and, justly considering the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of public societies, in the different countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, under the auspices of the sovereign, to be the best remedy for that defect, he has given, in his fanciful <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the New <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIS">Atlantis</a>, the delineation of a philosophical society on the most extended plan, for the improvement of all arts and sciences; a work which, though written in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and tinged with the colouring of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, is full of the noblest philosophic views. The plan of Lord Bacon, which met with little attention from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which he lived, was destined to produce its effect in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> not very distant. The scheme of a philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> by Cowley is acknowledged to have had a powerful influence in procuring the establishment of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II.; and Cowley's plan is manifestly copied in almost all its parts from that in the New Atlantis. The institution of the Royal Society of London was soon followed by the establishment of the Royal Academy. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> demy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and these two have served as models to the philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> of highest reputation in the other kingdoms of Europe. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of ages has shown, that improvements of a public <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> are best carried on by societies of liberal and ingenious men, uniting their labours without regard to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, or party, in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> pursuit alike interesting to all, whereby mutual prejudices are worn off, and a humane philosophical spirit is cherished. Men united together, and frequently meeting for the purpose of advancing the sciences, the arts, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, manufactures, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, may oftentimes suggest such hints to one another as may be improved to important ends; and such societies, by being the repositories of the observations and discoveries of the learned and ingenious, may from time to time furnish the world with useful publications which might otherwise be lost: for men of ingenuity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> may not choose to risk their reputation, by sending abroad unpatronized what a learned society might judge richly worth the public eye; or perhaps their circumstances being straitened, they may not be able to defray the expense of publication. Societies instituted for promoting knowledge may also be of eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, by exciting a spirit of emulation, and by kindling those sparks of genius which otherwise might for ever have been concealed; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, when possessed of funds sufficient for the purpose, they reward the exertions of the industrious and enterprising with pecuniary premiums or honorary medals, many important experiments and useful discoveries <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be made, from which the public may reap the highest advantages. Eminent instances of the beneficial effects of such institutions we have in the Royal Academy of Sciences at Paris, the Royal Society, and the Society instituted for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures, and Commerce, in London, and many others of a similar kind. Hereby a spirit of discovery and improvement has been excited among the ingenious in almost every nation; knowledge of various kinds, and greatly useful to mankind, has taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the dry and uninteresting speculations of schoolmen; and bold and erroneous hypotheses has been obliged to give way to demonstrative experiment. In short, since the establishment of these societies, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> learning and philosophy have more increased than they had done for many centuries before. As to those societies established for promoting industry, religion and morality, and relieving distress, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is laudable and excellent, and presents a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the philanthropy of modern times. We are happy to find, from the minutes of some of these societies, that their beneficial effects are already conspicuous. We will now give some account of the most eminent societies; arranging them under the three classes into which we have divided them: I. Religious and Humane Societies. II. Societies for Promoting Science and Literature. III. Societies for Encouraging Arts, Manufactures, &c. I. RELIGIOUS AND HUMANE SOCIETIES. 1. Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts, was instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William III. in 1701, in order to secure a maintenance for an orthodox clergy, and to make other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> for propagating the gospel in the plantations, colonies, and factories beyond the seas. To that end he incorporated the archbishops, several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and others of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, gentry, and clergy, to the number of 90, into one body, which, by the name of The Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts, was to plead and be implicated; to have perpetual succession, with privilege to purchase 2000l. a-year inheritance, and estates for lives or years, with other goods and chattels to any value. By its charter the society is authorized to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; and to meet annually on the third Friday in February for the purpose of choosing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, vice-president, and officers for the year ensuing; and on the third Friday in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, or oftener if there should be occasion, to transact business, and to depute persons to take subscriptions, and collect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> contributed for the purposes aforesaid; and of all moneys received and laid out, it is obliged to give account yearly to the lord-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> or keeper, the lord-chief-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the King's-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, the lord-chief-justice of the Common-pleas, or to any two of these magistrates. Of this society there is a standing committee at St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, to prepare matters for the monthly meeting, which is held at St Martin's library. Before the incorporation of the society for the propagation of the gospel in foreign parts, there had been formed, for the promoting of Christian knowledge both at home and in the colonies, a voluntary association of persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and respectability, who in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1699 began to hold stated meetings in London for that purpose, regulating themselves by the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and the canons of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and when the new society was formed, they had already transmitted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> and the West Indies 800l. worth of Bibles, Books of Common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a>, and treatises of practical religion, besides securing a tolerable maintenance to several clergymen on that continent. This association still fulfils under the denomination of The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, and has been productive of much good in the cities of London and Westminster; but upon the formation of the new society, into which all its original members were incorporated by name, the care which the voluntary association had taken of the colonies devolved of course upon the incorporated society; of which incorporation we believe the object has been sometimes mistaken, and the labours of its missionaries grossly misrepresented. It has by many been supposed that the society was incorporated for the sole purpose of converting the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> Americans; and it has been much blamed for sending missionaries into provinces where, in the common language of the complainers, a gospel-ministry was already established. But an impartial view of the rise and progress of the American provinces, now become independent states, will show the folly and injustice of those complaints. The English colonies in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America were in the last century formed and first peopled by religious men; who, made uneasy at home by their intolerant brethren, left the old world to enjoy in peace that first and chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, the free worship of God according to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. At one time Puritans were driven across the Atlantic by the episcopal church; at another, Churchmen were forced away by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">presbyterians</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as the revolutions of state threw the civil power into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the one or the other party; and not a few members of the CHURCH OF ROME were chafed to the wilds of America by the united exertions of both. It has been often observed, that people persecuted for their religion become for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> enthusiastically attached to it; and the conduct of those colonists was in perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> with this observation. Their zeal, inflamed by their violent removal to the other hemisphere, kept religion alive and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> among themselves; but their poverty disabled them from supplying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, by making provision for a ministry to instruct their offspring. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that the new Christian commonwealth, without the kindly assistance of its mother-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, would have been, in the words of the Roman historian, Res unius estatis. Against this danger a timely aid was to be provided by the society; which, as it consisted not of fanatical members, would not intrude the important business of the mission to fanatical preachers, who, though always ready for such spiritual enterprises, are never qualified to carry them on with success.
