It is required that the matters for which premiums are offered be delivered in without names, or any intimation to whom they belong; that each particular thing be marked in what manner each claimant thinks fit, such claimant sending with it a paper sealed up, having on the outside a corresponding mark, and on the inside the claimant's name and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>; and all candidates are to take notice, that no claim for a premium will be attended to, unless the conditions of the advertisement are fully complied with. No papers shall be opened but such as shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> premiums, unless where it appears to the society absolutely necessary for the determination of the claim: all the refuse shall be returned unopened, with the matters to which they belong, if inquired after by the marks within two years; after which time, if not demanded, they shall be publicly burnt unopened at some meeting of the society. All the premiums of this society are designed for that part of Great Britain called England, the dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and the town of Berwick upon Tweed, unless expressly mentioned to the contrary. No person shall receive any premium, bounty, or encouragement, from the society for any matter for which he has obtained or proposes to obtain a patent. No member of this society shall be a candidate for or intitled to receive any premium, bounty, or reward whatever, except the honorary medal of the society. The respectability of the members who compose it may be seen by perusing the list which generally accompanies their transactions. In the last volume (vol. xii.) it occupies no less than 43 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. Some idea may be formed of the wealth of this society, by observing that the list of their premiums fills 96 pages, and amounts to 250 in number. These consist of gold medals worth from 30 to 50s., and in a few instances to 100 guineas; and silver medals valued at 10 guineas. This society is one of the most important in Great Britain. Much money has been expended by it, and many are the valuable effects of which it has been productive. Among these we reckon not only the discoveries which it has excited, but the institution of other societies on the same principles to which it has given birth; and we do not hesitate to conclude, that future ages will consider the founding of this society as one of the most remarkable epochs in the history of the arts. We contemplate with pleasure the beneficial effects which must result to this nation and to mankind by the diffusion of such institutions; and rejoice in the hope that the active minds of the people of Great Britain, instead of being employed as formerly in controversies about religion, which engender strife, or in discussions concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of politics, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> of schemes inconsistent with the nature and condition of man, will soon be more generally united into associations for promoting useful knowledge and solid improvement, and for alleviating the distresses of their fellow creatures. 1. Society instituted at Bath for the Encouragement of Agriculture, Arts, Manufactures, and Commerce. It was founded in the year 1777 by several gentlemen who met at the city of Bath. This scheme met with a very favourable reception both from the wealthy and learned. The wealthy subscribed very liberally, and the learned communicated many important papers. On application to the London and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> societies instituted for the like purposes, they very politely offered their assistance. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> volumes of their transactions have already been published, containing very valuable experiments and observations, particularly respecting agriculture, which well deserve the attention of all farmers in the kingdom. We have consulted them with much satisfaction on several occasions, and have frequently referred to them in the course of this work; and therefore, with pleasure, embrace Societies for embracing the present opportunity of repeating our obligations. We owe the same acknowledgments to the Society for the Improvement of Arts, &c., of London. 3. Society for working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">Mines</a>, an association lately formed on the continent of Europe. This institution arose from the accidental meeting of several mineralogists at Skleno near Schenmuth in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, who were collected in order to examine a new method of amalgamation. Struck with the shackles imposed on mining by monopolizers of new and useful processes, they thought no method so effectual to break them, as forming a society, whose common labours should be directed to fix mining on its surest principles; and whose memoirs, spread all over Europe, might offer to every adventurer the result of the researches, of which they are the object. By these means they supposed, that there would be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of information collected; the interests of individuals would be lost in the general interest; and the one would materially assist the other. Imposture and quackery would, by the same means, be banished from a science, which must be improved by philosophy and experience; and the society, they supposed, would find, in the confidence which they inspired, the reward and the encouragement of their labours. They design, that the memoirs which they publish shall be short and clear; truth must be their basis, and every idle diffusion, every foreign digression, must be banished; politics and finance must be avoided, though the dissertations may seem to lead towards them; and they oblige themselves to oppose the affectation of brilliancies, and the ostentation of empty speculation, when compared with plain, simple, and useful facts. The object of the society is physical geography; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a> founded on chemistry; the management of ore in the different operations which it undergoes; subterranean geometry; the history of mining; foundries, and the processes for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> from the ores, either by fusion or amalgamation, in every instance applied to practice. The end of this institution is to collect, in the most extensive sense, everything that can assist the operations of the miner, and to communicate it to the different members, that they may employ it for the public good, in their respective countries. Each member must consider himself as bound to send to the society every thing which will contribute to the end of its institution; to point out, with precision, the several facts and observations; to communicate every experiment which occurs, even the unsuccessful ones, if the relation may seem to be advantageous to the public; to communicate to the society their examination of schemes, and their opinions on questions proposed by it; and to pay annually two ducats (about 18s. 6d.) to the direction every Easter. The society, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is bound to publish every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> that shall be communicated to it; to communicate to each member, at the member's expense, the memoirs, designs, models, productions, and every thing connected with the institution; to answer all the necessary demands made, relating in any respect to mining; and to give its opinion on every plan or project communicated through the medium of an honorary member. The great centre of all intelligence is to be at Zellerfield in Hartz, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>; but the society is not fixed to any one spot; for every particular state some practical mineralogist is nominated as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>. Among these are the names of Baron Born, M. Pallas, M. Charpentier, M. Prebra, and M. Henkel. Their office is to propose the members; to take care that the views of the society are pursued in the different countries where they reside; to answer the requests of the members of their manufactures, country who are qualified to make them; in case of the death of a director, to choose another; and the majority is to determine where the archives and the strong box is to be placed. All the eminent mineralogists in Europe are members of this society. It is erected on so liberal and so extensive a plan, that we entertain the highest hopes of its success; and have only to add, that we wish much to see the study of several other sciences pursued in the same manner. 4. The Society for the Improvement of Naval Architecture, was founded in 1791. The object of it is to encourage every useful invention and discovery relating to naval architecture as far as shall be in their power, both by honorary and pecuniary rewards. They have in view particularly to improve the theories of floating bodies and of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESISTANCE_OF_FLUIDS">resistance of <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>; to procure draughts and models of different vessels, together with calculations of their capacity, centre of gravity, tonnage, &c.; to make observations and experiments themselves, and to point out such observations and experiments as appear best calculated to further their designs, and most deserving those premiums which the society can bestow. But though the improvement of naval architecture in all its branches be certainly the principal object of this institution, yet the society do not by any means intend to confine themselves merely to the form and structure of vessels. Every subordinate and collateral pursuit will claim a share of the attention of the society in proportion to its merits; and whatever may have any tendency to render navigation more safe, salutary, and even pleasant, will not be neglected. This institution owes its existence to the patriotic disposition and extraordinary attention of Mr Sewell a private citizen of London, who (though engaged in a line of business totally opposite to all concerns of this kind) has been led, by mere accident, to take such ocular notice of, and make such observations on, the actual state of naval architecture in this country, as naturally occurred to a man of plain understanding, zealous for the honour and interest of his country, and willing to bestow a portion of that time for the public good, which men of a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> would rather have devoted to their own private advantage. His attention was the more seriously excited, by finding that it was the opinion of some private ship-builders, who, in a debate on the failure of one of our naval engagements, pronounced, that such "would ever be the case while that business (the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of our ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>) was not studied as a science, but carried on merely by precedent; that there had not been one improvement in our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> that did not originate with the French, who had naval schools and seminaries for the study of it; and that our ships were not a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> for those of that nation either singly or in a fleet, &c., &c." In a short time the society were enabled to offer very considerable premiums for particular improvements in the construction of our shipping, &c., &c. and also to encourage our philosophers, mathematicians, and mechanics, to make satisfactory experiments, tending to ascertain Societies for certain the laws of resistance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to solids of different forms, in all varieties of circumstance. On this head the reward is not less than one hundred pounds or a gold medal. Other premiums of 50, 30, and 20 guineas, according to the importance or difficulty of the particular subject or point of investigation, are likewise offered, for different discoveries, inventions, or improvements. The terms of admission into the society are a subscription of two guineas annually, or twenty guineas for life. 5. Society of Artists of Great Britain, which consists of directors and fellows, was incorporated by charter in 1765, and empowered to purchase and hold lands, not exceeding 1000l. a-year. The directors of this society, annually elected, are to consist of 24 persons, including the president, vice-president, treasurer, and secretary; and it is required that they be either painters, sculptors, architects, or engravers by profession. 6. British Society for Extending the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">Fisheries</a> and Improving the Sea-Coasts of this Kingdom, was instituted in 1786. The end and design of this society will best appear from their charter, of which we present an abstract. The preamble states, "the great want of improvement in fisheries, agriculture, and manufactures, in the Highlands and Islands of North Britain; the prevalence of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> from the want of employment in those parts; the prospect of a new nursery of seamen, by the establishment of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> towns and villages in that quarter. The act therefore declares, that the persons therein named, and every other person or persons who shall thereafter become proprietors of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> stock mentioned therein, shall be a distinct and separate body politic and corporate, by the name of The British Society for Extending the Fisheries and Improving the Sea-Coasts of this Kingdom: That the said society may raise a capital joint stock not exceeding 150,000l. to be applied to purchasing or otherwise acquiring lands and tenements in perpetuity, for the building thereon, and on no other land whatever, free towns, villages, and fishing stations: That the joint stock shall be divided into shares of 50l. each: That no person shall in his or her name possess more than ten shares, or 500l.: That the society shall not borrow any sum or sums of money whatsoever: That the sums to be advanced for this undertaking, and the profits arising therefrom, shall be divided proportionally to the sum subscribed; and that no person shall be liable for a larger sum than he or she the share have respectively subscribed: That one or two shares shall entitle to one vote and no more, in person or by proxy, at all meetings of proprietors; three or four shares to two votes; five, six, or seven shares, to three votes; eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shares to four votes; and ten shares to five votes and no more: That more persons than one inclining to hold in their joint names one or more shares shall be entitled to vote, by one of such persons, according to the priority of their names, or by proxy: That bodies corporate shall vote by proxy under their seal: That all persons holding proxies shall be proprietors, and that no one person shall hold more than five votes by proxy: That the affairs of the society shall be managed by a governor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> governor, and 13 other directors, to be elected annually on the 25th of March, from among the proprietors of the society, holding at least one full share, by signed lists of their names to be transmitted by the proprietors to the secretary of the society: that five proprietors, not being governor, director, or other officer, shall be in like manner annually elected to audit the accounts of the society: That there shall be one general meeting of the proprietors annually on the 25th of March: That occasional general meetings shall be called on the request of nine or more proprietors: That the general meetings of the proprietors shall make all bye-laws and constitutions for the government of the society, and for the good and orderly carrying on of the business of the same: That no transfer shall be made of the stock of the society for three years from the 16th of August 1786: That the cash of the society shall be lodged in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of England, bank of Scotland, or the royal bank of Scotland: That no director, proprietor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, or officer of the society, shall retain any sum or sums of money in his hands beyond the space of 30 days, on any account whatsoever: That all payments by the society shall be made by drafts on the said banks, under the hands of the governor or deputy-governor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-signed by the secretary or his deputy, and two or more directors: And that the books in which the accounts of the society shall be kept shall be open to all the proprietors." The institution of this public-spirited society was in a great measure owing to the exertions of the patriotic John Knox; who, in the course of 23 years, traversed and explored the Highlands of Scotland not fewer than 16 times, and expended several thousand pounds of his own fortune in pursuing his patriotic designs. 7. British <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">Wool</a> Society. See British Wool Society. SOCIETY Isles, a cluster of isles, so named by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook in 1769. They are situated between the latitudes of 16° 10' and 16° 55' south, and between the longitudes of 150° 37' and 152° west. They are eight in number; namely, Otahete, Huaheine, Ulietea, Otaha, Bolabola, Maurua, Tooouai, and Tabooyamanoo or Saunders's Island. The soil, productions, people, their language, religion, customs, and manners, are so nearly the same as at Otahete, that little need be added here on that subject. Nature has been equally bountiful in uncultivated plenty, and the inhabitants are as luxurious and as indolent. A plantain branch is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of peace, and exchanging names the greatest token of friendship. Their dances are more elegant, their dramatic entertainments have something of plot and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, and they exhibit temporary occurrences as the objects of praise or satire; so that the origin of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> may be already discerned among them. The people of Huaheine are in general flouter and fairer than those of Otahete, and this island is remarkable for its populousness and fertility. Those of Ulietea, on the contrary, are smaller and blacker, and much less orderly. Captain Cook put on shore a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> ewe at Bolabola, where a ram had been left by the Spaniards; and also an English boar and sow, with two goats, at Ulietea. If the valuable animals which have been transported thither from Europe should be suffered to multiply, no part of the world will equal these islands in variety and abundance of refreshments for future navigators.

SOCINIANS

Pages 62-63

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Christian heretics, so called from their founder Faustus Socinus (see Socinus). They maintain, "That <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who had no existence before he was conceived by the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; that the Holy Ghost is Socinians, no distinct person, but that the Father is truly and properly God. They own, that the name of God is given in the Holy Scriptures to Jesus Christ; but contend, that it is only a deputed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, which, however, invests him with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> sovereignty over all created beings, and renders him an object of worship to men and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. They deny the doctrines of satisfaction and imputed righteousness; and say that Christ only preached the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> to mankind, set before them in himself an example of heroic virtue, and sealed his doctrines with his blood. Original sin and absolute predetermination they esteem scholastic chimeras. They likewise maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, which they say becomes insensible at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and is raised again with the body at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, when the good shall be established in the possession of eternal felicity, while the wicked shall be confined to a fire that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not torment them eternally, but for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> in proportion to their deserts." This sect has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been indignant at being styled Socinians. They disclaim every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> leader; and professing to be guided solely by the word of God and the deductions of reason, they call themselves Unitarians, and affect to consider all other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, even their friends the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, as Polytheists. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> Unitarianism, as taught by Dr Priestley, is, however, a very different thing from Socinianism, as we find it in the Racovian catechism and other standard works of the sect. This far-famed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> has discovered, what escaped the sagacity of all the fraters poloni, that Jesus Christ was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> as well as Mary; that the evangelists mistook the meaning of Isaiah's prophecy, that "a virgin should conceive and bear a son;" that the applying of this prophecy to the birth of our Saviour, led them to conclude that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> was miraculous; and that we are not to wonder at this mistake, as the apostles were not always inspired, and were in general inconclusive reasoners. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of the writer in claiming the merit of such discoveries will appear in its proper colours to all our readers: the truth of his doctrine shall be considered in another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>.

SOCINUS

Pages 63-63

Lælius, the first author of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Socinians, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> in 1525. Being designed by his father for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he began very early to search for the foundation of that science in the Word of God; and by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> discovered that the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> taught many things contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>; when, being desirous of penetrating farther into the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the Scriptures, he studied Greek, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and even Arabic. In 1547 he left <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, to go and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>; and spent four years in travelling through France, England, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, and at length settled at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>. He by this means became acquainted with the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, who testified by their letters the esteem they had for him: but as he discovered to them his doubts, he was greatly suspected of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. He, however, conducted himself with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, that he lived among the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> enemies of his opinions, without receiving the least injury. He met with some disciples, who heard his instructions with respect; these were Italians who left their native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on account of religion, and wandered about in Germany and Poland. He communicated likewise his sentiments to his relations by his writings, which he caused to be conveyed to them at Sienna. He died at Zurich in 1562. Those who were of sentiments opposite to his, and were personally acquainted with him, confess that his outward behaviour was blameless. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">Paraphrase</a> on the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of St John; and other works are ascribed to him. Socinus, Faustus, nephew of the preceding, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCINIAN">Socinian</a> sect, was born at Sienna in 1539. The letters which his uncle Lælius wrote to his relations, and which infused into them many seeds of heresy, made an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon him; so that, knowing himself not innocent, he fled as well as the rest when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> began to persecute that family. He was at Lyons when he heard of his uncle's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and departed immediately to take possession of his writings. He returned to Tuscany; and made himself agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, that the charms which he found in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> posts he filled there, hindered him for twelve years from remembering that he had been considered as the person who was to put the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to the system of fanatical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, of which his uncle Lælius had made a rough draught. At last he went into Germany in 1574, and paid no regard to the grand duke's advices to return. He stayed three years at Basle, and studied divinity there, and having adopted a set of principles very different from the system of Protestants, he resolved to maintain and propagate them; for which purpose he wrote a treatise De Iesu Christo Servatore. In 1579 Socinus retired into Poland, and desired to be admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the Unitarians; but as he differed from them in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, on which he refused to be silent, he met with a repulse. However, he did not cease to write in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of their churches against those who attacked them. At length his book against James Paleologus furnished his enemies with a pretence to exasperate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Poland against him; but though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of it was sufficient to refute his accusers, Socinus thought proper to leave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>, after having resided there four years. He then lived under the protection of several Polish lords, and married a lady of a good family; but her death, which happened in 1587, so deeply afflicted him as to injure his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; and to complete his sorrow, he was deprived of his patrimony by the death of Francis de Medicis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> duke of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. The consolation he found in feeling his sentiments at last approved by several ministers, was greatly interrupted in 1598; for he met with a thousand insults at Cracow, and was with great difficulty saved from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the rabble. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was plundered, and he lost his goods; but this loss was not to uneasy to him as that of some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, which he extremely regretted. To deliver himself from such dangers, he retired to a village about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles distant from Cracow, where he spent the remainder of his days at the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Blonki, a Polish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, and died there in 1604. All Faustus Socinus's works are contained in the two first volumes of the Bibliotheca Fratrum Polonorum.

SOCMANS

Pages 63-63

Sokemans, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Socmen (Socmanni), are such tenants as hold their lands and tenements by focage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>. See Socage.

SOCOTORA

Pages 63-64

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lying between <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix; about 50 miles in length, and 22 in breadth. It is particularly noted for its fine aloes, known by the name of Socotrine Aloes. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the natives natives is a mixture of Mahometanism and Paganism; but they are civil to strangers who call there in their passage to the East Indies. It abounds in fruit and cattle; and they have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of their own, who is dependent on Arabia.

SOCRATES

Pages 64-67

the greatest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, was born at Alopece, a village near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, in the fourth year of the 77th Olympiad. His parents were of low <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; his father Sophroniscus being a flaxworker, and his mother Phaenareta a midwife. Sophroniscus brought up his son, contrary to his inclination, in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> employment; in which Socrates, though his mind was continually aspiring after higher objects, was not unsuccessful, for whilst he was a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, he is said to have formed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the habited Graces, which were allowed a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the citadel of Athens. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father he was left in such straitened circumstances as laid him under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of exercising that art to procure the means of subsistence, though he devoted, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, all the leisure which he could command, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. His distress, however, was soon relieved by Crito, a wealthy Athenian; who, remarking his strong propensity to study, and admiring his ingenious disposition and distinguished abilities, generously took him under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, and intrusted him with the instruction of his children. The opportunities which Socrates by this means enjoyed of attending the public lectures of the most eminent philosophers, so far increased his thirst after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, that he determined to relinquish his occupation, and every prospect of emolument which that might afford, in order to devote himself entirely to his favourite pursuits. Under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a> and Archelaus he prosecuted the study of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the usual manner of the philosophers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and became well acquainted with their doctrines. Prodicus the sophist was his preceptor in eloquence, Evenus in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, Thedorus in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and Damo in music. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCIBIADES">Alcibiades</a>, a woman no less celebrated for her intellectual than her personal accomplishments, whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was frequented by the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, had also some share in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of Socrates. Under such preceptors it cannot reasonably be doubted but that he became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of every kind of learning which the age in which he lived could afford; and being blessed with very uncommon talents by nature, he appeared in Athens, under the respectable characters of a good citizen and a true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Being called upon by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to take arms in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and severe struggle between Athens and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, he signalized himself at the siege of Potidea, both by his valour and by the hardiness with which he endured fatigue. During the severity of a Thracian winter, whilst others were clad in furs, he wore only his usual clothing, and walked barefoot upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. In an engagement in which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Alcibiades falling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> wounded, he advanced to defend him, and saved both him and his arms: and though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of valour was on this occasion unquestionably due to Socrates, he generously gave his vote that it might be bestowed upon Alcibiades, to encourage his rising merit. He served in other campaigns with distinguished bravery, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> on one occasion to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Xenophon, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> him, when covered with wounds, out of the reach of the enemy. It was not till Socrates was upwards of 60 years of age that he undertook to serve his country in any civil office, when he was chosen to represent his own district, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of five hundred. In this office, though he at first exposed himself to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> from the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in the forms of business, he soon convinced his colleagues that he was superior to them all in wisdom and integrity. Whilst they, intimidated by the clamours of the populace, passed an unjust <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> upon the commanders, who, after the engagement at the Arginian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, had been prevented by a storm from paying funeral honours to the dead, Socrates stood forth singly in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and to the last refused to give his suffrage against them, declaring that no force should compel him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and the laws. Under the subsequent tyranny he never ceased to condemn the oppressive and cruel proceedings of the thirty tyrants; and when his boldness provoked their resentment, so that his life was in hazard, fearing neither treachery nor violence, he still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to support with undaunted firmness the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of his fellow citizens. Having given these proofs of public virtue both in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and civil capacity, he wished to do still more for his country. Observing with regret how much the opinions of the Athenian youth were misled, and their principles and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> corrupted by philosophers who spent all their time in refined speculations upon nature and the origin of things, and by sophists who taught in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> the arts of false eloquence and deceitful reasoning; Socrates formed the wise and generous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of instituting a new and more useful method of instruction. He justly conceived the true end of philosophy to be, not to make an ostentatious display of superior learning and ability in futile disputations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ingenious conjectures, but to free mankind from the dominion of pernicious prejudices; to correct their vices; to inspire them with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of virtue; and thus conduct them in the path of wisdom to true felicity. He therefore assumed the character of a moral philosopher; and, looking upon the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Athens as his school, and all who were disposed to lend him their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> as his pupils, he seized every occasion of communicating moral wisdom to his fellow citizens. He passed the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his time in public; and the method of instruction of which he chiefly made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> was, to propose a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of questions to the person with whom he conversed, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to some unforeseen conclusion. He first gained the consent of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESPONDENT">respondent</a> to some obvious truths, and then obliged him to admit others from their relation or resemblance to those to which he had already assented. Without making use of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> argument or persuasion, he chose to lead the person he meant to instruct, to deduce the truths of which he wished to convince him, as a necessary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> from his own conceptions. He <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> conducted these conferences with such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, as to conceal his design till the respondent had advanced too far to recede. On some occasions he made use of ironical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that vain men might be caught in their own replies, and be obliged to confess their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. He never assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of a morose and rigid preceptor, but communicated useful instruction with all the ease and pleasantry of polite conversation. Though eminently furnished with every kind of learning, he preferred moral to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> wisdom. Convinced that philosophy Socrates. Philosophy is valuable, not as it furnishes questions for the schools, but as it provides men with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of life, he censured his predecessors for spending all their time in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> researches into nature, and taking no pains to render themselves useful to mankind. His favorite maxim was, Whatever is above us doth not concern us. He estimated the value of knowledge by its utility, and recommended the study of geometry, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and other sciences, only so far as they admit of a practical application to the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> object in all his conferences and discourses was, to lead men into an acquaintance with themselves; to convince them of their follies and vices; to inspire them with the love of virtue; and to furnish them with useful moral instructions. Cicero might therefore very justly say of Socrates, that he was the first who called down philosophy from heaven to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and introduced her into the public walks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> retirements of men, that she might instruct them concerning life and manners. Through his whole life this good man discovered a mind superior to the attractions of wealth and power. Contrary to the general practice of the preceptors of his time, he instructed his pupils without receiving from them any gratuity. He frequently refused rich presents, which were offered him by Alcibiades and others, though importunately urged to accept them by his wife. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men of Athens were his stewards: they sent him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, as they apprehended he wanted them; he took what his present wants required, and returned the rest. Observing the numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> which were exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> in Athens, he exclaimed, "How many things are there which I do not want!" With Socrates, moderation supplied the place of wealth. In his clothing and food, he consulted only the demands of nature. He commonly appeared in a neat but plain cloak, with his feet uncovered. Though his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> was only supplied with simple fare, he did not scruple to invite men of superior rank to partake of his meals; and when his wife, upon some such occasion, expressed her dissatisfaction on being no better provided, he desired her to give herself no concern; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his guests were wise men, they would be contented with whatever they found at his table; if otherwise, they were unworthy of notice. Whilst others, says he, live to eat, wise men eat to live. Though Socrates was exceedingly unfortunate in his domestic connection, he converted this infelicity into an occasion of exercising his virtues. Xantippe, concerning whose ill humour ancient writers relate many amusing tales, was certainly a woman of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and unmanageable spirit. But Socrates while he endeavored to curb the violence of her temper, improved his own. When Alcibiades expressed his surprise that his friend could bear to live in the same house with so perverse and quarrelsome a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, Socrates replied, that being daily inured to ill humour at home, he was the better prepared to encounter perverseness and injury abroad. In the midst of domestic vexations and public disorders, Socrates retained such an unruffled serenity, that he was never seen either to leave his own house or to return home with a disturbed countenance. In acquiring this entire dominion over his passions and appetites, he had the greater merit, as it was not effected without a violent struggle against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> propensities. Zopyrus, an eminent physiognomist, declared, that he discovered in the features of the philosopher evident traces of many vicious inclinations. The friends of Socrates who were present ridiculed the ignorance of this pretender to extraordinary sagacity. But Socrates himself ingenuously acknowledged his penetration, and confessed that he was in his natural disposition prone to vice, but that he had subdued his inclinations by the power of reason and philosophy. Through the whole of his life Socrates gave himself up to the guidance of unbiased reason, which is supposed by some to be all that he meant by the genius or daemon from which he professed to receive instruction. But this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is inconsistent with the accounts given by his followers of that daemon, and even with the language in which he spoke of it himself. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> sometimes calls it his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, and Apuleius his god; and as Xenophon attests that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of his master that the gods occasionally communicate to men the knowledge of future events, it is by means improbable that Socrates admitted, with the generality of his countrymen, the existence of those intermediate beings called daemons, of one of which he might fancy himself the peculiar care. It was one of the maxims of Socrates, "That a wise man <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> worship the gods according to the institutions of the state to which he belongs." Convinced of the weakness of the human understanding, and perceiving that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of philosophy had led his predecessors into futile speculations on the nature and origin of things, he judged it most consistent with true wisdom to speak with caution and reverence concerning the divine nature. The wisdom and the virtues of this great man, whilst they procured him many followers, created him also many enemies. The Sophists*, whose knavery and ignorance he took every opportunity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> to public contempt, became inveterate in their enmity against so bold a reformer, and devised an expedient, by which they hoped to check the current of his popularity. They engaged <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, the first buffoon of the age, to write a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, in which Socrates should be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> character. Aristophanes, pleased with so promising an occasion of displaying his low and malignant <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, undertook the task, and produced the comedy of The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">Clouds</a>, still extant in his works. In this piece, Socrates is introduced hanging in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> in the air, and thence pouring forth absurdity and profaneness. But the philosopher, showing in a crowded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> that he was wholly unmoved by this ribaldry, the satire failed of its effect; and when Aristophanes attempted the year following to renew the piece with alterations and additions, the representation was so much discouraged, that he was obliged to discontinue it. From this time Socrates continued for many years to pursue without interruption his laudable design of instructing and reforming his fellow-citizens. At length, however, when the inflexible integrity with which he had discharged the duty of a senator, and the firmness with which he had opposed every kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> corruption and oppression, had greatly increased the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his enemies, clandestine arts were employed to raise a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> against him. The people were industriously reminded, that Critias, who had been one of the most cruel of the thirty tyrants, and Alcibiades, who Socrates, who had insulted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, by defacing the public statues of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, and performing a mock representation of the Eleusinian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, had in their youth been disciples of Socrates; and the minds of the populace being thus prepared, a direct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> was preferred against him before the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature. His accusers were Anytus a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-dresser, who had long entertained a personal enmity against Socrates, for reprehending his avarice, in depriving his sons of the benefits of learning, that they might pursue the gains of trade; Melitus, a young rhetorician, who was capable of undertaking any thing for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>; and Lycon, who was glad of any opportunity of displaying his talents. The accusation, which was delivered to the senate under the name of Melius, was this: "Melius, son of Melius, of the tribe of Pythos, accuseth Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, of the tribe of Alopece. Socrates violates the laws, in not acknowledging the gods which the state acknowledges, and by introducing new divinities. He also violates the laws by corrupting the youth. Be his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> death." This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> was delivered upon oath to the senate; and Crito a friend of Socrates became surety for his appearance on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. Anytus soon afterwards sent a private message to Socrates, assuring him that if he would desist from censuring his conduct, he would withdraw his accusation. But Socrates refused to comply with so degrading a condition; and with his usual spirit replied, "Whilst I live I will never <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, nor speak otherwise than my duty requires." The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the accusation and the trial he spent in philosophical conversations with his friends, choosing to discourse upon any other subject rather than his own situation. When the day of trial arrived, his accusers appeared in the senate, and attempted to support their charge in three distinct speeches, which strongly marked their respective characters. Plato, who was a young man, and a zealous follower of Socrates, then rose up to address the judges in defence of his master; but whilst he was attempting to apologise for his youth, he was abruptly commanded by the court to sit down. Socrates, however needed no advocate. Ascending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> with all the ferocity of conscious innocence, and with all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of superior merit, he delivered, in a firm and manly tone, an unpremeditated defence of himself, which silenced his opponents, and ought to have convinced his judges. After tracing the progress of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> which had been raised against him to its true source, the jealousy and resentment of men whose ignorance he had exposed, and whose vices he had ridiculed and reproved, he distinctly replied to the several charges brought against him by Melitus. To prove that he had not been guilty of impiety towards the gods of his country, he appealed to his frequent practice of attending the public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> festivals. The crime of introducing new divinities, with which he was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>, chiefly as it seems on the ground of the admonitions which he professed to have received from an invisible power, he disclaimed, by pleading that it was no new thing for men to consult the gods and receive instructions from them. To refute the charge of his having been a corrupter of youth, he urged the example which he had uniformly exhibited of justice, moderation, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>; the moral spirit and tendency of his discourses; and the effect which had actually been produced by his doctrine upon the manners of the young. Then, disdaining to solicit the mercy of his judges, he called upon them for that justice which their office and their oath obliged them to administer; and professing his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and confidence in God, resigned himself to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The judges, whose prejudices would not suffer them to pay due attention to this apology, or to examine with impartiality the merits of the cause, immediately declared him guilty of the crimes of which he stood accused. Socrates, in this stage of the trial, had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to enter his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> against the punishment which the accusers demanded, and instead of the sentence of death, to propose some pecuniary <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERCEMENT">amercement</a>. But he at first peremptorily refused to make any proposal of this kind, imagining that it might be construed into an acknowledgment of guilt; and asserted, that his conduct merited from the state reward rather than punishment. At length, however, he was prevailed upon by his friends to offer upon their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> a fine of thirty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINA">mina</a>. The judges, notwithstanding, still remained inexorable: they proceeded, without farther delay, to pronounce sentence upon him; and he was condemned to be put to death by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a>. The sentence being passed, he was sent to prison; which, says Seneca, he entered with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and firmness with which he had opposed the thirty tyrants; and took away all ignominy from the place, which could not be a prison while he was there. He lay in fetters 30 days; and was constantly visited by Crito, Plato, and other friends, with whom he passed the time in dispute after his usual manner. Anxious to save so valuable a life, they urged him to attempt his escape, or at least to permit them to convey him away; and Crito went so far, as to assure him that, by his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with the jailor, it might be easily accomplished, and to offer him a retreat in Thessaly; but Socrates rejected the proposal, as a criminal violation of the laws; and asked them, whether there was any place out of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> which death could not reach. At length the day arrived when the officers to whose care he was committed delivered to Socrates early in the morning the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> order for his execution, and immediately, according to the law, fet him at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> from his bonds. His friends, who came thus early to the prison that they might have an opportunity of conversing with their master through the day, found his wife sitting by him with a child in her arms. Socrates, that the tranquillity of his last moments might not be disturbed by her unavailing lamentations, requested that she might be conducted home. With the most frantic expressions of grief she left the prison. An interesting conversation then passed between Socrates and his friends, which chiefly turned upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. In the course of this conversation, he expressed his disapprobation of the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>, and assured his friends that his chief support in his present situation was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, though not unmixed with doubts, of a happy existence after death. "It would be inexcusable in me (said he) to despise death, if I were not persuaded that it will conduct me into the presence of the gods, who are the most righteous governors, and into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and good men; but I derive confidence from the hope that something of man remains after death," death, and that the condition of good men will then be much better than that of the bad." Crito afterwards asked him, in what manner he wished to be buried? Socrates replied, with a smile, "As you please, provided I do not escape out of your <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>." Then, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the rest of his friends, he said, "Is it not strange, after all that I have said to convince you that I am going to the society of the happy, that Crito still thinks that this body, which will soon be a lifeless corpse, is Socrates? Let him dispose of my body as he pleases, but let him not at its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> mourn over it as if it were Socrates." Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the day he retired into an adjoining apartment to bathe; his friends, in the meantime, expressing to one another their grief at the prospect of losing so excellent a father, and being left to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the rest of their days in the solitary state of orphans. After a short interval, during which he gave some necessary instructions to his domestics, and took his last leave of his children, the attendant of the prison informed him, that the time for drinking the poison was come. The executioner, though accustomed to such scenes, shed tears as he presented the fatal cup. Socrates received it without change of countenance or the least appearance of perturbation: then offering up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> to the gods that they would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> him a prosperous passage into the invisible world, with perfect composure he swallowed the poisonous draught. His friends around him burst into tears. Socrates alone remained unmoved. He upbraided their pusillanimity, and entreated them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> a manly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> worthy of the friends of virtue. He continued walking till the chilling operation of the hemlock obliged him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> down upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. After remaining for a short time silent, he requested Crito (probably in order to refute a calumny which might prove injurious to his friends after his decease) not to neglect the offering of a cock which he had vowed to Eucalypus. Then, covering himself with his cloak, he expired. Such was the fate of the virtuous Socrates! A story, says Cicero, which I never read without tears. The friends and disciples of this illustrious teacher of wisdom were deeply afflicted by his death, and attended his funeral with every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of grief. Apprehensive, however, for their own safety, they soon afterwards privately withdrew from the city, and took up their residence in distant places. Several of them visited the philosopher Euclid of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, by whom they were kindly received. No sooner was the unjust condemnation of Socrates known through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, than a general indignation was kindled in the minds of good men, who universally regretted that so distinguished an advocate for virtue should have fallen a sacrifice to jealousy and envy. The Athenians themselves, so remarkable for their caprice, who never knew the value of their great men till after their death, soon became sensible of the folly as well as criminality of putting to death the man who had been the chief ornament of their city and of the age, and turned their indignation against his accusers. Melitus was condemned to death; and Anytus, to escape a similar fate, went into voluntary exile. To give a farther <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the sincerity of their regret, the Athenians for a while interrupted public business; decreed a general <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>; recalled the exiled friends of Socrates; and erected a statue to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> in one of the most frequented parts of the city. Socrates' death happened in the fifth year of the 96th olympiad, and in the 70th year of his age. Socrates left behind him nothing in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; but his illustrious pupils Xenophon and Plato have in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> supplied this defect. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of Socrates, written by Xenophon, afford, however, a much more accurate idea of the opinions of Socrates, and of his manner of teaching, than the Dialogues of Plato, who everywhere mixes his own conceptions and dictum with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and language of his master. It is related, that when Socrates heard Plato recite his Lyfs, he said, "How much does this young man make me say which I never conceived?" His distinguishing character was that of a moral philosopher; and his doctrine concerning God and religion was rather practical than speculative. But he did not neglect to build the structure of religious faith upon the firm foundation of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to natural appearances: He taught, that the Supreme Being, though invisible, is clearly seen in his works; which at once demonstrate his existence and his wise and benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>. He admitted, besides the one Supreme Deity, the existence of beings who possess a middle station between God and man, to whose immediate agency he ascribed the ordinary phenomena of nature, and whom he supposed to be particularly concerned in the management of human affairs. Hence he declared it to be the duty of every one, in the performance of religious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, to follow the customs of his country. At the same time, he taught, that the merit of all religious offerings depends upon the character of the worshipper, and that the gods take pleasure in the sacrifices of none but the truly pious. Concerning the human soul, the opinion of Socrates, according to Xenophon, was, that it is allied to the Divine Being, not by a participation of essence, but by a similarity of nature; that man excels all other animals in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of reason; and that the existence of good men will be continued after death in a state in which they will receive the reward of their virtue. Although it appears that on this latter topic he was not wholly free from uncertainty, the consolation which he professed to derive from this source in the immediate prospect of death, leaves little room to doubt that he entertained a real expectation of immortality: and there is reason to believe that he was the only philosopher of ancient Greece whose principles admitted of such an expectation (see <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, Part III. Chap.iv.). Of his moral system, which was in a high degree pure, and founded on the surest basis, the reader will find a short view in our article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">MORAL PHILOSOPHY</a>, No. 4. SOCRATES was also the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> historian of the 5th century, born at Constantinople in the beginning of the reign of Theodosius: he professed the law and pleaded at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, whence he obtained the name of Scholasticus. He wrote an ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> from the year 309, where Eusebius ended, down to 440; and wrote with great exactness and judgement. An edition of Eusebius and Socrates, in Greek and Latin, with notes by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, was published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1720.

SODA

Pages 67-68

the name given by the French chemists to the mineral alkali, which is found native in many parts of the world: it is obtained also from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and from the ashes of the kali, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Tafola. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, for an account of its properties and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after that article was written, soda and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a> were decomposed by means of <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol9.html#article-GALVANISM">galvanism</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, hitherto considered as simple substances, appear, from the experiments of Mr Davy, who first made the discovery, to be compounds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> and a metallic base. Mr Davy's conclusions have been controverted by some of the French chemists; and as the subject may perhaps in a few months receive some farther elucidation, we shall delay our account of the whole till we come to describe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> by which the experiments are conducted. See Through Galvanic. SODA is also a name for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in the stomach, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> heart-burn. See Medicine, No 275.

SODOM

Pages 68-68

formerly a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, famous in Scripture for the wickedness of its inhabitants, and their destruction by fire from heaven on account of that wickedness. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it stood is now covered by the waters of the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the lake <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a>. See Asphaltites.

SODOMY

Pages 68-68

an unnatural crime, so called from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Sodom, which was destroyed by fire for the same. The Levitical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> adjudged those guilty of this execrable crime to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and the civil law assigns the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> to it. The law of England makes it felony. There is no statute in Scotland against Sodomy; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> of the crime is therefore founded on the divine law, and practice makes its punishment to be burned alive.

SODOR

Pages 68-68

a name always conjoined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, in mentioning the bishop of Man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. Concerning the origin and application of this word, very different opinions have been formed by the learned. Buchanan (lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 34.) says, that before his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the name of Sodor was given to a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Man. In Gough's edition of Camden's Britannia (vol. iii. p. 701,) it is said, that after the Isle of Man was annexed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England, this appellation was given to a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> within mucket-thot of Man, in which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> stands, called by the Norwegians the Holm, and by the inhabitants the Peel. In support of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> is quoted A.D. 1505, in which Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Man confirms to Huon Heketh bishop of Sodor all the lands, &c. anciently belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Man. "Ecclesiam cathedralem sancti Germani in Holm Sodor vel Pele vocatam, ecclesiam sancti Patricii ibidem, et locum praefatum in quo ecclesia praefata fita fuit." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of either, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps of both, these accounts might be allowed; but neither of them is sufficient to account for the constant conjunction of Sodor and Man, in charters, registers, and histories. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> Sodor was a small town or island belonging to Man, it cannot be conceived why it is always mentioned before it, or rather why it should be mentioned at all in speaking of a bishop's diocese. To speak of the bishopric of Sodor and Man in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> would be as improper as it would be to call the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOLY_ISLAND">Holy Island</a> and Durham, or the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARLINGTON">Darlington</a> and Durham; the former being a small island and the latter a town belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> and diocese of Durham. Neither of these accounts, therefore, gives a satisfactory account of the original conjunction of Sodor and Man. The island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONA">Iona</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the bishop of the Isles resided, the cathedral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of which, it is said, was dedicated to our Saviour, in Greek Soter, hence Sotorfenfer, which might be corrupted into Sodorfenfer, a name frequently given by Danish writers to the western isles of Scotland. That we may be the more disposed to accede to this Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for this opinion tell us, that the name Icolmkill, which is often applied to this island, is also of Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, being derived from Columba, "a pigeon;" a meaning that exactly corresponds to the Celtic word Colum and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word Iona. We must confess, however, that we have very little <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in the conjectures of etymologists, and think that upon no occasion they alone can establish any fact, though when concurring with facts they certainly tend to confirm and explain them. It is only from historical facts that we can know to what Sodor was applied. It appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Orkneys, compiled by an old Icelandic writer, translated and enlarged by Torfaes, that the Æbude or Western isles of Scotland were divided into two clusters, Nordureys and Sudereys. The Nordureys, which were separated from the Sudereys by the point of Ardnamurchan, a promontory in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARGYLESHIRE">Argyleshire</a>, consisted of Muck, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">Egg</a>, Rum, Canna, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>, Raay, Barra, South Uist, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Uist, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BENBECULA">Benbecula</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, including Harris, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small isles. The Sudereys were, Man, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARRAN">Arran</a>, Bute, Cumra, Avon, Gid, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-ILA">Ila</a>, Colonfay, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURA">Jura</a>, Scarba, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, Iona, Tiree, Coll, Ulva, and other small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. All these, when joined together, and subject to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, made up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Man and the Isles. In the Norwegian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, Suder and Norder signify southern and northern, and ey or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AY">ay</a> an island. When the Æbude were under one monarch, the seat of empire was fixed in the Sudereys, and the Nordureys were governed by deputies; hence the former are much oftener mentioned in history than the latter; hence, too, the Sudereys often comprehend the Nordureys, as in our days Scotland is sometimes comprehended under England. Sudereys, or Suder, when anglicized, became Sodor; and all the Western isles of Scotland being included in one diocese under the Norwegian princes, the bishop appointed to superintend them was called the bishop of Man and the Isles, or the bishop of Sodor and Man. Since Man was conquered by Edward III. it has been separated from the other isles, and its bishops have exercised no jurisdiction over them. Should it now be asked, why then is the bishop of Man still called the bishop of Sodor and Man? we reply, that we have been able to discover no reason; but suppose the appellation to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the same way, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France has been kept up by the kings of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, for several centuries after the English were entirely expelled from France.

SOFA

Pages 68-69

in the east, a kind of alcove raised half a foot above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of a chamber <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other apartment; and used as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of state, where visitors of distinction are received. Among the Turks the whole floor of their state-rooms is covered with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, and on the window-side is raised a sofa or sopha, laid with a kind of mattock, covered with a carpet much richer than the other. On this carpet the Turks are seated, both men and women, like the tailors in England, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged, leaning against the wall, which is bolstered bolstered with velvet, satin, or other stuff suitable to the season. Here they eat their meals; only laying a skin over the carpet to serve as a tablecloth, and a round wooden board over all, covered with plates, &c.

SOFALA

Pages 69-69
or **CEVALA**, a kingdom of Africa, lying on the coast of Mozambique, near Zanzibar. It is bounded on the north by Monomotapa; on the east by the Mozambique tea; on the south by the kingdom of Sabia; and on the west by that of Manica. It contains mines of gold and iron, and a great number of elephants.
