It is governed by a king, tributary to the Portuguese, who built a fort at the principal town, which is of the same name, and of great importance for their trade to the East Indies. It is situated in a small island, near the mouth of a river. E. Long. 35° 40'. S. Lat. 20° 20'.

SOFFITA

Pages 69-69
or **SOFFT**, in Architecture, any timber ceiling formed of crofs beams of flying cornices, the square compartments or panelling of which are enriched with sculpture, painting, or gilding; such as those in the palaces of Italy, and in the apartments of Luxembourg at Paris.

SOFT

Pages 69-69
or **SOFT**, is also used for the underside or face of an architrave; and more particularly for that of the corona or larmier, which the ancients called lacunar, the French plafond, and we usually the drip. It is enriched with compartments of roses; and in the Doric order has 18 drops, disposed in three ranks, six in each, placed to the right of the guttae, at the bottom of the triglyphs.

SOFTENING

Pages 69-69

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, the mixing and diluting of colours with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>.

SOHO

Pages 69-69

the name of a set of works, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> manufactory of a variety of hardwares, belonging to the late Mr Boulton, situated on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, within two miles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a>; now so justly celebrated as to deserve a short historical detail. About 30 years ago the premises consisted of a small mill and a few obscure dwellings. Mr Boulton, in conjunction with Mr Fothergill, then his partner, at an expense of £9000, erected a handsome and extensive edifice, with a view of manufacturing metallic toys. The first productions consisted of buttons, buckles, watch-chains, trinkets, and such other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as were peculiar to Birmingham. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">Novelty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and variety, were however always conspicuous; and plated wares, known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> plate, comprising a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of useful and ornamental articles, became another permanent subject of manufacture. To open channels for the consumption of these commodities, all the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> was explored by the mercantile partner Mr Fothergill. A wide and extensive correspondence was thus established, the undertaking became well known, and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a>, by becoming his own merchant, eventually enjoyed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> profit. Impelled by an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the arts, and by the patriotic ambition of forming his favourite Soho into a fruitful seminary of artists, the proprietor extended his views; and men of taste and talents were now sought for, and liberally patronised. A successful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the French or moulded ornaments, consisting of vases, tripods, candelabra, &c., &c., extended the celebrity of the works. Services of plate and other works in silver, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a>, were added, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a> office was established in Birmingham. Mr Watt, the ingenious improver of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine, was afterwards taken into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with Mr Boulton; and they carried on at Soho a manufactory of steam-engines, not less beneficial to the public than lucrative to themselves. This valuable machine, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and excellencies of which are described in another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> (see STEAM-ENGINE), Mr Boulton proposed to apply to the operation of coining, and suitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> was erected at a great expense, for the purpose of being employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to make a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>-coining for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Artists of merit were engaged, and specimens of exquisite delicacy were exhibited; the works were also employed upon highly finished medals and private coins. To enumerate all the productions of this manufactory would be tedious (A). In a national view, Mr Boulton's undertakings are highly valuable and important. By collecting around him artists of various descriptions, rival talents have been called forth, and by successive competition have been multiplied to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> highly beneficial to the public. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> arts partook of the benefit, and became proportionally improved. A barren heath has been covered with plenty and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>; and Mr Boulton's works, which in their infancy were little known and attended to, now cover several acres, give employment to more than 600 persons, and are said to be the first of their kind in Europe.

SOIL

Pages 69-70

the mould covering the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in which vegetables grow. It serves as a support for vegetables, and as a reservoir for receiving and communicating their nourishment. Soils are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> triple compounds of the several reputed primitive earths, except the barytic. The magnesian likewise sparingly occurs. The more fertile soils afford also a small proportion of coaly substance arising from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, and some traces of marine acid and gypsum. The vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into clay, chalk, sand, and gravel, is well understood. Loam denotes any soil moderately adhesive; and, according to the ingredient that predominates, it receives the epithets of clayey, chalky, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, or gravelly. The intimate mixture of clay with the oxides of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> is called till, and is of a hard consistence and a dark reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Soils are found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> to contain their earthy ingredients in very different proportions. According to M. Giobert, fertile mould in the vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> amounts yearly to 40 inches, affords for each 100 parts, from 77 to 79 of flex, from 8 to 14 of argill, and from 5 to 12 of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a>; besides about one-half of carbonic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and nearly an equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, partly carbonic and partly hydrocarbonic. The same experimenter represents the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of barren soils in similar situations to be from 42 to 88 per cent. of flex, (A) It was at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in the year 1772, that Mr Eginton invented an expeditious method of copying pictures in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; but we do not know how far this method has succeeded. lex, from 20 to 30 of argill, and from 4 to 20 of calx. The celebrated Bergman found rich soils in the valleys of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, where the annual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of rain is 24 inches, to contain, for each 100 parts, 56 of siliceous sand, 14 of argill, and 30 of calx. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> fall of rain is 20 inches, fertile mixtures, according to M. Tillet, vary from 46 to 52 per cent. of filex, and from 11 to 17 of argill, with 37 of calx. Hence it appears that in dry countries rich earths are of a closer texture, and contain more of the calcareous ingredient, with less of the siliceous. Mr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> Young has discovered, that the value of fertile lands is nearly proportioned to the quantities of gas which equal weights of their soil afford by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOISSONS

Pages 70-70

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of Aisne and late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Soiflonnois. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name, under the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of the French monarchs. It contains about 12,000 inhabitants, and is a bishop's see. The environs are charming, but the streets are narrow, and the houses ill-built. The fine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> has one of the most considerable chapters in the kingdom; and the bishop, when the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> was absent, had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. The castle, though ancient, is not that in which the kings of the first race resided. Soissons is situated in a very pleasant and fertile valley, on the river Aisne, 30 miles west by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Rheims, and 60 north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 24'. N. Lat. 49° 23'.

SOL

Pages 70-70

in Music, the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the gamut, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. See Gamut. Sol., <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Sou, a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> made up of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> mixed with a little silver, and is worth upwards of an English halfpenny, or the 23rd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>. The sol when first struck was equal in value to 12 deniers Tournois, whence it was also called douzain, a name it still retains, though its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> value be changed; the sol having been since augmented by three deniers, and struck with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a> of a fleur-de-lis, to make it current for 15 deniers. Soon after the old sols were coined over again, and both old and new were indifferently made current for 15 deniers. In 1729, the value of the same sols was raised to 18 deniers. Towards the latter end of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV, the sol of 18 deniers was again lowered to 15; and by the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> it was reduced to the original value of 12. What it is at present posterity may perhaps discover. The Dutch have also two kinds of sols: the one of silver, called sols de gros, and likewise schelling; the other of copper, called also the stuyver. Sol., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, Astrology, &c. See Astronomy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLIUM">pallium</a>. Sol., in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; thus called from an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this metal is in a particular manner under the influence of the sun. Sol., in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes Or, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> in the arms of foreign princes. SOLÆUS, or Soleus, in Anatomy, one of the extensor muscles of the foot, rising from the upper and hinder parts of the tibia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIBULA">fibula</a>. SOLAN-GOOSE. See Pelicanus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOLANDRA

Pages 70-70

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a>, and to the order of polyandra; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 38th order, Tricocceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOLANUM

Pages 70-70

a genus of the monogynia order, belonging to the pentandria clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 28th order, Luride. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOLAR

Pages 70-70

something belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>. SOLAR-Spots. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SOLDÁN. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>.

SOLDANELLA

Pages 70-70

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas of pentandria, and order of monogynia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 21st order, Preciae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOLDER

Pages 70-71

SODDER, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Soder, a metallic or mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> used in soldering or joining together other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. Solders are made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>; usually observing, that in the composition there be some of the metal that is to be soldered mixed with some higher and finer metals. Goldsmiths usually make four kinds of folder, viz. folder of eight, where to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> parts of silver there is one of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or copper; folder of six, where only a sixth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is copper; folder of four, and folder of three. It is the mixture of copper in the folder that makes raised plate come always cheaper than flat. As mixtures of gold with a little copper are found to melt with less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> than pure gold itself, these mixtures serve as folders for gold: two pieces of fine gold are soldered by gold that has a small admixture of copper; and gold alloyed with copper is soldered by such as is alloyed with more copper: the workmen add a little silver as well as copper, and vary the proportions of the two to one another, so as to make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the folder correspond as nearly as may be to that of the piece. A mixture of gold and copper is also a folder for fine copper as well as for fine gold. Gold being particularly disposed to unite with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, proves an excellent folder for the finer kinds of iron and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> instruments. The folder used by plumbers is made of two pounds of lead to one of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>-tin. Its goodness is tried by melting it, and pouring the bigness of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-piece on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; for, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> good, there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> arise little bright shining flares therein. The folder for copper is made like that of the plumbers; only with copper and tin; and for very nice works, instead of tin, they sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of silver. Folder for tin is made of two-thirds of tin and one of lead, or of equal parts of each; but where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is any thing delicate, as in organ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a> is scarce discernible, it is made of one part of bismuth and three parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>. The pewterers use a kind of folder made with two parts of tin and one of bismuth; this composition melts with the least heat of any of the folders. Silver folder is that which is made of two parts of silver and one of brass, and used in soldering those metals. Spelter folder is made of one part of brass and two of spelter or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, and is used by the braziers and coppersmiths for soldering brass, copper, and iron. This folder is improved by adding to each ounce of it one <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNYWEIGHT">pennyweight</a> of silver; but as it does not melt without a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat, it cannot be used when it it is inconvenient to heat the work <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> copper and brass are soldered with silver. Though spelter folder be much cheaper than silver-folder, yet workmen in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> prefer the latter. And Mr Boyle informs us, that he has found it to run with too moderate a heat, as not much to endanger the melting of the delicate parts of the work to be soldered; and if well made, this silver folder will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> even upon the ordinary kind itself; and so fill up those little cavities that may chance to be left in the first operation, which is not easily done without a folder more easily fusible than the first made use of. As to iron, it is sufficient that it be heated to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> heat, and the two extremities, in this state, hammered together; by which means they became incorporated one with the other.

SOLDERING

Pages 71-71

the joining and fastening together of two pieces of the same metal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of two different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, by the fusion and application of some metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> on the extremities of the metals to be joined. To solder upon silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>: Take silver, five pennyweights; brass, four pennyweights; melt them together for soft folder, which runs soonest. Take silver, five pennyweights; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, three pennyweights; melt them together for hard folder. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">Beat</a> the folder thin, and lay it on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to be soldered, which must be first fitted and bound together with wire as occasion requires; then take <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a> in powder, and temper it like poy, and lay it upon the folder, letting it dry; then cover it with live coals, and blow, and it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> run immediately; take it presently out of the fire, and it is done. It is to be observed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any thing is to be soldered in two places, which cannot well be done at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, you must first solder with the harder folder, and then with the soft; for if it be first done with the soft, it will unfolder again before the other is fastened. Let it be observed, that if you would not have your folder run about the piece that is to be soldered, you must rub such places over with chalk.—In the soldering either of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, copper, or either of the metals above mentioned, there is generally used borax in powder, and sometimes rosin. As to iron, it is sufficient that it be heated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot, and the two extremities thus hammered together, by which means they will become incorporated with each other. For the finer kinds of iron and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> instruments, however, gold proves an excellent folder. This metal will dissolve twice or thrice its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of iron in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> very far less than that in which iron itself melts; hence if a small plate of gold is wrapped round the parts to be joined, and afterwards melted by a blow-pipe, it strongly unites the pieces together without any injury to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, however delicate.

SOLDIER

Pages 71-71

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> fitted to serve a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state in consideration of a certain daily pay. SOLDIER-Crab. See Cancer, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> SOLDIER. See Stratiotes, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

SOLECISM

Pages 71-71

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a false manner of speaking, contrary to the rules of grammar, either in respect of declension, conjugation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNTAX">syntax</a>.—The word is Greek, σολεικός, derived from the Soli, a people of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, who being transplanted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, lost the purity of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tongue, and became ridiculous to the Athenians for the improprieties into which they fell.

SOLEMN

Pages 71-71

something performed with much pomp, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, and expense. Thus we say, solemn feasts, solemn funerals, solemn games, &c.—In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, solemn signifies something authentic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> what is clothed in all its formalities.

SOLEN

Pages 71-71

Razor-sheath, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">Knife</a>-handle Shell; a genus belonging to the class of vermes, and order of testacea. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOLEURE

Pages 71-71

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and extremely neat town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of the same name. It contains about 4000 inhabitants, and is pleasantly seated on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AAR">Aar</a>, which here expands into a noble river. Among the most remarkable objects of curiosity in this town is the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Urs, which was begun in 1762 and finished in 1772. It is a noble edifice of a whitish grey <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, drawn from the neighbouring quarries, which admits a polish, and is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of rude marble. The lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is of the Corinthian, the upper of the Composite order. The façade, which consists of a portico, surmounted by an elegant tower, presents itself finely at the extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> street. It cost at least 82,000l. a considerable sum for such a small republic, whose revenue scarcely exceeds 12,000l. a-year. Soleure is surrounded by regular stone fortifications, and is 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-north-east of Bern, 27 south-south-west of Baffe, and 45 west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 20'. N. Lat. 47° 15'.

SOLFAING

Pages 71-72

in Music, the naming <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pronouncing the several notes of a song by the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, &c. in learning to sing it. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> notes in the French <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si, only four are used among us in singing, as mi, fa, sol, la: their office is principally, in singing, that by applying them to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the scale, it may not only be pronounced with more ease, but chiefly that by them the tones and semitones of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> scale may be better marked out and distinguished. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is obtained by the four syllables fa, sol, la, mi. Thus from fa to sol is a tone, also from sol to la, and from la to mi, without distinguishing the greater or less tone; but from la to fa, also from mi to fa, is only a semitone. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> then these be applied in this order, fa, sol, la, fa, sol, la, mi, fa, &c., they express the natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> from C; and if that be repeated to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>, we see by them how to express all the different orders of tones and semitones in the diatonic scale; and still above mi <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stand, fa, sol, la, and below it the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> la, sol, fa, and one mi is always distant from another an octave; which cannot be said of any of the rest, because after mi ascending come always fa, sol, la, which are repeated invertedly descending. To conceive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of this, it is to be remembered, that the first thing in learning to sing, is to make one raise a scale of notes by tones and semitones to an octave, and descend again by the same; and then to rise and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by greater intervals at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a>, as thirds and fourths, &c., and to do all this by beginning at notes of different pitch. Then those notes are represented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and spaces, to which these syllables are applied, and the learners taught to name each line and space thereby, which makes what we call solfège; the use whereof is, that while they are learning to tune the degrees and intervals of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> expressed by notes on a line or space, or learning a song to which no words are applied, they may not only do it the better by means of articulate sounds, but chiefly that by knowing the degrees and intervals expressed by those syllables, they may more readily know the places of the semitones, and the true distance of the notes. See the article SING-

SOLFATERRA

Pages 72-72

a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and Terra di Lavoro. This mountain appears evidently to have been a volcano in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is yet so hot, that the workmen employed there in making <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> need nothing else besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the ground for evaporating their liquids. Of this mountain we have the following account by Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>. "Near Afruni (another mountain, formerly a volcano likewise) rises the Solfaterra, which not only retains its cone and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a>, but much of its former heat. In the plain within the crater, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> issues from many parts, as also from its sides: here, by means of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and tiles heaped over the crevices, through which the smoke passes, they collect in an awkward manner what they call <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> armonico; and from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the plain they extract sulphur and alum. This spot, well attended to, might certainly produce a good revenue, whereas I doubt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have hitherto ever cleared 200l. a-year by it. The hollow found produced by throwing a heavy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on the plain of the crater of the Solfaterra, seems to indicate that it is supported by a sort of arched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> vault; and one is induced to think that there is a pool of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> beneath this vault (which boils by the heat of a subterranean fire still deeper), by the very moist <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> that issues from the cracks in the plain of the Solfaterra, which, like that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water, runs off a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, presented to it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> drops. On the outside, and at the foot of the cone of the Solfaterra, towards the lake of Agnano, water rushes out of the rocks so hot as to raise the quicksilver in Fahrenheit's thermometer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of boiling water (A); a fact of which I was myself an eye-witness. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, well worthy the observation of the curious, has been taken little notice of; it is called the Pisciarelli. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people of Naples have great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in the efficacy of this water; and make much of it in all cutaneous disorders, as well as for another disorder that prevails here. It seems to be impregnated chiefly with sulphur and alum. When you approach your <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to the rocks of the Pisciarelli, from whence this water issues, you hear a horrid boiling noise, which seems to proceed from the huge cauldron that may be supposed to be under the plain of the Solfaterra. On the other side of the Solfaterra, next the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, there is a rock which has communicated with the sea, till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it was cut away to make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Puzzole; this was undoubtedly a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, that ran from the Solfaterra when it was an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> volcano. Under this rock of lava, which is more than 70 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, there is a stratum of pumice and ashes. This ancient lava is about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; you meet with it abruptly before you come in sight of Puzzole, and it finishes as abruptly within about 100 paces of the town. The ancient name of the Solfaterra was Forum Vulcani; a strong <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of its origin from subterraneous fire. The degree of heat that the Solfaterra has preserved for so many ages, seems to have calcined the stones upon its cone and in its crater, as they are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and crumble easily in the hottest parts.

SOLICITOR

Pages 72-72

a person employed to take care of and manage suits depending in the courts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>. Solicitors are within the statute to be sworn, and admitted by the judges, before they are allowed to practice in our courts, in like manner as attorneys. There is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> officer of the law, next to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a>, who is styled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s solicitor-general; who holds his office by patent during the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, has the care and concern of managing the king's affairs, and has fees for pleading, besides other fees arising by patents, &c. He attends on the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and the attorney-general and he were anciently reckoned among the officers of the exchequer; they have their audience, and come within the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> in all other courts.

SOLID

Pages 72-73

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, a body whose parts are so firmly connected together, as not easily to give way <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> slip from each other; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> solid stands opposed to fluid. Geometricians define a solid to be the third <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of magnitude, or that which has three dimensions, viz. length, breadth, and thickness or depth. Solids are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> divided into regular and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>. The regular solids are those terminated by regular (A) "I have remarked, that after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is much less; which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> account for what Padre Torre says (in his book, intitled Histoire et Phenomenes du Veuf), that when he tried it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Monsieur de la Condamine, the degree of heat, upon Reaumur's thermometer, was 68°." and equal planes, and are only five in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, viz. the tetrahedron, which consists of four equal triangles; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBE">cube</a> or hexahedron, of six equal squares; the octahedron, of eight equal triangles; the dodecahedron, of twelve; and the icosahedron, of twenty equal triangles. The irregular solids are almost infinite, comprehending all such as do not come under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of regular solids; as the sphere, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, cone, parallelogram, prism, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLELOPIPED">parallelopiped</a>, &c. **Solids**, in **Anatomy**, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, ligaments, membranes, muscles, nerves and vessels, &c. The solid parts of the body, though equally composed of vessels, are different with regard to their consistence; some being hard and others soft. The hard, as the bones and cartilages, give firmness and stature to the body, and sustain the other parts; the soft parts, either alone or together with the hard, serve to execute the animal functions. See **Anatomy**. **Solidago**, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of *Syngenesia*, and to the order of *polygamia superflua*; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 49th order, *Compositae*. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**. **Solidity**, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, or body, by which it excludes all other bodies from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which itself possesses; and as it would be absurd to suppose that two bodies could possess one and the same place at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it follows, that the softest bodies are equally solid with the hardest. See **<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>**, No. 44, 173, &c. Among geometers, the solidity of a body denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or space contained in it, and is called also its solid content. The solidity of a cube, prism, cylinder, or parallelopiped, is had by multiplying its basis into its height. The solidity of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> or cone is had by multiplying either the whole base into a third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the height, or the whole height into a third part of the base. **Soliloquy**, a reasoning or discourse which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> holds with himself; or, more properly, according to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPIAS">Papias</a>, it is a discourse by way of answer to a question that a man proposes to himself. Soliloquies are become very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> stage; yet nothing can be more inartificial, or more unnatural, than an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>'s making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> speeches to himself, to convey his intentions to the audience. Where such discoveries are necessary to be made, the poets should rather take care to give the dramatic persons such confidants as may necessarily share their inmost thoughts; by which means they will be more naturally conveyed to the audience; yet even this is a shift which an accurate poet would not have occasion for. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and abuse of soliloquies deserve <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>: Soliloquies had need be very few, Extremely short, and spoke in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> too. Our lovers talking to themselves, for want Of others, make the pit their confidant: Nor is the matter mended yet, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> thus They trust a friend, only to tell it us. **Soliman II.**, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Turks, surnamed the Magnificent, was the only son of Selim I. whom he succeeded in 1520. He was educated in a manner very different from the Ottoman princes in general; for he was instructed in the maxims of politics and the secrets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. He began his reign by restoring those persons their possessions whom his father had unjustly plundered. He re-established the authority of the tribunals, which was almost annihilated, and bestowed the government of provinces upon none but persons of wealth and probity: "I would have my viceroys (he used to say) resemble those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that fertilize the fields through which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, not those torrents which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> everything before them." After concluding a truce with Ismael Sophy of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and subduing Gozeli Bey, who had raised a rebellion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, he turned his arms against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a> was taken in 1521, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> fell into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the year following, after an obstinate and enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. In 1526 he defeated and slew the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> in the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Mohatz. Three years after he conquered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUDA">Buda</a>, and immediately laid siege to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> itself. But after continuing 20 days before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and assaulting it 20 times, he was obliged to retreat with the loss of 80,000 men. Some time after he was defeated by the Persians, and disappointed in his hopes of taking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. He succeeded, however, in dispossessing the Genoese of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIO">Chio</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> which had belonged to that republic for more than 200 years. He died at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 76, while he was besieging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SZIGETH">Szigeth</a>, a town in Hungary, on the 30th August 1566. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the strictest probity, a lover of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and vigorous in the execution of it; but he tarnished all his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> by the cruelty of his disposition. After the battle of Mohatz he ordered 1500 prisoners, most of them gentlemen, to be ranged in a circle, and beheaded in presence of his whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Soliman thought nothing impossible which he commanded: A general having received orders to throw a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Drave, wrote him, that it was impossible. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> sent him a long band of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> with these words written on it: "The emperor Soliman, thy <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, orders thee to build a bridge over the Drave in spite of the difficulties thou mayest meet with. He informs thee at the same time, that if the bridge be not finished upon his arrival, he will hang thee with the very linen which informs thee of his will." **Solipuga**, or **Solifuga**, in **<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>**, the name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to a small venomous insect of the spider-kind, called by the Greeks *helicentrus*; both words signifying an animal which stings most in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and seas where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is most hot. Solinus makes this creature peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>; but this is contrary to all the accounts given us by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. It is common in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and some parts of Europe. Almost all the hot countries produce this venomous little creature. It lies under the sand to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> other insects as they go by; and if it meet with any uncovered part of a man, produces a wound which proves very painful; it is said that the bite is absolutely mortal, but probably this is not true. Solinus writes the word *solifuga*, and so do many others, erroneously deriving the name from the notion that this animal flies from the sun's rays, and buries itself in the sand. **Solis, Antonio de**, an ingenious Spanish writer, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and illustrious family, born at Placenza an Old Castile, in 1610. He was intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but his inclination toward <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> prevailed, and he cultivated it with great success. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> IV. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>

SOLITARIES

Pages 74-74

a denomination of nuns of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCANTARA">Alcantara</a>, instituted in 1676, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of which was to imitate the fervent penitent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of that saint. Thus they are to keep a continual silence, never to open their mouths to a stranger; to employ their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wholly in spiritual exercises, and leave their temporal concerns to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of maids, who have a particular superior in a separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>: they always go bare-footed, without sandals; gird themselves with a thick <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, and wear no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>.

SOLITARY

Pages 73-74

that which is remote from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of others of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>.

SOLOMON

Pages 74-74

the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel, renowned in Scripture for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and magnificent temple and other buildings. Towards the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he fulfilled all his former <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> by his apostacy from God; from which cause vengeance was denounced against his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. He died about 975 B.C.

SOLON

Pages 74-74

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wise men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, of Athenian parents, who were descended from Codrus. His father leaving little patrimony, he had recourse to merchandise for his subsistence. He had, however, a greater thirst after knowledge and fame than after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and made his mercantile voyages subservient to the increase of his intellectual treasures. He very early cultivated the art of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of moral and civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. When the Athenians, tired out with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and troublesome <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Megarensians, for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Salamis, prohibited any one, under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, to propose the renewal of their claim to that island, Solon thinking the prohibition dishonourable to the state, and finding many of the younger citizens desirous to revive the war, feigned himself mad, and took care to have the report of his insanity spread through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he composed an elegy adapted to the state of public affairs, which he committed to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Every thing being thus prepared, he fell into the market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> with the kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> on his head which was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> worn by sick persons, and, ascending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERALD">herald</a>'s stand, he delivered, to a numerous crowd, his lamentation for the desertion of Salamis. The verses were heard with general applause; and Pittacus seconded his advice, and urged the people to renew the war. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> was immediately repealed; the claim to Salamis was resumed; and the conduct of the war was committed to Solon and Pittacus, who, by means of a stratagem, defeated the Megarensians, and recovered Salamis. His popularity was extended through Greece in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a successful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> which he formed among the states in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> against the Corinthians. When dissensions had arisen at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> between the rich creditors and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> debtors, Solon was created archon, with the united powers of supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. He soon restored <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> between the rich and poor: He cancelled the debts which had proved the occasion of so much oppression; and ordained that in future no creditor should be allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the body of the debtor for his security: He made a new distribution of the people, instituted new courts of judicature, and framed a judicious code of laws, which afterwards became the basis of the laws of the twelve tables in Rome. Among his criminal laws are many wise and excellent regulations; but the code is necessarily defective with respect to those principles which must be derived from the knowledge of the true God, and of pure morality, as the certain foundations of national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. Two of them in particular were very exceptionable; the permission of a voluntary exile to persons that had been guilty of premeditated <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, and the appointment of a less severe <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> than for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEDUCTION">seduction</a>. Those who wish to see accurately stated the comparative excellence of the laws of Moses, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, and Solon, may consult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">Prize</a> Dissertations relative to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> and Revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> by Teyler's Theological <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, vol. ix. The interview which Solon is said to have had with Croesus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Lydia, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> remarks of the sage after surveying the monarch's wealth, the recollection of those remarks by Croesus when doomed to die, and the noble conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> on that occasion, are known to every schoolboy. Solon died in the island of Cyprus, about the 80th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">Statues</a> were erected to his memory both at Athens and Salamis. His thirst after knowledge <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the last: "I grow old (said he) learning many things." Among the aphorisms and precepts which have been ascribed to Solon, are the following: Laws are like cobwebs, that entangle the weak, but are broken through by the strong. He who has learned to obey, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> know how to command. In all things let reason be your guide. Diligently contemplate excellent things. In every thing that you do, consider the end.

SOLSTICE

Pages 74-74

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is in one of the solstitial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; that is, when he is at his greatest distance from the equator; thus called because he then appears to stand still, and not to change his distance from the equator for some time; an appearance owing to the obliquity of our sphere, and which those living under the equator are strangers to. The solstices are two in each year; theestival <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice, and the hyemal or winter solstice. The summer solstice is when the sun seems to describe the tropic of cancer, which is on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 22, when he makes the longest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>: the winter solstice is when the sun enters the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, or seems to describe the tropic of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">capricorn</a>, which is on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 22, when he makes the shortest day. This is to be understood as in our northern hemisphere; for in the southern, the sun's entrance

SOMERS

Pages 74-75

John, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a> in 1652. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards entered himself at the Middle Temple, where he studied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> vigour. In 1688 he was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> at their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, and argued with great learning and eloquence against the dispensing power. In the convention which met by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>'s summons, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 22, 1689, he represented Worcester; and was one of the managers for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons, at a conference with the House of Lords upon the word abdicated. Soon after the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> to the throne, he was appointed solicitor-general, and received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. In 1692 he was made attorney general, and in 1693 advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of lord keeper of the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of England. In 1695 he proposed an expedient to prevent the practice of clipping the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. In 1697 he was created lord Somers, baron of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVESHAM">Evesham</a>, and made lord high chancellor of England. In the beginning of 1700 he was removed from his post of lord chancellor, and the year after was impeached of high crimes and misdemeanors by the House of Commons, of which he was acquitted upon trial by the House of Lords. He then retired to a studious course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. In 1706 he proposed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> for the regulation of the law; and the same year was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> managers for the union between England and Scotland. In 1708 he was made lord president of the council; from which post he was removed in 1710, upon the change of the ministry. In the latter end of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s reign his lordship grew very infirm in Somers' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; which is supposed to be the reason that he held no other post than a seat at the council-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, after the accession of King George I. He died of an apoplectic fit in 1716. Mr Addison has drawn his character very beautifully in the Freeholder.

SOMERSETSHIRE

Pages 75-75

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, taking its name from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERTON">Somerton</a>, once the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, between 50° and 51° 27' <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between 1° 25' and 2° 50' west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> channel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the north east by a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, and on the east by Wiltshire. It is one of the largest counties in England, extending in length from east to west about 68 miles; in breadth, where broadest, from south to north, about 47; and 240 in circumference. It is divided into 42 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, in which are 3 cities, 32 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 1700 villages, 385 parishes of which 132 are vicarages, containing more than 1,000,000 acres, and about 273,750 souls. It sends 18 members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, viz. two for the county, two for Bristol, two for Bath, two for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, two for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>, two for Bridgewater, two for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ILCHESTER">Ilchester</a>, two for Milborne-port, and two for Minehead. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this county is very mild and wholesome, especially that of the hilly part. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general is exceeding rich, so that single acres very <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> produce forty or fifty bushels of wheat, and there have been instances of some producing sixty of barley. As there is very fine pasture both for sheep and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, it abounds in both, which are as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of a finer grain. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this abundance of black cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of cheese are made in it, of which that of Cheddar is thought equal to Parmesan. In the hilly parts are found coal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> calaminaris. Wood thrives in it as well as in any county of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It abounds also in peas, beans, beer, cider, fruit, wild fowl, and salmon; and its mineral waters are celebrated all over the world. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of this county, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and acquired, exceed those of any other in the kingdom, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> excepted. The woollen manufacture in all its branches is carried on to a very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and in some parts of the county great quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> are made. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> to these the produce of various other commodities in which it abounds is added, the amount of the whole must undoubtedly be very great. Its foreign trade must also be allowed to be very extensive, when it is considered that it has a large trade for coal, lead, and potteries, besides other ports, that of Bristol, a town of the greatest trade in England, next to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Besides small streams, it is well watered and supplied with fish by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Severn, Avon, Parrel, Froome, Axe, Torre, and Tone. Its greatest hills are Mendip, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTON">Poulton</a>, and Quantock, of which the first abounds in coal, lead, &c. The rivers Severn and Parrel breed very fine salmon. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Bristol.

SOMERTON

Pages 75-75

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, from whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> derives its name. It is 123 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; it has five streets, containing 25 houses, which are mostly built of the blue <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> from the quarries in the neighbourhood. It is governed by constables, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> for petty sessions. The mar-

SONATA

Pages 76-76

in Music, a piece <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, intended to be performed by instruments only; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to cantata, or a piece designed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. See Cantata. The sonata then, is properly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>, free, humorous composition, diversified with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of motions and expressions, extraordinary and bold strokes, figures, &c. And all this purely according to the fancy of the composer; who, without confining himself to any general rules of counterpoint, or to any fixed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, gives a loose to his genius, and runs from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, measure, &c. to another, as he thinks fit. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of composition had its rise about the middle of the 17th century; those who have most excelled in it were Baffani and Corelli. We have sonatas of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and even 8 parts, but usually they are performed by a single violin, or with two violins, and a thorough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> for the harpsichord; and frequently a more figured bass for the bass viol, &c. There are a thousand different species of sonatas; but the Italians usually reduce them to two kinds. Sonate de chiefa, that is, sonatas proper for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> music, which usually begin with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, suitable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and sanctity of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, after which they strike into a brisker, gayer, and richer manner. These are what they more peculiarly call sonatas. Sonate de camera, or sonatas for the chamber, are properly serenades of several little pieces, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, only composed to the same tune. They usually begin with a prelude or little sonata, serving as an introduction to all the rest; afterwards come the allemande, pavane, courant, and other serious dances; then jigs, gavots, minuets, chacons, prélècaillles, and other gay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>: the whole composed in the same tune or mode.

SONCHUS

Pages 76-76

Sow-thistle, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of Syngenesia, and to the order of Polygaminæ aquatilis; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranged under the 49th order, Compositæ. The receptacle is naked; the calyx is imbricated, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-shaped and conical; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> of the seed is simple, fleshy, and very soft; the seed is oval and pointed. There are 13 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; the maritimus, palustris, fruticosus, arvensis, oleraceus, tenerimus, plumieri, alpinus, floridanus, fibricus, tataricus, tuberosus, and canadensis. Four of these are natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.—1. Palustris, marsh sow-thistle. The stem is erect, from six to ten feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, branched and hairy towards the top; the leaves are firm, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, half pinnated, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, and sharp-pointed; the lower ones fugituate at the base: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and dispersed on the tops of the branches: the calyx is rough. It is frequent in marshes, and flowers in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> August.—2. Arvensis, corn sow-thistle. The leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a>, runcinate, and heart-shaped at the base; the root creeps under ground; the stem is three or four feet high, and branched at the top. It grows in corn-fields, and flowers in August.—3. Oleraceus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sow-thistle. The stalk is succulent, pinnular, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> high or more; the leaves are broad, embracing the stem, generally deeply sinuated, smooth, or prickly at the edges; the flowers are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow, numerous, in a kind of umbel, and terminal; the calyx is smooth. It is frequent in waste places and cultivated grounds.—4. Alpinus, blue-flowered sow-thistle. The stem is erect, purplish, branched, or simple, from three to five feet high: the leaves are large, smooth, and sinuated; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> segment large and triangular: the flowers are blue, and grow on hairy vilvíd pedicels, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> spikes: the calyx is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. This species is found in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>.

SONG

Pages 76-77

in Music, is applied in general to a single piece of music, whether contrived for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a>. SONG of Birds, is defined by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Duines Barrington to be a succession of three or more different notes, which are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> without interruption, during the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, with a musical <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of four crotchets in an adagio movement, or whilst a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> swings four seconds. It is affirmed, that the notes of birds are no more innate than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and that they depend upon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, as far as their organs <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> enable them to imitate the sounds which they have frequent opportunities of hearing: and their adhering so steadily, even in a wild state, to the same song, is owing to the nestlings attending only to the instruction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, whilst they disregard the notes of all others that may perhaps be singing round them. Birds in a wild state do not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sing above 10 weeks in the year, whereas birds that have plenty of food in a cage sing the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the year; and we may add, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> of no <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of birds ever sings. This is a wise provision of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, because her song would discover her nest. In the same manner, we may rationally account for her inferiority in plumage. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of singing is confined to the cock birds; and accordingly Mr Hunter, in dissecting birds of several species, found the muscles of the larynx to be stronger SON Stronger in the nightingale than in any other bird of the same size; and in all those instances, where he defeated both cock and hen, the same muscles were stronger in the cock. To the same purpose, it is an observation as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Pliny, that a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPON">capon</a> does not crow. Some have ascribed the singing of the cock-bird in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> solely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of pleasing his mate during incubation; others, who allow that it is partly for this end, believe it is partly owing also to another cause, viz., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and insects in the spring, which, as well as seeds, are the proper food of singing birds at that time of the year. Mr Barrington remarks, that there is no instance of any singing bird which exceeds our blackbird in size; and this, he supposes, may arise from the difficulty of its concealing itself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it called the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of its enemies, not only by its bulk, but by the proportionable loudness of its notes. This writer farther observes, that some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the song in a few kinds of birds correspond with the intervals of our musical <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, of which the cuckoo is a striking, and known instance; but the greater part of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> cannot be reduced to a musical scale; partly, because the rapidity is often so great, and it is also so uncertain when they may stop, that we cannot reduce the passages to form a musical bar in any time whatsoever; partly also, because the pitch of most birds is considerably higher than the most shrill notes of those instruments which have the greatest compass; and principally, because the intervals used by birds are commonly so minute, that we cannot judge of them from the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> intervals into which we divide our musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>.
