This writer apprehends, that all birds sing in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>; and in order to discover this key, he informs us, that the following notes have been observed in different birds, A, B flat, C, D, F, and G; and therefore E only is wanting to complete the scale; now these intervals, he says, can only be found in the key of F with a sharp third, or that of G with a flat third; and he supposes it to be the latter, because admitting that the first musical notes were learned from birds, those of the cuckoo, which have been most attended to, form a flat third, and most of our compositions are in a flat third, where music is simple, and consists merely of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>. As a farther <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that birds sing always in the same key, it has been found by attending to a nightingale, as well as a robin which was educated under him, that the notes reducible to our intervals of the octave were always precisely the same. Most people, who have not attended to the notes of birds, suppose, that every species sing exactly the same notes and passages: but this is by no means true; though it is admitted that there is a general resemblance. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> bird-catchers prefer the song of the Kentish goldfinches, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> chaffinches; and some of the nightingale fanciers prefer a Surry bird to those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>. Of all singing birds, the song of the nightingale has been most universally admired: and its superiority (deduced from a caged bird) consists in the following particulars; its tone is much more mellow than that of any other bird, though at the same time, by a proper exertion of its musical powers, it can be very brilliant. Another point of superiority is its continuance of long without a pause, which is sometimes no less than 20 seconds; and when respiration becomes necessary, it takes it with as much judgment as an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>-finger. The sky-lark in this particular, as well as in compass and variety, is only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to the nightingale. The nightingale also sings (if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> may be allowed) with superior judgment and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Mr Barrington has observed, that his nightingale, which was a very <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> bird, began softly like the ancient orators, referring its breath to swell certain notes, which by these means had a most astonishing effect. This writer adds, that the notes of birds, which are annually imported from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, both singly and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>, are not to be compared to those of European birds. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, formed by Mr Barrington, agreeably to the idea of M. de Piles in estimating the merits of painters, is designed to exhibit the comparative merit of the British singing birds; in which 20 is supposed to be the point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> perfection. | Philosopha- | Mellowness | Sprightly- | Flaming- | Compass & | Execution | |-------------|------------|-----------|----------|-----------|-----------| | Nightingale | 19 | 14 | 19 | 19 | 19 | | Sky-lark | 4 | 19 | 4 | 18 | 18 | | Wood-lark | 18 | 4 | 17 | 12 | 8 | | Tit-lark | 12 | 12 | 12 | 12 | 12 | | Linnet | 12 | 16 | 12 | 16 | 18 | | Goldfinch | 4 | 19 | 4 | 12 | 12 | | Chaffinch | 4 | 12 | 4 | 8 | 8 | | Greenfinch | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 6 | | Hedge-sparrow| 6 | 0 | 6 | 4 | 4 | | Aberdavine or siskin | 2 | 4 | 0 | 4 | 4 | | <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a>-poll | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | 4 | | Thrush | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 | | Blackbird | 4 | 0 | 2 | 2 | 2 | | Robin | 6 | 16 | 12 | 12 | 14 | | Wren | 0 | 12 | 0 | 4 | 2 | | Reed sparrow| 0 | 4 | 0 | 2 | 2 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> mock nightingale | 14 | 12 | 12 | 14 | 14 |

SONNA

Pages 77-77

a book of Mahometan traditions, which the orthodox muslims are required to believe.

SONNER

Pages 76-76

WILLIAM, an eminent English antiquary, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> in 1626. His first treatise was The Antiquities of Canterbury, which he dedicated to Archbishop Laud. He then applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and having made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it, he perceived that the old glossary prefixed to Sir Roger Twysden's edition of the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry I, printed in 1644, was faulty in many places; he therefore added to that edition notes and observations valuable for their learning, with a very useful glossary. His Treatise of Gavelkind was finished about 1638, though not published till 1660. Our author was zealously attached to King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I, and in 1648 he published a poem on his sufferings and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His skill in the Saxon tongue led him to inquire into most of the European languages <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. He assisted Dugdale and Dodsworth in compiling the Monasicon Anglicum. His Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1659. He died in 1669.

SONNERATIA

Pages 77-77

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of icelandia, and to the order of monogynia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SONNET

Pages 77-77

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> contained in 14 verses, viz., two stanzas <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of four verses each, and two of three, the first eight verses being all in three rhymes.

SONNITES

Pages 77-77

among the Mahometans, an appellation given to the orthodox muslims <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a>; in opposition to the several heretical sects, particularly the Shiites, or followers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>.

SOONTABURDAR

Pages 77-78

in the East Indies; an attendant, who carries a silver bludgeon in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> about two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and runs before the palanquin. He is inferior to the chubdar; the propriety of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> newaury requiring two soontaburdars for every chubdar in the train. The chubdar proclaims the approach of visitors, &c. He generally carries a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fil- ver <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> about five feet long in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and among the Nabobs he proclaims their praises aloud as he runs before their palanquins.

SOOT

Pages 78-78

a volatile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> arising from wood and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> along with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather, it is the smoke itself condensed and gathered to the sides of the chimney. Though once volatile, however, soot cannot be again resolved into vapour; but, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> distilled by a strong fire, yields a volatile alkali and empyreumatic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fixed matter remaining at the bottom of the distilling vessel. If burnt in an open fire, it flames with a thick smoke, whence other fuel is produced. It is used as a material for making sal ammoniac, and as a manure. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">AMMONIA</a>, mariate of, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Soot-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">COLOUR</a>-Making.

SOPHII

Pages 78-78
or SOFI, a title given to the emperor of Persia, importing as much as wise, sage, or philosopher. The title is by some said to have taken its rise from a young shepherd named Sophi, who attained to the crown of Persia in 1372; others derive it from the sophoi or sages anciently called magi. Volius gives a different account of the word: sophi in Arabic, he observes, signifies wool; and he adds, that it was applied by the Turks out of derision to the kings of Persia ever since Ishmael's time; because, according to their scheme of religion, he is to wear no other covering on his head but an ordinary red woollen stuff; whence the Persians are also called hazzellafesh, q. d. red-heads. But Bochart affirms us, that sophi in the original Persian language, signifies one that is pure in his religion, and who prefers the service of God in all things; and derives it from an order of religious called by the same name. The sophis value themselves on their illustrious extraction. They are descended in a right line from Houssain, second son of Ali, Mahomet's cousin, and Fatima, Mahomet's daughter.

SOPHIS

Pages 78-78
or Sofees, a kind of order of religious among the Mahometans in Persia, answering to what are otherwise called dervishes, and among the Arabs and Indians fakirs. Some will have them called sophis from a kind of coarse camlet which they wear, called sof, from the city Soof in Syria, where it is principally manufactured. The more eminent of those sophis are complimented with the title Schiek, that is, reverend, much as in Roman countries the religious are called reverend fathers. Schiek Sophi, who laid the foundation of the grandeur of the royal house of Persia, was the founder, or rather the restorer of this order: Ishmael, who conquered Persia, was himself a sophi, and greatly valued himself on his being so. He chose all the guards of his person from among the religious of this order; and would have all the great lords of his court sophis. The king of Persia is still grandmaster of the order; and the lords continue to enter into it, though it be now fallen under some contempt.

SOPHISM

Pages 78-78

in Logic, a specious argument having the appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, but leading to falsehood. Sophisms are reduced by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> into eight classes, an arrangement so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and comprehensive, that it is equally proper in present as in former times. 1. Ignoratio elenchi, in which the sophist seems to determine the question, while he does it only in appearance. Thus the question, "Whether the excess of wine be hurtful?" seems to be determined by proving, that wine revives the spirits and gives a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> courage: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> point is here kept out of sight; for still it may be hurtful to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, to fortune, and reputation. 2. Petitio principii, a begging of the question, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> taking for granted that which remains to be proved, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any one should undertake to prove that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is extended through all the parts of the body, because it resides in every member. This is affirming the same thing in different words. 3. Reasoning in a circle; as when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a> prove the Scriptures to be the word of God by the authority of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and the authority of the church from the Scriptures. 4. Non causa pro causa, or the afflicting of a false cause to any effect. Thus the supposed principle, that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> abhors a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>, was applied to explain the rising of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> before Galileo discovered that it was owing to the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. In this way the vulgar ascribe accidents to divine vengeance, and the heresies and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times are said to be owing to learning. 5. Fallacia accidentis, in which the sophist represents what is merely accidental as essential to the nature of the subject. This is nearly allied to the former, and is committed by the Mahometans and Roman Catholics. The Mahometans forbid wine, because it is sometimes the occasion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a> and quarrels; and the Roman Catholics prohibit the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, because it has sometimes promoted heresies. 6. By deducing an universal assertion from what is true only in particular circumstances, and the reverse: thus some men argue, "transcribers have committed many errors in copying the Scriptures, therefore they are not to be depended on." 7. By asserting anything in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> which is only true in a divided sense; so when the Scriptures assure us, that the worst of sinners may be saved, it does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that they shall be saved while they remain sinners, but that if they repent they may be saved. 8. By an abuse of the ambiguity of words. Thus Mr Hume reasons in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>: "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> is our only guide in reasoning concerning matters of fact; now we know from experience, that the laws of nature are fixed and invariable. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, testimony is variable and often false; therefore since our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for the reality of miracles rests solely on testimony which is variable, and our evidence for the uniformity of the laws of nature is invariable, miracles are not to be believed." The sophistry of this reasoning depends on the ambiguity of the word experience, which in the first proposition signifies the maxims which we form from our own observation and reflection; in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> it is confounded with testimony; for it is by the testimony of others, as well as our own observation, that we learn whether the laws of nature are variable or invariable. The Essay on Miracles may be recommended to those who wish to see more examples of sophistry; as we believe most of the eight <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of sophisms which we have mentioned are well illustrated by examples in that essay.

SOPHIST

Pages 78-79

an appellation assumed in the early periods of Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> by those who devoted their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of science. This appellation appearing too arrogant to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, he declined it, and wished to be called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; declaring that, though he could not consider himself as a wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, he was indeed a lover of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. True wisdom and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> are generally Sophocles generally united. The example of Pythagoras was followed by every man of eminence; while the name sophist was retained only by those who with a pomp of words made a magnificent display of wisdom upon a very slight foundation of knowledge. Those men taught an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> structure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and a false method of reasoning, by which, in argument, the worst might be made to appear the better reason (see <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOPHISM">Sophism</a>). In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> they were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> repute, and supported, not only by contributions from their pupils, but by a regular salary from the state. They were among the bitterest enemies of the illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, because he embraced every opportunity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> to contempt and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> their vain pretensions to superior knowledge, and the pernicious influence of their doctrines upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and morals of the Athenian youth.

SOPHISTICATION

Pages 79-79

the mixing of anything with what is not genuine; a practice too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the making up of medicines for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; as also among vintners, distillers, and others, who are accused of foreshortening their wines, spirits, oils, &c., by mixing with them cheaper and coarser materials; and in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the cheat is carried on so artfully as to deceive the best judges.

SOPHOCLES

Pages 79-79

the celebrated Greek tragic poet, the son of Sophilus an Athenian, was born at Colonn, and educated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Superior vigour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> in the exercises of the palestra, and skill in music, were the great accomplishments of young men in the states of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. In these, Sophocles excelled; nor was he less distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of his person. He was also instructed in the noblest of all sciences, civil polity and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>: from the first of these he derived an unshaken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which he served in some embassies, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> command with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERICLES">Pericles</a>; from the latter he was impressed with a pious reverence for the gods, manifested by the inviolable integrity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. But his studies were early devoted to the tragic muse; the spirit of Eschylus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> a fire to his genius, and excited that noble emulation which led him to contend with, and sometimes to bear away the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> from, his great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. He wrote 43 tragedies, of which 7 only have escaped the ravages of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: and having testified his love of his country by refusing to leave it, though invited by many kings; and having enjoyed the uninterrupted esteem and affection of his fellow citizens, which neither the gallant actions and sublime genius of Eschylus, nor the tender spirit and philosophic virtue of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, could secure to them, he died in the 91st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, about 406 years before Christ. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> was at Decelia, which the Lacedemonians had at that time seized and fortified; but Lycaon, the Spartan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, permitted the Athenians to inter their deceased poet; and they paid him all the honours due to his love of his country, integrity of life, and high poetic excellence. Eschylus had at once feigned the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the true sublime; to that eminence his claim could not be disputed. Sophocles had a noble elevation of mind, but tempered with so fine a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and so chastened a judgement, that he never passed the bounds of propriety. Under his conduct the tragic muse appeared with the chaste <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of some noble matron at a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> solemnity; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> is in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> in all her motions. From him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> received some additional embellishments; and Sophocles the drama the introduction of a third speaker, which made it more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and interesting: but his distinguished excellence is in the judicious disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, and so nice a connection and dependence of the parts on each other, that they all agree to make the event not only probable, but even necessary. This is peculiarly admirable in his "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OEDIPUS">Oedipus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> of Thebes;" and in this important point he is far superior to every other dramatic writer. The ingratitude of the children of Sophocles is well known. They wished to become immediate masters of their father's possessions; and therefore tired of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> life, they accused him before the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a> of insanity. The only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> the poet made was to read his tragedy of Oedipus at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONUS">Colonus</a>, which he had lately finished; and then he asked his judges, whether the author of such a performance could be taxed with insanity! The father upon this was acquitted, and the children returned home covered with shame and confusion. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> tragedies of Sophocles which still remain, together with the Greek Scholia which accompany them, have been translated into Latin by Johnson, and into English by Dr Franklin and Mr Potter.

SOPHORA

Pages 79-79

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of decandria, and to the order of monogynia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 32d order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOPORIFIC

Pages 79-79
or SOPORIFEROUS, a medicine that produces sleep. Such are opium, laudanum, the seed of poppies, &c. The word is formed from the Latin sopor "sleep." The Greeks in place of it use the word hypnotic.

SORBONNE

Pages 79-79

is also used in general for the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; as the assemblies of the whole body are held in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the Sorbonne; and the bachelors of the other houses of the faculty, as the house of Navarre, &c., come hither to hold their sorbonnique, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> for being admitted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>.

SORBUS

Pages 79-80
SERVICE-TREE, a genus of plants belonging to the class of icoandria, and to the order of trigynia. See Botany Index.—The aucuparia, mountain-ash, quicken-tree, quick-beam, or roan-tree, rises with a straight upright stem and regular branching head, twenty or thirty feet high or more, covered with a smooth grayish brown bark; pinnated leaves of eight or ten pair of long, narrow, ferrated folioles, and an odd one, smooth on both sides; and large umbellate clusters of white flowers at the sides and ends of the branches, succeeded by clusters of fine red berries, ripe in autumn and winter. There is a variety with yellow striped leaves. This species grows wild in many parts of this island in mountainous places, woods, and hedge-rows, often growing to the size of timber; and is admitted into most ornamental plantations, for the beauty of its growth, foliage, flowers, and fruit; the latter, in particular, being produced in numerous red large bunches all over the tree, exhibit a fine appearance in autumn and winter, till devoured by the birds, especially the blackbird and thrush, which are so allured by this fruit as to flock from all parts and feed on it voraciously.—In the island of Jura the juice of the berries is employed as an acid for punch. It is probable that this tree was in high esteem with the Druids; for it is more abundant than any other tree in the neighborhood of those Druidical circles of stones, so common in North Britain. It is still believed by some persons, that a branch of this tree can defend them from enchantment or witchcraft. Even the cattle are supposed to be preserved by it from danger. The dairy-maid drives them to the summer pastures with a rod of the rowan-tree, and drives them home again with the same. In Strathspey, we are told, a hoop is made of the wood of this tree on the 1st of May, and all the sheep and lambs are made to pass through it. The domestica, or cultivated service-tree, with eatable fruit, grows with an upright stem, branching 30 or 40 feet high or more, having a brownish bark, and the young shoots in summer covered with a mealy down; pinnated leaves of eight or ten pair of broadish deeply ferrated lobes and an odd one, downy underneath; and large umbellate clusters of white flowers at the sides and ends of the branches, succeeded by bunches of large, fleshy, edible red fruit, of various shapes and sizes. This tree is a native of the southern warm parts of Europe, where its fruit is used at table as a dessert, and it is cultivated here in many of our gardens, both as a fruit-tree and as an ornament to diversify hardy plantations.

SORCERY

Pages 80-81
or MAGIC; the power which some persons were formerly supposed to possess of commanding the devil and the infernal spirits by skill in charms and invocations, and of soothing them by fumigations. Sorcery is therefore to be distinguished from witchcraft; an art which was supposed to be practised, not by commanding evil spirits, but by compact with the devil. As an instance of the power of bad smells over demons or evil spirits, we may mention the flight of the evil spirit mentioned in Tobit into the remote parts of Egypt, produced, it is said, by the smell of the burnt liver of a fish. Lilly informs us, that one Evans having raised a spirit at the request of Lord Bothwell and Sir Kenelm Digby, and forgetting a fumigation, the spirit, vexed at the disappointment, pulled him without the circle, and carried him from his house in the Minories into a field near Battersea Causeway. King James, in his Daemonologia, has given a very full account of the art of sorcery. "Two principal things (says he) cannot well in that errand be wanted: holy water (whereby the devil mocks the papists), and some present of a living thing unto him. There are likewise certain cases and hours that they observe in this purpose. These things being all ready and prepared, circles are made, triangular, quadrangular, round, double, or single, according to the form of the apparition they crave. When the conjured spirit appears, which will not be while after many circumstances, long prayers, and much muttering and murmurings of the conjurors, like a papist priest dispatching a hunting maske—how soon, I say, he appears, if they have missed one jot of all their rites; or if any of their feet once fly over the circle, through terror of his fearfull apparition, he pales himself at that time, in his owne hand, of that due debt which they ought him; and otherwise would have delayed longer to have paid him: I mean, he carries them with him, body and soule." How the conjurors made triangular or quadrangular circles, his majesty has not informed us, nor does he seem to imagine there was any difficulty in the matter. We are therefore led to suppose, that he learned his mathematics from the same system as Dr Sacheverell, who, in one of his speeches or sermons, made use of the following simile: "They concur like parallel lines, meeting in one common centre." Another mode of consulting spirits was by the beryl, by means of a spectator or seer; who, to have a complete sight, ought to be a pure virgin, a youth who had not known woman, or at least a person of irreproachable life and purity of manners. The method of such consultation is this: The conjuror having repeated the necessary charms and adjurations, with the litany or invocation peculiar to the spirits or angels he wishes to call (for every one has his particular form), the seer looks into a crystal or beryl, wherein he will see the answer, represented either by types or figures; and sometimes, though very rarely, will hear the angels or spirits speak articulately. Their pronunciation is, as Lilly says, like the Irish, much in the throat. Lilly describes one of these beryls or crystals. It was, he says, as large as an orange, set in silver, with a cross at the top, and round about engraved the names of the angels Raphael, Gabriel, and Uriel. A delineation of another is engraved in the frontispiece to Aubery's Miscellanies. These sorcerers or magicians do not always employ their art to do mischief; but, on the contrary, frequently exert it to cure diseases inflicted by witches; to discover thieves; recover stolen goods; to foretell future events, and the fate of absent friends. On this account they are frequently called white witches. See Magic, Witchcraft, &c. Our forefathers were strong believers when they enacted, by statute 33 Hen. VIII. c. 8. all witchcraft and forcery to be felony without benefit of clergy; and again, by statute 1 Jac. I. c. 12. that all persons invoking any evil spirit, or consulting, covenanting with, entertaining, employing, feeding, or rewarding any evil spirit; or taking up dead bodies from their graves to be used in any witchcraft, forcery, charm, or enchantment; or killing or otherwise hurting any person by such infernal arts; should be guilty of felony without benefit of clergy, and suffer death. And if any person should attempt by forcery to discover hidden treasure, SORCERY or to restore stolen goods, or to provoke unlawful love, or to hurt any man or beast, though the same were not effected, he or she should suffer imprisonment and pillory for the first offence, and death for the second. These acts continued in force till lately, to the terror of all ancient females in the kingdom; and many poor wretches were sacrificed thereby to the prejudice of their neighbours and their own illusions, not a few having by some means or other confessed the fact at the gallows. But all executions for this dubious crime are now at an end; our legislature having at length followed the wise example of Louis XIV. in France, who thought proper by an edict to restrain the tribunals of justice from receiving informations of witchcraft. And accordingly it is with us enacted, by statute 9 Geo. II. c. 5, that no prosecution shall for the future be carried on against any person for conjuration, witchcraft, sorcery, or enchantment: But the misdemeanor of persons pretending to use witchcraft, tell fortunes, or discover stolen goods, by skill in the occult sciences, is still deservedly punished with a year's imprisonment, and standing four times in the pillory.

SOREX

Pages 81-81

the SHREW, a genus of animals belonging to the class of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, and order of ferae. See MAMMALIA <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SORITES

Pages 81-81

in Logic, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of reasoning in which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> are so linked together, that the predicate of the one becomes continually the subject of the next following, till at last a conclusion is formed by bringing together the subject of the first proposition and the predicate of the last. Such was that merry argument of Themistocles, to prove that his little son under ten years old governed the whole world. Thus: My son governs his mother; his mother me; I the Athenians; the Athenians the Greeks; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> commands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; Europe the whole world; therefore my son commands the whole world. See LOGIC, No. 96, 97.

SORREL

Pages 81-81

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the rumex, which grows in pastures and meadows, and is well known. The natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> boil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of the leaves in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and mix the juice when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of their rein-deer, which they esteem an agreeable and wholesome food. The Dutch are said to cultivate this plant for its usefulness in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> of woollen cloths <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; and we know that by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-leaved sorrel an excellent black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is, in many places of Scotland, given to woollen stuffs without the aid of copperas. As this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of dyeing does not in the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> injure the texture of the cloth, which continues to the last soft and silky, without that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> to the touch which it acquires when dyed black by means of copperas, our readers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably thank us for the following receipt, with which we have been favoured by a learned physician: Let the stuff to be dyed be well washed with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and water, and afterwards completely dried. Then of the common broad-leaved sorrel boil as much as shall make an acid decoction of sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> to let the stuff to be dyed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in it open and easy to be stirred. The greater quantity of sorrel that is used, the better will the colour be; and therefore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the pot <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cauldron will not hold enough at once, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> has been sufficiently boiled, it must be taken out and wrung, and a fresh quantity be boiled in the same juice or decoction. When the liquor is made sufficiently acid, strain it from the sorrel through a sieve, put the cloth or yarn into it, and let it boil for two hours, stirring it frequently. If stockings be among the stuff to be dyed, it will be expedient, after they have been an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> liquor, to turn them inside out, and at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hour let the whole be poured into a tub or any other vessel. The pot or cauldron must then be washed, and water put into it, with half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of logwood chips for every pound of dry yarn or cloth. The logwood and water should boil slowly for four hours; and then the cloth or yarn being wrung from the four liquor, and put into the logwood decoction, the whole must be suffered to boil slowly for four hours, stockings, if there be any, being turned inside out at the end of two hours. Of this last decoction there must, as of the former, be enough to let the cloth lie open and easy to be stirred while boiling. At the end of the four hours the cloth must be taken out, and among the boiling liquor, first removed from the fire, must be poured a Scotch pint or half an English gallon of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> urine for every pound of dry cloth or other stuff to be dyed. When this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> liquor has been stirred and become cold, the cloth must be put into it and suffered to remain well covered for 12 hours, and then dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; after which, to divest it of smell or any other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>, it may be washed in cold water, and dried for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Wood-SORREL. See OXALIS, BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SORREL-Colour, in the manege, is a reddish colour, generally thought to be a sign of a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>.

SORRENTO

Pages 81-81

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, with an archbishop's see. It is seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Naples, at the foot of a mountain of the same name, 17 miles south-east of Naples. It is the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Torquato Tasso. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 24'. N. Lat. 40° 36'.

SORTILEGE

Pages 81-82

(Sortilegium) a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a> performed by means of fates <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lots. The fates Pronoeia, famous in antiquity, consisted in putting a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of letters, or even whole words, into an urn; and then, after shaking them together, they were thrown on the ground; and whatever sentences could be made out from them, constituted the answer of the oracle. To this method of divination succeeded that which has been called the fates Homeriaca and fates Virgiliaca, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of inquiring into futurity, which undoubtedly took its rise from a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the oracular priests of delivering their answers in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; it subsisted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and being from them adopted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, it was not till after a long succession of centuries that it became exploded. Among the Romans it consisted in opening some celebrated poet at random, and among the Christians the Scriptures, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, from the first passage which presented itself to the eye, a prognostic of what would befall one's self or others, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> for conduct when under any exigency. There is good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that this was none of the vulgar errors; the greatest persons, philosophers of the best repute, admitted this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, when in prison, hearing this line of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Within three days I Phthia's shore shall see, immediately said, within three days I shall be out of the world; world; gathering it from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> meaning of the word Phthia, which in Greek is both the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and signifies corruption or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This prediction, addressed to Ælchines, was not easily forgotten, as it was verified. When this superstition passed from Paganism into Christianity, the Christians had two methods of consulting the divine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> from the Scriptures; the one, casually, to open the divine writings, and take their direction, as above mentioned; the other, to go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with a purpose of receiving, as a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the will of heaven, the words of the Scripture, which were singing at the instant of one's entrance. This unwarrantable practice of inquiring into futurity prevailed very generally in England till the beginning of the 18th century; and sometimes the books of Scripture, and sometimes the poems of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, were consulted for oracular responses. One remarkable instance is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I, who being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> during the civil wars, went one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to see the public library, where he was shown, among other books, a Virgil nobly printed and exquisitely bound. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKLAND">Falkland</a>, to divert the king, would have his majesty make a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of his fortune by the Sortes Virgilianae. Whereupon the king opening the book, the passage which happened to come up was this: *At, bello audacis populi vexatus et armis, Finibus extorris, complexu avulsius Iuli, Auxilium implorat; videtque indigna fiorum Funera: nec, cum se sub liges patres inique Tradiderat, regno aut optata luce fruatur; Sed cadat ante diem, mediaque inhumerato arena.* Eneid, lib. iv. Yet let a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, untamed and haughty foes, His peaceful entrance with dire arms oppose; Oppressed with numbers in the unequal field, His men discouraged, and himself expelled, Let him for succour sue from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, Torn from his subjects, and his son's embrace: First let him see his friends in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> slain, And their untimely fate lament in vain; And when at length the cruel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> shall cease, On hard conditions may he buy his peace. Nor let him then enjoy supreme command, But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> untimely by some hostile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> unburied on the barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Lord Falkland observing that the king was concerned at this accident, would likewise try his own fortune in the same manner, hoping he might fall upon some passage that would have no relation to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and thereby divert the king's thoughts from any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> which the other might have upon him; but the place he stumbled upon was as much suited to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> as the other had been to the king's; being the lamentation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a> for the untimely death of his son Palas*: for this lord's eldest son, a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an amiable character, had been slain in the first battle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWBURY">Newbury</a>. We have ourselves known several whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> has not always been regulated by judgement pursue this method of divination; and have generally observed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> has been despair or presumption. To such we beg leave to recommend one passage in Scripture which will never disappoint them: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.

SOTERIA

Pages 82-82

in antiquity, sacrifices offered to the gods for delivering a person from danger; as also poetical pieces composed for the same purpose.

SOUBISE

Pages 82-82

a town of France, in the department of Lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARENTE">Charente</a>, and late territory of Saintonge. It is situated on the river Charente, 22 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 2'. N. Lat. 45° 57'.

SOUDAN

Pages 82-82

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, situated between 11° and 16° N. Lat. and 26° and 30° E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. See Dar Fur.

SOUFFRIERE

Pages 82-83

a small town, situated at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, near the leeward extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Lucia. Of itself it is not entitled to much notice, but the adjacent ground is very remarkable. The declivities of the surrounding hills are cultivated, and afford <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a> of a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. The extremity of the south side of Souffriere bay runs into two steep hills of a conical shape, and nearly perpendicular, reckoned the highest on the island, and known by the appellation of the Sugar-Loaf Hills. It is impossible to ascend them; for although it was once attempted by two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, it is said that they never returned. Paffing the hills to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> of Souffriere, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> presents itself, extending from 15 to 20 miles from the back of the Sugar-Loaf Hills along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, being wholly cultivated, and divided into rich estates. It is intersected by numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of very clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which, by art, are made subservient to the purpose of sugar-making. The rains here are less frequent than on any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the sea, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> nearly so. There is a volcano in the vicinity of this town. After passing one or two small hills, the smell of sulphur is sensibly felt before any vestige of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is perceived. The first thing discerned is a rivulet of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> running water, feeding forth streams nearly in a state of ebullition, from which the volcano soon comes into view, situated Souffriere situated in a hollow, and surrounded by hills on every side. There are many pits in the hollow, of a black and thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which appears to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">Lava</a> is ejected by flow degrees, and there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of it in the centre of the hollow, forming a fort of hill. The lava is said to be a sulphur mixed with calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and some saline body. Small quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> have been found in a perfect state; and there is a rivulet of good water in the opening, at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the hollow. When the bottom of it is stirred, the water is very hot, so much so as not to be touched. The liquid running from the pits is strongly impregnated with sulphur, and very much resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> sold in the shops, called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> sulphura.

SOUGH

Pages 82-82

among miners, denotes a passage dug underground, to convey off waters from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. See Mine.

SOUL

Pages 83-83

the principle of perception, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, intelligence, and volition, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; which, since the earliest era of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, has furnished questions of difficult <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, and materials of keen and important controversy (see <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> III, chap. ii. iii. iv. v.; and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">Resurrection</a>, No. 42—48.). In the fourth volume of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Literary and Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a very valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> by Dr Ferriar, proving, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> apparently complete, that every part of the brain has been injured without affecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of thought. An abridgement of that memoir would weaken its reasoning; which, built on matters of fact and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, appears to us to have shaken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATERIALISTS">Materialists</a> from its very foundation. Soul of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">Brutes</a>. See Brutes.

SOUND

Pages 83-83

in Physics, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which expresses a simple idea; it is that primary information which we obtain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> things by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of hearing. See Acoustics. Sound, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, denotes in general any strait <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inlet of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> between two headlands. It is given by way of eminence to the strait between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, joining the German ocean to the Baltic, being about three miles over. See Denmark, No. 32, and Elsinore. SOUND-Board, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an organ, and that which makes the whole machine play. It is a reservoir into which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, drawn in by the bellows, is conducted by a port-vent, and thence distributed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> placed over the holes of its upper part. The wind enters them by valves, which open by pressing on the keys, after the registers are drawn, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is prevented from going into any of the other pipes, besides those in which it is required.

SOUND-BOARD ALSO

Pages 83-83

d also denotes a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> board placed over the head of a public speaker, to enlarge <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> extend and strengthen his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>-boards are found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to be of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, as their distance from the speaker is too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> to be impressed with sufficient force. But sound-boards over a pulpit have frequently a good effect, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is constructed of a proper thickness, and according to particular principles. SOUND-Port, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> placed in the inside of a violin, &c., as a prop between the back and belly of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, and nearly under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>.

SOUNDING

Pages 83-85

the operation of trying the depth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the bottom, by means of a plummet sunk from a ship to the bottom. There are two plummets used for this purpose in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; one of which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, weighing about 8 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 9 pounds; and the other the deep-sea lead, which weighs from 25 to 30 pounds; and both are shaped like the frustum of a cone or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. The former is used in shallow waters, and the latter at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from the shore; particularly on approaching the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> after a sea-voyage. Accordingly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> employed for this purpose are called the deep-sea lead-line, and the hand lead-line. The hand lead-line, which is usually 20 fathoms in length, is marked at every two or three fathoms; so that the depth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> may be ascertained either in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night. At the depth of two and three fathoms, there are marks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; at 5 fathoms, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rag; at 7, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> rag; at 10, black leather; at 13, black leather; at 15, a white rag; and at 17, a red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">ditto</a>. Sounding with the hand lead, which is called heaving the lead by leamen, is generally performed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who stands in the main-chains to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a>. Having the line quite ready to run out without interruption, he holds it nearly at the distance of a fathom from the plummet; and having swung the latter backwards and forwards three or four times, in order to acquire the greater velocity, he swings it round his head, and thence as far forward as is necessary; so that, by the lead's sinking whilst the ship advances, the line may be almost perpendicular when it reaches the bottom. The person sounding then proclaims the depth of the water in a kind of song resembling the cries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAWKERS">hawkers</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the mark of five fathoms is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the surface of the water, he calls, 'By the mark five!' and as there is no mark at four, six, eight, &c., he estimates those numbers, and calls, 'By the dip four,' &c. If he judges it to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> or an half more than any particular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, he calls, 'And a quarter five! and a half four,' &c. If he conceives the depth to be three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> more than a particular number, he calls it a quarter less than the next; thus, at four fathoms and three fourths he calls 'A quarter less five!' and so on. The deep sea lead is marked with two knots at 20 fathoms, three at 30, four at 40, and so on to the end. It is also marked with a single knot in the middle of each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, as at 25, 35, 45 fathoms, &c. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this lead more effectually at sea, or in deep water on the sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, it is usual previously to bring to the ship, in order to retard her course: the lead is then thrown as far as possible from the ship on the line of her drift, so that, as it sinks, the ship drives more perpendicularly over it. The pilot, feeling the lead strike the bottom, readily discovers the depth of the water by the mark on the line nearest its surface. The bottom of the lead being also well rubbed over with tallow, retains the distinguishing marks of the bottom, as shells, ooze, gravel, &c., which naturally adhere to it. The depth of the water, and the nature of the ground, which is called the soundings, are carefully marked in the log-book, as well to determine the distance of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from the shore, as to correct the observations of former pilots. A machine for the same purpose has been invented by Mr Massey, of which the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is given: "The importance of obtaining true soundings at sea must Sounding be admitted by every seaman; and it is rather singular, that no other method than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> lead has hitherto been brought into use; as its imperfections are very generally acknowledged. "Many vessels have been lost, by depending upon the soundings taken in the usual way. The difficulty of obtaining the true perpendicular, and the uncertainty as to the exact moment when the lead strikes the bottom, upon which the accuracy of the result depends, must always prevent the possibility of obtaining the true depth, while the ship has any considerable way upon her. Indeed, it has been acknowledged by experienced seamen, during some experiments, made at various times, in the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, that they could not depend upon the common lead, when going five or six knots in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, in ten or twelve fathoms of water. When the depth is considerable, the vessel must be hove to, which is an operation attended with great loss of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and sometimes considerable injury to the sails; and during a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, this inconvenience must be particularly felt. "True soundings may be taken with this machine in thirty fathoms water, without the trouble of heaving the vessel to, although she may be going at the rate of six miles in the hour. True soundings may also thus be obtained in very deep water, where it is not possible to take them by the common lead. "Fig. 1. represents the sounding machine. \(a\) is the founding <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, \(i\), \(2\), with two dials: the hand of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">dial</a> \(i\) makes one revolution when the weight has descended twenty fathoms, the other revolves once when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> amounts to five hundred fathoms. A rotator, \(b\), similar to that attached to the log, communicates with the wheel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the dials \(i\), \(2\), by means of the rod \(c\), on which there are three universal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, \(3\), \(4\), and \(5\). This rod is supported during the descent of the weight, by the drop, \(d\), at the end of which is a fork, \(6\), and a friction wheel, \(7\). "When the machine is to be used, a founding line is fastened to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, \(e\); and one of the vanes of the rotator is slipped into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> \(8\); the rotator <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> then be in the position indicated by the dotted lines, \(x\). The indices must be set at \(o\), and the cover or lid, \(f\), be shut. The machine must then be projected perpendicularly into the sea. As soon as it reaches the surface, the resistance of the water forces the dotted rotator, \(x\), out of the spring \(8\), and it assumes its perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> as represented by the rotator \(b\). As the machine descends, it is evident the rotator will revolve, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> be communicated freely past the friction wheel \(7\), and the universal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> \(5\), to the wheel work of the dials \(i\), \(2\), and thus indicate the space passed through in fathoms. When the machine has arrived at the bottom, the rotator, as it is no longer buoyed up by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> of the water, will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the bottom, quitting the fork of the drop \(d\), which will also fall from its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, and in its descent, by means of the locking rod \(9\), prevent the rotator from revolving as the machine is drawn up. When at the bottom, the rotator will be in the position of the dotted lines \(y\). "This machine, simple in its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and scarcely more liable to accident than the common lead, ascertains, with the utmost precision, the perpendicular depth, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of descent through the water. No mistake can arise from that common source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, the drift or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-way of the ship during the time of descent; nor does an operation of such importance depend upon Sounding, the uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> caused by the lead striking the bottom, on which the accuracy of the common log altogether depends, and which, it is well known, frequently and materially misleads the best seaman: for though a thousand fathoms of line were paid out, in the smallest depth of water, no inaccuracy could arise, as the perpendicular depth, at the point of heaving, would be registered on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>. The only inconvenience experienced would be the additional labour necessary for hauling in the excess of line. The most inexperienced person may use this machine, without risk of error, in the most turbulent sea, and during the night. "The advantages already enumerated would render the founding machine of great importance; but there are other properties of still more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. "To heave a ship to, in order to obtain soundings, on a lee shore, in stormy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, is a very disagreeable operation, attended with much trouble, and loss of way; also with considerable danger to the ship's sails; indeed, it would often, under such circumstances, be attended with great hazard to the safety of the ship. To avoid these unpleasant consequences, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> sometimes adopts a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, which he conceives to be the least exceptionable alternative, by running on without founding at all. "To prove how much inconvenience and danger are avoided by Maffey's lead, it is enough to state, that soundings may be taken in depth from 60 to 80 fathoms, while the ship is under way, at the rate of three miles an hour; and as the rate of falling may be still materially reduced, without entirely stopping the vessel, or altering her course, so may soundings be had, to any depth required, while she is under way. "In order more clearly to show the superiority of this machine, and make it apparent, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of stray-line veered out does not at all affect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of the result: suppose the common lead thrown from the mizen chains of the ship, which may be represented by the point \(a\) of the triangle \(abc\) (fig. 2.), and that the ship Fig. 2. has moved forwards through the space equal to the line \(bc\), while the lead has descended through the line \(ac\); it is evident, that it is impossible, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, to ascertain the exact depth, as a quantity of line, equal to \(<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a>\), would be paid out, whereas the true depth is equal only to the line \(ac\), which is much less. But the case is very different when the patent founding machine is used, as the operation ceases when it has reached the bottom; nor is the stray-line, \(ab\), whatever its length, at all taken into the account. "It has been extremely difficult, and sometimes impossible, to obtain soundings in very deep water with the common lead, which may perhaps be thus accounted for. The common line which is used for founding, though, if left to itself, it would sink in water, yet its descent would be much slower than that of the lead, separately; it consequently follows, that the lead must be so much impeded by carrying the line with it, that when it does reach the bottom, there will be scarcely any sensible check to enable the seaman to know the precise moment. Indeed, if he can ascertain even this to a certainty, he still cannot depend upon the truth of his soundings; for if there be the least drift or current, the line itself will assume a curve, similar to that of the line of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KITE">kite</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. These two causes will always operate..." After so fully describing the principle of the patent founding machine, it is scarcely necessary to prove, that it is liable to neither of the foregoing objections; and it may be sufficient to say, that, as it will certainly find its way to the bottom, if a sufficient portion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-line be allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against its being checked in its progress, and the certainty of its having reached the bottom may be ascertained by the arming, there can be no doubt of the practicability of its obtaining foundings, in any depth, and no reasonable doubt of their correctness when obtained. From the construction of this machine, it might be imagined, that the rotator would impede its motion through the water, and that it could not descend so rapidly as the common lead; but during repeated trials, in thirteen fathoms water, in which the rotator was frequently detached, and the lead suffered to descend alone, there was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> perceptible in the time of their descent, though an excellent quarter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> stop watch was used during the experiment, to detect any change. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> shows how very uniformly the times of descent corresponded with the depths in fathoms, during a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of trials made on the river Mersey, with the patent lead, weighing 14 pounds. The manner of conducting these experiments was such as is deserving of perfect reliance. Two pilots, of well-known ability and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, were employed: one threw the lead, and the other, the moment he found, by the slackening of the rope, that the weight had arrived at the bottom, cried 'stop,' to a third person who held the watch. | Time of descent | Fathoms | |----------------|---------| | 2 seconds | 2 1/2 | | 2 1/2 | 3 | | 3 | 4 | | 5 | 8 | | 5 1/2 | 8 1/2 | | 6 | 10 | | 6 | 10 | | 7 | 11 1/2 | Taken when under sail, at upwards of five knots in the hour. Several captains and masters in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> have made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the log and founding machine, and given very favourable reports of their performance; and it has been adopted by order of the Navy Board in the British navy.*

SOUP

Pages 85-85

a strong decoction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other substances. Portable or dry soup is a kind of cake formed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the gelatinous parts of animal substances till the watery parts are evaporated. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of soup is chiefly used at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and has been found of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage. The following receipt <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> show how it is prepared. Of calves feet take 4; leg of beef 12 lbs.; knuckle of veal 3 lbs.; and leg of mutton 10 lbs. These are to be boiled in a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the scum taken off as usual; after which the soup is to be separated from the meat by straining and pressure. The meat is then to be boiled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in other water; and the two decoctions, being added together, must be left to cool, in order that the fat may be exactly separated. The soup must then be clarified with five or six whites of eggs, and a sufficient quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> added. The liquor is then strained through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, and evaporated on the water-bath to the consistence of a very thick paste; after which it is spread rather thin upon a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, then cut into cakes, and lastly dried in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">stove</a> until it becomes brittle; these cakes are kept in well closed bottles. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> may be used to make a portable soup of the flesh of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>; and aromatic herbs may be used as a seasoning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> thought proper. These tablets or cakes may be kept four or five years. When intended to be used, the quantity of half an ounce is put into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> glass of boiling water, which is to be covered, and set upon hot ashes for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, or until the whole is entirely dissolved. It forms an excellent soup, and requires no addition but a small quantity of salt. SOUR-CROUTE. See CROUTE. SOUR-Gourd, or African Calabash-tree. See ADANSONIA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOUTH

Pages 86-86

one of the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> from which the winds blow. SOUTH <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a>, is that vast body of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> interposed between <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It does not, however, strictly speaking, reach quite to the continent of Asia, excepting to the northward of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>: for the water interposed between the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and the peninsula <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned has the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean. The South sea then is bounded on one side by the western coast of America, through its whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, from the unknown regions in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to the straits of Magellan and Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a>, where it communicates with the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Atlantic. On the other side, it is bounded by the coast of Asia, from the northern promontory of Tchukotkoi Nefs, to the peninsula of Malacca already mentioned.
