Thence it is bounded to the southward by the northern coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORNEO">Borneo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACASSAR">Macassar</a>, New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, which divide it from the Indian ocean. Then, wathing the eastern coast of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of New Holland, it communicates with that vast body of water encompassing the whole southern part of the globe, and which has the general name of the Southern ocean all round. Thus does this vast ocean occupy almost the semicircumference of the globe, extending almost from one pole to the other, and about the equatorial parts extending almost $180^\circ$ in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, or $12,500$ of our miles. The northern parts of the Pacific ocean are entirely destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; not a single island having yet been discovered in it from the latitude of $40^\circ$ north and upwards, excepting such as are very near the coast either of Asia or America; but in the southern part there are a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Till very lately the South sea was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> unknown. From the great extent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> which covers the southern part of the globe, it was imagined that much more land existed there than in the northern regions: but that this could not be justified merely from that circumstance, is plain from what has been advanced under the article AMERICA, No 3—24; and the southern continent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> known by the name of Terra Australis, has eluded the search of the most expert navigators sent out from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and France by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> authority. See TERRA AUSTRALIS. SOUTH Sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>. See COMPANY.

SOUTHAMPTON

Pages 86-86

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> in England. It is commodiously seated on an arm of the sea; is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of good trade, and well inhabited. It is surrounded by walls and several watch-towers, and had a strong castle to defend the harbour, now in ruins. It is a corporation and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of an earldom, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 26. N. Lat. 50. 55.

SOUTHERN

Pages 86-86

Thomas, an eminent dramatic writer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> in 1660, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the university there. He came young to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but instead of that devoted himself to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of plays. His Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Loyal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">Brother</a>, was introduced in 1682, when the Tory <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> was triumphant in England; and the character of the Loyal Brother being intended to compliment James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, he rewarded the author when he came to the throne with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. On the Revolution taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he retired to his studies, and wrote several plays, from which he is supposed to have derived a very handsome subsistence, being the first who raised the advantage of play-writing to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third night. The most finished of all his plays is Oroonoko, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Slave, which is built on a true story related in one of Mrs Behn's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOVELS">novels</a>. Mr Southern died in 1746, in the 86th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which he spent in a peaceful serenity, having, by his commission as a soldier, and the profits of his dramatic works, acquired a handsome fortune; and being an exact economist, he improved what fortune he gained to the best advantage. He enjoyed the longest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of all our poets; and died the richest of them, a very few excepted. His plays are printed in two vols 12mo. SOUTHERN Continent. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">AMERICA</a>, No 3—24, and TERRA AUSTRALIS. SOUTHERNWOOD. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">ARTEMISIA</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SOUTHWARK

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, and a suburb of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, being separated from that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> only by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. See LONDON, No 96. SOW. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUS">SUS</a>, MAMMALLA <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Sow, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> works, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lump of metal they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at once in the iron <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. SOVEREIGN

Pages 82-82

in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, is applied to the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> magistrates of an independent government or state; because their authority is only bounded by the laws of God and the laws of the state; such are kings, princes, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">Prerogative</a>, &c. SOVEREIGN Power, or Sovereignty, is the power of making laws; for wherever that power resides, all others must conform to it, and be directed by it, whatever appearance the outward form and administration of the government may put on. For it is at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the option of the legislature to alter that form and administration by a new edict or rule, and to put the execution of the laws into whatever <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it pleases: and all the other powers of the state must obey the legislative power in the execution of their several functions, or else the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> is at an end. In our constitution the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> ascribes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> of sovereignty: but that is to be understood in a qualified <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, i.e. as supreme magistrate, not as sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>; as the legislative power is vested in the king, lords, and commons, not in any of the three estates alone. SOU. See Sol.

SOWING

Pages 86-86

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the depositing any kind of seed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> for a future crop. See AGRICULTURE. Drill-Sowing. See DRILL-Sowing. SOY. See DOLICHOS.

SOZOMENUS

Pages 86-86

Hermias, an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> historian of the 5th century, was born in Bethelia, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. He was educated for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and became a pleader at Constantinople. He wrote an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">Abridgment</a> of Ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, in two books, from the ascension of our Saviour to the year 323. This compendium is lost; but a continuation of it in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> books, written at greater length, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the year 440, is still extant. He seems to have copied <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, who wrote a history of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The style of Sozomenus is perhaps more elegant; but in other respects he falls far short of that writer, displaying throughout his whole book an amazing credulity and a superstitious <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to monks and the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The best edition of Sozomenus is that of Robert Stephen in 1544. He has been translated and published by Valerius, and republished with additional notes by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1720, in 3 vols folio.

SPA

Pages 86-155

a town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia and bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, famous for its mineral waters, lies in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 50. N. Lat. 50. 30. about 21 miles south-east from Liege, and 7 south-west from Lomburg. It is situated at one end of a deep valley on the banks of a small rivulet, and is surrounded on all sides by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The sides of these mountains next to Spa are rude and uncultivated, presenting a rugged appearance as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> shattered by the convulsions of earthquakes; but as they are strewed with tall oaks and abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> around forms a wild, romantic, and beautiful landscape. The access to the town town is very beautiful. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> winds over the mountains till it descends to their bottom, when it runs along a smooth valley for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a mile and a half. The town consists of four streets in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, and contains about 400 inhabitants. Spa has no wealth to boast of. It can scarcely furnish the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to its own inhabitants during the winter, and almost all the luxuries which are requisite for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> concourse of affluent visitors during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> are carried from Liege by women. Its only source of wealth is its mineral waters. No sooner does the warm season commence, than crowds of valetudinarians arrive, as well as many other persons who are attracted solely by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of amusement, and some from less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> motives. The inhabitants, who spend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight months of the year without seeing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a stranger, wait for the return of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> with impatience. The welcome found of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> brings multitudes from the town, either to gratify their curiosity, or to offer their services in the hopes of securing your employment while you remain at Spa. Immediately after your arrival, your name and designation is added to the printed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the annual visitors; for which you pay a stated sum to the bookellers, who has a patent for this purpose from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> bishop of Liege. This list not only enables one to know at a glance whether any friends or acquaintance are residing there, but also to distinguish persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and fashion from adventurers, who seldom have the effrontery to insert their names. There are two different ways of accommodating the visitors at Spa with lodging and necessaries. People may either lodge at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a>, where everything is furnished them in a splendid and expensive style; or they may take up their residence in private lodgings, from which they may send for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> to a cook's shop. Among the people who visit Spa, there are many persons of the first rank and fashion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Perhaps indeed there is no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Europe to which so many kings and princes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>; but it is also visited by many self-created <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, who, under the titles of counts, barons, marquises, and knights, contrive by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, and artifices, to prey upon the rich and inexperienced. The manners established at Spa are conducive both to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and amusement. Every body rises early in the morning, at six o'clock or before it, when a great many horses stand ready saddled for those who choose to drink the Sauveniere or Geronfere waters at a little distance from Spa. After this healthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> generally breakfast together at Vauxhall, a magnificent and spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. At this place a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of card-tables are opened every forenoon, round which many persons assemble and play for stakes to a very considerable amount. A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> too is generally held once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> at Vauxhall, besides two balls at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> rooms near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTON">Poulton</a> in the middle of the town. The most remarkable waters at Spa are, 1. The Poulton, situated in the middle of the town; 2. The Sauveniere, a mile and a half east from it; 3. Groifbeck, near to the Sauveniere; 4. Tonnelet, situated a little to the left of the road which leads to the Sauveniere; 5. Geronfere, two miles south from Spa; 6. Warroz, near to the Tonnelet; 7. Sarts or Nivelet, in the district of Sarts; 8. Chevron or Bru, in the principality of Slavellot; 9. Couve; 10. Beverfe; 11. Sige; 12. Geremont. These four last are near Malmedy. Dr Brownrigg was the first person who discovered that fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or, as it is now generally called, carbonic acid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the Spa waters, and actually separated a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> fluid, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> it to different degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> from 110° to 170° of Fahrenheit. From 20 ounces 7 drams and 14 grains apothecaries <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the Poulton <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, he obtained 8 ounces 2 drams and 50 grains. Since <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1765, when Dr Brownrigg read a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on this subject before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, the waters of Spa have been often analysed, but perhaps by none with more accuracy than by Dr Ash, who published a book on the chemical and medicinal properties of these waters in 1788. We shall present the result of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of the five principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. | Fountains | Quantity of Water | Ounces of Gas | <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">Solid</a> contents | Aerated Lime | Aerated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a> | Aerated Mineral Alkali | Aerated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> | Aerated Selenite | Aerated Vegetah | Aerated Alkali | |-----------|------------------|---------------|----------------|--------------|-----------------|------------------------|-------------|----------------|---------------|---------------| | Pouhon | 33 | 35.75 | 16.25 | 2.75 | 9.50 | 2.25 | 1.75 | | | | | Geronfere | 32.75 | 24.75 | 5.50 | 2.50 | 1.75 | 0.75 | 0.50 | | | | | Sauveniere| 32.50 | 33.50 | 3.75 | 1.50 | 0.75 | 0.50 | 1 | | | | | Groifbeck | 32.25 | 35.50 | 5.25 | 1.50 | 1 | 0.75 | | | | | | Tonnelet | 32 | 40.75 | 2.00 | 0.25 | 0.75 | 1 | | | | | The Pouhon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> rises from the hill to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Spa, which consists of argillaceous schistus and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> slate. The other fountains rise from the surrounding hills to the south-east, south-west, and north-west of the town; and this ridge of mountains is formed of calcareous earths mixed with siliceous substances. The surface of the mountains is covered with woods, interspersed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> boggy swamps filled with mud and water. The Pouhon is considered as the principal spring at Spa, being impregnated with a greater quantity of iron than any of the rest, and containing more fixed air than any except the Tonnelet. It is from this spring that the Spa water for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> is bottled; for which the demand is so great, that, according to the best information which Mr Thickneffe could obtain, the quantity exported amounts to 200,000 or 250,000 bottles annually. This exported water is inferior in its virtue to that which is drunk on the spot; for the evil effects into which it is collected are injudiciously exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and dust, for several hours before they are corked, by which means a considerable part of its volatile ingredients must be evaporated; for it has been found by experiment, that by exposing it to a gentle heat, air-bubbles ascend in great numbers. It is in its greatest perfection when collected in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; it is then pellucid, colourless, and without smell, and almost as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> as distilled water. It varies in its heat from $52^\circ$ or $53^\circ$ to $67^\circ$ of Fahrenheit's thermometer. The Géronfère is a much weaker chalybeate water than the Pouhon; and as it is exceedingly nauseous, and tastes and smells like rotten eggs, it certainly contains some hepatic gas. This is a circumstance which Dr Ash seems not to have attended sufficiently. The Sauvemiere water also, when newly taken from the well, smells a little of sulphur. The Groiibek contains more alkali, and almost as much gas as the Pouhon, and has been celebrated for its good effects in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of calculous concretions. The Tonnelet contains more gas than any of the rest. So small is the quantity of any fossil body held in suspension by the aerial acid in it, and so volatile is the gas, that it begins to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> off very rapidly the moment it is taken out of the well, and in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> is entirely gone. Dr Ash informs us, that in the neighbourhood of this well, the cellars, on any approaching change of weather, are found to contain much fixed air; and the best prognostic which they have of rain is the aversion which cats show to be carried into these cellars. The Spa waters are diuretic, and sometimes purgative. They exhilarate the spirits with an influence much more benign than wine or spirituous liquors, and they are more cooling, and allay thirst more effectually than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> water. They are found beneficial in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of weakness and relaxation, either partial or universal; in nervous disorders; in obstructions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> and spleen; in cases where the blood is too thin and putrefied; in cases of excessive discharges proceeding from weakness; in the gravel and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and in most cases where a strengthening remedy is wanted. But they are hurtful in confirmed obstructions attended with fever, where there is no free outlet to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as in ulcerations of the lungs. They are also injurious to bilious and plethoric constitutions, when used before the body is cooled by proper evacuations. **SPACE.** See **<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>**, Part II. Chap. iv. **SPACE,** in **<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>,** denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, or that which fills the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> or distance between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> that terminate it. **SPADIX,** in **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>,** anciently signified the receptacle of the palms. It is now used to express every flower-stalk that is protruded out of a spathe or sheath. The spadix of the palms is branched; that of all other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> simple. This last case admits of some variety; in *canna*, *dracontium*, and *póthos*, the florets cover it on all sides; in *arum*, they are disposed on the lower part only; and in *zephyra* on one side. See **BOTANY**. **SPAGIRIC ART,** a name given by old authors to that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> which works on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and is employed in the search of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s stone. **SPAHSIS,** horsemen in the Ottoman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, chiefly raised in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. The great strength of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> seignior's army consists in the janissaries, who are the foot, and the spahis, who are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">SPAIN</a>.** The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Spain, which occupies by situation far the greater portion of the south-western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Europe, is bounded on the north by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a> and Pyrenean mountains, which separate it from France; on the east by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the south by the straits of Gibraltar, which divide it from the African kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>; and on the west, partly by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, but chiefly by the narrow kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. This last is the only <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> boundary of the Spanish territory, and consists of ideal lines, except in three parts, where the river Minho to the north, and the Douro and the Chanza, till its junction with the Guadiana to the east, rather more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> limits. From <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Ortegal in N. Lat. $43^\circ 44'$, to the rock of Gibraltar, in N. Lat. $35^\circ 57'$, the continent of Spain extends through nearly $8^\circ$ of latitude, while its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from west to east, viz. from Cape <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a> in Long. $9^\circ 17'$ W. from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> to Cape Creus, or Croix, in Long. $3^\circ 30'$ E. from the same meridian, comprehends nearly $13^\circ$ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. In British miles, its length from north to south, viz. from Cape Penas to Gibraltar, may be estimated at $550$ miles, while its medium breadth may be computed at $440$. According to De Laborde, its superficial extent, exclusive of Portugal, is $25,137$ <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> French leagues, or about $21,000$ square English leagues. Besides the continental part of Spain, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> comprehends several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Mediterranean, especially <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a>, and Ibiza; the Canary islands, and several places on the north-western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; the Philippine and Ladrones islands; together with an immense territory both in North and South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, comprehending <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, or New Spain, New Mexico, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>, &c., in North America, and in the southern part of that continent, the greatest portion of Terra Firme, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, almost the whole of Paraguay, with an extensive territory lying on the banks of the river Plate. The usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Spanish continent is into fourteen provinces, viz. those of Catalonia, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, and Navarre, on the confines of France; Biscay, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, on the shores of the Atlantic; Leon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, on the side of Portugal; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> chiefly on the straits of Gibraltar; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, on the shores of the Mediterranean; Old and New Castile in the centre. The latest writer on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> of Spain, De Laborde, reckons only 13 provinces, as he includes Granada under Andalusia. In the following table we have brought together the most important circumstances respecting each of these provinces, viz. their subdivisions, extent in square British miles, <a class="xref" | Cabrera | | | | | Island of Minorca. | Iviza | 110 | 27,000 | | | | | 360 | | | Some account of these provinces <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Andalusia, Aragon, Asturias, Biscay, Castile, Catalonia, Estremadura, Galicia, Granada, Leon, Murcia, Navarre, Valencia, Iviza, Majorca and Minorca; but, for the best view of their present state, we must refer our readers to De Laborde's View of Spain, vols i. ii. and iii. or to Playfair's Geography, vol. i. In its general appearance, Spain presents a pleasing variety of hill and dale, mountain and valley. It must be regarded as a mountainous country, its plains being few in number and of small extent. The most remarkable of these occupies the centre of the kingdom, especially New Castile, which forms the most elevated tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> country to be found in Europe, having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> elevation of more than 300 fathoms above the level of the sea. The country is well wooded, and abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; but these are often very deficient in water, and... Spain, especially on its eastern coast, is remarkable for the dryness of its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. Notwithstanding this aridity, however, most parts of the kingdom teem with fertility, and native verdure and high cultivation render the scenery delightful. Here and there, indeed, occurs a tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> utterly incapable of cultivation; but, in general, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has done much more for the country than the labour of its inhabitants. The soil is said to be in general light, and easily wrought; but on many parts of the eastern coast it is composed chiefly of a stiff loam or clay. The most fertile parts of the kingdom are in Valencia, on the coast of Granada, in the kingdom of Old Castile, and in several parts of those of New Castile and Leon. The soil of Catalonia is very discouraging, except in the valleys, and the same may be said of all the provinces bordering on the Pyrenees; the soil of Extremadura, though naturally good, has been so long abandoned to itself, that it has almost ceased to produce, and that of Andalusia has a very mixed character. The soil of Murcia is uncommonly arid; that of the Asturias cold; that of Galicia extremely wet. In the neighbourhood of Cartagena there is an extensive tract, which is so covered with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> as to form a desert as sterile and untameable as any on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plains of Africa or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. We have said that Spain is a mountainous country. The chain of the Pyrenees, common to it and France, is by no means the most considerable in point either of elevation or extent; though that chain may be regarded as the common root or origin of all the rest. From the western corner of the Pyrenees a vast ridge branches off through Navarre, Biscay, Asturias, and Galicia, terminating only at Cape Finisterre, and Cape Ortegal. This ridge is the Cantabrian mountains, and is distinguished into several subordinate groups, denominated from the principal towns situated in their vicinity. Thus we have the mountains of Mondonedo in Galicia. In general, these groups are called Sierras, from the jagged or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a> appearance of their tops; as the Sierra de la Aflurias, Sierra d'Avala, &c. The subordinate mountains that extend from the Sierra of the Asturias in the north, to the Alpujaras in the south, run in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> lines; and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> prevails in the mountains of Saint Andero, which join the Pyrenees. From the mountains of Biscay arises a main ridge, which, after proceeding a little to the south, divides into three or four branches. Of these the most northerly chain separates the provinces of Old Castile and New Castile, extending to the confines of Portugal, and called the mountains of Guadarrama. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> branch divides the principal part of New Castile from the province of La Mancha, running from the north-east to the south-west, as far as Badajoz in Extremadura. The most remarkable part of this chain is the Sierra of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUADALUPE">Guadalupe</a>. South of these runs the Sierra Morena, or Sable mountains, rendered classical by the inimitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Cervantes. This is the last chain till we reach the Alpujaras, that extend through the provinces of Granada and Andalusia. Of these mountains there are two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which, in elevation, exceed Mont Perdu, the highest of the Pyrenees, viz., the Pico de Venleta, in the Sierra Nevada, or snowy mountains of Granada, which is elevated more than 1784 fathoms above the level of the ocean, and the peak of Mulahaten, in the same chain, raised above 1824 fathoms, which is within 76 fathoms of the peak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. The principal capes and promontories of the Spanish continent are, Cape Creus, Cape St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTOINE">Antoine</a>, opposite promontory the island of Ibiza; Cape Palas, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>; Cape de Gatte, near <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMERIA">Almeria</a>, and the promontory on which stands the town of Gibraltar, all on the coast of the Mediterranean; and Cape Machicaco, Cape Penas, Cape Ortegal, the promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERROL">Ferrol</a>, Cape Finisterre, and Cape Trafalgar, on the coasts of the Atlantic. The principal bays and gulfs on the coast of Spain, pursuing the same course, are the following; the bay gulfs of Valencia, the bay of Alicante, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Cartagena, the bay of Almeria, the bay of Gibraltar, the harbour of Cadiz, the bay of Corunna, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Groyne, and the bay of Biscay. The rivers of Spain are intimately connected with the Rivers, mountains from which they derive their source, and between the chains of which they generally flow. The most important are, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EBRO">Ebro</a>, rising in the mountains of Santillana in the Asturias, and running in a south-eastern direction between the Castiles and Valencia on the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the provinces of Navarre, Aragon, and Catalonia, on the other, till it reaches the Mediterranean, at a small distance from Tortola; the Xacar, rising in the Sierra of Cuenca in New Castile, and flowing into the Mediterranean considerably to the southward of Valencia; the Segura, rising in a mountain of the same name, traversing the province of Murcia, and meeting the Mediterranean about midway in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of that province, and Alicante. These flow into the Mediterranean, and there are several other rivers of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, which pour their waters into the same sea, and which we can merely enumerate. These are the Ter at Gerona, the Llobregate at Barcelona, and the Miñares, passing by Segorbe. The rivers which flow into the Atlantic are, the Guadalquivir, rising at the foot of Mount Segura, from the opposite side of which originates the river of the same name, flowing with a sluggish course through the province of Andalusia, and meeting the Atlantic a little to the north-west of Xeres; the Guadiana, rising among some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> to the north-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALCARAZ">Alcaraz</a> in New Castile, and passing between the Sierra Morena and the Sierra de Guadalupe, till, near Badajoz, it enters the kingdom of Portugal, and runs nearly in a southerly direction, till it meets the Atlantic at Ayamonte; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, rising among the mountains of Albaracin in New Castile, and running westerly till, at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCANTARA">Alcantara</a>, it becomes a river of Portugal; the Douro, rising in Old Castile near Soria, and passing by Valladolid and Zamora, near which it forms a part of the boundary of Portugal; the Minho, rising in the mountains of Galicia, and running to the south-west, till it meets the Atlantic to the north of Camina. The only other river of any importance in this direction is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>, supposed to be the Lethe of the poets, which rises in Galicia, and flows into the sea below Viara. If we except the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of small lakes from which we have said the river Guadiana takes its rise, there are, in Spain, few lakes that merit particular notice. The most remarkable of these is the lake of Abulfera, in the province of Valencia. This lake begins near the village of Catarroja, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> south of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Valencia, and extends nearly four leagues as far as Cullera. When Spain. It is full; it is about four leagues long, two in breadth, and five in circumference; but it is so shallow, that small boats can scarcely float in it. To supply the deficiency of water, an engine is employed, by which the neighboring waters are drawn into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the lake; and any superabundant water occasioned by heavy rains, is carried off into the sea by means of an artificial opening. This lake contains a great many fish, and numerous aquatic birds make it their haunt. On certain days in the year the inhabitants of Valencia make incursions hither to shoot the birds, and the surface of the lake is at these times covered with boats. Many parts of the kingdom of Spain abound in large tracts of wood. Extensive forests are found in Catalonia, the Asturias, Galicia, and in the Sierra Morena. It is in the mountainous chains that the forests of Spain are most remarkable; and there are few of these heights, except in the snowy regions of the Sierra Nevada, but what are covered with wood almost to their summits. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Spain is as delightful as that of any part of Europe; and though at certain seasons of the year the eastern coast is subject to excessive heat and drought, and the north-western to almost perpetual rains, the temperature is in general mild, and the air salubrious. The climate of Spain has been admirably depicted by M. A. de Humboldt; and we shall here present to our readers the substance of his remarks, as they are related by De Laborde, in his view of Spain. No country of Europe presents a configuration so singular as Spain. It is this extraordinary form which accounts for the dryness of the soil in the interior of the Castiles, for the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, the want of rivers, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of temperature which is observable between Madrid and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, two towns situated under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude. The interior of Spain is, as we have seen, an elevated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, which is higher than any of the same kind in Europe, occupying a large extent of country. The mean height of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> at Madrid is 26 inches 2½ lines. It is therefore 1½ lower than the mean height of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> at the level of the ocean. This is the difference of the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> that is experienced by all bodies exposed to the air at Madrid, and at Cadiz and Bordeaux. At Madrid the barometer falls as low as 25 inches 6 lines, and sometimes even lower. The following is a table of the variations in the height of the barometer during the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months of the year 1793. | Months | Maximum | Minimum | Mean Height of the Mercury | |--------|---------|---------|---------------------------| | | Inches | Lines | Inches | Lines | Inches | Lines | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> | 26 | 5.8 | 25 | 9.8 | 26 | 2.6 | | February| 26 | 5.3 | 25 | 6.2 | 26 | 1.6 | | <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> | 26 | 4.7 | 25 | 6.0 | 25 | 1.6 | | April | 26 | 4.4 | 25 | 6.9 | 26 | 1.6 | | May | 26 | 4.6 | 25 | 10.5 | 26 | 0.8 | | June | 26 | 4.3 | 25 | 11.8 | 26 | 1.6 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> | 26 | 4.3 | 25 | 11.5 | 26 | 2.4 | | August | 26 | 3.2 | 25 | 11.5 | 26 | 1.4 | | September| 26 | 4.3 | 25 | 11.5 | 26 | 1.7 | From the mean height of the barometer at Madrid, Spain, we find that capital to be elevated 309½ fathoms above the level of the ocean. Madrid, consequently, stands as high as the town of Innsbruck, situated in one of the highest defiles of the Tyrol, while its elevation is 15 times greater than that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and three times greater than that of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. According to M. Thalacker, the mineralogist, who has taken several heights with the barometer in the environs of Madrid, the elevation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at San <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ILDEFONSO">Ildefonso</a> is 593 fathoms, which is higher than the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>, and is, strictly speaking, in the regions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, which generally float from 550 to 600 fathoms high. The height of the plain of the Castiles has an evident effect on its temperature. We are astonished at not finding oranges in the open air under the same latitude as that of Tarentum, part of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, Thessaly, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; but the mean temperature of Madrid is very little superior to that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>, Paris, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and is nearly the same with that of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> and Rome. The following table shews the mean temperature at Madrid and at Rome, during the first nine months of the years 1793 and 1807. | Months | Deg. of Fahrenheit | Deg. of Fahrenheit | |--------|-------------------|-------------------| | January| 39° 3 | 40° 11' 15" | | February| 43 24 | 47 49 30 | | March | 47 54 | 50 15 45 | | April | 52 19 30" | 54 34 30 | | May | 59 4 30 | 65 56 15 | | June | 72 32 15 | 72 30 | | July | 77 13 30 | 79 15 | | August | 81 34 30 | 79 15 | | September| 65 45 | 72 34 30 | Thus, the mean temperature at Madrid appears to be 59° of Fahrenheit, while that of the coasts of Spain, from the 41° to the 36° of Lat. is between 63½° and 68° of Fahrenheit. In the former climate we find that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees will not flourish in perfection, while in the latter we see banana trees, heliconias, and even sugarcanes, growing in situations that are sheltered from the cold winds. Spain presents few species of animals that are not found in the other parts of southern Europe. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, we may remark, as peculiar to Spain, the genet, (genetta genetta). The bear is found in several parts of the great Pyrenean chain, especially on some of the mountains of Aragon, as well as those of Occar and Reynosa in Old Castile. Wolves are met with in all the higher and mountainous parts of the country, and wild boars on the mountains of Navarre, on the Pinar, and the Sierra de Carafcoy, in the kingdom of Valencia. The roebuck is found on some of the mountains of Navarre, and the lynx and the ibex on those of Cuenca in New Castile, in the valleys of Aure and Gijon, as well as in the Pyrenees. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a> is the horse, for which this kingdom has been famous in all ages. The Spanish horses horses have probably originated from the Barbis of the north of Africa, supposed to be the immediate offspring of the Arabian breed. The Spanish mules are also excellent, and the ass is here no ignoble animal, though not equal to those of Arabia. There is little remarkable in the breed of cattle, but the Merino sheep have long been distinguished, and are perhaps superior to any in the world for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>, if not for the delicacy of the mutton. The flocks of Merino sheep are sometimes extremely large, and Mr. Townsend mentions one nobleman who possessed not fewer than 40,000. The whole number in the kingdom may be estimated at about 5,000,000. These animals were, by a special code, called the Moifa, authorized to travel from one province to another, according as the season presented the best pasturage in the mountains or the plains. The fleece of the Merino sheep is esteemed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> in value to that of any other breed. Of the birds more peculiarly found in Spain, the vulture, pernicopterus, the cuculus glandarius, cuculus tridactyla, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOTACILLA">motacilla</a> hispanica, hirundo mellia, and hirundo rupestris, are the most remarkable. Fresh-water fishes are very plentiful in the Spanish rivers; but those in most esteem are from the small river Tormes in Old Castile, where have been taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a> of 20 lbs. weight. The tench of the lakes near Tobar in New Castile, are remarkably fine and delicate, and are taken in great abundance every year, during the months of May and June. The fish taken on the coasts are much the same as those of the other countries bordering on the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. The tuna was formerly taken on the eastern coast, where it formed a particular branch of the fishery, but is now, we believe, little regarded. Among the Spanish insects, the most remarkable are, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTHARIDES">cantharides</a>, (meloe sefectorius), and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERMES">kermes</a> insect (coccus ilicis). The latter insect is much cultivated as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, especially in the territory of Bujalance, and of Fernan Nunes in the kingdom of Cordova, as also in the vicinity of the town of De las Aguas, four leagues from Alicante, and near the river Henares, in New Castile. The evergreen oaks on which these animals feed, present in the spring, a most singular appearance, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> nidi of the kermes, with which their leaves are covered. No country of Europe of the same extent, furnishes such an ample field for the researches of the botanist, as Spain; and indeed its botany constitutes a very important part of its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The mountainous districts are clothed with the ever-green oak, the common oak, the chestnut, and in some places various species of pine; but their most useful production is the cork tree. The smaller heights produce the wild olive, the almond, the thyme, the laurel, the bay, the cypress, Canary and Portugal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> jessamine, and the Provence rose. The vine, the palm tree, the orange, the lemon and the olive, are so nearly naturalized as to require but little cultivation; and the same may be said of the kali (saltpeter), which is produced in large quantities on the coasts, and furnishes the best kind of kelp, commonly called barilla, used in the manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> and glats. The plains and valleys are covered with many of those plants which form some of the greatest ornaments of our flower gardens, as the tulip, several species of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, the peony, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> flower, the orange and martagon lily, the jonquil, several species of narcissus and hyacinth, and above all the rhododendron. The mountains, however, exhibit the greatest variety of botanical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. Those most worthy of the visits and researches of the enterprising botanist, are, the Sierra de Guadalupe in Extremadura; the mountains of Moncayo in Aragon; of Pineda, Guadarrama, and Cuerca, in New Castile; of Carofoyo, in the kingdom of Murcia; of Peña-Colosa, Mongi, Aytona, and Mariola, in the kingdom of Valencia, and the Pyrenees. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, was, before the discovery of the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> islands, one of the most important objects of Spanish cultivation, and numerous sugar <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> were established along the coast of the Mediterranean, especially in the kingdom of Granada. At the conquest of that Moorish kingdom, not fewer than fourteen sugar plantations and two mills, were found within the province. Some sugar canes are still cultivated in the kingdom of Valencia, but the manufacture of sugar is discontinued, and the canes are used only for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. There is, we believe, still a manufacture for sugar from Spanish canes in Granada. Spain has long been celebrated for the riches of its minerals, mineral kingdom, and it may still be considered as the Mexico and Peru of Europe. There are few metals which may not be found in this kingdom; and, till the discovery of America put the Spaniards in possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> which far surpass their own in produce, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver mines of Spain were thought to be nearly the richest in the world. At present, no gold mines are wrought, but grains of that metal are found disseminated in ferruginous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>, forming a vein that passes through a mountain near the village of San Ildefonso in Old Castile. Spangles of gold are found intermixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERY">emery</a>, in a mine near Alocer in Extremadura, and in the territory of Molena in Aragon; and this metal is occasionally found in the sand of two rivers; the Agueda, in the kingdom of Leon, which rises from the mountains of Xalama, and the Tagus in New Castile, especially in the vicinity of Toledo. Silver is much more abundant, but most of its mines have also been abandoned. We believe the only silver mine now in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, is that of the Sierra de Guadalupe, near the village of Logroño, where the silver is found mixed with micaceous schistus. The most remarkable silver mines formerly worked are those of Alrodovado del Campo; of Zalamea on the road to Alocer in Extremadura; of Almazara near Carthagena; three in the Sierra Morena, about a league from Guadalcanal, in the kingdom of Seville, and another about two leagues from Linarejos, in the kingdom of Jaen. This last mine was well known both to the Carthaginians and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; while Spain was under the dominion of the former it belonged to Himilce, the wife of Asdrubal. After having been long abandoned, it was again wrought in the 17th century, when a vein of ore five feet in diameter was discovered; at present, however, it is no longer in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Mines of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> are found near Pamplona in Navarre, near Salva Tierra in Alava; near Escarray, and at the foot of the mountains of Guadarrama in Old Castile; near Lorea in Murcia; near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTREUSE">Chartreuse</a> of the Val de Cristo in Valencia; in the Sierra de Guadalupe in Extremadura; in the mountains near Cordova; near Riotinto, and at la <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> de los Conejos in Seville; in the district of Albuladui in Granada, and near Lé- narez in the kingdom of Jaen. There are numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> mines, especially near Tor- tosa in Catalonia; at Zoma, Benifiques, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">Plan</a> in Aragon; near Logroño and Alcofer in Extremadura; in the mountain Guadarrama in Old Castile; near los Alumbres and Lorca in Murcia; at Alcaniz and Con- stantina in Seville, and at the district of Linarex in Jaen. The mines of iron are abundant, and need not be enumerated. Of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> there are two mines, both in the district of La Mancha. One of these is at Alen- dia, near Almodovar; the other at the foot of the Sier- ra Morena. There is only one mine of cobalt, viz., in the province of Aragon, found in the valley of Gefton. There are two mines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> in Valencia; one about two leagues from Alicante in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> mountains of Alcoray; the other between Valencia and San Felipe; and two others in the same province, that produce native mercury, but none of these are worked. The most abundant mine of mercury and cinnamon united is in the district of La Mancha, on the borders of Cordova. It is situated in a hill of sandstone which rests on slate. The whole length of the hill is traversed by two princi- pal veins, both of which were wrought by the Romans. The whole of this mine was lately wrought by the agents of the king, and its produce was very abundant. Plumbago is found in a thick vein intermixed with feld- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, about a league from the village of Real Monasterio, in the kingdom of Seville. Mines of sulphur occur, both in Aragon and Murcia; jet has been found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- trict of Old Colmenar, i.e., Old Castile; and there is good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the presence of coal at several places in Catalonia, in the Asturias, New Castile, and Aragon; but it is said that no coal mines have as yet been open- ed. The marbles of Spain are very numerous and valuable. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, veined with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, is procured near Barcelona; many dendritic marbles occur near Tortosa. Near the town of Molina, in Aragon, is found a gra- nular marble spotted with red, yellow, and white. At the village of Salinos, in the district of Guipuzcoa, is a beautiful blue pyritical marble, containing marine shells. From Monte Sagarru, near Segorbia, in the province of Valencia, are procured several fine marbles, which were held in great estimation even by the Romans. The pro- vince of Granada, however, contains more valuable va- rieties of this beautiful mineral than all the rest of Spain; of these some of the principal are the following. A pure white statuary marble, of which the whole moun- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> of Filabra, near Almeria, is composed; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-co- lored marble from a mountain near Antequera; an exquisitely beautiful wax-coloured alabaster, from the vicinity of the city of Granada; and a finely veined marble from the Sierra Nevada. Of the Spanish mineral waters the following are the most celebrated. The principal cold springs are, a he- patic water in the town of Buron, in Valencia; a car- bonated water at Gerona, in Catalonia; a saline purga- tive water at Vacia-Madrid, three leagues from the ca- pital, and another of a similar nature near Toledo. The principal hot springs are, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of Abu-Zu- lema, at Javal-Cohol, near Brea; a hepatic spring used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALHAMA">Alhama</a> de Granada; another near Almeria, in the province of Granada, to which are at- tached both bathing and vapour baths: all these were discovered, or at least brought into general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, by the Moors. A very copious hot spring near Merida, in Extremadura, made use of by the Romans. The Calda de Bonar, in the neighbourhood of Leon, a spring of tepid water frequented by the Romans, and still exhibi- ting the ruins of baths and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>. A very hot spring near Orense, in Galicia. A spring at Alhama, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALATAYUD">Calatayud</a>, in Aragon, formerly much frequented, but now in a state of neglect. The Fuente de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUZOT">Buzot</a>, near Alicante, a saline spring of the tempera- ture of 104° Fahrenheit. A very copious and hot spring at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHENA">Archena</a>, near Murcia, where still remain the ruins of Roman and Moorish baths. A hepatic spring near Armellino, in Old Castile. Among the natural curiosities of Spain, we may parti- cularize the mountain of Montserrat in Catalonia (see curiosities, Montserrat); the insulated hill of rock felt near the town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARDONA">Cardona</a>, in Catalonia (see <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a>, No. 22); the subterranean lake contained within a cavern in the neighbourhood of the Cava Perella, in the island of Minorca; the stalactite cave called St Michael's, on the west side of the rock of Gibraltar, and the river Guadiana, which appears and disappears several times in the course of its progress to the sea. The various groups of islands that are subject to Spain Spani- have long been distinguished by particular names. Thus islands. Majorca, Minorca, Cabrera and Dragonera, were called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> Insulae Baleares, and are still named the Balearic Isles; while Iviça and Formentera form a lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a>, denominated the Pitiusae Isles. Of these islands, the latter were taken possession of by the Car- thaginians nearly 700 years before the Christian era; and about 200 years after that entering people made themselves masters of the Balearic Isles. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, all these islands long maintained a state of piratical independence, and only Majorca was ever com- pletely subject to the Romans. In the time of Augustus we are told that the Balearic Isles were so infested with rabbits, that the inhabitants sent deputies to Rome for assistance to destroy these formidable invaders of their plantations. In the year 426 of the Christian era, these islands came into the possession of the Vandals, from whom they were taken at the end of the 8th century by the African Moors. At the beginning of the 9th century they were seized on by a fleet sent into the Me- diterranean by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>; but they were soon after reconquered by the Moors, who maintained the sove- reignty in these islands till, in 1228, they were finally dispossessed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> James grandson of Alphonso II., king of Aragon. Though Spain appears to have been known to the Names of Phoenicians nearly 1000 years before the birth of Christ, Spain. it seems to have been little regarded by the Greeks till after the period when <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> composed his history. Some part of this country was probably the Tartessus of Scripture, from which the Phoenicians imported gold, silver, and other precious commodities into Judea. When the Greeks had established a colony at Marcellis, they must have been well acquainted with at least the northern part of this peninsula, to which they gave the names of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IBERIA">Iberia</a> and Celtiberia, from two nations who then inhabited the country, and of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HISPANIA">Hispania</a>, from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> situation in the west of the then known world. The name Hispania, from which its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> appellation Spain is derived, was bestowed on it by the Romans; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of this name is uncertain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a> of Spain were doubtless a Celtic tribe, which probably passed into this peninsula from the adjoining continent of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, though at a very early period they appear to have been mixed with a colony of Mauritani, or Moors from the coast of Africa. The Celtic inhabitants, or Celtiberi, seem to have possessed the northeast of the peninsula, while the Mauritani occupied the southern and south-western districts. Nothing certain is known respecting the early state of Spain, till the commencement of the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the Romans and the Carthaginians, in the middle of the third century before Christ. Not long before this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>, probably at the beginning of the century, the latter people had possessed themselves of Catalonia, when their general Hamilcar Barcas is said to have founded the city of Barceno, the modern Barcelona. The Carthaginian colony, however, seems to have been rather a mercantile than a warlike settlement, and the Celtiberi were more the allies than the subjects of their African neighbours. Of the contests carried on between the Carthaginians and the Romans, till the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> subjugation of the former, and the consequent occupation of all their territories by the Roman republic, we have given an account under the articles Carthage and Rome. We shall here briefly consider the state of Spain at the time of its occupation by the Romans, and relate the events to which that occupation gave rise, and which are less connected with the more immediate transactions of the Punic wars. At the time of the Roman conquest, Spain, though prodigious quantities of silver had been carried out of it by the Carthaginians and Tyrians, was yet a very rich country. In the most ancient times, indeed, its riches are said to have exceeded what is related of the most wealthy country in America. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> affirms us, that when the Phoenicians first arrived in Spain, they exchanged their naval commodities for such immense quantities of silver, that their ships could neither contain nor sustain its load, though they used it for ballast, and made their anchors and other implements of silver. When the Carthaginians first came to Spain, they found the quantity of silver nothing lessened, since the inhabitants at that time made all their utensils, and even mangers, of that precious metal. In the time of the Romans this amazing plenty was very much diminished; however, their gleanings were by no means despisable, since in the space of nine years they carried off 111,542 pounds of silver, and 4995 of gold, besides an immense quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> and other things of value (A). The Spaniards were always remarkable for their bravery, and some of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>'s best troops were brought from thence; but as the Romans penetrated farther into the country than the Carthaginians had done, they met with nations whose love of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> was equal to their valour, and whom the whole strength of their empire was scarcely able to subdue. Of these the most formidable were the Numantines, Cantabrians, and Asturians. In the time of the third Punic war, one Viriathus, a celebrated hunter, and afterwards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of a gang of banditti, took upon him the command of some Numantines who had been in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Carthage, and ventured to oppose the Roman power in that part of Spain called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>, now Portugal. The praetor, named Veillius, who commanded in those parts, marched against him with 10,000 men; but was defeated and killed, with the loss of 4000 of his troops. The Romans immediately dispatched another praetor with 10,000 foot and 1300 horse: but Viriathus having first cut off a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of 4000 of them, engaged the rest in a pitched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; and having entirely defeated them, reduced great part of the country. Another praetor, who was sent with a new army, met with the same fate; so that, after the destruction of Carthage, the Romans thought proper to send a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> named Quintus Fabius, who defeated the Lusitanians in several battles, and regained two important places which had long been in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the rebels. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of Fabius's consulship, Viriathus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the war with his usual success, till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> thought proper to send against him the consul Q. Caecilius Metellus, an officer of great valour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. With him Viriathus did not choose to venture a pitched battle, but contented himself with acting on the defensive; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the Romans recovered a great many cities, and the whole of Tarraconian Spain was obliged to submit to their yoke. The other consul, named Servilianus, did not meet with the same success; his army was defeated in the field, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> was nearly taken by Viriathus. Notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> of Metellus, however, he could not withstand the intrigues of his countrymen against him, and he was not allowed to finish the war he had begun with so much success. In resentment for this he took all imaginable pains to weaken the army under his command: he disbanded the flower of his troops, exhausted the magazines, let the elephants die, broke in pieces the arrows which had been provided for the Cretan archers, and threw them into a river. Yet, after all, the army which he gave up to his successor Q. Pompeius, consisting of 30,000 foot and 2000 horse, was sufficient to have crushed Viriathus if the general had known how to use it. But, instead of opposing Viriathus with success, the imprudent consul procured much more formidable enemies. The Termantians and Numantines, who had hitherto kept themselves independent, offered very advantageous terms of peace and alliance with Rome; but Pompeius insisted on their delivering up their arms. Upon this war was immediately commenced. The consul with great confidence invested Numantia; but being repulsed with considerable loss, he sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before Termantia, where he was attended with still worse success. The very first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the Termantines killed 700 of his legionaries; took a great convoy which was coming to (A) In this account we must allow something for the exaggerations of fabulous historians. There is no doubt, however, that Spain was at this time immensely rich, and if we may believe Strabo, there was then a mine near Carthage which yielded every day 25,000 drams of silver, or about 300,000l. per annum. Spain. The Roman camp; and having defeated a considerable body of their horse, pushed them from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> to post till they came to the edge of a precipice, where they all tumbled down, and were dashed to pieces. In the mean time Servilius, who had been continued in his command with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of proconsul, managed matters so ill, that Viriathus surrounded him on all sides, and obliged him to sue for peace. The terms offered to the Romans were very moderate; being only that Viriathus should keep the country he at that time possessed, and the Romans remain masters of all the rest. This peace the proconsul was very glad to sign, and afterwards procured its ratification by the senate and people of Rome. The next year Q. Pompeius was continued in his command against the Numantines in Farther Spain, while Q. Servilius Cepio, the new consul, had for his province Hither Spain, where Viriathus had established his new state. Pompeius undertook to reduce Numantia by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> aside the stream of the Durius, now the Douro, by which it was supplied with water; but, in attempting this, such numbers of his men were cut off, that, finding himself unable to contend with the enemy, he was glad to make peace with them on much worse terms than they had offered of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>. The peace, however, was ratified at Rome; but in the meantime Cepio, desirous of showing his prowess against the renowned Viriathus, prevailed on the Romans to declare war against him without any provocation. As Cepio commanded an army greatly superior to the Lusitanians, Viriathus thought proper to sue for peace; but finding that Cepio would be satisfied with nothing less than a surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, he resolved to stand his ground. In the mean time, the latter having bribed some of the intimate companions of Viriathus to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> him in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, he by that infamous method put an end to a war which had lasted 14 years, very little to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the republic. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Viriathus, the Romans with like treachery ordered their new consul Popilius to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with the Numantines. His infamous conduct met with the reward it deserved; the Numantines lying out, put the whole Roman army to flight with such slaughter, that they were in no condition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. Manlius, who succeeded Popilius, met with still worse success; his great army, consisting of 30,000 men, was utterly defeated by 4500 Numantines, and 20,000 of them killed in the pursuit. The remaining 10,000, with their general, were pent up by the Numantines in such a manner that they could neither advance nor retreat, and would certainly have been all put to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or made prisoners, had not the Numantines, with a generosity which their enemies never possessed, offered to let them depart upon condition that a treaty should be concluded with them upon very moderate terms. This the consul very willingly promised, but found himself unable to perform. On the contrary, the people, not satisfied with declaring his treaty null and void, ordered him to be delivered up to the Numantines. The latter refused to accept him, unless he had along with him the 10,000 men whom they had relieved as before related. At last, after the consul had remained a whole day before the city, his successor Furius, thinking this a sufficient recompense to the Numantines for breaking the treaty, ordered him to be received again into the camp. However, Furius did not chuse to engage with such a desperate and resolute enemy as the Numantines had showed themselves; and the war with them was discontinued till the year 133 B.C., when Scipio Emilianus, the destroyer of Carthage, was sent against them. Against this renowned general the Numantines with all their valour were not able to contend. Scipio, having with the utmost care introduced strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> among his troops, and reformed the abuses which his predecessors had suffered in their armies, by degrees brought the Romans to face their enemies, which at his arrival they had absolutely refused to do. Having then ravaged all the country round the town, it was soon blocked up on all sides, and the inhabitants began to feel the want of provisions. At last they resolved to make one desperate attempt for their liberty, and either to break through their enemies, or perish in the attempt. With this view they marched out in good order by two gates, and fell upon the works of the Romans with the utmost fury. The Romans, unable to stand this desperate shock, were on the point of yielding, when Scipio, hurrying to the places attacked, with no fewer than 20,000 men, the unhappy Numantines were at last driven into the city, where they sustained for a little longer the miseries of famine. Finding at last, however, that it was altogether impossible to hold out, it was resolved by the majority to submit to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of the Roman commander. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> was not universally approved. Many shut themselves up in their houses, and died of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, while even those who had agreed to surrender repented their offer, and setting fire to their houses, perished in the flames with their wives and children, so that not a single Numantine was left alive to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> the triumph of the conqueror of Carthage. After the destruction of Numantia the whole of Spain submitted to the Roman yoke; and nothing remarkable happened till the times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a>, when a pretorian army was cut off in Spain by the Lusitanians.
