It turned out to be the same with Smollet's story of the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> crows, which some body was said to have vomited. Upon inquiry at the inn where the West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> gentleman had lodged, no such gentleman had been seen there. It was found afterwards he had never left the West Indies. Still, however, the veracity of the widow was not disputed; and some dark and secret transaction was suspected. But the whole affair was at length explained by discovering that she was somewhat deranged by melancholy. And the cries which she had at first imagined she had heard were afterwards imitated by some rogueish person, who was highly amused with spreading terror among the credulous. 5. Drunkenness also has the power of creating spectres. Its natural effect in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> is to derange the understanding, to throw it off its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and to give full scope to that passion which has a natural disposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> an ascendancy; and sometimes it excites passions which scarcely seem to exist at any other time. It makes some men licentious, some furious, some all benevolence and kindness, some from being cowards it renders undaunted heroes. It seldom, if ever, excites fear; and therefore it may be thought strange that men should imagine they see ghosts when intoxicated. But it must be remarked, that the ghouls which the drunkard sees, he sees not with the same alarm and terror as men who are sober. He is not afraid of them. He has the courage to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with them, and even to fight with them, if they give him provocation. A man returning home intoxicated, affirmed that he had met with the devil; and that after a severe encounter he had vanquished him and brought him to the ground, to which he had nailed him fast by driving his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> through his body. Next morning the staff was found stuck with great violence into a heap of turfs! 6. Many apparitions of spectres have no other origin than the artifices of the waggish or self-interested. Dr Plot, in his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, relates a marvellous story, which will illustrate this assertion. Soon after the murder of King Charles I. a commission was appointed to survey the king's house at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>, woods, and other demesnes to that manor belonging; and one Collins, under a feigned name, hired himself as secretary to the commissioners, who, upon the 13th of October 1649, met, and took up their residence in the king's own rooms. His majesty's bed-chamber they made their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> their pantry, and the presence-chamber was the place where they sat for the dispatch of business. His majesty's dining-room they made their wood yard, and stored it with the wood of the famous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>-oak from the High Park, which, that nothing might be left with the name of king about it, they had dug up by the roots, and split and bundled up into faggots for their firing. Things being thus prepared, they sat on the 16th of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> for the dispatch of business; and in the midst of their first debate there entered a large black dog (as they thought), which made a dreadful howling, overturned two or three of their chairs, and then crept under a bed and vanished. This gave them the greater surprise, as the doors were kept constantly locked, so that no real dog could get in or out. The next day their surprise was increased, when fitting at dinner in a lower room, they heard plainly the noise of persons walking over their heads, though they well knew the doors were all locked, and there could be no body there. Presently after they heard also all the wood of the king's oak brought by parcels from the dining-room, and thrown with great violence into the presence chamber; as also all the chairs, stools, tables, and other furniture, forcibly hurried about the room; their papers containing the minutes of their transactions were torn, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>-glass broken. When all this noise had ceased, Giles Sharp, their secretary, proposed to enter first into these rooms; and in presence of the commissioners, from whom he received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>, he opened the doors, and found the wood spread about the room, the chairs toiled about and broken, the papers torn, the ink-glass broken (as has been said), but not the least track of any human creature, nor the least reason to suspect one, as the doors were all fast, and the keys in the custody of the commissioners. It was therefore unanimously agreed, that the power who did this mischief must have entered the room at the key-hole. The night following, Sharp the secretary, with two of the commissioners servants, as they were in bed in the same room, which room was contiguous to that where the commissioners lay, had their bed's feet lifted up so much higher than their heads, that they expected to have their necks broken, and then they were let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> at once with so much violence as shook the whole house, and more than ever terrified the commissioners. On the night of the 19th, as all were in bed in the same room for greater safety, and lights <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> by them, the candles in an instant went out with a sulphurous smell; and that moment many trenchers of wood were hurled about the room, which next morning were found to be the same their honours had eaten on the day before, which were all removed from the pantry, though not a lock was found opened in the whole house. The next night they fared still worse; the candles went out as before; the curtains of their honours beds were rattled to and fro with great violence; their honours received many cruel blows and bruises, by eight great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>-dishes and a number of wooden trenchers being thrown on their beds, which being heaved off, were heard rolling about the room, though in the morning none of these were to be seen. This night likewise they were alarmed with the tumbling down of oaken billets about their beds, and other frightful noises; but all was clear in the morning, as if no such thing happened. The next night the keeper of the king's house and his dog lay in the commissioners room, and then they had no disturbance. But on the night of the 22d, though the dog lay in the room as before, yet the candles went out, a number of brick-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a> fell from the chimney into the room, the dog howled piteously, their bed clothes were all stripped off, and their terror increased. On the 24th they thought all the wood of the king's oak was violently thrown down by their bed sides; they counted 64 billets that fell, and some hit and shook the beds in which they lay; but in the morning none were found there, nor had the door been opened where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a> wood was kept. The next night the candles were put out; the curtains rattled, and a dreadful crack like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> was heard; and one of the servants running in haste, thinking his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was killed, found three dozen of trenchers laid smoothly under the quilt by him. But all this was nothing to what succeeded afterwards: The 29th, about midnight, the candles went out, something walked majestically through the room, and opened and shut the windows; great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> were thrown violently into the room, some of which fell on the beds, others on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>; and at about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> after one a noise was heard as of forty cannon discharged together, and again repeated at about eight minutes distance. This alarmed and raised all the neighbourhood, who coming into their honours room, gathered up the great stones, four score in number, and laid them by in the corner of a field, where, in Dr Plot's time, who reports this story, they were to be seen. This noise, like the discharge of cannon, was heard through all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for 16 miles round. During these noises, which were heard in both rooms together, the commissioners and their servants gave one another over for lost, and cried out for help; and Giles Sharp, snatching up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, had well nigh killed one of their honours, mistaking him for the spirit, as he came in his shirt from his own room to theirs. While they were together, the noise was continued, and part of the tiling of the house was stript off, and all the windows of an upper room were taken away with it. On the 30th at midnight something walked into the chamber treading like a bear; it walked many times about, then threw the warming-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a> violently on the floor; at the same time a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of broken glass, accompanied with great stones and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, came pouring into the room with uncommon force. These were all found in the morning to the astonishment and terror of the commissioners, who were yet determined to go on with their business. But on the first of November the most dreadful <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of all ensued: Candles in every part of the room were lighted up, and a great fire made; at midnight, the candles all yet burning, a noise like the bursting of a cannon was heard in the room, and the burning billets were tossed about by it even into their honours beds; who called Giles and his companions to their relief, otherwise the house had been burnt to the ground; about an hour after the candles went out as usual, the crack as if many cannon was heard, and many pailfuls of green flinging water were thrown upon their honours beds; great stones were also thrown in as before, the bed curtains and bedsteads torn and broken, the windows shattered, and the whole neighbourhood alarmed with the most dreadful noises; nay, the very rabbit-stealers that were abroad that night in the warren were so terrified, that they fled for fear and left their ferrets behind them. One of their honours this night spoke, and, in the name of God, asked what it was, and why it disturbed them so? No answer was given to this; but the noise ceased for a while, when the spirit came again; and, as they all agreed, brought with it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> devils worse than itself. One of the servants now lighted a large <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and set it in the door-way between the two chambers, to see what passed; and as he watched it, he plainly saw a hoof striking the candle and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLESTICK">candlestick</a> into the middle of the room, and afterwards making three scrapes over the snuff, scraped it out. Upon this the same person was so bold as to draw a sword; but he had scarce got it out when he felt another invisible hand holding it too, and pulling it from him; and at length prevailing, struck him so violently on the head with the pommel, that he fell down for dead with the blow. At this instant was heard another burst like the discharge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROADSIDE">broadside</a> of a ship of war, and at about a minute or two's distance each no less than 19 more such: these shook the house so violently, that they expected every moment it would fall upon their heads. The neighbours, on this, as has been said, being all alarmed, flocked to the house in great numbers, and all joined in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and psalm singing; during which the noise still continued in the other rooms, and the discharge of cannons was heard as from without, though no visible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> was seen to discharge them. But what was the most alarming of all, and put an end to their proceedings effectually, happened the next day as they were all at dinner, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in which they had signed a mutual agreement to reserve a part of the premises out of the general survey, and afterwards to share it equally amongst themselves, (which paper they had hid for the present under the earth in a pot in one corner of the room, and in which an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-tree grew), was consumed in a wonderful manner, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> taking fire with which the pot was filled, and burning violently with a blue fume, and an intolerable stench; so that they were all driven out of the house, to which they could never again be prevailed upon to return. This wonderful contrivance was all the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the memorable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Collins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, otherwise called Funny Joe, who having hired himself as secretary, under the name of Giles Sharp, by knowing the private traps belonging to the house, and the help of pulvis fulminans and other chemical preparations, and letting his fellow-servants into the scheme, carried on the deceit without discovery to the very last; insomuch that the Dr Plot, in his Natural History, relates the whole for fact, and concludes in this grave manner, "That though tricks have been often played in affairs of this kind, many of the things above related are not reconcileable by juggling; such as the loud noises, beyond the power of man to make without such instruments as were not there; the tearing and breaking the beds; the throwing about the fire; the hoof treading out the candle; and the striving for the sword, and the blow the man received from the pommel of it." Spectre of the Broken, a singular phenomenon observed on the top of the Broken, one of the Hartz <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, of which M. Haue has given the following account. "After having been here (says he) for the thirtieth time, and having procured information respecting the above-mentioned atmospheric phenomenon, I was at length, on the 23rd of May 1797, fortunate as to have the pleasure of seeing it; and perhaps my description may afford satisfaction to others who visit the Broken through curiosity. The sun rose about four o'clock, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> being quite serene towards the east, his rays could pass without any obstruction over the Heinrichshöhe. In the south-west, how- About a quarter past four I went towards the inn, and looked round to see whether the atmosphere would permit me to have a free prospect to the south-west; when I observed, at a very great distance towards Achtermannshöhe, a human figure of a monstrous size. A violent gust of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> having almost carried away my hat, I clapped my hand to it by moving my arm towards my head, and the colossal figure did the same. The pleasure which I felt on this discovery can hardly be described; for I had already walked many a weary step in the hopes of seeing this shadowy image, without being able to gratify my curiosity. I immediately made another movement by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> my body, and the colossal figure before me repeated it. I was desirous of doing the same thing once more—but my colossus had vanished. I remained in the same position, waiting to see whether it would return; and in a few minutes it again made its appearance on the Achtermannshöhe. I paid my respects to it a second time, and it did the same to me. I then called the landlord of the Broken; and having both taken the same position which I had taken alone, we looked towards the Achtermannshöhe, but saw nothing. We had not, however, stood long, when two such colossal figures were formed over the above eminence, which repeated our compliments by bending their bodies as we did; after which they vanished. We retained our position; kept our eyes fixed on the same spot, and in a little the two figures again stood before us, and were joined by a third. Every movement that we made by bending our bodies these figures imitated—but with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the phenomenon was sometimes weak and faint, sometimes strong and well defined. Having thus had an opportunity of discovering the whole secret of this phenomenon, I can give the following information to such of my readers as may be desirous of seeing it themselves. When the rising sun, and according to analogy the calf will be the same at the setting sun, throws his rays over the Broken upon the body of a man standing opposite to fine light <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> floating around or hovering past him, he needs only fix his eyes steadfastly upon them, and, in all probability, he will see the singular spectacle of his own shadow extending to the length of five or six hundred feet, at the distance of about two miles before him." SPECULARIS <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a>, composed of large plates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> thinness. (See TALC, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>). The white variety with large and broad leaves, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Jinglafis and Mufcory glafs, is imported in great quantities; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>-painters cover their pictures with it; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a>-makers sometimes use it instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and minute objects are usually preserved between two plates of it, for examination by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>.

SPECULATIVE

Pages 193-196

something relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of some art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> science, in contradistinction to practical. SPECULUM for reflecting telescopes, is made of a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> consisting of 32 parts fine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> copper, one of brafs, 15 of grain-tin, and three of white arsenic. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> given by the late J. Edwards, who was rewarded by the Board of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">Longitude</a>, for disclosing it to the public, was published in the Speculum Nautical <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a> for 1787, and is as follows: Melt the copper in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> crucible, employing some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>, composed of two parts of tartar and one of nitre; when melted, add to it the brafs and the silver. Let the pure tin be melted in another crucible, also with some black flux. Take them both from the fire, and pour the melted tin into the fused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> in the large crucible. Stir the whole well with a dry spatula of birch, and pour off the fused metal immediately into a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The sudden chill of the water <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> cause the fluid metal to divide into an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small particles, which will cool instantly. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the copper be completely saturated, the fracture of one piece of this mixed metal will appear bright, and of a gleamy look, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of pure quicksilver. But if it is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, it wants a little more tin. To ascertain the required proportion, melt a small quantity, known by weights, of the mixed metal, with a known very small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of tin; and, if necessary, repeat the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> with different doses, till the fracture of the new mixture looks as already described. Having now ascertained the necessary addition of tin that is required, proceed to the last melting of the whole metal, together with the additional <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> dose of tin; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> the whole, observing the same cautions as before; and you will find that the mixture will melt with a much less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> than that for the first fusion. Have ready as many ounces of white arsenic in coarse powder as there are pounds in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the metal; wrap up the arsenic in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and put it, with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of tongs, into the crucible; stir it well with the spatula, retaining the breath to avoid the arsenical fumes or vapours (which however are not found to be hurtful to the lungs) till they disappear; take the crucible off the fire, clear away the dross from the top of the metal, pour in about one ounce of powdered rosin, with as much nitre, in order to give the metal a clean surface, and pour out the metal into the moulded flasks. The speculum should be moulded with the concave surface downwards, and many small holes should be made through the sand upwards, to discharge the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The moulding sand from Highgate near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, used by the founders, is as good as any for casting these metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> metal should be taken out from the sand of the flasks whilst it is hot, or else it may happen to crack if left to cool within. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELESCOPE">TELESCOPE</a>. But in addition to what has now been said, we must notice some other information relative to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>, polishing, and other important circumstances connected with the method of preparing the most perfect speculum for telescopes. The metal being taken out of the flask, as already noticed, and this should be done as soon as it has become <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and while it is yet red hot, care must be taken to keep the face downwards to prevent it from sinking. Holding it in that position by the git, force out the sand from the hole in the middle of the mirror with a piece of wood or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the speculum in an iron pot, with a large quantity of hot ashes or small coals, so as to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the speculum in them a sufficient depth. If the sand is not forced out of the hole in the manner above directed, the metal, by sinking as it cools, will... will embrace the sand in the middle of the speculum so tight, as to cause it to crack before it becomes entirely cold. And if the metal be not taken out of the sand, and put in a pot with hot ashes or coals to anneal it, the moisture from the sand will always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the metal. Let the speculum remain in the ashes till the whole is become quite cold. The git may be easily taken off by marking it round with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fine half round <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and giving it then a gentle blow. The metal is then to be rough ground and figured. But before we proceed to describe that process, it may be proper to give an account of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> for the speculum of a reflecting telescope, which has been employed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success, by Rochon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the marine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at Brest. Of this composition the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient is platinum; which, in grains, must be purified in a strong fire by means of nitre and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of glass, or that flux which in the English glass-houses is called by the workmen sandifer. To the platinum, when purified, add the eighth part of the metal employed in the composition of common specula; for tin without red copper would not produce a good effect. This mixture is then to be exposed to the most violent heat, which must be still excited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a> that disengages itself from nitre when thrown into the fire. One melting would be insufficient; five or six are requisite to bring the mixture to perfection. It is necessary that the metal should be in a state of complete fusion at the moment when it is poured into the mould. By this process I have been enabled (says the author) to construct a telescope with platinum, which magnifies the diameters of objects five hundred times, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of clearness and distinctness requisite for the nicest observations. The large speculum of platinum weighs fourteen pounds; it is eight inches in diameter, and its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> is five feet. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price of platinum will, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, forever prevent it from coming into general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for the speculaums of telescopes, we thought it proper to notice this discovery, and shall now proceed to the grinding of the speculum. For accomplishing this object, a very complicated process is recommended in Smith's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, and one not much more simple, by Mr Mudge in the 67th volume of the Philosophical Transactions; but according to Mr Edwards, whose speculaums are confessedly the best, neither of these is necessary. Besides a common grindstone, all the tools that he made use of are a rough grinder, which serves also as a polisher, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. When the speculum was cold, he ground its surface bright on a common grindstone, previously brought to the form of the gage; and then took it to the rough grinder. The tool is composed of a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and tin, or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>, and is made of an elliptical form, of such dimensions, that the shortest diameter of the ellipse is equal to the diameter of the mirror or speculum, and the longest diameter is to the shortest in the proportion of ten to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. This rough grinder may be fixed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood, in order to raise it higher from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>; and as the metal is ground upon it with fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERY">emery</a>, Mr Mudge, with whom, in this particular, Mr Edwards agrees, directs a hole or pit to be made in the middle of it as a lodgement for the emery, and deep grooves to be cut out across its surface with a graver for the same purpose. By means of a handle, fixed on the back of the metal with soft cement, the speculum can be whirled round upon this grinder so rapidly, that a common labourer has been known to give a piece of metal, four inches in diameter, to good a face and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> as to fit it for the holes in the space of two hours. The emery, however fine, will break up the metal very much; but that is remedied by the subsequent processes of honing and polishing. When the metal is brought to a true figure, it must be taken to a convex tool, formed of some stones from a place called Edgedon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUDLOW">Ludlow</a> and Bishop's Castle. The common blue stones, used by many opticians for this purpose, will scarcely touch the metal of Mr Edwards's speculaums; but where they must be employed for want of the others, as little water should be used as possible when the metal is put upon them; because it is found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> that they cut better when but barely wet, than when drenched with water. The stones, however, from Edgedon are greatly preferable; for they cut the metal more easily, and having a very fine grain, they bring it to a smooth face. These stones are directed by Mr Mudge to be cemented in small pieces upon a thick round piece of marble, or of metal made of tin and lead like the former composition, in such a manner, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> between the stones may run straight from one side to the other; so that placing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in each of these divisions, they may be cleared from one end to the other of the cement which rises between the stones. As soon as the stones are cemented <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, this tool must be fixed in the lathe, and turned as exactly true to the gage as possible. It should be of a circular figure, and but very little larger than the metal intended to be figured upon it. If it be made considerably larger, it will grind the metal into a larger sphere and a bad figure; and if it be made exactly of the same size, it will <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> the metal indeed into a figure truly spherical, but will be apt to shorten its focus, unless the metal and tool be worked alternately upwards. On these accounts, Mr Edwards recommends it to be made about one twentieth part longer in diameter than the speculum, because he has found that it does not then alter its focus; and he earnestly dissuades the use of much water on the hone pavement at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of using it; otherwise, he says, that the metal in different parts of it will be of different degrees of brightness. The metal being brought to a very fine face and figure by the bed of stones, is ready to receive a polish, which is given to it by the elliptical rough grinder covered with pitch. With respect to the consistency of this pitch, Mr Mudge and Mr Edwards give very different directions. Whilst the former says that it should be neither too hard nor too soft, the latter affirms that the harder the pitch is, the better figure it will give to the metal. Pitch may be easily made of a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> by adding a proper quantity of rosin; and when it is hardened in this way, it is not so brittle as pitch alone, which is hardened by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>. Mr Edwards advises to make the mixture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> so hard as to receive, when cold, an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> from a moderate pressure of the nail of one's finger. When the elliptical tool is to be covered with this mixture, it must be made pretty warm, and in that state have the mixture poured upon it when beginning to cool in the crucible. Our author Speculum. author recommends this coating to be made everywhere of about the thickness of half a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and to give it the proper form, it must, when somewhat cool, be pressed upon the face of the mirror, which has first been dipped in cold water, or covered over with very fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> paper. If it be not found to have taken the exact figure from the first pressure, the surface of the pitch must be gently warmed, and the operation repeated as before. All the superfluous pitch is now to be taken away from the edge of the polisher with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and a hole to be made in the middle, accurately round, with a conical piece of wood. This hole should go quite through the tool, and should be made of the same size, or somewhat less than the hole in the middle of the speculum. Mr Edwards says, that he has always found that small mirrors, though without any hole in the middle, polish much better, and take a more correct figure, for the polisher's having a hole in the middle of it. The polisher being thus formed, it must be very gently warmed at the fire, and divided into several squares by the edge of a knife. These, by receiving the small portion of metal that works off in polishing, will cause the figure of the speculum to be more correct than if no such squares had been made. Mr Mudge directs the polisher to be strewed over with very fine patty; but Mr Edwards prefers Colcothar of vitriol. Patty (says he) gives to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> a white lustre, or, as workmen call it, a silver hue; but good colcothar of vitriol will polish with a very fine and high black lustre, so as to give the metal finished with it the complection of polished <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>. To know if the colcothar of vitriol is good, put some of it into your mouth, and if you find it dissolves away it is good; but if you find it hard, and crunch between your teeth, then it is bad, and not well burned. Good colcothar of vitriol is of a deep red, or of a deep purple colour, and is soft and oily when rubbed between the fingers; bad colcothar of vitriol is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> red colour, and feels harsh and gritty. The colcothar of vitriol should be levigated between two surfaces of polished steel, and wrought with a little water; when it is worked dry, you may add a little more water, to carry it lower down to what degree you please. When the colcothar of vitriol has been wrought dry three or four times, it will acquire a black colour, and will be low enough, or sufficiently fine, to give an exquisite lustre. This levigated colcothar of vitriol must be put into a small phial, and kept with some water upon it. When it is to be used, every part of the pitch-polisher must be first brushed over with a fine camel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, which has been dipped in pure water, and rubbed gently over a piece of dry clean <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. The washed colcothar of vitriol is then to be put upon the polisher; and Mr Edwards directs a large quantity of it to be put on at once, so as to saturate the pitch, and form a fine coating. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or third application of this powder be found necessary, it must be used very sparingly, or the polish will be destroyed which has been already attained. When the metal is nearly polished, there will always appear some black mud upon its surface, as well as upon the tool. Part of this must be wiped away with some very soft wash <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>; but if the whole of it be taken away, the polishing will not be so well completed. With respect to the parabolic figure to be given to Vol. XIX. Part II. the mirror, Mr Edwards assures us, that a very little experience in these matters will enable any one to give it with certainty, by polishing the speculum in the common manner, only with crofs strokes in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, upon an elliptical tool of the proper dimensions. Speculum, a looking glass or mirror, capable of reflecting the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Speculum, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for dilating a wound, or the like, in order to examine it attentively. See Surgery. Speech, in general, the art or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of expressing a person's thoughts by means of articulate sounds, which we call words. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, and Oratory, Part IV. Speed, John, an English historian, was born at Farington, in Cheshire, in the year 1542. He was by profession a taylor, and freeman of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of merchant tailors in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London. In 1636, he published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which was afterwards reprinted in folio, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Theatre of the Empire of Great Britain. His Genealogies of Scripture were first bound up with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> in 1611, when the first edition of the present translation was printed. In 1614 appeared his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Great Britain, which has been translated into Latin; and in 1616 he published his Cloud of Witness, in octavo. He lived in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> 57 years with his wife, by whom he had twelve sons and six daughters; and died in 1629. He was interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Giles's, Cripplegate, London, where a monument was erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Speedwell. See Veronica, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Spell, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> consisting of some words of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> power, generally attended with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>.—In order to explain it, we will produce a few examples. On St Agnes's night, 21st of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, take a row of pins, and pull out every one, one after another, saying a Pater-noster on sticking a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> in your sleeve, and you will dream of him or her you shall marry. Another method to see a future spouse in a dream. Grofe's Prose. The party inquiring must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> from that in which he <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> resides, and on going to Glengarry, bed must knit the left <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a> about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-legged <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>, letting the other garter and stocking alone; and as he rehearses the following verses, at every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMA">comma</a> knit a knot: This knot I knit, To know the thing I know not yet; That I may see The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (woman) that shall my husband (wife) be; How he goes, and what he wears, And what he does all days and years. Accordingly, in a dream, he will appear with the insignia of his trade or profession. Another, performed by charming the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, thus: At the first appearance of the new moon, immediately after the new year's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, (though some say any other new moon is as good,) go out in the evening, and stand over the spars of a gate or file, and, looking on the moon, repeat the following lines: All <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> to the moon! all hail to thee! I prither, good moon, reveal to me This night who my husband (wife) must be. Immediately Immediately after you must go to bed, when you will dream of the person destined for your future husband or wife.

SPELLING

Pages 196-196

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of orthography which teaches the true manner of resolving words into their syllables. All words are either simple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, as *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>*, *diffuse*; *done*, *undone*; and the rules for dividing each must be such as are derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in general, or from the established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of speaking; which, for the English language, are reduced to the following rules: 1. A consonant between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a> must be joined with the latter in spelling, as *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>*, *verily*, *generous*; except, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> *x*, which is joined to the first, as in *flaxen*, *oxen*, &c., and compound words, as in *upon*, *unused*, &c. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> consonant must be divided, as in *letter*, *monner*, &c. 3. Those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a> which can begin a word must not be parted in spelling, as in *defraud*, *reprove*, *distinct*; however, this rule is found sometimes to fail; for though *gn* begins a word, as *gnaw*, *gnat*, &c., yet it must be divided in spelling, as in *cognizance*, *imaginary*, &c. 4. Those consonants which cannot begin a word must be divided, as *ld* in *seldom*, *lt* in *multitude*, *mp* in *temper*, *rd* in *ardent*; but in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> syllables there are exceptions, as *tl* in *<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>*, *dl* in *handle*, &c. 5. When two vowels come together, and are both of them distinctly founded, they must be separated in spelling, as in *coeval*, *mutual*, &c. 6. The grammatical terminations or endings must be separated in spelling, as *ed* in *winged*, *ed* in *deliverance*, *ing* in *hearing*, *ance* in *deliverance*, &c. 7. Compound words must be resolved into their simple or component words, as *upon*, *into*, *nevertheless*, *notwithstanding*, &c.

SPELMAN

Pages 196-196

Sir Henry, an eminent English antiquarian, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and born at Cengham, near Lynn in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, about the year 1561. He was knighted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. who had a particular esteem for him on account of his known capacity for business; and he employed him several times in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> on public affairs. When he was about 50 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he went to reside in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; where falling into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> to which his own genius had always inclined him, he collected all such books and MSS. as concerned the subject of antiquities, either foreign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>. In 1626, he published the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his well-known Glossary, which he never carried beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> L; because, as some have suggested, he had said things under "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">Magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>," and "Maximum consilium," that could not then have appeared without giving offence. Upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> all his papers came into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of his son Sir John Spelman, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who had abilities to have completed his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> death had not prevented him. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part was afterwards published by Sir William Dugdale; but with all the marks of a scanty unfinished performance. The next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he entered upon was an edition of the English Councils, of which he published the first volume about two years before his death, leaving the second volume, as well of this as of his Glossary, to be published by Sir William Dugdale. Sir Henry wrote several other things, all relating to ancient laws and customs, and died in 1641. His Posthumous Works were published in folio, 1698, under the inspection of Mr Gibbon, afterwards bishop of London.

SPENCE

Pages 196-197
Joseph, an eminent writer, was fellow of New College, Oxford, where he took the degree of A.M. in 1727. About that time he became first known as an author, by an Essay on Pope's Odyssey, in which some particular beauties and blemishes of that work are considered; a work of great merit, and which for sound criticism and candid dilution is almost without a parallel. He was elected professor of poetry by the university in 1728, and held that office ten years, which is as long as the statutes will allow. His History of Stephen Duck was first published in 1731; but it was afterwards much altered, and prefixed to an edition of Duck's poems. About this time he travelled into Italy as tutor to the earl of Lincoln, afterwards duke of Newcastle.—In 1736 he republished Gorboduc, at Mr Pope's desire, with a preface giving an account of the author, the earl of Dorset. He quitted his fellowship in 1742, upon being presented by the Society of New College to the rectory of Great Harwood in Buckinghamshire.—He never refused in his living; but paid it an annual visit, distributing large sums of money among the poor, and providing for many of their children. The same year he was made professor of modern history at Oxford. In 1747 he published Polyetess; or an inquiry concerning the agreement between the works of the Roman poets and the remains of ancient artists, being an attempt to illustrate them mutually from each other. This work was treated by Gray with a contempt which it did not deserve. He raises objections because the author did not illustrate his subject from Greek writers; that is, because he failed to execute what he never undertook. He was installed prebendary of the seventh stall at Durham the 24th May 1754. He published the same year, "An Account of the Life, Character, and Poems, of Mr Blacklock, student of philosophy at Edinburgh;" which was afterwards prefixed to his Poems. The prose pieces which he printed in the Museum he collected and published, together with some others, in a pamphlet called Moralities, by Sir Harry Beaumont. Under the same name he published "Crito, or a Dialogue on Beauty;" and "A particular Account of the emperor of China's Gardens near Pekin, in a letter from F. Attiret, a French missionary now employed by that emperor to paint the apartments in those gardens, to his friend at Paris." Both these treatises are printed in Dodley's fugitive pieces, as is also "A Letter from a Swiss Officer to his friend at Rome;" which Mr Spence first published in the Museum. In 1758 he published "A Parallel, in the Manner of Plutarch, between a most celebrated man of Florence and one scarce ever heard of in England." This was also inserted in the fugitive pieces. The same year he made a journey into Scotland, which he described in an affectionate letter to Mr Shenstone, published in Hall's Collection of Letters, 1758. In 1764 he was very well described by Mr James Ridley, in his admirable Tales of the Genii, under the name of Phelos Ecneps (his name read backwards), derivate of the groves. A letter from Mr Spence to that ingenious moralist, under the same signature, is preserved in the 3d volume of "Letters..." In 1768 he published "Remarks and Dissertations on Virgil, with some other classical observations, by the late Mr Holdsworth." On the 29th of August the same year he was unfortunately drowned in a canal in his garden at Byfleet in Surrey. He was found flat upon his face at the edge of the canal, where the water was so shallow as not even to cover his head. The accident, it was supposed, for he was quite alone, was owing to a fit. The duke of Newcastle possessed some manuscript volumes of anecdotes collected by Mr Spence, from which Dr Johnson was permitted to insert many extracts in his Lives of the Poets.

SPENCER

Pages 197-197

Dr John, an eminent divine, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in 1630, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He was chosen fellow of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in 1663. In 1667 he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Corpus Christi College, and preferred to the deanery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a> in 1677. He died on the 29th of May 1695. His works are: 1. The Righteous Ruler; a sermon on Proverbs xxix. 2. preached <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 28, 1660. 2. A Discourse concerning Prodigies, wherein the vanity of prelacies by them is reprehended, and their true and proper ends asserted and vindicated. To this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was afterwards added, A Discourse concerning vulgar prophecies, wherein the vanity of receiving them as the certain indications of any future event is exposed; and some marks of distinction between true and pretended prophets are laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. 3. A Latin Dissertation concerning Urim and Thummim. 4. His famous treatise De legisbus Hebræorum ritualibus et earum rationibus. The intention of this book, as he informs us himself, was to vindicate the Deity from the imputation of acting from arbitrary and fantastical motives. It has been highly and justly esteemed both for the elegance of style and the uncommon erudition and found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> which it displays. It has, however, (that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it particularly which endeavours to deduce some of the Jewish ceremonies from the practices of their heathen neighbours), alarmed many persons, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> such a doctrine, if it could be proved, would derogate from the Divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and undermine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>. But this is so far from being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, that Dr Spencer's attempt, whether successful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not, deserves the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, because it has a tendency to throw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on an important and difficult subject.

SPENSER

Pages 197-197

Edmund, the poet, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the year 1553, and descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of the Spencers in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>. All we know concerning his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> is, that he was admitted a fellow of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and matriculated in 1569. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> began his intimacy with Mr Gabriel Harvey, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of genius and a poet. In 1576, having completed his degrees in arts, he left the university, as it is conjectured, for want of subsistence, and retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England. Here he had the misfortune to become enamoured of his Rosalind, who, after flattering his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for a time, at length preferred his happier rival. Spenser <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> till the year 1578, when at the persuasion of his friend Mr Harvey he removed to London, where that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> introduced him to Mr Sidney (afterwards Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Sidney). Concerning his first introduction to Sir Philip, there is indeed a different story, which was first told by the writer of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, prefixed to his works in 1679, and transcribed by Hughes, Cibber, and several others; which, nevertheless, is certainly not true. The purport of it is, that Spenser, being unknown to this Mecenas of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and sent in the 9th <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a> of the first book of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">Fairy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>; that, on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, Sir Philip ordered his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> to give the bearer 50l.; on reading a little farther 50l. more; then 200l. bidding him to make haste and pay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, lest he should give the poet his whole estate. The story tells prettily enough; but it is very certain, that the Fairy Queen was begun <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after his acquaintance with Sir Philip. By this universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of genius, however, he was presented to Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, who honoured him with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of poet-laureat. About this time he finished his Shepherd's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">Calendar</a>, which was first printed in 1579; and in the following year, being recommended by his patron to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Leicester, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> as secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Grey of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a>, then appointed lord-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Lord Grey was recalled in 1582, and with him Spenser returned to London, where he continued till after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir Philip Sidney in 1586; a loss which he bewailed to the end of his life. The following year, our poet, having obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of 3000 acres of forfeited lands in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork in Ireland, set out for that kingdom, took possession of his estate, and fixed his residence in the castle of Kilcolman, which had belonged to the earl of Desmond. In this retirement he resumed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the Fairy Queen; and continued in Ireland till, being visited by his old friend Sir Walter Raleigh in 1589, he came over with him to England, but returned to Ireland the year following, where he fell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with a country girl, and married her. Soon after his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, he paid another visit to his native country, where we also find him in 1596. In the following year he returned once more to Kilcolman; but on the rebellion of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRONE">Tyrone</a>, who ravaged the whole county of Cork, he was obliged to fly for safety with his family to England, where, in the year 1599, he died in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> poverty (A). He was buried in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, according to his request, near Chaucer. A monument was erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> by Ann countess of Dorset. We know but little of his character as a man; as a poet, considering the age in which he lived, he deserves our utmost veneration. He wrote various pieces besides those above mentioned. His whole works, with his life by Hughes, were published in six volumes 12mo, in 1715 and 1750.

SPERGULA

Pages 197-198
SURREY, a genus of plants belonging to the class of decandra; and in the natural system arranged (A) This is Camden's account, and it has been generally believed; but Mr Malone, the last editor of Shakespeare's works, by examining the patent roll, 33 Eliz. p. 3, has discovered, that in February 1600-1 Spenser obtained from Queen Elizabeth an annuity or pension of 50l. during his life; a sum equivalent to 200l. at present. Sperm, arranged under the 22d order, Caryophyllaceae. See Botany Index.

SPERMACETI

Pages 198-198

a whitish, unctuous, flaky substance, prepared from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, but chiefly from the brains of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of whale called physeter macrocephalus. The method of preparing spermaceti kept a secret; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is said to be this: The brains being taken out of the animal, are then, as some say, melted over a gentle fire, poured into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>, and when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> melted again; and this process is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till they are purified. Others say, that after being pressed and drained they are more thoroughly purified by steeping them in a ley of alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and quicklime. The brains are then washed, and cut into thin flakes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> slices with woollen knives. One filth is said to afford some tons of brains. Good spermaceti is glossy and semitransparent, in fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flakes; soft and unctuous to the touch, yet dry and friable; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, somewhat like <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and of a faint smell like that of tallow. Some adulterate it with wax; but the deceit is discovered, either by the smell of the wax or by the dulness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Some also sell a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of oil taken from the tail of the whale instead of that from the brain; but this kind turns <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> as soon as exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Indeed it is apt in general to grow yellowish, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a rancid fishy smell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not carefully secured from the air. The more perfectly it has been purified at first, the less susceptible it is of these alterations; and after it has been changed, it may be rendered white and sweet again by steeping it afresh in a ley of alkaline salt and quicklime. It melts in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and congeals again as it cools. Spermaceti is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in medicine. Quincy says it is a noble remedy in the asthma, &c., though chiefly used in bruises, inward hurts, and after delivery. For internal use, it may be dissolved in aqueous liquors into the form of an emulsion, by trituration with almonds, the yolk or white of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, and more elegantly by macerations; or made into a lochock, by mixing two drams of it with a suitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of yolk of egg, then adding half an ounce of fresh drawn oil of almonds, and an ounce of balmatic syrup. Spermaceti is not capable of being dissolved by caustic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, and of forming soaps, like other oily matters; but it is altogether soluble in oils, and unites by liquefaction with wax and resins; and in these forms is applied externally. But it is certain, its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and that which makes it so much in vogue in many places, is its softening the skin. Whence it comes to be used by the ladies in pastes, washes, &c. Spermaceti candles are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> manufacture: they are made smooth, with a fine glost, free from rings and scars, superior to the finest wax candles in colour and lustre; and, when genuine, leave no spot or stain on the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cloth, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. A method has been lately proposed by Dr Smith Gibbes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, to convert animal muffle into a substance much resembling spermaceti. The process is remarkably simple: Nothing more is necessary than to take a dead carcase and expose it to a stream of running <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>: it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> be changed to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of fatty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. To remove the offensive smell, a quantity of nitrous acid may then be poured upon it, which uniting with the fetid matter, the fat is separated in a pure state. This acid indeed turns it yellow, but it may be rendered white and pure by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the oxygenated muriatic acid. Mr Gibbes brought about the same change in a much shorter time. He took three lean pieces of mutton and poured on them the three mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and he perceived that at the end of three days each was much altered; that in the nitrous acid was much softened, and on separating the acid from it, he found it to be exactly the same with that which he had before got from the water; that in the muriatic acid was not in that time so much altered; the vitriolic acid had turned the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>.

SPERMACOCE

Pages 198-198

Burton-wood, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of tetrandria; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 47th order, Belliaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SPEUSIPPUS

Pages 198-198

an Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, the nephew and successor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. Contrary to the practice of Plato, Speusippus required from his pupils a fixed gratuity. He placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the Graces in the school which Plato had built. On account of his infirm state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> carried to and from the academy in a vehicle. On his way thither he one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> met <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a>, and saluted him; the surly philosopher refused to return the salute, and told him, that such a feeble wretch ought to be ashamed to live; to which Speusippus replied, that he lived not in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, but in his mind. At length, being wholly incapacitated, by a paralytic stroke, for the duties of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, he resigned it to Xenocrates. He is said to have been of a violent temper, fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and exceedingly avaricious. Speusippus wrote many philosophical works, which are now lost, but which <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> thought sufficiently valuable to purchase at the expense of three talents. From the few fragments which remain of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, it appears that he adhered very strictly to the doctrine of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>.

SPEY

Pages 198-198

a river of Scotland, rising from a lake of the same name in Badenoch, and, after a tortuous course of 76 miles, passes by Rothes castle, and falls into the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at Garnoch near <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>. Mr Pennant tells us, that the Spey is a dangerous neighbour to Cattle Gordon, overflowing frequently in a dreadful manner, as appears by its ravages far beyond its banks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the river is wide and full of gravel, and the channel very shifting. In 1746 the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> passed this river at Belly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, near Cattle Gordon, when the channel was so deep as to take an officer, from whom Mr Pennant had the account, and who was six feet four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, up to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>. The banks are here very high and steep; so that had not the rebels been intimidated in such a manner as to neglect opposition, the passage must have been attended with considerable loss. On this river there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> salmon-fishery; about 1700 barrels full are caught in the season, and the shore was formerly rented for about 1200l. per annum: now it is probably doubled.

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a> and Medicine, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and perfect corruption <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the parts. SPHÆRANTHUS, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the

SPHAGNUM

BOG-MOSS, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of cryptogamia and order of musci. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Os SPHENOIDES, the seventh bone of the cranium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skull. See ANATOMY, No. II.

SPHERE

Pages 199-199

is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> contained under one uniform round surface, every point of which is equally distant from a certain point in the middle called its centre; and is formed by the revolution of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> about its diameter. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">GEOMETRY</a>. Projection of the Sphere. See Projection. Sphere, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, that concave orb <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> expanse which invests our globe, and in which the heavenly bodies appear to be fixed, and at an equal distance from the eye. The better to determine the places of the heavenly bodies in the sphere, several circles are supposed to be described on the surface thereof, hence called the circles of the sphere: of these some are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circles, as the equinoctial, ecliptic, meridian, &c. and others small circles, as the tropics, parallels, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">GEOGRAPHY</a>; and ASTRONOMY, paffim. Armillary Sphere. See Geography. Sphere of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">Activity</a> of a Body, is that determinate space or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to which, and no farther, the effluvia continually emitted from that body reach; and where they operate according to their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>.

SPHERES

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, the same with metallic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>, for telescopes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other purposes. See MIRROR.

SPHEROID

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> approaching to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a sphere. It is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the entire revolution of a semi-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELLIPSIS">ellipsis</a> about its axis. When the revolution is made round the largest axis, the spheroid is called prolate; and when round the shortest, oblate. This last is the figure of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and probably of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>.
