the sole intention is to point out the proportion of ingredients, the specific gravities are computed only to four places, which will always give the answer true to \( \frac{1}{1000} \)th part. In the last, which is more immediately interesting to the merchant in his transactions with the excise office, the computation is carried one place further. The consideration of the first of these two tables will furnish some useful information to the reader who is interested in the philosophy of chemical mixture, and who endeavours to investigate the nature of those forces which connect the particles of tangible matter. These vary with the distance of the particle; and therefore the law of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, like that of universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, is to be discovered by measuring their sensible effects at their various distances. Their change of distance is seen in the change of density or specific gravity. Did the individual densities of the water and spirit remain unchanged by mixture, the specific gravity would change by equal differences in the series of mixtures on which this table is constructed; for the bulk being always the same, the change of specific gravity must be the difference between the weight of the gallon of water which is added and that of the gallon of spirit which is taken out. The whole difference of the specific gravities of spirits and water being 1.750 parts in 10,000, the augmentation by each successive change of a measure of spirit for a measure of water would be the 100th part of this, or 17.5. But, by taking the successive differences of density as they occur in the table, we see that they are vastly greater in the first additions of water, being then about 10; after which they gradually diminish to the medium quantity 17\(\frac{1}{2}\), when water and spirits are mixed in nearly equal bulks. The differences of specific gravity still diminish, and are reduced to 9, when about 75 parts of water are mixed with 25 of spirit. The differences now increase again; and the last, when 99 parts of water are mixed with one part of spirit, the difference from the specific gravity of pure water is above 14. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> effect, therefore, of the addition of a measure of water to a great quantity of spirit is greater than the similar effect of the addition of a measure of spirits to a great quantity of water. What we call mechanical effect is the local motion, the change of distance of the particles, that the corporeal forces may again be in equilibrio. Observe, too, that this change is greater than in the proportion of the distance of the particles; SPIRITOUS particles; for the density of water is to that of spirits nearly as 6 to 5, and the changes of specific gravity are nearly as 6 to 3. We also see that the changing cause, which produces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> condensation of each ingredient, ceases to operate when 75 parts of water have been mixed with 25 of alcohol: for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of specific gravity, from diminishing comes now to increase; and therefore, in this particular state of composition, is equable. Things are now in the same state as if we were mixing two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> which did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> on each other, but were mutually disseminated, and whose specific gravities are nearly as 9 to 10; for the variation of specific gravity may be considered as the 100th part of the whole difference, in the same manner as 17.7 would have been had water and alcohol sustained no contraction. The imagination is greatly assisted in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of geometrical quantity by exhibiting it in its own form. Specific gravity, being an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of density (a notion purely geometrical), admits of this illustration. Therefore let AB (fig. 2) represent the bulk of any mixture of water and alcohol. The specific gravity of water may be represented by a line of such a length, that AB shall be the difference between the gravities of alcohol and water. Suppose it extended upwards, towards a, till B a is to A a as 10,000 to 8250. It will suit our purpose better to represent it by a parallelogram a BF e, of any breadth BF. In this case the difference of the specific gravities of alcohol and water will be expressed by the parallelogram ABFE. If there were no change produced in the density of one or both ingredients, the specific gravity of the compound would increase as this parallelogram does, and AGHE would be the augmentation corresponding to the mixture of the quantity AG of alcohol with the quantity GB of water, and so of other mixtures. But, to express the augmentation of density as it really obtains, we must do it by some curvilinear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> DABCHD, which varies at the rate determined by Sir Charles Blagden's experiments. This area must be precisely equal to the rectangle ABFE. It must therefore fall without it in some places, and be deficient in others. Let DMHKC be the curve which corresponds with these experiments. It is evident to the mathematical reader, that the ordinates LM, GH, IK, &c. of this curve are in the ultimate ratio of the differences of the observed specific gravities. If A a, b b, &c. are each = s, the little spaces a a b b, &c. will be precisely equal to the differences of the specific gravities 0.8250; 0.8387; 0.8516; &c. corresponding to the different mixtures of water and alcohol. The curve cuts the side of the parallelogram in K, where the ordinate GK expresses the mean variation of density 0.0017.5. IK is the smallest variation. The condensation may be expressed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a curve dmGfk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to DMGKF, making Dd = AE. The condensation is now represented by the spaces comprehended between this last curve and the abscissa AGB, reckoning those <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on the other side of it. This shows, not only that the condensation is greatest in the mixture AG × GB, but also that in mixing such a compound with another AI × IB, there is a rarefaction. Another curve ANOPB may be drawn, of which the ordinates LN, GP, IO, &c. are proportional to the areas ALmd, AGmD, AIkGmd (=AGmd—GIk), &c. This curve shows the whole condensation. This manner of representing the specific gravities of mixtures will suggest many curious inferences to such as will consider them in the manner of Bozovich, with a view to ascertain the nature of the forces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> and chemical affinities: And this manner of viewing the subject becomes every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> more promising, in consequence of our improvements in chemical knowledge; for we now see, that mechanism, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> forces, are the causes of chemical action. We see in almost every case, that chemical affinities are comparable with mechanical prejudices; because the conversion of a liquid into a vapour or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a> is prevented by atmospheric pressure, and produced by the great chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> heat. The action of heat, therefore, or of the cause of heat, is a mechanical action, and the forces are common mechanical forces, with which we are familiarly acquainted. "It may be also remarked in the column of contractions, that in the beginning the contractions augment nearly in the proportion of the quantity of spirits (but more slowly); whereas, in the end, the contractions are nearly in the duplicate proportion of the quantity of water. This circumstance deserves the consideration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. We have represented it to the eye by the curve n g h d." We should here take some notice of the attempt made to elude some part of the duties, by adding some ingredient to the spirits. But our information on this subject is not very exact; and besides it would be doing no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the trader to put fraud more in his power. There are some facts which make a very great augmentation of density, but they render the liquor unpalatable. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> is frequently used with this view; 16 grains of refined sugar dissolved in 1000 grains of proof spirits gave it no fuliginous taste, and increased its specific gravity from 0.920 to 0.925, which is a very great change, equivalent to the addition of 9 grains of water to a mixture of 100 grains of alcohol and 80 of water.

SPOILATION

Pages 219-219

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is an injury done by one clerk <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> incumbent to another, in taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his benefice without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> thereto, but under a pretended <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. It is remedied by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> to account for the profits so taken. This injury, when the jus patronatus, or right of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOWSON">advowson</a>, doth not come in debate, is cognizable in the spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> first presents A to a benefice, who is instituted and inducted thereto; and then, upon pretence of a vacancy, the same patron presents B to the same living, and he also obtains <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> and induction. Now if A disputes the fact of the vacancy, then that clerk who is kept out of the profits of the living, whichever it be, may sue the other in the spiritual court for the spoliation, or taking the profits of his benefice. And if there be tried, whether the living were or were not vacant; upon which the validity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> clerk's pretensions must depend. But if the right of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> comes at all into dispute, as if one patron presented A, and another patron presented B, there the ecclesiastical court hath no cognizance, provided the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a> sued for amount to a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the value of the living, but may be prohibited at the instance of the patron by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s writ of indicavit. So also if a clerk, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of title, ejects another from his parsonage, this injury must be redressed in the temporal courts; for it depends upon no question determinable by the spiritual law (as plurality of benefices or no plurality, vacancy or no vacancy), but is merely a civil injury.

SPOLETO

Pages 218-219

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the marquisate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a> and duchy of Urbino, on the east by Farther Abruzzo, on the south by Sabina and the patrimony of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORVIETO">Orvieto</a> and Perugino. It is about 55 miles in length and 40 in breadth. It was anciently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Umbria, and now belongs to the pope.—The name of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is also Spoleto. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but in 1793 was ruined by an earthquake; from whence it has never recovered itself.

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a foot consisting of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> syllables, as omnis.

SPONDIAS

Pages 219-219

Brazilian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jamaica Plum, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of decandria. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SPONGIA

Pages 219-219

Sponge; a genus of animals belonging to the class of vermes, and order of zoophyta. It is fixed, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, and very torpid, growing in a variety of forms, composed either of reticulated fibres, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> masses of small spines interwoven together, and clothed with a living gelatinous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, full of small mouths or holes on its surface, by which it sucks in and throws out the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Fifty <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> have already been discovered, of which 10 belong to the British coasts. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. So early as the days of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> sponges were supposed to possess animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; the persons employed in collecting them having observed them shrink when torn from the rocks, thus exhibiting symptoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. The same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> prevailed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Pliny: But no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was paid to this subject till <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Marigliani examined them, and declared them vegetables. Dr Peyronell, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> which he sent to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in the year 1752, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1757, affirmed they were not vegetables, but the production of animals; and Spengia has accordingly described the animals, and the processes which they performed in making the sponges. Mr Eliotwood, in the year 1762, was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to discover these animals. For this purpose he dissected the sponge urens, and was surprised to find a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> of the genus of nemertes or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> colopendra, which had pierced their way through the soft substance of the sponge in quest of a safe retreat. That this was really the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, he was fully assured of, by inspecting a number of specimens of the same sort of sponge, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> fresh from the sea. He put them into a glass filled with seawater; and then, instead of seeing any of the little animals which Dr Peyronell described, he observed the papillae or small holes with which the papillae are surrounded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> and dilate themselves. He examined another variety of the same species of sponge, and plainly perceived the small tubes inspire and expire the water. He therefore concluded, that the sponge is an animal, and that the ends or openings of the branched tubes are the mouths by which it receives its nourishment, and discharges its excrements.

SPORADIC DISEASES

among physicians, are such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> particular persons at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> season, and in any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they are distinguished from epidemical and endemical diseases.
