SPOTSWOOD

Pages 219-220

John, archbishop of St Andrew's in Scotland, was descended from the lairds of Spotswood in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERSE">Merse</a>, and was born in the year 1565. He was educated in the university of Glasgow, and succeeded his father in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Calder when but 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In 1621 he attended Lodowick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lennox as his chaplain, in an embassy to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France for confirming the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> amity between the two nations, and returned in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>'s retinue through England. When he entered into the archbishopric of Glasgow, he found there was not 100l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> of yearly revenue left; yet such was his care for his successors, that he greatly improved it, and much to the satisfaction of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>. After having filled this see 11 years, he was raised to that of St Andrew's in 1615, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> and metropolitan of all Scotland. He presided in several assemblies for restoring the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and bringing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of uniformity with that of England. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. nor was he less valued by SPR King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I, who was crowned by him in 1633, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>-church of Holyroodhouse. In 1635, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Kinnoch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of Scotland, our primate was advanced to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>; but had scarcely held it four years, when the confusions beginning in Scotland, he was obliged to retire into England; and being broken with age, grief, and sickness, died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1639, and was interred in Westminster-abbey. He wrote A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Church of Scotland from the year 203 to the reign of King James VI. in folio.

SPRAT

Pages 220-220

Dr Thomas, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, was born in 1616. He had his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and after the Restoration entered into holy orders. He became fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, chaplain to George <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, and chaplain in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. In 1667 he published the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Royal Society, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Mr Cowley; who, by his last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, left to his care his printed works and MSS. which were accordingly published by him. In 1668 he was installed prebendary of Westminster; in 1682, was appointed canon of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>; in 1683, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Westminster; and in 1684, consecrated to the bishopric of Rochester. He was clerk of the closet to King Jas. II.; in 1685, was made dean of the chapel royal; and the year following, was appointed one of the commissioners for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs. In 1692 his lordship, with several other persons, was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> by two men, who drew up an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, in which they whose names were subscribed declared their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to restore King James; to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, dead <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alive; and to be ready with 30,000 men to meet King James when he should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. To this they put the names of Sancroft, Sprat, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, and others. The bishop was arrested, and kept at a messenger's under a strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, for eleven days. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was searched, and his papers seized, among which nothing was found of treasonable appearance, except one memorandum, in the following words: Thorough-paced doctrine. Being asked at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> the meaning of the words, he said that, about 20 years before, curiosity had led him to hear Daniel Burgels preach; and that being struck with his account of a certain kind of doctrine, which he said entered at one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, and pacing through the head went out at the other, he had inserted the memorandum in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-book, that he might not lose the substance of so strange a sermon. His innocence being proved, he was set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, when he published an account of his examination and deliverance; which made such an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> upon him, that he commemorated it through life by an yearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of thanksgiving. He lived to the 79th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and died May 20, 1713. His works, besides a few poems of little value, are, "The History of the Royal Society;" "The Life of Cowley;" "The Answer to Sorbiere;" "The History of the Rye-house Plot;" "The Relation of his own Examination;" and a volume of "Sermons." Dr Johnson says, "I have heard it observed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> justness, that every book is of a different kind, and that each has its distinct and characteristic excellence." SPRAT. See CLupea, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SPRAY

Pages 220-220

the sprinkling of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which is driven from the top of a wave in stormy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. It differs from foam-drift, as being only blown occasionally from the broken surface of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wave; whereas the latter continues to fly horizontally along the sea, without intermission, during the excess of a tempest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hurricane.

SPRING

Pages 223-223

Ver., in cosmography, denotes one of the seasons of the year; commencing, in the northern parts of the world, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> enters the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Aries, which is about the 16th day of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and ending when the sun leaves Gemini; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, more strictly and generally, the spring begins on the day when the distance of the sun's meridian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> from the zenith, being on the increase, is at a medium between the greatest and least. The end of the spring coincides with the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. See Summer. Elater SPRING, in Physics, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> or endeavour of certain bodies, to return to their first state, after having been violently put out of it by compressing, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> them. This faculty is, by philosophers, usually denominated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> force, or elasticity. SPRING-Tide. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Tide. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">SPRINGS</a>. See Burning-Springs.

SPRIT

Pages 223-223

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pole which crosses the sail of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> diagonally, from the mast to the upper hindmost corner of the sail, which it is used to extend and elevate; the lower end of the sprit rests in a sort of wreath or collar called the smother, which encircles the mast in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. SPRITSAIL. See Sail and Ship. SPRITSAIL-Topsail. See Sail and Ship. SPRUCE-TREE. See Pinus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SPRUCE-Beer, a cheap and wholesome liquor, which is thus made: Take of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> 16 gallons, and boil the half of it. Put the water thus boiled, while in full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to the reserved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, which should be previously put into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> or other vessel; then add 16 pounds of treacle or molasses, with a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> spoonfuls of the essence of spruce, stirring the whole well together; add half a pint of yeast, and keep it in a temperate situation, with the bung hole open, for two days, till the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> be abated. Then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> it up or bottle it off, and it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be fit for being drunk in a few days afterwards. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and perhaps in other countries, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spruce-firs abound, instead of adding the essence of the spruce at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with the molasses, they make a decoction of the leaves and small branches of these trees, and find the liquor equally good. It is a powerful antiscorbutic, and may prove very useful in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> voyages.

SPUN-YARN

Pages 223-223

among sailors, is a kind of line made from rope yarn, and used for seizing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fastening things together. SPUNK. See Boletus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SPUNGING

Pages 223-223

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, the cleaning of the inside of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> with a sponge, in order to prevent any sparks of fire from remaining in it, which would endanger the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of him that should load it again.

SQUADRON

Pages 223-223

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, denotes a body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> whose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men is not fixed; but is usually from 100 to 200. SQUADRON of Ships, either implies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of ships employed on any particular expedition, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a naval armament.

SQUADS

Pages 223-223

in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, are certain divisions of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> into so many squads, generally into three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of forming companies into as many squads of inspection as it has sergeants and corporals, is proved by those regiments who have practised that method; as by it the irregularity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> is considerably restrained, their dress improved, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the regiment in general most remarkably forwarded. Every officer should have a roll of his company by squads.

SQUALL

Pages 223-223

a sudden and violent blast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, usually occasioned by the interruption and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVERBERATION">reverberation</a> of the wind from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. These are very frequent in the Mediterranean, particularly that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it which is known by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, as produced by the repulsion and new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> which the wind meets with in its passage between the various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Archipelago.

SQUALUS

Pages 223-223

the Shark; a genus of fishes arranged by Linnaeus under the class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHIBIA">amphibia</a>, and the order of nantes, but by Gmelin referred to the class of pisces, and order of chondropterygi. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. SQUAMARIA. See Lathrea, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

SQUAMOUS

Pages 223-223

in Anatomy, a name given to the spurious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> false sutures of the skull, because composed of squamas or scales like those of fishes.

SQUARE

Pages 223-229

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRILATERAL">quadrilateral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> both equilateral and equangular. See Geometry. SQUARE-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">Roof</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, No. 33, and 34. Hollow SQUARE, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a body of foot drawn. drawn up with an empty space in the middle, for the colours, drums, and baggage, faced and covered by the pikes every way to keep off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. Square, among Mechanic, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> consisting of two rules <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> branches, fastened perpendicularly at one end of their extremities, so as to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>. It is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and laying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> perpendiculars. T Square, or Tee Square, an instrument used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, so called from its resemblance to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> T. Square-Rigged, an epithet applied to a ship whose yards are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It is also used in contradistinction to all vessels whose sails are extended by stays or lateen-yards, or by booms and gaffs; the usual situation of which is nearly in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>; and hence, Square-Sail, is a sail extended to a yard which hangs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, as distinguished from the other sails which are extended by booms and stays placed obliquely. This sail is only used in fair winds, or to fend under in a tempest. In the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is furnished with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a>, which is then attached to its bottom, and removed when it is necessary to scud. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCUDDING">Scudding</a>. Squaring, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATURE">Quadrature</a> of the Circle, signifies the finding a square exactly equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of a given circle. This problem however has not been, and probably cannot be, strictly resolved by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> admitted principles of geometry; mathematicians having hitherto been unable to do more than to find a square that shall differ from the area of any proposed circle by as small a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> as they please. The quadrature of the circle is a problem of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of difficulty, and indeed may be regarded as identical with another geometrical problem, namely, the Rectification of the circle, or the finding a straight line equal to its circumference; for the area of a circle is equal to that of a rectangle contained by the radius and a straight line equal to half the circumference (Geometry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. VI. Prop. 3.) therefore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a straight line exactly equal to the circumference could be found, a rectilineal space precisely equal to the area might also be found, and the contrary. But although no perfectly accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the problem has been obtained under either form, we can always find approximate values of the area and circumference; and therefore it is now customary to apply the terms quadrature and rectification of the circle also to these. The problem of the quadrature of the circle appears to have engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of geometers at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; for we are told that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>, who lived about 500 years before Christ, attempted its solution while confined in prison on account of his philosophical opinions. We are ignorant of the result of his researches; but although we cannot suppose they were attended with any success, we may reasonably conclude that we are indebted to them for the discovery of some of the properties of the figure, which are now known as elementary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> in geometry. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> of Chios was likewise engaged in trying to resolve the same problem, and it was no doubt in the course of his inquiries into this subject that he discovered the quadrature of the curvilinear space, which is now known by the name of the Lune of Hippocrates. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this discovery may be briefly explained as follows. Let ABCD be a circle (Plate D. fig. 1.), H its centre, AC its diameter, ADC a triangle <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, having its sides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">AD</a>, DC equal to one another. On D as a centre, with DA or DC as a radius, let the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> AEC be described, then shall the curvilinear space bounded by the semicircle ABC and the quadrant arch AEC (which is the Lune of Hippocrates) be equal to the rectilineal triangle ADC. For because circles are to one another as the squares of the radii (Geometry, Sect. VI. Prop. 4.) the circle having DA for its radius <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be to the circle having HA for its radius as the square of DA to the square of HA, that is, as 2 to 1; hence the former of these circles will be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the latter, and consequently one fourth of the former will be equal to one half of the latter; that is, the quadrant AEC will be equal to the semicircle ABC; from these equals take away the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> space bounded by the diameter AC and the arch AEC, and there will remain the triangle ADC equal to the luneal space AECBA. Although Hippocrates's discovery has led to no important conclusion either relating to the quadrature of the circle or that of any other curve, yet at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was made it might be regarded as of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, chiefly because it showed the possibility of exhibiting a rectilineal figure equal to a space bounded by curved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, a thing which we have reason to suppose was then done for the first time, and might have been fairly doubted, considering the insuperable difficulty that was found to attend the quadrature of the circle or its rectification. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> speaks of two persons, viz. Bryson and Antiphon, who about his time, or a little earlier, were occupied with the quadrature of the circle. The former appears, according to the testimony of Alexander Apollonius, to have erred most egregiously; he having concluded that the circumference was exactly 3\(\frac{1}{7}\) times the diameter. And the latter seems to have proceeded pretty much in the same manner as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> afterwards did in squaring the parabola, that is, by first inscribing a square in the circle, then an inscribed triangle in each of the segments of the curve, having for its base a side of the square; and next again a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of triangles in the segments, having for their bases the sides of the former series, and so on: this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of procedure however, could not be attended with any success, as it is well known that the spaces thus formed do not, as in the case of the parabola, admit of being absolutely summed. It may naturally be supposed that Archimedes exerted his utmost efforts to resolve this problem; and probably it was only after long meditation on the subject that he lost all hopes of success, and contented himself with that approximation to the ratio of the diameter to the circumference which is contained in his treatise De Circuli Dimensione, which has been preserved from the period in which he wrote, about 250 years before Christ, to the present times. He found his approximation to the ratio, by supposing a regular polygon of 96 sides to be described about the circle, and another of the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sides to be inscribed in it, and by showing that the perimeter of the circumscribing polygon was less than \(3\frac{1}{7}\), or \(3\frac{1}{7}\) times the diameter, but that the perimeter of the inscribed figure was greater than \(3\frac{1}{7}\) times the Squaring the diameter; now the circumference of the circle being 1/6 than the perimeter of the one polygon but greater than that of the other, it follows that the circumference must be less than \(3\frac{1}{7}\) times the diameter, but greater than \(3\frac{4}{7}\) times; so that, taking the first of these limits as being expressed by the smallest numbers, the circumference will be to the diameter as \(3\frac{1}{7}\) to 1, or as 22 to 7 nearly. Although the approximate ratio investigated by Archimedes be the oldest known to have been found in the western world, yet one more accurate seems to have been known at a much earlier period in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. This we learn from the Institutes of Akbar (Ayeen Akberry) where it is said that the Hindoos suppose the diameter of a circle to be to its circumference as 1250 to 3927. Now this ratio, which is the same as that of 1 to 3.1416, when found in the simplest and most elementary manner must have required the inscription of a polygon of 768 sides in the circle, and must have been attended with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> extractions of the square root, each carried as far as ten places of figures. We learn from Simplicius that Nicomedes and Apollonius both attempted to square the circle, the former by means of a curve which he called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUADRATRIX">Quadratrix</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of which, however, is ascribed to Dinostratus, and the latter also by the help of a curve denominated the slitter to the tortuous line or spiral, and which was probably no other than the quadratrix of Dinostratus; the nature of which, and the manner of its application to the subject in question, we shall briefly explain. Let AFB be a quadrant of a circle (fig. 2.) and C its centre; and conceive the radius CF to revolve uniformly about C from the position CA until at last it coincide with CB; while at the same time a line DG is carried with an uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> from A towards CB; the former line continuing always parallel to the latter, until at last they coincide; both motions being supposed to begin and end at the same instant. Then the point E in which the revolving radius CF and the moveable line DG intersect one another will <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> a certain curve line AEH, which is the Quadratrix of Dinostratus. Draw EK, FL both perpendicular to CB; then because the radius AC and the quadrant arch AFB are uniformly <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the same time by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> D and F, the contemporaneous spaces described will have to one another the same ratio as the whole spaces; that is, AD : AF :: AC : <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>; hence we have AC : AB :: DC, or EK : FB. Now as the moveable point F approaches to B, the ratio of the straight line EK to the arch FB will approach to, and will manifestly be ultimately the same as the ratio of the straight line EK to the straight line FL, which again is equal to the ratio of CE to CF; therefore the ratio of the radius AC to the quadrant arch AFB is the limit of the ratio of CE to CF, and consequently equal to the ratio of CH to CB, H being the point in which the quadratrix meets CB. Since therefore CH : CB :: CA or CB : quad. arch AFB, if by any means we could determine the point H, we might then find a straight line equal to the quadrant arch, (by finding a third <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to CH and CB) and consequently a straight line equal to the circumference. The point H, however, cannot be determined by a geometrical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and therefore all the ingenuity evinced by the person who first thought of this method of rectifying the circle (which certainly is considerable) has been unavailing. The Arabs, who succeeded the Greeks in the cultivation of the sciences, would no doubt have their pretended squarers of the circle. We however know nothing more than that some one of them believed he had discovered that the diameter being unity, the circumference was the square root of 10; a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> mistake; for the square root of 10 exceeds 3.162; but Archimedes had demonstrated that the circumference was less than 3.143. It appears that, even during the dark ages, some attempts were made at the solution of this famous problem, which however have always remained in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> buried in the dust of old <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>. But upon the revival of learning the problem was again agitated by different writers, and particularly by the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> De Cufa, who distinguished himself by his unfortunate attempt to resolve it. His mode of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, which had no <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation in geometry, led him to conclude, that if a line equal to the sum of the radius of a circle and the side of its inscribed square were made the diameter of another circle, and an equilateral triangle were inscribed in this last, the perimeter of this triangle would be equal to the circumference of the other circle. This pretended quadrature of the cardinal's was refuted by Regiomontanus; and indeed the task was not difficult; for, according to his construction, the diameter being 1, the circumference was greater than \(3\frac{1}{7}\); a conclusion which must be absurd, seeing that Archimedes had demonstrated that it must be less than that number. It would be trespassing too much upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> of our readers, were we to mention all the absurd and erroneous attempts which have been made during the last three centuries to square the circle. In a supplement to Montucla's excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, Histoire des Mathematiques, we find upwards of forty pretenders to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this discovery enumerated. These were almost all very ignorant of geometry; and many of them were wild visionaries, pretending to discover inexplicable relations between the plain truths of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and the most mysterious doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. If those who have sought the quadrature of the circle had been previously initiated in the doctrines of geometry, although they missed attaining the object they had in view, yet they could not have failed to have extended the boundaries of the science by the discovery of many new propositions. From such persons, however, as have generally pursued this inquiry, no improvement whatever of the science was to be expected; although, indeed, in some instances, it has derived advantage from the labours of such as have undertaken to expose the absurdity of their conclusions; as in the case of Metius, who in refuting the quadrature of one Simon à Picquet, found a much nearer approximation to the ratio of the diameter to the circumference than had been previously known, at least in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, viz., that of 113 to 355, which reduced to decimals is the same as the ratio of 1 to 3.1415929, differing from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> only in the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of decimals. Among the most remarkable of those who have recorded their own folly by publishing erroneous resolutions of the problem, we may reckon the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger. Full of self-conceit, he believed that, enterings, Squaring. tering upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of geometry, he could not fail to surmount by the force of his genius those obstacles which had completely foiled the progress of all preceding inquirers. He gave the result of his meditations to the world in 1592, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Nova Cyclomeria; but he was refuted by Clavius, by Vieta, and others, who showed that the magnitude he had assigned to the circumference was a little less than the perimeter of the inscribed polygon of 192 sides, which proved beyond a doubt that he was wrong. Scaliger, however, was not to be convinced of the absurdity of his conclusion; and indeed, in almost every instance, pretenders to this discovery have not been more remarkable for their folly in committing absurd blunders, than for their obstinacy in maintaining that they were in the right, and all who held a contrary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>. The famous Hobbes came also upon the field about the year 1650, with pretensions not only to the quadrature of the circle, but also to the trisection of an angle, the rectification of the parabola, &c.; but his pretended solutions were refuted by Dr Wallis. And this circumstance afforded him occasion to write not only against geometers, but even against the science of geometry itself. We find it recorded by Montucla, as a sort of phenomenon, that one Richard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, an English Jesuit, having happened upon what he conceived to be a quadrature of the circle, which he published under the title, Chrysaëpsis seu Quadratura Circuli, suffered himself at last to be convinced by some of his friends that he was wrong both in his quadrature of the circle, and in his rectification of the spiral. But a solution of the same problem found out by one Mathulen of Lyons, did not produce in the end so much advantage to its author. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in 1728 announced to the learned world that he had discovered both the quadrature of the circle and a perpetual motion; and he was so certain of the truth of these discoveries, that he consigned 1000 ecus (about 125l.) to be paid to any one who should demonstrate that he was deceived in either. The task was not difficult. Nicole of the Academy of Sciences demonstrated that he was wrong, and he himself allowed it; but he hesitated to pay the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which Nicole had relinquished in favour of the Hôtel Dieu of Lyons. The affair went before a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, which adjudged the money to be paid, as Nicole had defined it, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. At a later period, viz. in 1753, the Chevalier de Caufans, a French officer, and a man who was never expected to be a mathematician, suddenly found a quadrature of the circle in procuring a circular piece of turf to be cut; and rising from one truth to another, he explained by his quadrature the doctrine of original sin, and the Trinity. He engaged himself by a public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to deposit with a notary the sum of 300,000 francs, to be wagered against such as should oppose him, and he actually lodged 10,000, which were to devolve to him who should demonstrate his error. This was easily done, as it resulted from his discovery that a circle was equal to its circumference square, that is, a part to the whole! Some persons came forward to answer his challenge, and in particular a young lady sued him at one of the courts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> judged that the Chevalier's fortune ought not to suffer on account of his whim; for, setting aside this piece of folly, in every other respect he was a worthy man. The procedure was therefore foiled, and the wager declared void. We shall not enter farther into the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of these vain and absurd attempts to resolve this important problem, but proceed to state what has actually been done by men of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> minds and real mathematical acquirements towards its solution. And in the first place it may be observed that the problem admits of being propounded under two different forms: for it may be required to find either the area of the whole circle, or, which is the same thing, the length of the whole circumference; or else to find the area of any proposed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a> or segment, or, which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>, the length of the arch of the sector or segment. The former is termed the definite and the latter the indefinite quadrature of the circle. The latter evidently is more general than the former, and includes it as a particular case. Now if we could find by any means a finite algebraic equation that should express the relation between any proposed arch of a circle, and some known straight line, or lines, the magnitude of one or more of which depended on that arch, then we would have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> rectification of the arch, and consequently a rectification or quadrature also of the whole circle. We here speak of an analytical solution of the problem; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, however, who were almost entirely ignorant of this branch of mathematical science, must have endeavoured to treat it entirely upon geometrical principles. It is now well known, however, that all geometrical problems may be subjected to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>; and that it is only by such a mode of proceeding they have in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> been resolved. With respect to the definite quadrature of the circle, it is commonly understood that no unexceptionable demonstration of its impossibility has hitherto been published. It is true that James Gregory, in his vera circuli et Hyperbolae quadratura, has given what he considered as such a demonstration; but it has been objected to, particularly by Huygens, one of the best geometers of his time. We are, however, certain that the ratio of the diameter to the circumference, as also, that the ratio of the square of the diameter to the square of a straight line equal to the circumference, cannot be expressed by rational numbers, for this has been strictly demonstrated by Lambert, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> for 1761. A demonstration is also given in Legendre's Geometrie. As to the indefinite quadrature, if Newton's demonstration of the 28th lemma of the first book of his Principia be correct, the thing ought to be absolutely impossible. For the object of that proposition is to prove that in no oval figure whatever, that returns into itself, can the area cut off by straight lines at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> be universally found by an equation of a finite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a>, and composed of a finite number of terms. If this be true, then it will be impossible to express any sector of a circle taken at pleasure in finite terms. It is however to be remarked, that the accuracy of the reasoning by which Newton has attempted to establish the truth of the general proposition has been questioned by no less a geometer than D'Alembert; and indeed we know one oval curve, which returns into itself, and which according to Newton's proposition ought therefore not to admit of an indefinite quadrature; yet this is by no means the case, for it does really admit of such a quadrature. The curve we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> is the lemniscata, the equation of which is \((x^2+y^2)^2=ax(x^2-y^2)\), where \(x\) and \(y\) denote its coordinates. squaring ordinates, and \(a\) is put for a given line. The figure of the curve is nearly that of the numeral character 8. Upon the whole then we may infer that an unexceptionable demonstration of the impossibility of expressing either the whole circle, or any propoed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> of it, by a finite equation, is still among the desiderata of mathematics. We come now to speak of the different methods which have been found for approximating to the area or the circumference. We have already noticed the approximation to the ratio of the diameter to the circumference found by Archimedes, and the earlier and more accurate approximation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> mathematicians. Archimedes' ratio is the only one found by the ancients in the western world that has descended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, and it appears to have been the most accurate known, until about the year 1535, when Metius, in refuting a pretended quadrature, found the more accurate ratio of \(\frac{11}{7}\) to \(\frac{355}{113}\), as we have already noticed. About the same time Vieta, and Adrianus Romanus published their ratios expressed in decimals, the former carrying the approximation to ten decimals instead of six, (which was the number of accurate figures expressed by Metius's ratio), and the latter extending it to 17 figures. Vieta also gave a kind of series, which being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to infinity, gave the value of the circle. These approximations, however, were far exceeded by that of Ludolph Van Ceulen, who in a work published in Dutch in 1610, carried it as far as 36 figures, showing that if the diameter were unity, the circumference would be greater than \(3.141592653589793\ldots\), but less than the same number with the last figure increased by an unit. This work was translated into Latin by Snellius, and published under the title, *De Circulo et <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPERBOLA">Hyperbola</a> Quadratura*. In finding this approximation, Van Ceulen followed the method of Archimedes, doubling continually the number of sides of the inscribed and circumscribed polygons, until at length he found two which differed only by an unit in the 36th place of decimals in the numbers expressing their perimeters. This, however, must have been rather a work of patience than of genius; and indeed the labour must have been prodigious. He seems to have valued highly this singular effort, for in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Archimedes, whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> was adorned with a sphere and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, in commemoration of his discovery of the proportion which these solids bear to one another, he requested that the ratio he had found might be inscribed on his tomb, which was accordingly done.

STAFF

Pages 236-236

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> ordinarily used to rest on in walking. The staff is also frequently used as a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> weapon both of offence and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; and for several other purposes. Staff, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pole erected in different parts of a ship, whereon to hoist and display the colours. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these is reared immediately over the stern, to display the ensign; another is fixed on the bowsprit, to extend the jack; three more are erected at the three mast heads, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> formed by their upper ends, to show the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> or pendant of the respective squadron or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> to which the ship is appropriated. See Ensign, Mast, Jack, and Pendant. Staff, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> matters, consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>-general, adjutant-general, and majors of brigade. The staff properly exists only in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. See Quarter-Master General, &c. Regimental Staff, consists in the adjutant, quarter-master, chaplain, surgeon, &c. Staff, in music, five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, on which, with the intermediate spaces, the notes of a song or piece of music are marked. Fore-Staff. See Fore Staff.

STAFFA

Pages 236-236

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> of Scotland, remarkable for its basaltic pillars. It was visited by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, who communicated the following account of it to Mr Pennant. "The little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Staffa lies on the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, about three leagues <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONA">Iona</a>, or Icolmkill: its greatest length is about an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, and its breadth about half a one. On the east side of the island is a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> where boats generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>; a little to the southward of which the first appearance of pillaris is to be observed; they are small; and instead of being placed upright, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on their sides, each forming a segment of a circle. From thence you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a small cave, above which the pillars, now grown a little larger, are inclining in all directions: in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in particular, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of them very much resembles the ribs of a ship. From hence having passed the cave, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it is not low-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, you must do in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, you come to the first range of pillars, which are still not above half as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as those a little beyond. Over against this place is a small island, called in Esse Boo-fha-la, separated from the main by a channel not many fathoms wide. This whole island is composed of pillars without any stratum above them; they are still small, but by much the nearest formed of any about the place. "The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the island, for at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water it is divided into two, makes a kind of a cone, the pillars converging together towards the centre: on the other they are in general laid down flat: and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> next to the main, you see how beautifully they are packed together, their ends coming out <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> which they form. All these have their transverse sections exact, and their surfaces smooth; which is by no means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the large ones, which are cracked in all directions. I must question, however, if any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this whole island of Boo-fha-la is two feet in diameter. "The main island opposite to Boo-fha-la, and farther towards the north-west, is supported by ranges of pillars pretty erect, and, though not tall (as they are not uncovered to the base), of large diameters; and at their feet is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> pavement, made by the upper sides of such as have been broken off, which extends as far under water as the eye can reach. Here the forms of the pillars are apparent; there are of three, four, five, six, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sides; but the numbers of five and six are by much the most prevalent. The largest I measured was of seven; it was four feet five inches in diameter. "The surfaces of these large pillars, in general, are rough and uneven, full of cracks in all directions; the transverse figures in the upright ones never fail to run in their true directions. The surfaces upon which we walked were often flat, having neither concavity nor convexity; the larger <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, however, was concave, though some were very evidently convex. In some places, the interstices within the perpendicular figures were filled up with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>: in one place, a vein passed in among the mass of pillars, carrying here and there small threads of spar. Though they were broken and cracked through in all directions, yet their perpendicular figures might easily be traced: from whence it is easy to infer, that whatever the accident might have been that caused the dillocation, it happened after the formation of the pillars. "From hence proceeding along shore, you arrive at Fingal's cave. Its dimensions I have given in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: | Length of the cave from the rock without | Feet. | |-----------------------------------------|-------| | From the pitch of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> | 371 | | Breadth | 6 | Footnotes: [1] <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">Stadtholder</a> had in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> his representatives, who had the first place and the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in all the councils, and the first of whom was always first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of their high mightinesses. In 1749 the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> stadtholder was created by the states-general, governor-general and supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the East and West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> companies; dignities which gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of authority and power, and which had never been conferred upon any of his predecessors, nor had they hitherto been made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. He had his representatives in the several chambers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and chose their directors out of a nomination of three qualified persons. The prince enjoyed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> in Zealand from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his elevation to the stadtholderate. The revenues of the stadtholderate of the seven United Provinces were reckoned (including the 25,000 guilders which the prince enjoyed annually as the first member of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state, and what he had from the India company's dividends) to amount to 300,000 guilders a-year. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-general of the union, his serene highness had 120,000 guilders per annum; besides 24,000 from Friesland, and 12,000 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of captain-general of those provinces. In times of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> the state allowed extraordinary sums to the captain-general for the expense of every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. All these powers and privileges were held by the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> previous to the revolutionary war of France. The influence of the usurper of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> has extended to the states of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and attached them as a province to France under the name of a kingdom, at the head of which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Bonaparte. STÆHELINA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of syngenesia, and order of polygamy aquilis; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 49th order, Compositae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STAFFORD

Pages 237-237

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 5. N. Lat. 53. 0. It stands on the river Sow, has two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches, a fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and a flourishing cloth-manufacture. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and is 135 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>.

STAFFORDSHIRE

Pages 237-238

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, by Cheshire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a> and Derbyshire on the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a> and Cheshire on the west. The length is reckoned 62 miles, the breadth 33, and the circumference 180. It contains five <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, 150 parishes, 810,000 acres, 18 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 4 K. inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, except in those parts that are called the Moorlands and Woodlands, and about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, is good, especially upon the hills, where it is accounted very fine. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in the northern mountainous parts is not fertile; but in the middle, where it is watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, the third river in England, it is both fruitful and pleasant, being a mixture of arable and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> grounds. In the south, it abounds not only with corn, but with mines of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and pits of coal. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of this county, besides the Trent, which runs almost through the middle of it, and abounds with salmon, are the Dove and Tame, both of which are well stored with fish. In this county are also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and meres <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pools, as they are called; which, having streams either running into them or from them, cannot be supposed to be of any great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> to the air; they yield plenty of fish. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of the county are medicinal waters, impregnated with different sorts of minerals, and consequently of different qualities and virtues; as those at Hints and Bredfordhouse, which are mixed with bitumen; those at Ingleside, Codswalwood, and Willoughbridge <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>, which are sulphureous. Of the saline kind are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRINE">Brine</a>-pits at Chertley, Epson, Pensnet-clofe, of which very good <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is made. There is a well at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>-under-Lyme that is said to cure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s evil; another called Elderswell near Blemhill, said to be good for sore eyes; and a third called the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPA">Spa</a>, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLVERHAMPTON">Wolverhampton</a>. Great flocks of sheep are bred in this county, especially in the moorlands, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it; but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is said to be somewhat coarser than that of many other counties. Of this wool, however, they make a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, particularly felts. In the low grounds along the rivers are rich pastures for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle; vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> and cheese are made. In the middle and southern parts not only grain of all kinds, but a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> are raised. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> produces also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, iron; marble, alabaster, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>; coal, salt, and marbles of several sorts and colours; brick-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, fullers earth, and potters clay, particularly a sort used in the glass manufacture at Amblecot, and sold at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>-pence a bushel; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pipe clay; a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-clay earth called slip, used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> divers vessels; red and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> ochres; fire-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> for hearths of iron furnaces, ovens, &c.; iron-stones of several sorts; bloodstones, or haematites, found in the brook <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">Tent</a>, which, when wet a little, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> draw red <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> like ruddle; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>-stones, and grind-stones. For <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> the country is well supplied with turf, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>, and coal of several sorts, as cannel-coal, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>-coal, and pit-coal. The peacock-coal is so called, because, when turned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it displays all the colours of the peacock's tail; but it is fitter for the forge than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>. Of the pit-coal there is an inexhaustible store: it burns into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> ashes, and leaves no such cinder as that of the Newcastle coal. It is not used for malting till it is charred, and in that state it makes admirable winter-fuel for a chamber. This county is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Lichfield and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> circuit. It sends ten members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; namely, two for the county, two for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lichfield, two for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, two for Newcastle-under-Lyme, and two for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TAMWORTH">Tamworth</a>. STAG. See Cervus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. STAG-Beetle. See Lucanus, Entomology Index.

STAGE

Pages 238-238

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> drama, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and representation, included between the pit and the scenes, and answering to the proscenium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pulpitum of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">Playhouse</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a>. STAGGERS. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STAHL

Pages 238-238

GEORGE ERNEST, an eminent German chemist, was born in Franconia in 1665, and chosen professor of medicine at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, when a university was founded in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in 1694. The excellency of his lectures while he filled that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, the importance of his various publications, and his extensive practice, soon raised his reputation to a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height. He received an invitation to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> in 1716, which having accepted, he was made counsellor of state and physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. He died in 1734, in the 75th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Stahl is without doubt one of the greatest men of which the annals of medicine can boast; his name marks the commencement of a new and more illustrious era in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>. He was the author of the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLOGISTON">phlogiston</a>, which, though now completely overturned by the discoveries of Lavoisier and others, was not without its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; as it served to combine the scattered fragments of former chemists into a system, and as it gave rise to more accurate experiments and a more scientific view of the subject, to which many of the subsequent discoveries were owing. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> maintained its ground for more than half a century, and was received and supported by some of the most eminent men which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> has produced; a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the ingenuity and the abilities of its author. He was the author also of A Theory of Medicine, founded upon the notions which he entertained of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> dominion of mind over body; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, he affirmed, that every muscular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is a voluntary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the mind, whether attended with consciousness <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not. This theory he and his followers carried a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> too far, but the advices at least which he gives to attend to the state of the mind of the patient are worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of physicians. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Experimenta et Observationes Chymicae et Phylaceae, Berlin, 1731, 8vo. 2. Dissertations Medicinae, Hall, 2 vols 4to. This is a collection of theses. 3. Theoria Medica vera, 1737, 4to. 4. Opusculum Chymico-phylaceum, 1740, 4to. 5. A Treatise on Sulphur, both Inflammable and Fixed, written in German. 6. Negotium Otiolium, Hall, 1720, 4to. It is in this treatise chiefly that he establishes his system concerning the action of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> upon the body. 7. Fundamenta Chymicae Dogmatiae et Experimentalis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, 1747, 3 vols 4to. 8. A treatise on Salts, written in German. 9. Commentarium in Metallurgiam Becheri, 1723. STAINING or COLOURING OF BONE, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">HORN</a>, MARBLE, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">PAPER</a>, WOOD, &c. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>.

STAIRCASE

Pages 238-238

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, an ascent inclosed between walls, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a balustrade consisting of stairs or steps, with landing places and rails, serving to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the several stories of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. See Architecture, No 89, &c.

STALACTITES

Pages 238-238

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, crystalline spars formed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, conical, round, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> bodies, composed of various crusts, and usually found hanging in form of icicles from the roofs of grottoes, &c.

STALAGMITIS

Pages 238-239

a genus of the monocota order, belonging belonging to the polygamy class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricocca. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STALE

Pages 239-239

among sportmen, a living fowl put in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to allure and bring others where they may be taken. For want of these, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, his entrails taken out, and dried in an oven in his feathers, with a stick thrust through to keep it in a convenient posture, may serve as well as a live one. STALE is also a name for the urine of cattle. ANIMATED STALK. This remarkable animal was found by Mr Ives at Cuddalore; and he mentions several kinds of it; some appearing like dry straws tied together, others like grass; some have bodies much larger than others, with the addition of two fealy imperfect wings; their neck is no bigger than a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, but twice as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as their bodies; their heads are like those of a hare, and their eyes vertical and very bright. They live upon flies, and catch these insects very dexterously with the two fore-feet, which they keep doubled up in three parts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to their head, and dart out very quick on the approach of their prey; and when they have caught it, they eat it very voraciously, holding it in the same manner as a squirrel does its food. On the outer <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the fore-feet are several very sharp hooks for the easier catching and holding of their prey; while, with the other feet, which are four in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, they take hold of trees <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other thing, the better to surprise whatever they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in wait for. They drink like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, putting their mouths into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Their excrements, which are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, are almost as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the body of the animal, and as the natives say, dangerous to the eyes.

STALLION

Pages 239-239
or STONE-HORSE, in the manege, a horse designed for the covering of mares, in order to propagate the species. See Equus, Mammalia Index.

STAMFORD

Pages 239-239

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England; situated on the river Welland, on the edge of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, containing five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches, several good streets, and fine buildings. It had formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, the students of which removed to Brazen Nose college in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. It has no considerable manufactories, but deals chiefly in malt. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. c. 31. N. Lat. 54° 42'.

STAMINA

Pages 239-239

in the animal body, are defined to be those simple original parts which existed first in the embryo <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; and by whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, augmentation, and accretion by additional juices, the animal body at its utmost bulk is supposed to be formed.

STAMP-DUTIES

Pages 239-239

a branch of the perpetual revenue. See Revenue. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> there is a tax imposed upon all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, whereon any legal proceedings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> private instruments of almost any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> whatsoever are written; and also upon licences for retailing wines, of all denominations; upon all almanacs, newspapers, advertisements, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, dice, &c. These imposts are very various; being higher or lower, not so much according to the value of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> transferred, as according to the nature of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>. The highest do not exceed six pounds upon every sheet of paper or skin of parchment; and these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> duties <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> chiefly upon grants from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and upon certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> proceedings, without any regard to the value of the subject. There are in Great Britain no duties on the registration of deeds or writings, except the fees of the officers who keep the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>; and these are seldom more than a reasonable recompense for their labour. The crown derives no revenue from them. The stamp-duties constitute a tax which, though in some instances it may be heavily felt, by greatly increasing the expense of all mercantile as well as legal proceedings, yet (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> moderately imposed) is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the public in general, by authenticating instruments, and rendering it much more difficult than formerly to forge deeds of any standing; since, as the officers of this branch of the revenue vary their stamps frequently, by marks perceptible to none but themselves, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that would forge a deed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, must know and be able to counterfeit the stamp of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> also. In France and some other countries the duty is laid on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> itself, not on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in which it is contained; as, with us too in England (besides the stamps on the indentures), a tax is laid, by statute 8 Ann. c. 9, on every apprentice-fee; of 6d. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> if it be sold or under, and 1s. in the pound if a greater sum: but this tends to draw the subject into a thousand nice difficulties and disputes concerning the nature of his contract, and whether taxable or not; in which the farmers of the revenue are sure to have the advantage. Our general method answers the purposes of the state as well, and consults the ease of the subject much better. The first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the stamp duties was by statute 5 and 6 W. and M. c. 21, and they have since, in many instances, been increased to five times their original amount.

STANCHION

Pages 239-239
or STANCHIONS, a sort of small pillars of wood or iron used for various purposes in a ship; as to support the decks, the quarter-rails, the nettings, the awnings, &c. The first of these are two ranges of small columns fixed under the beams, throughout the ship's length between decks; one range being on the starboard and the other on the larboard side of the hatchways. They are chiefly intended to support the weight of the artillery.

STAND

Pages 239-239

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> from two hundred and an half to three hundred of pitch.
