STANHOPE PHILIP DORMER

Pages 239-241
earl of Chesterfield, was born in 1695, and educated in Trinity-hall, Cambridge; which place he left in 1714, when, by his own account, he was an absolute pedant. In this character he went abroad, where a familiarity with good company soon convinced him he was totally mistaken in almost all his notions: and an attentive study of the air, manner, and address of people of fashion, soon polished a man whose predominant desire was to please; and who, as it afterwards appeared, valued exterior accomplish- Lord Stanhope, he got an early seat in parliament; and in 1722, succeeded to his father's estate and titles. In 1728, and in 1745, he was appointed ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary to Holland; which high character he supported with the greatest dignity; serving his own country, and gaining the esteem of the states general. Upon his return from Holland, he was sent lord-lieutenant of Ireland; and during his administration there, gave general satisfaction to all parties. He left Dublin in 1746, and in October succeeded the earl of Harrington as secretary of state, in which post he officiated until February 6th 1748. Being seized with a deafness in 1732 that incapacitated him for the pleasures of society, he from that time led a private and retired life, amusing himself with books and his pen; in particular, he engaged largely as a volunteer in a periodical miscellaneous paper called *The World*, in which his contributions have a distinguished degree of excellence. He died in 1773, leaving a character for wit and abilities that had few equals. He distinguished himself by his eloquence in parliament on many important occasions; of which we have a characteristic instance, of his own relating. He was an active promoter of the bill for altering the style; on which occasion, as he himself writes in one of his letters to his son, he made so eloquent a speech in the house, that every one was pleased, and said he had made the whole very clear to them; "when (says he), God knows, I had not even attempted it. I could just as soon have talked Celtic or Sclavonian to them, as astronomy; and they would have understood me full as well." Lord Chesterfield, one of the greatest mathematicians in Europe, and who had a principal hand in framing the bill, spoke afterwards, with all the clearness that a thorough knowledge of the subject could dictate; but not having a flow of words equal to Lord Chesterfield, the latter gained the applause from the former, to the equal credit of the speaker and the auditors. The high character Lord Chesterfield supported during life, received no small injury soon after his death, from a fuller display of it by his own hand. He left no issue by his lady, but had a natural son, Philip Stanhope, Esq., whose education was for many years a close object of his attention, and who was afterward envoy extraordinary at the court of Dresden, but died before him. When Lord Chesterfield died, Mr Stanhope's widow published a course of letters, written by the father to the son, filled with instructions suitable to the different gradations of the young man's life to whom they were addressed. These letters contain many fine observations on mankind, and rules of conduct; but it is observable that he lays a greater stress on exterior accomplishments and address, than on intellectual qualifications and sincerity; and allows greater latitude to fashionable pleasures than good morals will justify, especially in paternal instructions. Hence it is that a celebrated writer, and of manners somewhat different from those of the polite earl of Chesterfield, is said to have observed of these letters, that "they inculcate only the morals of a whore, with the manners of a dancing-master." Dr John Stanhope, an eminent divine, was born at Hertfordshire in Derbyshire, in the year 1660. His father was rector of that place, vicar of St Margaret's church in Leicester, and chaplain to the earls of Chesterfield and Clare. His grandfather, Dr George Stanhope, was chaplain to James I. and Charles I.; had the chancellorship of York, where he was also a canon-rectory, held a prebend, and was rector of Welldrake in that county. He was for his loyalty driven from his home with eleven children; and died in 1642. Our author was sent to school, first to Uppingham in Rutland, then at Leicester; afterwards removed to Eaton; and thence chosen to King's college in Cambridge, in the place of W. Cleaver. He took the degree of B. A. in 1681; M. A. 1683; was elected one of the syndics for the university of Cambridge, in the bursaries of Alban Francis, 1687; minister of Quoi near Cambridge, and vice-proctor, 1688; was that year preferred to the rectory of Tring in Hertfordshire, which after some time he quitted. He was in 1689 presented to the vicarage of Lewisham in Kent by Lord Dartmouth, to whom he had been chaplain, and tutor to his son. He was also appointed chaplain to King William and Queen Mary, and continued to enjoy that honour under Queen Anne. He commenced D. D. July 5th 1697, performing all the offices required to that degree publicly and with great applause. He was made vicar of Deptford in 1703; succeeded Dr Hooper as dean of Canterbury the same year; and was thrice chosen prolocutor of the lower house of convocation. His uncommon diligence and industry, assisted by his excellent parts, enriched him with a large stock of polite, solid, and useful learning. His discourses from the pulpit were equally pleasing and profitable; a beautiful intermixture of the clearest reasoning with the purest diction, attended with all the graces of a just elocution. The good Christian, the solid divine, and the fine gentleman, in him were happily united. His conversation was polite and delicate, grave without preciseness, facetious without levity. His piety was real and rational, his charity great and unselfish, fruitful in acts of mercy, and in all good works. He died March 18th 1728, aged 68 years; and was buried in the chancel of the church at Lewisham. The dean was twice married: first to Olivia Cotton, by whom he had one son and four daughters. His second lady, who was sister to Sir Charles Wager, survived him, dying October 11th 1732, aged about 54. One of the dean's daughters was married to a son of Bishop Burnet. Bishop Moore of Ely died the day before Queen Anne; who, it has been said, designed our dean for that see when it should become vacant. Dr Felton says, "The late dean of Canterbury is excellent in the whole. His thoughts and reasoning are bright and solid. His style is just, both for the purity of the language and for the strength and beauty of expression; but the periods are formed in so peculiar an order of the words, that it was an observation, nobody could pronounce them with the same grace and advantage as himself." His writings, which are an inestimable treasure of piety and devotion are, A Paraphrase and Comment upon the Epistles and Gospels, 4 vols, 1753, 8vo. Sermons at Boyle's Lectures, 1756, 4to. Fifteen Sermons, 1750, 8vo. Twelve Sermons on several Occasions, 1727, 8vo. Thomas à Kempis, 1666, 8vo. Epictetus's Morals, with Simplicius's Comment, and the Life of Epictetus, 1700, 8vo. Parson's Christian Directory, 1716, 8vo. Rochefoucauld's Maxims, 1766, 8vo. A Funeral Sermon on Mr Richard Sare bookseller, 1724, two editions 4to. Twenty Sermons, published singly between Stanhope, between the years 1692 and 1724. Private Prayers Stanislaus for every Day in the Week, and for the several Parts of each Day; translated from the Greek Devotions of Bishop Andrews, with Additions, 1735. In his translations, it is well known, Dr Stanhope did not confine himself to a strict and literal version: he took the liberty of paraphrasing, explaining, and improving upon his author; as will evidently appear (not to mention any other work) by the slightest perusal of St Augustine's Meditations, and the Devotions of Bishop Andrews.

STANISLAUS LIECZINSKI

Pages 241-242
king of Poland, was born at Leopolis the 20th of October 1677. His father was a Polish nobleman, distinguished by his rank and the important offices which he held, but still more by his firmness and courage. Stanislaus was sent ambassador in 1704 by the assembly of Warsaw to Charles XII. of Sweden, who had conquered Poland. He was at that time 27 years old, was general of Great Poland, and had been ambassador extraordinary to the Grand Signior in 1699. Charles was so delighted with the frankness and sincerity of his deportment, and with the firmness and sweetness which appeared in his countenance, that he offered him the crown of Poland, and ordered him to be crowned at Warsaw in 1705. He accompanied Charles XII. into Saxony, where a treaty was concluded with King Augustus in 1705, by which that prince resigned the crown, and acknowledged Stanislaus king of Poland. The new monarch remained in Saxony with Charles till 1707, when they returned into Poland and attacked the Russians, who were obliged to evacuate that kingdom in 1708. But Charles being defeated by Peter the Great in 1709, Augustus returned into Poland, and being assisted by a Russian army, obliged Stanislaus to retire first into Sweden, and afterwards into Turkey. Soon after he took up his residence at Weissenburg, a town in Alsace. Augustus dispatched him his envoy to France to complain of this; but the duke of Orléans, who was then regent, returned this answer: "Tell your king, that France has always been the asylum of unhappy princes." Stanislaus lived in obscurity till 1725, when Louis XV. espoused the princess Mary his daughter. Upon the death of King Augustus in 1733, he returned to Poland in hopes of remounting the throne of that kingdom. A large party declared for him; but his competitor the young elector of Saxony, being supported by the emperor Charles VI. and the empress of Russia, was chosen king, though the majority was against him. Dantzig, to which Stanislaus had retired, was quickly taken, and the unfortunate prince made his escape in disguise with great difficulty, after hearing that a price was set upon his head by the Russians. When peace was concluded in 1736 between the emperor and France, it was agreed that Stanislaus should abdicate the throne, but that he should be acknowledged king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania, and continue to bear these titles during life; that all his effects and those of the queen his spouse should be restored; that an amnesty should be declared in Poland for all that was past, and that every person should be restored to his possessions, rights, and privileges: that the elector of Saxony should be acknowledged king of Poland by all the powers who acceded to the treaty; that Stanislaus should be put in peaceable possession of the duchies of Lorraine and Bar; but that immediately after his death these duchies should be united for ever to the crown of France. Stanislaus succeeded a race of Stanislaus princes in Lorraine, who were beloved and regretted; and his subjects found their ancient sovereigns revived in him. He took then the pleasure which he had so long desired, the pleasure of making men happy. He visited his new subjects; he embellished Nancy and Lunéville; he made useful establishments; he founded colleges and built hospitals. He was engaged in these noble employments, when an accident occasioned his death. His night-gown caught fire, and burnt him so severely before it could be extinguished, that he was seized with a fever, and died the 23rd of February 1766. His death occasioned a public mourning; the tears of his subjects indeed are the best eulogium upon this prince. In his youth he had accustomed himself to fatigue, and had thereby strengthened his mind as well as his constitution. He lay always upon a kind of mattress, and seldom required any service from his domestics. He was temperate, liberal, adored by his vassals, and perhaps the only nobleman in Poland who had any friends. He was in Lorraine what he had been in his own country; gentle, affable, compassionate, treating his subjects like equals, participating their sorrows and alleviating their misfortunes. He resembled completely the picture of a philosopher which he himself has drawn. "The true philosopher (said he) ought to be free from prejudices, and to know the value of reason: he ought neither to think the higher ranks of life of more value than they are, nor to treat the lower orders of mankind with greater contempt than they deserve: he ought to enjoy pleasures without being a slave to them, riches without being attached to them, honours without pride or vanity: he ought to support disgraces without either fearing or courting them: he ought to reckon what he possesses sufficient for him, and to regard what he has not as useless: he ought to be equal in every fortune, always tranquil, always gay: he ought to love order, and to observe it in all his actions: he ought to be severe to himself, but indulgent to others: he ought to be frank and ingenious without rudeness, polite without falsehood, complacent without baseness: he ought to have the courage to disregard every kind of glory, and to reckon as nothing even philosophy itself." Such was Stanislaus in every situation. His temper was affectionate. He told his treasurer one day to put a certain officer on his list, to whom he was very much attached: "In what quality (said the treasurer) shall I mark him down?" "As my friend" (replied the monarch). A young painter conceiving hopes of making his fortune if his talents were made known to Stanislaus, presented him with a picture, which the courtiers criticised severely. The prince praised the performance, and paid the painter very generously: then turning to his courtiers, he said, "Do ye not see, gentlemen, that this poor man must provide for his family by his abilities? if you discourage him by your censures, he is undone. We ought always to assist men; we never gain anything by hurting them." His revenues were small; but were we to judge of him by what he did, we should probably reckon him the richest potentate in Europe. A single instance will be sufficient to show the well-judged economy with which his benevolent plans were conducted. He gave 18,000 crowns to the magistrates of Bar to be employed in purchasing grain, when at a low price, to be sold out again to the poor at a moderate rate when Stanislaus the price should rise above a certain sum. By this arrangement (say the authors of Dictionnaire Histo- rique), the money increases continually, and its good effects may in a short time be extended over the whole province. He was a protector of the arts and sciences: he wrote several works of philosophy, politics, and morality, which were collected and published in France in 1765, in 4 vols, 8vo, under the title of Oeuvres de Philosophe Bien- faisant, "the works of the Benevolent Philosopher."

STANLEY

Pages 242-242

THOMAS, a learned English writer in the 17th century, was the son of Sir Thomas Stanley of Cumberlow-Green in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>. He was born at Cumberlow about 1644, and educated in his father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, whence he removed to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He afterwards travelled; and, upon his return to England, prosecuted his studies in the Middle Temple. He married, when young, Dorothy, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir James Engan of Flower, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>. He wrote, 1. A volume of Poems. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, and Lives of the Philosophers. 3. A Translation of Echylus, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a>; and several other works. He died in 1678.

STANNARIES

Pages 242-242

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and works where tin is dug and purified; as in Cornwall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, &c.

STANNARY COURTS

Pages 242-242

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> and Cornwall, for the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> among the miners therein. They are held before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-warden and his substitutes, in virtue of a privilege granted to the workers in the tin-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> there, to sue and be sued only in their own courts, that they may not be drawn from their benches, which is highly profitable to the public, by attending their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits in other courts. The privileges of the miners are confirmed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, 33 Edw. I. and fully expounded by a private statute, 50 Edw. III., which has since been explained by a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, 16 Car. I. c. 15. What relates to our present purpose is only this: That all miners and labourers in and about the stannaries shall, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their working therein, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONA">bona</a> fide, be privileged from suits of other courts, and be only pleaded in the stannary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in all matters, excepting pleas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and member. No writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> lies from hence to any court in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; as was agreed by all the judges, in 4 Jac. I. But an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lies from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of the court to the under-warden; and from him to the lord-warden; and thence to the privy-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Cornwall, when he hath had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of the same. And from thence the appeal lies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> himself, in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>.

STANZA

Pages 242-242

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> regularly adjusted to each other; so much of a poem as contains every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> relation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a> used in that poem.

STAPELIA

Pages 242-242

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class pentandria and order dignya, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> orders arranged under the Succulentae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.—This singular tribe of plants is peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> deserts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. They are extremely succulent. From this peculiarity of structure, the power of retaining <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to support and nourish them, they are enabled to live during the prevalent droughts of those arid regions. On this account the stapelia has been compared to the camel; and we are told that, by a very apt similitude, it has been denominated "the camel of the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>." We must confess ourselves quite at a loss to see the propriety <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> aptitude of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>. In many parts of the animal and vegetable economy there is doubtless a very obvious and striking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>; but this analogy has been often carried too far; much farther than fair experiment and accurate observation <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> support. It is perhaps owing to this inaccuracy in observing the peculiarity of structure and diversity of functions, that a resemblance is supposed to exist, as in the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, where in reality there is none. The camel is provided with a bag or fifth stomach, in addition to the four with which ruminant animals are furnished. This fifth stomach is destined as a reservoir to contain water; and it is sufficiently capacious to receive a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of that necessary fluid, equal to the wants of the animal, for many days: and this water, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it remains in the fifth stomach, is said to be perfectly pure and unchanged. The stapelia, and other succulent plants, have no such reservoir. The water is equally, or nearly so, diffused through the whole plant. Every vessel and every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> is fully distended. But besides, this water, whether it be received by the roots, or absorbed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, has probably undergone a complete change, and become, after it has been a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> within the plant, a fluid possessed of very different qualities. The peculiar economy in the stapelia, and other succulent plants, seems to exist in the absorbent and exhalant systems. The power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> is as much increased as the power of the exhalant or perspiratory vessels is diminished. In these plants, a small quantity of nourishment is required. There is no <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> to be formed, no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fruit to be produced. They generally have very small leaves, often are entirely naked; so that taking the whole plant, a small surface only is exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and consequently a much smaller proportion of water is decomposed than in plants which are much branched and furnished with leaves. Two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of stapelia only were known at the beginning of the century. The unfortunate Forskal, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of Niebhur, who was sent out by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> to explore the interior of Arabia, and who fell a sacrifice to the pestilential diseases of those inhospitable regions, discovered two new species. Thunberg, in his Prodromus, has mentioned five more. Forty new species have been discovered by Mr Masson of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEW">Kew</a> Gardens, who was sent out by his present Majesty for the purpose of collecting plants round the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope. Descriptions of these, with elegant and highly finished coloured engravings, have lately been published. They are chiefly natives of the extensive deserts called Karroo, on the western side of the Cape.

STAPLE

Pages 242-243

primarily signifies a public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> market, whither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, &c., are obliged to bring their goods to be bought by the people; as the Greve, or the places along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of wines and corn, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, whither the merchants of other parts are obliged to bring those commodities. Formerly, the merchants of England were obliged to carry their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and other like staple commodities of this realm, in order to expose them by wholesale; and these staples were appointed to be constantly kept at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>-upon-Tyne, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, Westminster, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>; in each whereof a public mart was appointed to be kept, and each of them had a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the mayor of the staple, for deciding differences, held according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-merchant, in a summary way.

STAR

Pages 243-244

in Fortification, denotes a small fort, having five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, or salient and re-entering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, flanking one another, and their faces 90 or 100 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR_CHAMBER">STAR-CHAMBER</a>, (camera stellata), a famous, or rather infamous, English tribunal, said to have been so called either from a Saxon word signifying to fleer or govern; or from its punishing the crimen stellatus, or cozenage; or because the room wherein it sat, the old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-chamber of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Westminster, (Lamb. i.8.) which is now converted into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a>-office, and forms the eastern side of New-Palace yard, was full of windows; or, (to which Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, 4 Inst. 66. accedes), because haply the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> thereof was at the first garnished with gilded stars. As all these are merely conjectures, (for no stars are now in the roof, nor are any said to have remained there so late as the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>), it may be allowable to propose another conjectural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>, as plausible perhaps as any of them. It is well known, that, before the banishment of the Jews under Edward I. their contracts and obligations were denominated in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> records flarra or flarrs, from a corruption of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> word, betar, a covenant. (Tovey's Angl. Judaic. 32. Selden. tit. of hon. ii. 34. Uxor Ebraica. i. 14.). These stars, by an ordinance of Richard I. preserved by Hoveden, were commanded to be enrolled and deposited in chests under three keys in certain places; one, and the most considerable, of which was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s exchequer at Westminster; and no star was allowed to be valid, unless it was found in some of the said repositories. (Mandorat in Scac. P. 6. Edw. I. prefixed to Maynard's year-book of Edw. II. fol. 8. Madox hist. exch. c. vii. § 4, 5, 6.). The room at the exchequer, where the chests containing these stars were kept, was probably called the star-chamber; and, when the Jews were expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, was applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the king's council, sitting in their judicial capacity. To confirm this, the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the star-chamber is mentioned in any record, it is said to have been situated near the receipt of the exchequer at Westminster: (the king's council, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, justices, and other lages, were assembled en la chaumbre des efeilles pres la receipt at Westminster. Claus. 41 Edw. III. m. 13.). For in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, when the meaning of the Jewish stars were forgotten, the word star-chamber was naturally rendered in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> French, la chaumbre des efeilles, and in law Latin camera stellata; which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be the style in Latin till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of that court. This was a court of very ancient original; but new-modelled by statutes 3 Hen. VII. c. 1. and 21 Henry VIII. c. 20. consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> lords spiritual and temporal, being privy-counsellors, together with two judges of the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, without the intervention of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. Their jurisdiction extended legally over riots, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, misbehaviour of sheriffs, and other notorious misdemeanors, contrary to the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Yet this was afterwards (as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clarendon informs us) stretched "to the afflicting of all proclamations and orders of state; to the vindicating of illegal commissions and grants of monopolies; holding for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> that which pleased, and for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> that which profited; and becoming both a court of law to determine civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, and a court of revenue to enrich the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>: the council-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> by proclamations enjoining to the people that which was not enjoined by the laws, and prohibiting that which was not prohibited; and the star-chamber, which consisted of the same persons in different rooms, confining the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> and disobedience to those proclamations by very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fines, imprisonments, and corporal severities: so that any disrespect to any acts of state, or to the persons of state-men, was in no time more penal, and the foundations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> never more in danger to be destroyed." For which reasons, it was finally abolished by statute 16 Car. I. c. 10. to the general joy of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. See King's-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>. There is in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> (Hist. MSS. vol. i. No. 126.), a very full, methodical, and accurate account of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and course of this court, compiled by William Hudson of Gray's Inn, an eminent practitioner therein. A short account of the same, with copies of all its process, may also be found in 18 Rym. Feod. 192, &c. STAR-Board, the right side of the ship when the eye of the spectator is directed forward. STAR-Fish. See Asterias, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. STAR-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">Shot</a>, a gelatinous substance frequently found in fields, and supposed by the vulgar to have been produced from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> called a falling-star: but, in reality, is the half-digested food of herons, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-mews, and... and the like birds; for these birds have been found when newly shot, to disgorge a substance of the same kind. **STAR-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>**, in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, a name given to certain extraneous fossil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, in form of short, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> somewhat crooked columns, composed of several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, each resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a radiated star, with a greater or smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rays in the different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>: they are usually found of about an inch in length, and of the thickness of a goose-quill. Some of them have five angles or rays, and others only four; and in some the angles are equidistant, while in others they are irregularly so: in some also they are short and blunt, while in others they are long, narrow, and pointed; and some have their angles very short and obtuse. The several joints in the same specimen are usually all of the same thickness; this, however, is not always the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>: but in some they are larger at one end, and in others at the middle, than in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body; and some species have one of the rays bifid, so as to emulate the appearance of a five-rayed kind. **STAR-Thistle.** See *Centaurea*. **STAR-Wort.** See *Aster*.

STARCH

Pages 244-245

a fecula <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sediment, found at the bottom of vessels wherein wheat has been steeped in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, of which fecula, after separating the bran from it, by passing it through sieves, they form a kind of loaves, which being dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or an oven, is afterwards cut into little pieces, and so sold. The best starch is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, soft, and friable, and easily broken into powder. Such as require fine starch, do not content themselves, like the flaxmen, with refuse wheat, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the finest grain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is as follows: The grain, being well cleaned, is put to ferment in vessels full of water, which they expose to the sun while in its greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; changing the water twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, for the space of eight or twelve days, according to the season. When the grain bursts easily under the finger, they judge it sufficiently fermented. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> perfected, and the grain thus softened, it is put, handful by handful, into a canvas-bag, to separate the flour from the husks; which is done by rubbing and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> it on a plank laid across the mouth of an empty vessel that is to receive the flour. As the vessels are filled with this liquid flour, there is seen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> at top a reddish water, which is to be carefully scummed off from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and clean water is to be put in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which, after stirring the whole together, is also to be strained through a cloth or sieve, and what is left behind put into the vessel with new water, and exposed to the sun for some time. As the sediment thickens at the bottom, they drain off the water four or five times, by inclining the vessel, but without passing it through the sieve. What remains at bottom is the starch, which is cut in pieces to get out, and left to dry in the sun. When dry, it is laid up for use. The following mill, was invented by M. Baumé for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> potatoes, with a view to extract starch from them. He had a grater made of plate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, in a cylindrical form (fig. 1) about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches in diameter, and about eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; the bars made by stumping the holes are on the inside. This grater is supported upon three feet AAA, made of flat iron bars, seven feet high, strongly rivetted to the grater; the bottom of each foot is bent horizontally, and has a hole in it which receives a screw, as at A, fig. 4. A little below the upper end of the three feet is fixed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> piece B (fig. 1 and 4), divided into three branches, and rivetted to the feet. This cross piece not only serves to keep the feet at a proper distance from each other, and to prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a>; but the centre of it having a hole cut in it, serves to support an axis or spindle of iron, to be presently described. The upper end of this cylindrical grater has a diverging border of iron C (fig. 1, 4, and 7), about ten inches in diameter at the top, and five inches in height. Within this cylindrical grater is placed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> grater (fig. 2 and 3), in the form of a cone, the point of which is cut off. The latter is made of thick plate iron, and the bars of the holes are on the outside; it is fixed, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> end at the bottom, as in fig. 4. At the upper end of the cone is rivetted a small triangle, or cross piece of iron, consisting of three branches D (fig. 2), in the middle of which is made, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole, to receive an axis or spindle; to give more resistance to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the cone, it is strengthened by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of iron E, which is fixed to the grater by means of rivets, and has also a square hole made in it, to let the axis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through. Fig. 3 represents the same cone seen in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>; the base F has also a cross piece of three branches, rivetted to a hoop of iron, which is fixed to the inner surface of the cone; the centre of this cross piece has also a square hole for the passage of the axis. Fig. 5 is a spindle or axis itself; it is a square <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of iron about sixteen inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and more than half an inch thick; round at the bottom, and also towards the top, where it fits into the cross piece I, fig. 7, and B, fig. 1 and 4; in these pieces it turns round, and by them it is kept in its place. It must be square at its upper extremity, that it may have a handle, about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches long, fixed to it, by means of which the conical grater is turned round. At G, (fig. 5), a small hole is made through the axis, to receive a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> H, by means of which the conical grater is kept at its proper height within the cylindrical one. Fig. 6 is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>'s-eye view, in which the mill is represented placed in an oval tub, like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>-tub. I is the fore-mentioned triangular iron cross, fixed with screws to the side of the tub; the centre of it has a round hole, for the axis of the mill to move in when it is used. Fig. 7 represents the mill in the oval tub; it is placed at one end of it, that the other end may be left free for any operation to be performed in it which may be necessary. A part of the tub is cut off, that the inside of it, and the manner of fixing the mill, may be seen. That the bottom of the tub may not be worn by the screws which pass through the feet of the mill, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> board, about an inch thick, and properly shaped, is placed under the mill. When we wish to make use of this mill, it is to be fixed by the feet, in the manner already described; it is also fixed at the top, by means of the cross piece I, fig. 6, and 7. The tub is then to have water poured into it as high as K, and the top of the mill is to be filled with potatoes, properly washed and cut; the handle L is to be turned round, and the potatoes, after being ground between between the two graters, go out gradually at the lower part, being afflited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> produced in the water by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the mill. To prepare starch from potatoes, says M. Baumé, any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of these roots may be taken, and soaked in a tub of water for about an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>; they are afterwards to have their fibres and shoots taken off, and then to be rubbed with a pretty strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is apt to lodge in the inequalities of their surface, may be entirely removed; as this is done, they are to be washed, and thrown into another tub full of clean water. When the quantity which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to make use of has been thus treated, those which are too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> are to be cut into pieces about the size of eggs, and thrown into the mill; that being already fixed in the oval tub, with the proper quantity of water: the handle is then turned round, and as the potatoes are grated they pass out at the bottom of the mill. The pulp which collects about the mill must be taken off from time to time with a wooden spoon, and put aside in water. When all the potatoes are ground, the whole of the pulp is to be collected in a tub, and mixed up with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantity of clean water. At the same time, another tub, very clean, is to be prepared, on the brim of which are to be placed two wooden rails, to support a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> sieve, which must not be too fine. The pulp and water are to be thrown into the sieve; the flour passes through with the water, and fresh quantities of water are successively to be poured on the remaining pulp, till the water runs through as clear as it is poured in. In this way we are to proceed till all the potatoes that were ground are used. The pulp is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> thrown away as useless; but it should be boiled in water, and used as food for animals; for it is very nourishing, and is about 3/5ths of the whole quantity of potatoes used. It is farther to be observed that the liquor which has passed through the sieve is turbid, and of a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, on account of the extractive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which is dissolved in it; it deposits, in the space of five or six hours, the flour which was suspended in it. When all the flour is settled to the bottom, the liquor is to be poured off and thrown away, being useless; a great quantity of very clean water is then to be poured upon the flour remaining at the bottom of the tub, which is to be stirred up in the water, that it may be washed, and the whole is to stand quiet till the day following. The flour <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> then be found to have settled at the bottom of the tub; the water is again to be poured off as useless, the flour washed in a fresh quantity of pure water, and the mixture passed through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> sieve pretty fine, which will retain any small quantity of pulp which may have passed through the hair sieve. The whole must once more be suffered to stand quiet till the flour is entirely settled; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the water above it is perfectly clear and colourless, the flour has been sufficiently washed; but if the water has any tenible appearances either of colour or of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the flour must be again washed, as it is absolutely necessary that none of the extractive matter be suffered to remain. When the flour is sufficiently washed, it may be taken out of the tub with a wooden spoon; it is to be placed upon wicker frames covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and dried, properly defended from dust. When it is thoroughly dry, it is to be passed through a silk sieve, that if any clotted lumps should have been formed they may be divided. It is to be kept in glass vessels stoppered with paper only. A patent was granted in 1796 to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> William Murray for his discovery of a method by which starch may be extracted from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-chesnuts. It is as follows: Take the horse-chesnuts out of the outward green prickly husks; and either by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, or other tool, or else with a mill adapted for that purpose, very carefully pare off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> rind, being particular not to leave the smallest speck, and to entirely eradicate the sprout or growth. Next take the nuts, and rasp, grate, or grind them fine into water, either by hand, or by a mill adapted for that purpose. Wash the pulp, which is thereby formed in this water, as clean as possible, through a coarse horse-hair sieve; this again wash through a finer sieve, and then again through a still finer, constantly adding clean water, to prevent any starch from adhering to the pulp. The last process is, to put it with a large quantity of water (about four gallons to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of starch) through a fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>, muslin, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, so as entirely to clear it of all bran or other impurities. As soon as it settles, pour off the water; then mix it up with clean water, repeating this operation till it no longer imparts any green, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, or other colour to the water. Then drain it off till nearly dry, and set it to bake, either in the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> starch, or else spread out before a brisk fire; being very attentive to stir it frequently to prevent its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, that is to say, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to a paste or jelly, which, on being dried, turns hard like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. The whole process should be conducted as quickly as possible. Mention is here made of a mill which may be employed to grind the horse-chesnuts; but it is not described; perhaps the one described above for grinding potatoes might answer the purpose.

STARK

Pages 245-246

Dr. William, known to the public by a volume containing Clinical and Anatomical Observations, with some curious Experiments on Diet, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1740; but the family from which he sprung was Scotch, and respectable for its antiquity. His grandfather John Stark of Killermont was a covenanter; and having appeared in arms against his sovereign at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Bothwell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> in the year 1679, became obnoxious to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and, to conceal himself, withdrew into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. There is reason to believe that he had not imbibed either the extravagant zeal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> manners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> party to which he adhered; for after residing a few years in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which he had chosen for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his banishment, he married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Thomas Stewart, Esq. of Balymore in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Ireland; who, being descended of the noble family of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a>, would not probably have matched his daughter to such an exile as a ruthless fanatic of the last century. By this lady Mr. Stark had several children; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son Thomas, who settled at Manchester as a wholesale <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>-draper, and married Margaret Stirling, daughter of William Stirling, Esq. of Northwoodside, in the neighbourhood of Glasgow, was the father of the subject of this article. Another of his sons, the reverend John Stark, was minister of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>; and it was under the care of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> that our author received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, which, when we consider the character of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and reflect on the relation between him and his pupil, we may presume was calculated to store the mind of Dr Stark with those virtuous principles which influenced his conduct through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. From Lecropt young Stark was sent to the university of Glasgow, where, under the tuition of the doctors Smith and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>, with other eminent masters, he learned the rudiments of science, and acquired that mathematical accuracy, that logical precision, and that contempt of hypotheses, with which he prosecuted all his future studies. Having chosen physic for his profession, he removed from the university of Glasgow to that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, where he was soon distinguished, and honoured with the friendship of the late Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who was not more eminently conspicuous for the superiority of his own genius, than quick-minded in perceiving, and liberal in encouraging, genius in his pupils. Having finished his studies at Edinburgh, though he took there no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, Mr Stark, in the year 1765, went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and devoted himself entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic and the elements of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>; and looking upon anatomy as one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> pillars of both these arts, he endeavoured to complete with Dr Hunter what he had begun with Dr Monro; and under these two eminent professors he appears to have acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of anatomical knowledge. He likewise entered himself about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a pupil at St George's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; for being disgusted, as he often confessed, with the inaccuracy or want of candour observable in the generality of practical writers, he determined to obtain an acquaintance with diseases at a better school and from an abler master; and to have from his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> a standard, by which he might judge of the experience of others. With what industry he prosecuted this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and with what success his labours were crowned, may be seen in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of Clinical and Anatomical Observations, which were made by him during his attendance at the hospital, and were published after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by his friend Dr Carmichael Smyth. These observations give the public no cause to complain of want of candour in their author; for whatever delicacy he may have observed, when relating the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of patients treated by other physicians, he has related those treated by himself with the utmost impartiality. Whilst attending the hospital, he likewise employed himself in making experiments on the blood, and other animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>; and also in a course of experiments in chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a>; but though accounts of these experiments were left behind him, we believe they have not yet been given to the public. In the year 1767 Mr Stark went abroad, and obtained the degree of M.D in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, publishing an inaugural dissertation on the dyerery. On his return to London, he recommenced his studies at the hospital; and when Dr Black was called to the chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in Edinburgh, which he has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> filled with so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to himself and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the university, Dr Stark was solicited by several members of the university of Glasgow to stand a candidate for their professorship of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of physic, rendered vacant by Dr Black's removal to Edinburgh. This however Dr Stark declined, being influenced by the advice of his English friends, who wished to detain him in London, and having likewise some prospects of an appointment in the hospital. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time he had commenced (1769) a series of experiments on diet, which he was encouraged to undertake by Sir John Pringle and Dr Franklin, whose friendship he enjoyed, and from whom he received many hints respecting both the plan and its execution. These experiments, or rather the imprudent zeal with which he prosecuted them, proved, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his friends, fatal to himself; for he began them on the 12th of July 1769 in perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and vigour, and from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, though his health varied, it was seldom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> ever good, till the 23rd of February 1770, when he died, after suffering much uneasiness. His friend and biographer Dr Smyth thinks, that other causes, particularly chagrin and disappointment, had no small share in hastening his death; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> was intimately acquainted with his character and disposition, his opinion is probably well-founded, though the pernicious effects of the experiments are visible in Dr Stark's own journal. When he entered upon them, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of his body was 12 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> 3 lb. avoidupois, which in a very few days was reduced to 11 stone 10 lb. 8 oz.; and though some kinds of food increased it, by much the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of what he used had a contrary effect, and it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on the whole to decrease till the day of his death. This indeed can excite no wonder. Though the professed object of his experiments was to prove that a pleasant and varied diet is equally conducive to health with a more strict and simple one, most of the dishes which he ate during these experiments were neither pleasant nor simple, but compounds, such as every stomach must nauseate. He began with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; from which he proceeded to bread, water, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; then to bread, water, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives; then to bread and water with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; afterwards he tried bread and water with roast goose; bread and water with boiled beef; stewed lean of beef with the gravy and suet without bread; stewed lean of beef with the gravy, oil of fat or suet and water; flour, oil of fat, water and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; flour, water, and salt; and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of others infinitely more disagreeable to the stomach than even these, such as bread, fat of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAM">ham</a>, infusion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> with sugar; and bread or flour with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and the infusion of rosemary. But though we consider Dr Stark's experiments as whimsical, it cannot be denied that they indicate eccentricity of genius in the person who made them; and such of our readers as think genius <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, may perhaps be of opinion, that he derived a ray from the celebrated Napier the inventor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a>, who was his ancestor by both parents. At any rate, these experiments, of which a full account is given in the same volume with his clinical and anatomical observations, display an uncommon degree of fortitude, perseverance, self-denial, and zeal for the promoting of useful knowledge in their author; and with respect to his moral character, we believe it is with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> that Dr Smyth compares him to Cato, by applying to him what was said of that virtuous Roman by Sallust—"Non divitiis cum divite, neque faciotione cum faciiose; sed cum strenuo virtute, cum modesto pudore, cum innocente abfinititia certabat; eafe, quam videri, bonus malebat."* STARLING. See <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STURNUS">STURNUS</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> In-Catilinarium.

STARLINGS

Pages 246-247
or STERLINGS, the name given to the strong pieces of timber which were driven into the bed of the river to protect the piles, on the top of which were laid the flat beams upon which were built... Starlings the bases of the stone piers that support the arches of London bridge. In general, starlings are large piles placed on the outside of the foundation of the piers of bridges, to break the force of the water, and to protect the stone work from injury by floating ice. They are otherwise called jettes, and their place is often supplied by large stones thrown at random round the piers of bridges, as may be seen at Stirling bridge when the river is low; and as was done by Mr Smeaton's direction round the piers of the centre arch of London bridge, when it was thought in danger of being undermined by the current. STATE OF A CONTROVERSY. See ORATORY, Part I. No. 14.

STATES

Pages 247-247
or ESTATES, a term applied to several orders or classes of people assembled to consult of matters for the public good. Thus states-generals, in the old government of Holland, is the name of an assembly consisting of the deputies of the seven United Provinces. These were usually 30 in number, some provinces sending two, others more; and whatever resolution the states-general took was confirmed by every province, and by every city and republic in that province, before it had the force of a law. The deputies of each province, of what numbersoever they were, had only one voice, and were esteemed as but one person, the votes being given by provinces. Each province presided in the assembly in its turn, according to the order settled among them. Guelderland presided first, then Holland, &c. States of Holland were the deputies of eighteen cities, and one representative of the nobility, constituting the states of the province of Holland; the other provinces had likewise their states, representing their sovereignty; deputies from which made what was called the states-general. In an assembly of the states of a particular province, one dissenting voice prevented their coming to any resolution.

STATICE

THRIFT, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class of pentandra, and order of pentagynia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 48th order, Aggregatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STATICS

Pages 247-248

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> improvements in knowledge have made it necessary to introduce into physico-mathematical science. It was found convenient to distribute the doctrines of universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> into two classes, which required both a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of consideration and different principles of reasoning. Till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> little science of this kind was possessed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, from whom we have received the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the centre of gravity, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>, are the foundations of our knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> mechanics; and his theory of the equilibrium of floating bodies contains the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our hydrotatical knowledge. But it was as yet limited to the simplest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; and there were some in which Archimedes was ignorant, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> was mistaken. The marquis Guido Ubaldi, in 1578, published his theory of mechanics, in which the doctrines of Archimedes were well explained and considerably augmented. Stevinus, the celebrated Dutch engineer, published about 20 years after an excellent system of mechanics, containing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> principles which now form the science of equilibrium among <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies. In particular, he gave the theory of inclined planes, which was unknown to the ancients, though it is of the very first importance in almost every machine. He even states in the most express terms the principle afterwards made the foundation of the whole of mechanics, and published as a valuable discovery by Varignon, viz., that three forces, whose directions and intensities are as the sides of a triangle, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> each other. His theory of the pressure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">hydrostatics</a>, is no less estimable, including every thing that is now received as a leading principle in the science. When we consider the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, even of the most learned, of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> or phycico-mathematical knowledge, we must consider these performances as the works of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> genius; and we regret that they are so little known, being lost in a crowd of good writings on those subjects which appeared soon after. Hitherto the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> had been turned entirely to equilibrium, and the circumstances necessary for producing it. Mechanicians indeed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, that the energy of a machine might be somehow measured by the force which could be opposed or overcome by its intervention; but they did not remark, that the force which prevented its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, but did no more than prevent it, was an exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of its energy, because it was in immediate equilibrium with the pressure exerted by that part of the machine with which it was connected. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this opposed force was less, or the force acting at the other extremity of the machine was greater, the mechanicians knew that the machine would move, and that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> would be performed; but what would be the rate of its motion or its performance, they hardly pretended to conjecture. They had not studied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of moving forces, nor conceived what was done when motion was communicated. The great Galileo opened a new field of speculation in his work on Local Motion. He there considers a change of motion as the indication and exact and adequate measure of a moving force; and he considers every kind of pressure as competent to the production of such changes.—He contented himself with the application of this principle to the motion of bodies by the action of gravity, and gave the theory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>, which remains to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> without change, and only improved by considering the changes which are produced in it by the resistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton took up this subject nearly as Galileo had left it. For, if we except the theory of the centrifugal forces arising from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>, and the theory of pendulums, published by Huygens, hardly anything had been added to the science of motion. Newton considered the subject in its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and in his mathematical principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> he considers every conceivable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of moving force, and determines the motion resulting from its action.—His first application of these doctrines was to explain the celestial motions; and the magnificence of this subject caused it to occupy for a while the whole attention of the mathematicians. But the same work contained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> equally conducive to the improvement of common mechanics, and to the complete understanding of the mechanical actions of bodies. Philosophers began to make these applications also. They saw that every kind of work which is to be performed by a machine may be considered abstractedly as a retarding force; that the impulse of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, which are employed as moving powers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> by means of pressures which they exert on the impelled point of the machine; and that the machine itself may be considered as an assemblage of bodies moveable in certain limited circumstances, with determined directions and proportions of velocity. From all these considerations resulted a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> condition of a body acted on by known powers. And they found, that after all conditions of equilibrium were satisfied, there remains a surplus of moving force. They could now state the motion which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ensue, the new resistance which this will excite, the additional power which this will absorb; and they at last determined a new kind of equilibrium, not thought of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> mechanicians, between the resistance to the machine performing work and the moving power, which exactly balance each other, and is indicated, not by the rest, but by the uniform motion of the machine. In like manner, the mathematician was enabled to calculate that precise motion of water which would completely absorb, or, in the new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, balance the superiority of pressure by which water is forced through a sluice, a pipe, or canal, with a constant velocity. Thus the general doctrines of motion came to be considered in two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view, according as they balanced each other in a state of rest or of uniform motion. These two ways of considering the same subject required both different principles and a different manner of reasoning. The first has been named Statics, as expressing that rest which is the test of this kind of equilibrium. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> has been called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYNAMICS">Dynamics</a> or Universal Mechanics, because the different kinds of motion are characteristic of the powers or forces which produce them. A knowledge of both is indispensible necessary for acquiring any useful practical knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>; and it was ignorance of the doctrines of accelerated and retarded motions which made the progress of practical mechanical knowledge so very slow and imperfect. The mechanics, even of the moderns, before Galileo, went no further than to state the proportion of the power and resistance which would be balanced by the intervention of a given machine, or the proportion of the parts of a machine by which two known forces may balance each other. This view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> introduced a principle, which even Galileo considered as a mechanical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-AXIOM">axiom</a>, viz., that what is gained in force by means of a machine is exactly compensated by the additional time which it obliges us to employ. This is false in every instance, and not only prevents improvement in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of machines, but leads us into erroneous maxims of construction. The true principles of dynamics teach us, that there is a certain proportion of the machine, dependent on the kind and proportion of the power and resistance, which enables the machine to perform the greatest possible work. It is highly proper therefore to keep separate these two ways of considering machines, that both may be improved to the utmost, and then to blend them together in every practical discussion. Statics therefore is preparatory to the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of mechanics; but it does not hence derive all its importance. It is the sole foundation of many useful parts of knowledge. This will be best seen by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> enumeration. 1. It comprehends all the doctrines of the excitement and propagation of pressure through the parts of solid bodies, by which the energies of machines are produced. A pressure is exerted on the impelled point of a machine, such as the float-boards or buckets of a mill-wheel. This excites a pressure at the pivots of its axle, which act on the points of support. This must be understood, both as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> and intensity, that it may be effectually resisted. A pressure is also excited at the acting tooth of the cog-wheel on the same axle, by which it urges round another wheel, exciting similar pressures on its pivots and on the acting tooth perhaps of a third wheel.—Thus a pressure is ultimately excited in the working point of the machine, perhaps a wiper, which lifts a heavy flamer, to let it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> again on some matter to be pounded. Now statics teaches us the intensities and direction of all those pressures, and therefore how much remains at the working point of the machine unbalanced by resistance. 2. It comprehends every circumstance which influences the stability of heavy bodies; the investigation and properties of the centre of gravity; the theory of the construction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, vaults, and domes; the attitudes of animals. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRENGTH_OF_MATERIALS">strength of materials</a>, and the principles of construction, so as to make the proper adjustment of strength and strain in every part of a machine, edifice, or structure of any kind. Statics therefore furnishes us with what may be called a theory of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>, and gives us proper instructions for framing floors, roofs, centres, &c. 4. Statics comprehends the whole doctrine of the pressure of fluids, whether liquid or aeriform, whether arising from their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> or from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> action. Hence therefore we derive our knowledge of the stability of ships, or their power of maintaining themselves in a position nearly upright, in opposition to the action of the wind on their sails. We learn on what circumstances of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and flowage this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> depends, and what will augment or diminish it. Very complete examples will be given in the remaining part of this work of the advantages of this separate consideration of the condition of a machine at rest and in working motion; and in what yet remains to be delivered of the hydraulic doctrines in our account of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER_WORKS">Water-Works</a> in general, will be perceived the propriety of stating apart the equilibrium which is indicated by the uniform motion of the fluid. The observations too which we have to make on the strength of the materials employed in our edifices or mechanical structures, will be examples of the investigation of those powers, pressures, or strains, which are excited in all their parts.

STATIONARY

Pages 248-248

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the state of a planet when, to an observer on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, it appears for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to stand still, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remain immoveable in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the heavens. For as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, to such an observer, have sometimes a progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and sometimes a retrograde one, there must be some point between the two where they must appear stationary.

STATISTICS

Pages 248-249
