In the first place, a small branch 13, 13, is taken off from the injection-pipe immediately below the cistern, and conducted to the top of the cylinder, where it is furnished with a cock. The spout is so adjusted, that no more runs from it than what will keep a constant supply of a foot of water above the piston to keep it tight. Every time the piston comes to the top of the cylinder, it brings this water along with it, and the surplus of its evaporation and leakage runs off by a waste-pipe 14, 14. This water necessarily becomes almost boiling hot, and it was thought proper to employ its surplus for supplying the waste of the boiler. This was accordingly practised for some time. But Mr Beighton improved this economical thought, by supplying the boiler from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>-pipe, 2, 2, the water of which must be still hotter than that above the piston. This contrivance required attention to many circumstances, which the reader will understand by considering the perspective and profile. The education-pipe comes out of the bottom of the cylinder at 1 with a perpendicular part, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> sidewise below, and is shut at the extremity 1. A deep cup 5 communicates with it, holding a metal valve nicely fitted to it by grinding, like the key of a cock. To secure its being always air-tight, a slender stream of water trickles into it from a branch 6 of the waste-pipe from the top of the cylinder. The education-pipe branches off at 2, and goes down to the hot well, where it turns up, and is covered with a valve. In the perspective view may be observed an upright pipe 4, 4, which goes through the head of the boiler, and reaches to within a few inches of its bottom. This pipe is called the feeder, and rises about three or four feet above the boiler. It is open at both ends, and has a branch 3, 3, communicating with the bottom of the cup 5, immediately above the metal valve, and also a few inches below the level of the entry 2 of the education-pipe. This communicating branch has a cock by which its passage may be diminished at pleasure. Now suppose the steam in the boiler to be very strong, it will cause the boiling water to rise in the feeding pipe above 3, and coming along this branch, to rise also in the cup 5, and run over. But the height of this cup above the surface of the water in the boiler is such, that the steam is never strong enough to produce this effect. Therefore, on the contrary, any water that may be in the cup 5 will run off by the branch 3, 3, and go down into the boiler by the feeding pipe. These things being understood, let us suppose a quantity of injected water lying at the bottom of the Steama-cylinder. It will run into the education-pipe, fill the crooked branch 1, 1, and open the valve in the bottom of the cup (its weight being supported by a wire hanging from a flender spring), and it will fill the cup to the lowest con-level of the entry 2 of the education-pipe, and then trivance flow along 3, 3, and supply the boiler by the feeder 4, 4. What more water runs in at 1 will now go along the education pipe 2, 2, to the hot well. By properly adjusting the cock on the branch 3, 3, the boiler may be supplied as fast as the waste in steam requires. This is a most ingenious contrivance, and does great honour to Mr Beighton. It is not, however, of much importance. The small quantity which the boiler requires may be immediately taken even from a cold cistern, without sensibly diminishing the production of steam: for the quantity of heat necessary for raising the sensible heat of cold water to the boiling temperature is small, when compared with the quantity of heat which must then be combined with it in order to convert the water into steam. For the heat expended in boiling off a cubic foot of water is about five times as much as would bring it to a boiling heat from the temperature of 55°. No difference can be observed in the performance of such engines, and of those which have their boilers supplied from a brook. It has, however, the advantage of being purged of air; and when an engine must derive all its supplies from pit water, the water from the education-pipe is vastly preferable to that from the top of the cylinder. We may here observe, that many writers (among them the Abbé Boffet), in their descriptions of the steam-engine, have drawn the branch of communication 3, 3, from the feeding-pipe to a part of the crooked pipe 1, 1, lying below the valve in the cup 5. But this is quite erroneous; for, in this case, when the injection is made into the cylinder, and a vacuum produced, the water from the boiler would immediately rush up through the pipes 4, 3, and spout up into the cylinder: so would the external air coming in at the top of the feeder. This contrivance has also enabled us to form some judgement of the internal state of the engine during the absence of performance. Mr Beighton paid a minute attention to form some the situation of the water in the feeders and education, judgement of the internal state of the pipe of an engine, which seems to have been one of the internal state which has yet been erected. It was lifting a co of the column of water whose weight was four-sevenths of the fine during prelude of the air on its piston, and made 16 strokes, of the performance, fix feet each, in a minute. This is acknowledged by all to be a very great performance of an engine of this form. He concluded that the elasticity of the steam in the cylinder was never more than one-tenth greater or less than the elasticity of the air. The water in the feeder never rose more than three feet and a half above the surface of the boiling water, even though it was now lighter by 1/7th than cold water. The education-pipe was only four feet and a half long (vertically), and yet it always discharged the injection water completely; and allowed some to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the feeder. This could not be if the steam was much more than one-tenth weaker than air. By grasping this pipe in his hand during the rise of the piston, he could guess very well whereabouts the surface of the hot water in it rested during the motion, and he never found it supported so high as four feet. Therefore the steam in the cylinder had at least eight-ninths of of the elasticity of the air. Mr Buat, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of an engine which is erected at Montrelais, in France, by an English engineer, and has always been considered as the pattern in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, finds it necessary to suppose a much greater variation in the strength of the steam, and says, that it must have been one-fifth stronger and one-fifth weaker than common air. But this engine has not been nearly so perfect. Its lift was not more than one-half of the pressure of the atmosphere, and it made but nine strokes in a minute.—At W is a valve covering the mouth of a small pipe, and surrounded with a cup containing water to keep it air-tight. This allows the air to escape which had been extricated from the water of half injection. It is driven out by the first strong puff of steam which is admitted into the cylinder, and makes a noise in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a>. The valve is therefore called the fitting-valve. To finish our description, we observe, that besides the safety valve g (called the PUPPET CLACK), which is loaded with about 3 pounds on the square inch (though the engine will work very well with a load of 1 or 2 pounds), there is another DISCHARGER 10,10, having a clack at its extremity supported by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. Its use is to discharge the steam without doors, when the machine gives over working. There is also a pipe SI near the bottom of the boiler, by which it may be emptied when it needs repairs or cleaning. There are two small pipes II,II, and 12,12, with cocks called GAGE-PIPES. The first descends to within two inches of the surface of the water in the boiler, and the second goes about 2 inches below that surface. If both cocks emit steam, the water is too low, and requires a recruit. If neither give steam, it is too high, and there is not sufficient room above it for a collection of steam. Lastly, there is a filling pipe Q, by which the boiler may be filled when the machine is to be let to work. The engine has continued in this form for many years. The only remarkable change introduced has been the manner of placing the boiler. It is no longer placed below the cylinder, but at one side, and the steam is introduced by a pipe from the top of the boiler into a flat box immediately below the cylinder. The use of this box is merely to lodge the regulator, and give room for its motions. This has been a very considerable improvement. It has greatly reduced the height of the building. This was formerly a tower. The wall which supported the beam could hardly be built with sufficient strength for withstanding the violent shocks which were repeated without ceasing; and the buildings seldom lasted more than a very few years. But the boiler is now set up in an adjoining shed, and the gudgeons of the main beam rest on the top of upright pots, which are framed into the joints which support the cylinder. Thus the whole moving parts of the machine are contained in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> frame of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>, and have little or no connection with the flight walls of the building, which is merely a cage to hold the machine, and protect it from the weather. It is now time to inquire what is to be expected from this machine, and to ascertain the most advantageous proportion between the moving power and the load that is to be laid on the machine. It may be considered as a great pulley, and is indeed sometimes so constructed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> at the ends of the working beam being completed to a circle. It must be unequally loaded that it may move. It is loaded, during the working stroke, by the pressure of the atmosphere on the piston side, and by the column of water to be raised and the pump-gear on the pump side.—During the returning stroke it is loaded, on the piston side, by a small part of the atmospheric pressure, and on the pump side by the pump gear acting as a counter weight. The load during the working stroke must therefore consist of the column of water to be raised and this counter weight. The performance of the machine is to be measured only by the quantity of water raised in a given time to a given height. It varies, therefore, in the joint proportion of the weight of the column of water in the pumps, and the number of strokes made by the machine in a minute. Each stroke consists of two parts, which we have called the working and the returning stroke. It does not, therefore, depend simply on the velocity of the working stroke and the quantity of water raised by it. If this were all that is to be attended to, we know that the weight of the column of water should be nearly 3/4ths of the pressure of the atmosphere, this being the proportion which gives the maximum in the common pulley. But the time of the returning stroke is a necessary part of the whole time elapsed, and therefore the velocity of the returning stroke equally merits attention. This is regulated by the counter weight. The number of strokes per minute does not give an immediate proof of the goodness of the engine. A small load of water and a great counter weight will ensure this, because these conditions will produce a brisk motion in both directions.—The proper adjustment of the pressure of the atmosphere on the piston, the column of water to be raised, and the counter weight, is a problem of very great difficulty; and mathematicians have not turned much of their attention to the subject, although it is certainly the most interesting question that practical mechanics affords them. Mr Boulton has solved it very shortly and simply, upon Mr Boulton's supposition, that the working and returning stroke should be made in equal times. This, indeed, is generally aimed at in the erection of these machines, and they are not reckoned to be well arranged if it be otherwise. We doubt of the propriety of the maxim. Supposing, however, this condition for the present, we may compute the loadings of the two ends of the beam as follows. Let \(a\) be the length of the inner arm of the working beam, or that by which the great piston is supported. Let \(b\) be the outer arm carrying the pump rods, and let \(W\) be a weight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to all the load which is laid on the machine. Let \(c^2\) be the area of the piston; let \(H\) be the height of a column of water having \(c^2\) for its base, and being equal in weight to the pressure exerted by the steam on the under side of the piston; and let \(h\) be the pressure of the atmosphere on the same area, or the height of a column of water of equal weight. It is evident that both strokes will be performed in equal times, if \(h \cdot c^2 - W \cdot b\) be equal to \((h - H) \cdot c^2 \cdot a + W \cdot b\). The first of these quantities is the energy of the machine during the working stroke, and the second expresses the similar energy during the returning stroke. This equation gives us \[ W = \frac{2 \cdot h \cdot c^2 \cdot a - H \cdot c^2 \cdot a}{2 \cdot b} = \frac{(2 \cdot h - H) \cdot c^2 \cdot a}{2 \cdot b}. \] If we suppose the arms of the lever equal and $H = h$, we have $W = \frac{h}{2}$; that is, the whole weight of the outer end of the beam should be half the pressure of the air on the great piston. This is nearly the usual practice; and the engineers express it by saying, that the engine is loaded with seven or eight pounds on the square inch. This has been found to be nearly the most advantageous load. This way of expressing the matter would do well enough, if the maxim were not founded on erroneous notions, which hinder us from seeing the state of the machine, and the circumstances on which its improvement depends. The piston bears a pressure of 15 pounds, it is said, on the square inch, if the vacuum below it be perfect; but as this is far from being the case, we must not load it above the power of its vacuum, which very little exceeds eight pounds. But this is very far from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. When the cylinder is tight, the vacuum is not more than $\frac{1}{15}$th deficient, when the cylinder is cooled by the injection to the degree that is every day practicable, and the piston really bears during its descent a pressure very near to 14 pounds on the inch. The load must be diminished, not on account of the imperfect vacuum, but to give the machine a reasonable motion. We must consider not only the moving force, but also the quantity of matter to be put in motion. This is so great in the steam-engine, that even if it were balanced, that is, if there were suspended on the piston arm a weight equal to the whole column of water and the counter weight, the full pressure of the atmosphere on the steam piston would not make it move twice as fast as it does. This equation by Mr Boffin is moreover essentially faulty in another respect. The W in the first member is not the same with the W in the second. In the first it is the column of water to be raised, together with the counter weight. In the second it is the counter weight only. Nor is the quantity H the same in both cases, as is most evident. The proper equation for ensuring the equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the two strokes may be had in the following manner. Let it be determined by experiment what portion of the atmospheric pressure is exerted on the great piston during its descent. This depends on the remaining elasticity of the steam. Suppose it $\frac{c}{a}$ths: this we may express by $a \cdot b$, $a$ being $\frac{c}{a}$ths. Let it also be determined by experiment what portion of the atmospheric pressure on the piston remains unbalanced by the steam below it during its ascent. Suppose this $\frac{c}{a}$ths, we may express this by $b \cdot h$. Then let W be the weight of the column of water to be raised, and c the counter weight. Then, if the arms of the beam are equal, we have the energy during the working stroke $= a \cdot h - W - c$, and during the returning stroke it is $= c - b \cdot h$. Therefore $c - b \cdot h = a \cdot h - W - c$; and $c = \frac{h(a + b) - W}{2}$; which, on the above supposition of the values of $a$ and $b$, gives us $c = \frac{h - W}{2}$. We shall make some use of this equation afterwards; but it affords us no information concerning the most advantageous proportion of $h$ and W, which is the material point. We must consider this matter in another way: And furthering the that we may not involve ourselves in unnecessary difficulties, let us make the case as simple as possible, and suppose the arms of the working-beam to be of equal length. We shall first consider the adjustment of things at the outer end of the beam. Since the sole use of the steam is to give room for the adjustment of the atmospheric pressure by its rapid condensation, it is admitted into the cylinder only to allow the things at the piston to rise again, but without giving it any impetus at the end of the pulse. The pump-rods must therefore be returned to beam con- the bottom of the working barrels by means of a presidered ponderancy at the outer end of the beam. It may be the weight of the pump-rods themselves, or may be considered as making part of this weight. A weight at the end of the beam will not operate on the rods which are suspended there by chains, and it must therefore be attached to the rods themselves, but above their respective pump-barrels, so that it may not lose part of its efficacy by immersion in the water. We may consider the whole under the notion of the pump-gear, and call it p. Its office is to depress the pump-rods with sufficient velocity, by overcoming the resistances arising from the following causes: 1. From the inertia of the beams and all the parts of the apparatus which are in motion during the descent of the pump-rods. 2. From the loss of weight sustained by the immersion of the pump-rods in water. 3. From the friction of all the pistons and the weight of the plug-frame. 4. From the resistance to the piston's motion, arising from the velocity which must be <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the water in passing through the descending pistons. The sum of all these resistances is equal to the pressure of some weight (as yet unknown), which we may call m. When the pump-rods are brought up again, they bring along with them a column of water, whose weight we may call w. It is evident that the load which must be overcome by the pressure of the atmosphere on the steam piston consists of w and p. Let this load be called L, and the pressure of the air be called P. If p be L, no water will be raised; if p be 0, the rods will not descend: therefore there is some intermediate value of p which will produce the greatest effect. In order to discover this, let g be the fall of a heavy body in a second. The descending mass is p: but it does not descend with its full weight; because it is overcoming a set of resistances which are equivalent to a weight m, and the moving force is $p - m$. In order to discover the space through which the rods will descend in a second, when urged by the force $p - m$ (supposed constant, notwithstanding the increase of velocity, and consequently of m), we must institute this proportion $p : p - m = g : g(p - m)$. The fourth term of this analogy is the space required. Let t be the whole time of the descent in seconds. Then $t^2 : t^2 = \frac{g(p - m)}{p} : \frac{t^2 g(p - m)}{p}$. This last term is is the whole descent or length of the stroke accomplished in the time \( t \). The weight of the column of water, which has now got above the piston, is \( w = L - p \). This must be lifted in the next working stroke through the space \( \frac{t^2 g (p - m)}{p} \). Therefore the performance of the engine must be \( \frac{t^2 g (p - m) (L - p)}{p} \). That this may be the greatest possible, we must consider \( p \) as the variable quantity, and make the fluxion of the fraction \( \frac{p - m \times L - p}{p} = 0 \). This will be found to give us \( p = \sqrt{Lm} \); that is, the counter weight or preponderancy of the outer end of the beam is \( \frac{\rho}{\sqrt{Lm}} \). This gives us a method of determining \( m \) experimentally. We can discover by actual measurement the quantity \( L \) in any engine, it being equal to the unbalanced weights on the beam and the weight of the water in the pumps. Then \( m = \frac{\rho^2}{L} \). Also we have the weight of the column of water \( = L - p = L - \sqrt{Lm} \). When therefore we have determined the load which is to be on the outer end of the beam during the working stroke, it must be distributed into two parts, which have the proportion of \( \sqrt{Lm} \) to \( L - \sqrt{Lm} \). The first is the counter weight, and the second is the weight of the column of water. If \( m \) is a fraction of \( L \), such as an aliquot part of it; that is, if \[ m = \frac{L}{1}, \frac{L}{2}, \frac{L}{3}, \frac{L}{4}, \frac{L}{5}, \ldots \] The circumstance which is commonly objected to us by local considerations is the quantity of water, and the depth from which it is to be raised; that is, \( w \); and it will be convenient to determine everything in conformity to this. We saw that \( w = L - \sqrt{Lm} \). This gives us \( L = \frac{w + m^2}{4} + \frac{m}{2} + w \), and the counter weight \( p = \frac{w + m^2}{4} + \frac{m}{2} \). Having thus ascertained that distribution of the load on the outer end of the beam which produces the greatest effect, we come now to consider what proportion of moving force we must apply, so that it may be employed to the best advantage, or so that any expense of power may produce the greatest performance. It will be so much the greater as the work done is greater, and the power employed is less; and will therefore be properly measured by the quotient of the work done divided by the power employed. The work immediately done is the lifting up the weight \( L \). In order to accomplish this, we must employ a pressure \( P \), which is greater than \( L \). Let it be \( L + y \); also let \( s \) be the length of the stroke. If the mass \( L \) were urged along the space \( s \) by the force \( L + y \), it would acquire a certain velocity, which we may express by \( \sqrt{s} \); but it is impelled only by the force \( y \), the rest of \( P \) being employed in balancing \( L \). The velocities which different forces <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> by impelling a body along the same space are as the square roots of the forces. Therefore \( \sqrt{L + y} : \sqrt{y} = \sqrt{s} : \sqrt{\frac{s}{L + y}} \).

STEATOMA

Pages 306-307

a kind of encysted tumor, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, soft, without pain, and without discolouring the skin.

STEEL

Pages 312-314

Sir Richard, was born about the year 1676 in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> one branch of the family was possessed of a considerable estate in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEXFORD">Wexford</a>. His father, a counsellor at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> in Dublin, was private secretary to James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>; but he was of English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>; and his son, while very young, being carried to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he put him to school at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">Charter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, whence he was removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MERTON">Merton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. Our author left the university, which he did without taking any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, in the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. This step was highly displeasing to his friends; but the ardour of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> rendered him deaf to any other proposal. Not being able to procure a better station, he entered as a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> guards, notwithstanding he thereby lost the succession to his Irish estate. However, as he had a flow of good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, a generous openness and frankness of spirit, and a sparkling vivacity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, these qualities rendered him the delight of the soldiery, and procured him an ensign's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> in the guards. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as he had made choice of a profession which set him free from all the ordinary restraints in youth, he spared not to indulge his inclinations in the wildest excesses. Yet his gallantries and revels did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without some cool hours of reflection; it was in these that he drew up his little treatise intitled... The Christian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">Hero</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may believe himself, to be a check upon his passions. For this purpose it had lain some time by him, when he printed it in 1701, with a dedication to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cutts, who had not only appointed him his private secretary, but procured for him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in Lord Lucas's regiment of Footmen. The same year he brought out his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> called The Funeral, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Grief à la <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">Mode</a>. This play procured him the regard of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William, who resolved to give him some influential marks of his favour; and though, upon that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his hopes were disappointed, yet, in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s reign, he was appointed to the profitable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of gazetteer. He owed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> to the friendship of Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sunderland, to whom he had been recommended by his schoolfellow Mr Addison. That gentleman also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> him an helping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in promoting the comedy called The Tender Husband, which was acted in 1704 with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success. But his next play, The Lying Lover, had a very different fate. Upon this rebuff from the stage, he turned the same humorous current into another channel; and early in the year 1709, he began to publish the Tatler: which admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> was undertaken in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with Dr Swift. His reputation was perfectly established by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and, during the course of it, he was made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the stamp-duties in 1710. Upon the change of the ministry the same year, he joined the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, who had several years entertained a friendship for him; and upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>'s dismission from all employments in 1711, Mr Steele addressed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of thanks to him for the services which he had done to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. However, as our author still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to hold his place in the stamp-office under the new administration, he wisely declined the discussion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> subjects; and, adhering more closely to Mr Addison, he dropt the Tatler, and afterwards, by the assistance chiefly of that steady friend, he carried on the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, much improved, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The Spectator. The success of this paper was equal to that of the former; which encouraged him, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of it, to proceed upon the same design in the character of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>. This was opened in the beginning of the year 1713, and was laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in October the same year. But in the course of it his thoughts took a stronger turn to politics: he engaged with great warmth against the ministry; and being determined to prosecute his views that way by procuring a seat in the house of commons, he immediately removed all obstacles thereto. For that purpose he took care to prevent a forcible dismission from his post in the stamp-office, by a timely resignation of it to the earl of Oxford; and at the same time gave up a pension, which had been till this time paid him by the queen as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to the late Prince George of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. This done, he wrote the famous Guardian upon the demolition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, which was published August 7, 1713; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> being dissolved next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the Guardian was soon followed by several other warm political tracts against the administration. Upon the meeting of the new parliament, Mr Steele having been returned a member for the borough of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKBRIDGE">Stockbridge</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, took his seat accordingly in the house of commons; but was expelled thence in a few days after, for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the close of the paper called the Englishman, and one of his political pieces intitled the Crisis. Presently after his expulsion, he published proposals for writing the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the duke of Marlborough; at the same time he also wrote the Spinster; and, in opposition to the Examiner, he set up a paper called the Reader, and continued publishing several other things in the same spirit till the death of the queen. Immediately after which, as a reward for these services, he was taken into favour by her successor to the throne, King George I. He was appointed surveyor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> stables at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, governor of the royal company of comedians, put into the commission of the peace for the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, and in 1715 received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. In the first parliament of that king, he was chosen member for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOROUGHBRIDGE">Boroughbridge</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; and, after the suppression of the rebellion in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, was appointed one of the commissioners of the forfeited estates in Scotland. In 1718, he buried his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife, who had brought him a handsome fortune and a good estate in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>; but neither this, nor the ample additions lately made to his income, were sufficient to answer his demands. The thoughtless vivacity of his spirit often reduced him to little shifts of wit for its support; and the project of the fish pool this year owed its birth chiefly to the projector's necessities. This vessel was intended to carry fish alive, and without waiting, to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdom: but notwithstanding all his towering hopes, the scheme proved very ruinous to him; for after he had been at an immense expense in contriving and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> his vessel, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the patent, which he had procured, it turned out upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> project. His plan was to bring salmon alive from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but these fish, though supplied by this contrivance with a continual stream of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> while at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, yet uneasy at their confinement, shattered themselves to pieces against the sides of the pool; so that when they were brought to market they were worth very little. The following year he opposed the remarkable peerage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> in the house of commons; and, during the course of this opposition to the court, his licence for acting plays was revoked, and his patent rendered ineffectual, at the instance of the lord chamberlain. He did his utmost to prevent so great a loss; and finding every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> avenue of approach to his royal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> effectually barred against him by his powerful adversary, he had recourse to the method of applying to the public, in hopes that his complaints would reach the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> of his sovereign, though in an indirect course, by that canal. In this spirit he formed the plan of a periodical paper, to be published twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, under the title of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a>; the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of which came out on the 2d of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1719-20. In the mean time, the misfortune of being out of favour at court, like other misfortunes, drew after it a train of more. During the course of this paper, in which he had assumed the feigned name of Sir John Edgar, he was outrageously attacked by Mr Dennis, the noted critic, in a very abusive pamphlet, entitled The Character and Conduct of Sir John Edgar. To this insult our author made a proper reply in the Theatre. While he was struggling with all his might to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself from ruin, he found time to turn his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> against the mischievous South Sea scheme, which had nearly brought... brought the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> to ruin in 1720; and the next year he was restored to his office and authority in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a> in Drury-Lane. Of this it was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he made an additional advantage, by bringing his celebrated comedy called the Conscious Lovers upon that stage, where it was acted with prodigious success; so that the receipt there must have been very considerable, besides the profits accruing by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the copy, and a purse of £500, given to him by the king, to whom he dedicated it. Yet notwithstanding these ample supplies, about the year following, being reduced to the utmost extremity, he sold his share in the play-house; and soon after commenced a law-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with the managers, which in 1726 was decided against him. Having now again, for the last time, brought his fortune, by the most heedless profusion, into a desperate condition, he was rendered altogether incapable of retrieving the loss, by being seized with a paralytic disorder, which greatly impaired his understanding. In these unhappy circumstances, he retired to his seat at Languanor near Caerphilly in Wales, where he died on the 21st of September 1729, and was privately interred, according to his own desire, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Caerphilly. Among his papers were found the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of two plays, one called The Gentlemen, founded upon the Eunuch of Terence, and the other intitled The School of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">Action</a>, both nearly finished. Sir Richard was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of undiminished and extensive benevolence, a friend to the friendless, and, as far as his circumstances would permit, the father of every orphan. His works are chaste and manly. He was a stranger to the most distasteful appearance of envy or malevolence; never jealous of any man's growing reputation; and so far from arrogating any praise to himself from his conjunction with Mr Addison, that he was the first who desired him to distinguish his papers. His great fault was want of economy; and it has been said of him, he was certainly the most agreeable and the most innocent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> that ever trod the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> of dissipation.

STEEL-YARD

Pages 307-307

is one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> presents which science has made to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in defectude in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, is in most nations of the world the only <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for ascertaining the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of bodies. What is translated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, is in fact steelyard, being the word used by the Arabs to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> for their instrument, which is a steelyard. It is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in all the Asiatic nations. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATERA">patera</a> of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and seems to have been more confided in by them than the balance; for which reason it was used by the goldsmiths, while the balance was the instrument of the people.—Non aurificis patera sed populari trutina examinare. Cic. de Orat. 238. The steelyard is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> of unequal arms, and, in its most perfect form, is constructed much like a common balance. It hangs in three (fig. 1,) resting on the nail C, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> L for holding the goods hangs by a nail D on the short arm BC. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> weight P hangs by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of tempered <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, made sharp in the inside, that it may bear by an edge on the long arm CA of the steelyard. The under edge of the centre nail C, and the upper edge of the nail D, are in the straight line formed by the upper edge of the long arm. Thus the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of suspension are in one straight line. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of the steelyard is perpendicular to the line of the arms, and plays between the fleers. The short arm may be made so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a>, that, together with the scale, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> balance the long arm unloaded. When no goods are in the scale, and the counter weight with its hook are removed, the steelyard acquires a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its centre of gravity being below the axis of suspension. The rules for its accurate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> are the same as for a common balance.

STEEPLE

Pages 314-314

an appendage erected generally on the western end of churches, to hold the bells. Steeples are denominated from their form, either spires <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> towers: the first are such as ascend continually diminishing either conically or pyramidally; the latter are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> parallelopipeds, and are covered a-top <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a>-like.

STEERING

Pages 314-314

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, the art of directing the ship's way by the movements of the helm; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of applying its efforts to regulate her course when the advances. The perfection of steering consists in a vigilant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the ship's head, so as to check every deviation from the line of her course in the first instant of its motion; and in applying as little of the power of the helm as possible. By this she <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> run more uniformly in a straight path, as declining less to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left; whereas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a greater effort of the helm is employed, it will produce a greater declination from the course, and not only increase the difficulty of steering, but also make a crooked and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> track through the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. See Helm.—The helmsman should diligently watch the movements of the head by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, or stars; because, although Steering, the course is in general regulated by the compass, yet the vibrations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> are not so quickly perceived as the fallies of the ship's head to the right or left, which, if not immediately restrained, will acquire additional velocity in every instant of their motion, and demand a more powerful impulse of the helm to reduce them; the application of which will operate to turn her head as far on the contrary side of her course. —The phrases used in steering a ship vary according to the relation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to her course. Thus, if the wind is fair or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, the phrases used by the pilot or officer who superintends the steerage are, port, starboard, and steady. The first is intended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the ship's course farther to the right; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is to guide her farther to the left; and the last is designed to keep her exactly in the line wherein she advances, according to the course prescribed. The excesses of the first and second movements is called hard-a-port, and hard-a-starboard; the former of which gives her the greatest possible inclination to the right, and the latter an equal tendency to the left.—If, on the contrary, the wind is foul or scant, the phrases are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUFF">luff</a>, thus, and no nearer; the first of which is the order to keep her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the wind; the second, to retain her in her present situation; and the third to keep her fails full. In a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of steering the ship is usually divided amongst a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the most expert sailors, who attend the helm in their turns; and are accordingly called timoneers, from the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> timonier, which signifies "helmsman." The steerage is constantly superintended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-masters, who also attend the helm by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>. In merchant ships every seaman takes his turn in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, being directed therein by the mate of the watch, or some other officer.—As the safety of a ship, and all contained therein, depends in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> on the steerage or effects of the helm, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> by which it is managed should often be diligently examined by the proper officers. Indeed, a negligence in this important duty appears almost unpardonable, when the fatal effects which may result from it are duly considered.

STEEVENS

Pages 314-315

GEORGE, the most successful of all the editors and commentators of Shakespeare, was born in the year 1735. We know nothing respecting his parents, but they appear to have been in affluent circumstances. Our author received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>-upon-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and had Gibbon the historian for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> at that school. From hence he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">Eton</a>, and in a few years was admitted a fellow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but no mention is made of his peculiar course of studies. It appears, however, that he had little relish for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> at Cambridge to academical honours. On the first establishment of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, he accepted of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>; but he spent the concluding years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in almost total seclusion from the world, seldom mingling with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, but in the shops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a>, in the Shakespeare gallery, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the morning conversations of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks. Although not an original writer, we cannot in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> refuse him a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the first literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when we consider the works he illustrated, and the learning, sagacity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and general knowledge which he brought to the task. With a versatility of talents, lents, he was eminent both by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> excellence lay in his critical knowledge of an author's text; and the best specimen of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abilities is his edition of Shakespeare, in which he has left every competitor far behind him. He had studied the age of Shakespeare, and employed his persevering industry in becoming acquainted with the writings, manners, and laws of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> peculiarities, whether of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> or customs, which prevailed in different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, but more particularly in those where Shakespeare passed the early years of his life. He was continually increasing this store of knowledge, by the acquisition of the obsolete publications of a former age, which he spared no expense to obtain. His critical sagacity and observation were constantly employed in calling forth the hidden meanings of the dramatic bard, and of course enlarging the display of his beauties. This advantage is apparent from his last edition of Shakespeare, which contains so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> a portion of new, interesting, and accumulated instruction. In preparing it for the press, he gave an instance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and perseverance without example. To this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he exclusively devoted a period of 18 months, during which he left his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> every morning at one o'clock, going to his friend Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Read's chambers in Barnard's-inn, without any consideration of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> or the season, and there he found a sheet of the Shakespeare <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-press ready for correction. Thus, while the printers slept the editor was awake, by which means he completed, in less than 20 months, his splendid edition of Shakespeare in 15 vols. octavo; a labour almost incredible, and by which the energy and persevering powers of his mind were fully proved. He probably rested satisfied with being a commentator from the particular habits of his life, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the name of Shakespeare. But at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was a classical scholar of the first order, and well acquainted with the belles lettres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and particularly that of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His genius was strong and original; his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> abundant; his imagination of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and his sentiments enlivened with the most brilliant expressions. His eloquence was logical and animated; his descriptions were true to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, his figures so curiously selected, and so happily grouped, that he might be regarded as a speaking Hogarth. He scattered his wit and his humour too freely around him, and they were not lost for want of gathering. Mr Steevens had a very handsome fortune, which he managed with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. His generosity was equal to his fortune; and though not profuse of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to flabby beggars, few persons distributed with more liberality to truly deserving objects. He possessed all the graces of outward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a>, at a period when civility and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> were characteristics of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. He bequeathed his valuable Shakespeare, illustrated with about 1500 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Spencer; his Hogarth perfect, with the exception of one or two pieces, to Mr Windham; and his corrected copy of Shakespeare, with 200 guineas, to his friend Mr Read. He died in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1800, about 65 years of age.

STEGANOGRAPHY

Pages 315-315

the art of secret <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of writing in ciphers, known only to the persons corresponding. See Cipher.

STELLARIA

Pages 315-315

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas decandria, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 22nd order, Caryophyllaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STELLATE

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to leaves which grow not less than six at a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, and are arranged like the rays of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>.

STELLERA

Pages 315-315

German Groundsel, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas octandria; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system arranged under the 31st order, Vepreculie. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STELLIONATE

Pages 315-315

in the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a kind of crime committed by a fraudulent bargain, where one of the parties sells a thing for what it is not; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I sell an estate for my own which belongs to another, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convey a thing as free and clear which is already engaged to another, or put off <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, &c.

STEM

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a plant arising out of the root, and which sustains the leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, &c. By washing and rubbing the stems of trees, their annual increase is promoted; for the method of doing which, see the article Tree. STEM of a Ship, a circular piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> into which the two sides of a ship are united at the fore-end; the lower end of it is fastened to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and the bowsprit rests upon its upper end. The stem is formed of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two pieces, according to the size of the vessel; and as it terminates the ship forward, the ends of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">wales</a> and planks of the sides and bottom are let into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> or channel, in the midst of its surface, from the top to the bottom; which operation is called rabbling. The outside of the stem is usually marked with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of feet, according to its perpendicular height from the keel. The intention of this is to ascertain the draught of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> at the fore-part, when the ship is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-voyage, &c. The stem at its lower end is of equal breadth and thickness with the keel, but it grows proportionally broader and thicker towards its upper extremity. See Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>.

STEMMATA

Pages 315-315

in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of insects, are three smooth hemispheric dots, placed generally on the top of the head, as in most of the hymenoptera and other classes. The name was first introduced by Linnaeus.

STEMODIA

Pages 315-315

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas didynamia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 40th order, Perforatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STEMPHYLIA

Pages 315-315

a word used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to express the husks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the remains of the pressings of wine. The same word is also used by some to express the remaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of the olives, after the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is pressed out.

STEMPHYLITES

Pages 315-315

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a sort of wine pressed hard from the husks.

STEMPLES

Pages 315-315

in mining, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bars of wood in the shafts which are sunk to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. In many places the way is to sink a perpendicular hole, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shaft, the sides of which are strengthened from top to bottom with wood-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from falling in; the transverse pieces of wood are called stemples, and by means of these the miners in some places descend, without using any rope.

STEMSON

Pages 315-315

in a ship, an arching piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> fixed within the apron, to reinforce the scarf thereof, in the same manner as the apron supports the scarf of the stern. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships it is usually formed of two pieces.

STENOGRAPHY

Pages 315-322

STENOGRAPHY (A). CHAP. I. The art of stenography, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, was known and practised by most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> civilized nations. The Egyptians, who were distinguished for learning at an early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, at first expressed their words by a delineation of figures called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>. A more concise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of writing seems to have been afterwards introduced, in which only a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the symbol or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> was drawn. This answered the purpose of shorthand in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. After them the Hebrews, the Greeks, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>*, adopted different methods of abbreviating their words and sentences, suited to their respective languages. The initials, the finals, or radicals, often served for whole words; and various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of these sometimes formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>. Arbitrary marks were likewise employed to determine the meaning, and to assist legibility; and it seems probable that every writer, and every author of antiquity, had some peculiar method of abbreviation, calculated to facilitate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of his own sentiments, and intelligible only to himself. It is also probable, that some might by these means take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the heads of a discourse or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>; but few, very few, it is presumed, could have followed a speaker through all the meanders of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and noted with precision every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>, as it dropt from his mouth, in a manner legible even to themselves. To arrive at such consummate perfection in the art was reserved for more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, and is still an acquisition by no means general. In every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, till about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 16th century, the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of abbreviating (viz. substituting the initials or radicals, with the help of arbitraries, for words) appears to have been employed. Till then no regular <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> had been invented expressly for stenography, when an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the name of Willis invented and published one (B). His plan was soon altered and improved, or at least pretended to be so. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> succeeded another; and at intervals, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years past, some men of ingenuity and application have composed and published systems of stenography, and doubtless have themselves reaped all the advantages that attend it. But among the various methods that have been proposed, and the different plans that have been adopted by individuals, none has yet appeared fortunate enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> general approbation; or proved sufficiently simple, clear, and concise, to be universally studied and practised. Some systems are replete with unmeaning symbols, perplexing arbitraries, and ill-judged contractions; which render them so difficult to be attained by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> capacity, or ordinary application, that it is not to be wondered at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have sunk into neglect, and are now no longer known (c). Other systems, by being too prolix, by containing a multiplicity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and those characters not simple or easily remembered, become ineffectual to the purpose of expedition, and are only superior in obscurity to a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Some, again, not only reject all arbitraries and contractions, but even prepositions and terminations; which last, if not too lavishly employed and badly devised, highly contribute to promote both expedition and legibility; and though they reduce their characters to fewer than can possibly express the various modifications of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, yet they make nearly one half of them complex. In the disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>, there is the greatest perplexity in most systems. A dot is sometimes substituted for all the vowels indiscriminately, and the judgement is left to determine which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> out of any dot is intended to express; or a minute space is allotted them; so that unless they be arranged with mathematical precision they cannot be distinguished from one another; but such a minute <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of short-hand, which should teach us to write down in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as well as in small bounds, what we wish to preserve of what we hear. Nor is the plan of lifting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> and putting the next consonant in the vowel's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in the middle of words, less liable to objections; or that of representing all the vowels by distinct characters, being obviously ill calculated for facility and dispatch. (A) The value of stenography is not unknown to the learned; and the care and success with which it has been lately cultivated in these kingdoms <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, soon render it an object of general attention. No one, however, appears to us to have simplified and improved the art so much as Dr Mavor, author of Universal Stenography, who has liberally permitted us to present our readers with a complete view of his scheme. To those who wish to become proficient in Short-writing, we earnestly recommend his entire publication (printed for Cadell and Davis, Strand, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>), which in many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of the first reputation now forms a deserved clasbook. (B) Mr Locke says, a regular method of short-writing seems to be known and practised only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. This is not now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; and indeed there is no reason to doubt whether characters may not be invented to express the various sounds, or letters, employed in any language, either ancient or modern. (C) A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of writers on stenography. Mr Addy, Alridge, Angell, Annet, Blandemore, Blissett, Botley, Bridges, Byrom, Coles, Crofs, Dix, Everardt, Ewen, Facey, Farthing, Gibbs, Graeme, Gurney, Heath, Holdsworth, Hopkins, Jeake, Labourer, Lane, Lyle, Macauley, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACON">Macon</a>, Mavor, Metcalfe, Nicholas, Palmer, Rich, Ridpath, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHELTON">Shelton</a>, Steele, Tanner, Taylor, Thicknesse, Tiffen, Webster, Weston, Williamson, Willis, B. D. and Willis, &c. dispatch, and consequently inadmissible into any useful system. It is to be confessed, that the person who first proposed the omission of vowels in the middle of words (D), which it is obvious are not wanted, and invented letters, which could be connected as in a running hand without lifting the pen in the middle of the word, made a real improvement on the works of his predecessors. But, in fine, most systems, either in their plan or execution, labour under some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> defect, attended with circumstances highly discouraging to the learner, and which in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> defeat the end of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, by being too complicated to be learned with ease and remembered with accuracy, or to be practised with the expedition which is requisite; and so difficult to be deciphered, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can scarcely read what he has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> written. To obviate these defects; to provide against prolixity and conciseness, which might occasion obscurity; to exhibit a system founded on the simplest principles, which might be easily learned and read, and yet be capable of the utmost expedition—were the motives that gave rise to the present attempt. This method will be found different from any yet published, and superior to all in the disposition of the vowels and the facility of arranging them; the confusion in placing which seems to detract from the merit of the best performances on the subject; and it may be affirmed, without ostentation, that characters simpler in their form, and more perfect in their union, have not been applied to the art of stenography. As well as it could be determined, the simplest characters are appropriated to the letters most usually employed: indeed, as far as possible, those which are complex have been rejected; but as it was an object always kept in view that the writing should be on a line, a few are admitted into the alphabet for that reason. The characters for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> and triple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a> are the easiest that could be invented, consistent with perspicuity (E); for care has been taken to provide against all obscurity which might arise by adopting letters too similar in their formation; and with respect to the prepositions and terminations, those which occur most frequently are expressed by the simplest characters, which will be found perfectly easy in their application. The arbitrariness are few in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> (F), and the arbitrary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a>, as they are entirely from the letters of the alphabet, and chosen from some thousands of words in common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, will well repay the learner for an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s trouble in committing them to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. The last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> lays down a scheme of abbreviation, comprised in a few rules, perfectly easy to be understood and practised by proficient in this art, which we hope will answer the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the author, and will be found free from the perplexity complained of in many systems where abbreviation is admitted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> rules are new, are so easy, so extensive in their use, and so consistent with expedition and legibility, if applied with judgment, that they alone might suffice. The learner is however advised by no means to adopt any of them, till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has convinced him that they may be used without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> or injury to legibility. All abbreviating rules are suited to those only who have made some progress in the stenographic art; for although they certainly promote expedition in a wonderful manner, and afford the greatest ease to a proficient, yet a learner, as expedition is not his first, though his ultimate view, should admit of nothing that in the least renders the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> difficult. CHAP. II. The English alphabet consists of twenty-five letters; the first of which are vowels, a, e, i, o, u, and y; and the other twenty consonants, b, c, d, f, g, h, k, l, m, n, p, q, r, s, t, v, x, and z. This alphabet, as is observed by the best grammarians that have written on the language, is both defective and redundant in expressing the various modifications of sound. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">Custom</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> has assigned some letters a place, when others would with much more propriety express the same sound: and to this may be added, that several letters, sometimes in one word, seem to be admitted for no other reason than to perplex a young beginner or a foreigner, as an obstruction to true <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, and to add to the apparent length of the word, when they are entirely quiescent and useless. That this is the genius of the orthography of our language must be perceived by the most superficial observer; but no modern tongue is absolutely free from the same exceptions. In particular, the French has a great number of dormant letters, which, it is obvious, render the pronunciation more difficult and perplexing to learners (G). But as it is neither our business nor our intention to propose a mode of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPELLING">spelling</a> different from that in common use, when applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-hand writing (since several innovators in orthography have fallen into contempt, and their plans have been only preserved as beacons to warn others of the folly of endeavouring to subvert established principles); we shall only observe,† <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">Preface</a> that in stenography, where the most expeditious and concise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>. concise method is the best, if consistent with perspicuity, the following simple rules are studiously to be regarded and practised. Rule I. All quiescent consonants in words are to be dropped; and the orthography to be directed only by the pronunciation: which being known to all, will render this art attainable by those who cannot spell with precision in long hand. Rule II. When the absence of consonants, not entirely dormant, can be easily known, they may often be omitted without the least obscurity. Rule III. Two or sometimes more consonants may, to promote greater expedition, be exchanged for a single one of nearly similar sound; and no ambiguity as to the meaning ensue (H). Rule IV. When two consonants of the same kind or same sound come together, without any vowel between them, only one is to be expressed; but if a vowel or vowels intervene, both are to be written: only observe, if they are perpendicular, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, or oblique <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, they must only be drawn a size longer than usual; and characters with loops must have the size of their heads doubled. Might is to be written mit, fight fit, machine maishin, enough enuf, laugh laf, prophet profet, physics fisiks, through thro', foreign foron, sovereign soveren, palm jam, receipt recpt, write rite, wright rit, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> island, knavery nevvy, temptation tentation, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> nife, stick flk, thigh thi, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> honur, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> indiment, acquaint aquaint, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> knos, &c. Strength strenth, length lenth, friendship frenship, connect conekt, commandment comament, conjunct conjunt, humble humle, lumber lumer, slumber slumer, number numer, exemplary examlary, &c. Rocks rox, acts akt or akt, facts faks or fax, districts distrixs, or distrix, affects afeks or afex, afflicts affiks or affix, conquer konkr, &c. Letter leter, little little, command comand, error eror, terror teror, &c. But in remember, moment, miter, and such like words, where two consonants of the same name have an intervening vowel, both of them must be written. These four rules, with their examples, being carefully considered by the learner, will leave him in no doubt concerning the disposition and management of the consonants in this scheme of short-writing; we shall therefore proceed to lay down rules for the application of the vowels with ease and expedition. Rule I.
