Vowels, being only simple articulate sounds, though they are the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONNECTIVES">connectives</a> of consonants, and employed in every word and every syllable, are not necessary to be inserted in the middle of words; because the consonants, if fully pronounced, with the assistance of connection, will always discover the meaning of a word, and make the writing perfectly legible. Rule II. If a vowel is not strongly accented in the incipient syllable of a word, or if it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a>, it is likewise to be omitted; because the sound of the incipient vowel is often implied in that of the first consonant, which will consequently supply its place. Rule III. But if the vowel constitutes the first or last syllable of a word, or is strongly accented at its beginning or end, that vowel is continually to be written. Rule IV. If a word begins or ends with two or more vowels though separated, or when there is a coalition of vowels, as in diphthongs and triphthongs; only one of them is to be expressed, which must be that which agrees best with the pronunciation. Rule V. In monosyllables, if they begin or end with a vowel, it is always to be inferred, unless the vowel be mute at the end of a word. Such are the general principles of this art; in vindication and support of which it will be needless to offer any arguments, when it is considered that brevity and expedition are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> objects, if consistent with legibility; and the subsequent specimens in the orthography recommended will, we hope, be sufficient to show that there is no real deficiency in the last mentioned particular. As the whole of this art depends upon a regular method and a simple alphabet, we have not only endeavoured to establish the former on satisfactory principles, but have been careful to appropriate, according to the comparative frequency of their occurrence, such charac- (H) By this rule likewise q and v in the middle of words, but never in the beginning, may be exchanged for k and f, when they admit of an easier connecting with the following character, or will make the writing appear neater. ters for the letters as, after repeated trials and alterations, were conceived to be the best adapted for dispatch. The stenographic alphabet consists of 18 distinct characters (viz. two for the vowels and the rest for the consonants), taken from lines and semicircular curves; the formation and application of which we shall now explain, beginning with the vowels. For the three first vowels, a, e, and i, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMA">comma</a> is appropriated in different positions; and for the other three, o, u, and y, a point. The comma and point, when applied to a, and o, is to be placed, as in the Plate DVII. at the top of the next character; when for e and u, opposite to the middle; and when for i and y, at the bottom. This arrangement of the vowels is the most simple and distinct that can easily be imagined. Places at the top, the middle, and the bottom of characters, which make three different positions, are as easily distinguished from one another as any three separate characters could be; and a comma is made with the same facility as a point. Simple lines may be drawn four different ways; perpendicular, horizontal, and with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of about 45 degrees to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left. An ascending oblique line to the right, which will be perfectly distinct from the rest when joined to any other character, may likewise be admitted. These characters being the simplest in nature, are assigned to those five consonants which most frequently occur, viz. l, r, t, c hard or k, and c soft or s. Every circle may be divided with a perpendicular and horizontal line, so as to form likewise four distinct characters. These being the next to lines in the simplicity of their formation, we have appropriated them for b, d, n, and m. The characters expressing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of the consonants are all perfectly distinct from one another; eight only remain which are needful, viz. f, g or j, h, p, q, v, w, and x; to find characters for which we must have recourse to mixed curves and lines. The characters which we have adopted are the simplest in nature after those already applied, admit of the easiest joining, and tend to preserve lineality and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> in the writing. It must be observed that we have no character for c when it has a hard sound, as in castle; or soft, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; for it naturally takes the sound of k or s, which in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> will be sufficient to supply its place. R likewise is represented by the same character as l; only with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, r is written with an ascending stroke (i), and l with a descending; which is always to be known from the manner of its union with the following character; but in a few monosyllables where r is the only consonant in the word, and consequently stands alone, it is to be made as is shown in the alphabet for distinction's sake. Z, as it is a letter seldom employed in the English language, and only a coarser and harsher expression of s, must be supplied by s whenever it occurs; as for Zedekiah write Sedekiah, &c. CHAP. IV. The prepositions and terminations in this scheme are so simple, that the greatest benefit may be reaped from them, and very little trouble required to attain them; and terms as the incipient letter or the incipient consonant of all nations, the prepositions and of several of the terminations is used to express the whole. But although in Plate DVII. sufficient specimens are given of the manner of their application, that the learner of less ingenuity or more slow perception may have every assistance, we have subjoined the following directions. Rule I. The preposition is always to be written without joining, yet so near as plainly to show what word it belongs to; and the best way is to observe the same order as if the whole was to be connected. Rule II. A preposition, though the same letters that constitute it may be met with in the middle or end of a word, is never to be used, because it would expose to obscurity. Rule III. Observe that the preposition omni is expressed by the vowel e in its proper position; and for anti, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTA">anta</a>, ante, by the vowel a, which the radical part of the word will easily distinguish from being only simple vowels. The first rule for the prepositions is (allowing such exceptions as may be seen in the Plate) to be observed for the terminations; and also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, mutatis mutandis; except that whenever sis, fis, fys, cious, tius, and ces occur, they are to be expressed as directed in the fourth rule for the consonants, whether in the beginning, middle, or end of words (k). Rule IV. The terminative character for tion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SION">sion</a>, cion, cian, tian, is to be expressed by a small circle joined to the nearest letter, and turned to the right; and the plurals tions, sions, cions, cians, tians, tience, by a dot on the same side. Rule V. The terminative character for ing, is to be expressed likewise by a small circle, but drawn to the left hand; and its plural ings by a dot (i). Rule VI. The plural sign s is to be added to the terminative characters when necessary. Rule VII. The separated terminations are never to be used but in polysyllables or words of more syllables than one. These rules duly observed will point out a method as concise and elegant as can be desired, for expressing the most (1) The character for h, when lineality requires it, may be made from the bottom and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> (see Plate DVII.). And often h may be omitted entirely, or a vowel may be substituted in its stead, without any injury to legibility, it being rather a breathing than letter. (k) But in a few words where three horizontal characters meet, it will be better to express the fis, &c. by the semieliptical character in Plate DVII., opposite tious. (i) In horizontal characters, by the left hand is meant the top, and by the right the space below the letter (i.e. ing joined, Plate DVII.). In all other characters the right and left positions will naturally be known. most frequent and longest prepositions and terminations in the English language. If it should be thought necessary to increase their number by the addition of others, it will be an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for any one of the least discernment to do so, by proceeding on the principles before laid down. CHAP. V. Though a more concise method of writing, or more numerous abbreviations, may not be indispensably necessary, if the foregoing directions be practised for a considerable time, yet contractions will be found extremely useful and convenient to those who have attained a proper knowledge of the subject, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to a greater degree of expedition, at the same time that they diminish the labour of writing. It has been observed in the introduction, that abbreviations are only to be employed by proficient in this art; because expedition is not the first, though the ultimate, object in view; and that an easy legibility is of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the learner; which, however, cannot be preserved, if he adopts too soon those very rules which in time will afford him the greatest ease when applied with judgment. The following short and practical rules will be found, we hope, fully adequate to every purpose for which they were intended, and are far superior in the facility of their application to any which we have seen. RULE I. The usual abbreviations in long hand are always to be followed; as Mr for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>, M.D. for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Physic, and Abp. for Archbishop, &c. RULE II. Substantives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADJECTIVES">adjectives</a>, verbs, and participles, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> to the meaning, are to be expressed by their initial consonant with the distinguishing marks exhibited in Plate DVII. viz. a substantive must have the dot exactly over its initial consonant; an adjective must have a dot under it; a verb is to be expressed by a comma over its initial consonant; and a participle by a comma under (M). These being the four principal parts of speech will be sufficient; and an adept will never be at a loss to know when he can with safety apply this rule to them. RULE III. To render the writing more legible, the last letter of the word may be joined to the first, and the proper mark applied. RULE IV. The constituent or radical part of words, especially if they are long, will often serve for the whole, or sometimes the first syllable: as, we ought to moderate our ex. by our circum.; a man's man. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> shape his for. RULE V. All long words without exception may have their prepositions or terminations expressed by the incipient consonant of such preposition or termination. RULE VI. When there is a great dependence between the parts of a sentence, the initial letter will often suffice; as L. is the capital of Great B.; the eldest S. of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Great B. is styled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of W. Every one, it is presumed, will allow this to be perfectly legible in long-hand, then why may it not in stenography? RULE VII. The terminations nos and less may be omitted; as faithfulness is only to be written faithful; forwardness, forward; headless, heed; stubborness, stubborn, &c. RULE VIII. The second and third persons of verbs, ending in eth and eth, may be expressed by s; as, he loves, thou teachest; instead of he loveth, thou teachest; or even without s; as, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, &c. RULE IX. Words may often be entirely omitted, and yet no ambiguity ensue; as, In beginning God created heaven and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, for In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. RULE X. When there is an immediate repetition of a sentence or word, a line is to be drawn under the sentence or word to be repeated; as, Amen, Amen, Amen, is to be written Amen; but if any words intervene before a word or sentence is to be repeated, the line must be drawn as before, and a or mark of omission placed where the repetition should begin; as, Is it just the innocents should be condemned a reviled? The CONTENTS of the STENOGRAPHIC PLATES. Fabricius's Reply to Pyrrhus. As to my poverty, you have indeed, Sir, been rightly informed. My whole estate consists in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> appearance, and a little spot of ground, from which by my own labour I draw my support. But if by any means you have been persuaded to think, that this poverty makes me less considered in my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or in any degree unhappy, you are extremely deceived. I have no reason to complain of fortune, she supplies me with all that nature requires; and if I am without luxuries, I am also free from the desire of them. With these I confess I should be more able to succour the necessitous, the only advantage for which the wealthy are to be envied; but as small as my possessions are, I can still contribute something to the support of the state and the affluence of my friends. With regard to honours, my country places me, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> as I am, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the richest: for Rome knows no qualifications for great employments but virtue and ability. She appoints me to officiate in the most august ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; she entrusts me with the command of her armies; she confides to my care the most important negotiations. My poverty does not lessen the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and influence of my counsels in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; the Roman people honour me for that very poverty which you consider as a disgrace; they know the many opportunities I have had in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to enrich myself without incurring censure; they are convinced of my disinterested zeal for their prosperity; and if I have any thing to complain of in the return they make, it is only the excess of their applause. What value then can I set upon your <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver! What king can add anything to my fortune! Always attentive to discharge the duties incumbent (M) The dot or comma being placed thus will never occasion them to be mistaken for vowels, because they should always be on one side or other; whereas the mark for parts of speech may constantly be placed exactly over or under. incumbent on me, I have a mind free from self-reproach, and I have an honest fame. Dodley's Preceptor. Letter to a Friend against waste of Time. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">Converse</a> often with yourself, and neither lavish your time, nor suffer others to rob you of it. Many of our hours are stolen from us, and others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> insensibly away; but of both these losses the most shameful is that which happens through our own neglect. If we take the trouble to observe, we shall find that one considerable part of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is spent in doing evil, and the other in doing nothing, or in doing what we should not do. We <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">don</a>'t seem to know the value of time, nor how precious a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> is; nor do we consider that every moment brings us nearer our end. Reflect upon this, I entreat you, and keep a strict account of time. Procrastination is the most dangerous thing in life. Nothing is properly ours but the instant we breathe in, and all the rest is nothing; it is the only good we possess; but then it is fleeting, and the first comer robs us of it. Men are so weak, that they think they oblige by giving of trifles, and yet reckon that time as nothing for which the most grateful person in the world can never make amends. Let us therefore consider time as the most valuable of all things; and every moment spent, without some improvement in virtue or some advancement in goodness, as the greatest sublunary loss. St Paul's Speech before Agrippa and Festus. I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I shall answer for myself this day before thee, touching all things whereof I am accused of the Jews: especially because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews, wherefore I beseech thee to hear me patiently. My manner of life from my youth, which was at first among mine own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, know all the Jews, which knew me from the beginning (if they would testify), that, after the straitest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of our religion I lived a Pharisee. And now I stand and am judged for the hope of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> made by God unto our fathers: unto which promise our twelve tribes instantly serving God day and night hope to come; for which hope's sake, King Agrippa, I am accused of the Jews. Why should it be thought a thing incredible with you, that God should raise the dead, when God himself has given assurance of it unto all men, in that he hath raised Christ from the dead? As for my own part, most noble Festus, I own I once verily thought that even I myself ought to do many things contrary to the name of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAZARETH">Nazareth</a>. Which thing I also did in Jerusalem. I punished the saints oft in every synagogue, and compelled them to blaspheme; and being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them even unto strange cities. In pursuit of which, as I went to Damascus, with authority and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from the chief priests: At mid-day, O king, I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in the way a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from heaven, above the brightness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, shining about me, and them which journeyed with me. And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> speaking unto me, and saying in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> tongue, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, Saul, why persecutest thou me? It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. And I said, Who art thou, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>? And he said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest. But rise, and stand upon thy feet: for I have appeared unto thee for this purpose, to make thee a minister and a witness both of these things which thou hast seen, and of those things in which I will appear unto thee. Whereupon, O king Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision: but thowed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the coasts of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God. For these causes the Jews caught me in the temple, and went about to kill me. Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great, saying none other things than those which the prophets and Moses did say should come: That Christ should suffer, and that he should be the first that should rise from the dead, and should show light unto the people, and to the Gentiles. This is the real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>: Believe me, I am no pestilent fellow, nor mover of sedition; but always endeavour all that lies in me to preserve a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> void of offence towards God and towards man: nor can the Jews prove the things whereof they now accuse me. Neither am I, Festus, besides myself; but I speak thus freely before the king, because he knows these things to be fact; yea, I am fully persuaded the king knows them all to be fact; for they were not done in a corner. King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest. And would to God that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were altogether such as I am except these bonds. Holmes's Rhetoric. Pope to Atterbury. Once more I write to you as I promised, and this once I fear will be the last; the curtain will soon be drawn between my friend and me, and nothing left but to wish you a long good night; may you enjoy a state of repose in this life not unlike that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> which some have believed is to succeed it, where we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> utterly forgetful of that world from which we are gone, and ripening for that to which we are to go. If you retain any memory of the past, let it only image to you what has pleased you best; sometimes present a dream of an absent friend, or bring you back an agreeable conversation. But, upon the whole, I hope you will think less of the time past than the future; as the former has been less kind to you than the latter infallibly will be. Do not envy the world your studies: They will tend to the benefit of men, against whom you can have no complaint; I mean, of all posterity: and, perhaps, at your time of life, nothing else is worth your care. What is every year of a wise man's life but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">centurion</a> or critic on the past? Those whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> is the shortest, live long enough to laugh at one half of it: The boy despises the infant, the man the body, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> both, and the Christian all. You may now begin to think your manhood was too much a puerility; and you will never suffer your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to be but a second infancy. The toys and baubles of your childhood are hardly now more below you than those toys of our riper and our declining years; the drums and rattles of ambition, and the dirt and bubbles of avarice. At this time, when you are cut off from a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and made a citizen of the world at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, you should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> your talents not to serve a party, or a few, but all mankind. Your genius should mount above that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a>, in which its participation and neighbourhood with earth hath long involved it: To shine abroad, and to heaven, ought ought to be the business and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of your present situation. Remember it was at such a time that the greatest lights of antiquity dazzled and blazed the most in their retreat, in their exile, or in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. But why do I talk of dazzling or blazing? it was then that they did good, that they gave light, and that they became guides to mankind. Those aims alone are worthy of spirits truly great, and such I therefore hope will be yours. Resentment indeed may remain, perhaps cannot be quite extinguished, in the noblest minds; but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> will never harbour there: Higher principles than those of the first, and better principles than those of the latter, will infallibly influence men whose thoughts and whose hearts are enlarged, and cause them to prefer the whole to any part of mankind, especially to so small a part as one's single self. Believe me, my Lord, I look upon you as a spirit entered into another life, as one just upon the edge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>, where the passions and affections must be much more exalted, and where you ought to despise all little views and all mean retropects. Nothing is worth your looking back; and therefore look forward, and make (as you can) the world look after you; but take care it be not with pity, but with esteem and admiration. I am, with the greatest sincerity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for your fame as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, your, &c. The above most charming and most affectionate letter was written about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before Atterbury bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> was sent into banishment, and is universally admired.

STENTOROPHONIC TUBE

a speaking <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>; thus called from Stentor, a person mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>. See TRUMPET.

STEP

Pages 322-322

in a ship, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> of wood fixed on the decks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bottom of a ship, and having a hole in its upper side, fitted to receive the heel of a mizzen capstan. The steps of the main and foremasts of every ship rest upon the kelson, to which they are firmly secured by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, bolts, or spike-nails. The step of the mizen-mast usually rests upon the lower deck.

STEPHANIUM

Pages 322-322

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clasps; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 47th order, Stellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>.

STEPHANOPHORUS

Pages 322-322

in antiquity, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Pallas, who presided over the rite. It was usual for every god to have a chief priest; that of Pallas was the Stephanophorus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> was called Dadouchus.—Stephanophorus was also a priest who assisted the women in the celebration of the festival Thesmophoria.

STEPHANUS BYZANTINUS

Pages 322-322

an able grammarian, who lived in the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sixth century. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, in which he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of observations, borrowed from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which showed the origin of cities and colonies, of which we have nothing remaining but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> by Hermolaus the grammarian; but from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> the learned have received great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and Sionius, Calaubon, Scaliger, Salmasius, &c. have employed themselves in illustrating it.

STEPHEN

Pages 322-322
or St Stephen's Day, a festival of the Christian church, observed on the 26th of December, in memory of the first martyr St Stephen.

STEPHENS

Pages 322-322

a family of printers deservedly celebrated. They flourished at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the revival of learning, and contributed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> towards dispelling the cloud of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> which had so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> overshadowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Some of the classics before the 16th century were in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> lost, and all of them were exceedingly corrupted. By their abilities and indefatigable industry these defects were supplied, and the learned were furnished with beautiful and correct editions of the Greek and Roman authors. Thus the world was not only supplied with an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of amusement and instruction in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writings; but it is to the ardour which they inspired, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of elegance which they displayed, that the present advanced state of literature is in a great measure owing. [Merged from HENRY STEPHENS, p.322] the first of these illustrious men, was born in France, soon after the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, perhaps about the year 1465. He settled as a printer at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and was probably patronized by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. A great proportion of the books which he published were Latin: They are printed in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and are not inelegant, though some of them abound rather too much in contractions. He died about the year 1520, and left behind him three sons, Francis, Robert, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. His widow married Simeon de Colines (Colineus in Latin), who thus got possession of Henry's printing-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the profession till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

STERAGE

on board a ship, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship next below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-deck, before the bulk-head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cabin, where the steersman stands, in most ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. See Steering.

STERCORARIANS

Pages 328-328
or STERCORANISTÆ, formed from *stercus* "dung," a name which those of the Roman church anciently gave to such as held that the host was liable to digestion, and all its consequences, like other food.

STERCULIA

Pages 328-328

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clade monocotyledons; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 38th order, tricocceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STEREOGRAPHIC PROJECTION

Pages 328-328

is the projection of the circles of the sphere on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of some one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle, the eye being placed in the pole of that circle. See Projection of the Sphere.

STEREOMETER

Pages 328-328

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> invented in France for measuring the volume of a body, however <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, without plunging it in any liquid. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the volume of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> contained in a vessel be measured, when the vessel contains air only, and also when it contains a body whose volume is required to be known, the volume of air ascertained by the first measurement, deducting the volume ascertained by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the volume of the body itself. Again, if the volume of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of air be inversely as the pressure to which it is subjected, the temperature being supposed constant, it will be easy to deduce, from the mathematical relations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, the whole bulk if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two bulks under two known pressures be obtained by experiment. Suppose that the first pressure is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the second, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the second volume of air double the first, and the difference equal to 50 cubic inches; the first volume of air will likewise be 50 cubic inches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the stereometer is to ascertain this difference at two known pressures. The instrument is a kind of funnel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> (fig. 1) composed of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a> A, in which the body is placed, and the tube B as uniform in the bore as can be procured. The upper edge of the capsule is ground with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERY">emery</a>, that it may be hermetically closed with a glass cover M lightly greased. A double <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> is ruled on the tube, having two sets of graduations; one to denote the length, and the other the capacities, as determined by experiment. When this instrument is used, it must be plunged into a vessel of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, with the tube very upright, till the mercury rise within and without to a point C of the scale. See fig. 2. The capsule is then closed with the cover, which being greased will prevent its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> air and that contained within the capsule and tube. In this situation of the instrument, the internal air is compressed by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, expressed by the length of the mercury in the tube of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>. The instrument is then elevated, still keeping the tube in the vertical position. It is thus represented, fig. 2, second position. The mercury descends in the tube, but not to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the external surface, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of mercury DE remains suspended in the tube, the height of which is known by the scale. The interior air is less compressed.

STEREOMETRY

Pages 328-331

formed of στερεός <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, and μέτρον <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> which teaches how to measure solid bodies, i.e., to find the solidity <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> solid contents of bodies; as globes, cylinders, cubes, vessels, ships, &c.

STEREOTOMY

Pages 331-331

formed from στερεός, and τομή, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a>, the art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> solids, or making sections thereof; as walls and other membranes in the profiles of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>.

STEREOTYPE PRINTING

Pages 331-331

a method of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>, which was introduced into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by William Ged of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> before the middle of the 18th century, and which has been revived of late, and greatly improved by the French. It has also been brought into practice in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Stanhope, who has produced some beautiful specimens of it. Some persons seem disposed to dispute the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Ged, seeing that the same method of printing by wooden blocks was practised by the Chinese and Japanese many hundred years ago. See Ged, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of, and Printing.

STERILITY

Pages 331-331

barrenness, in opposition to fertility. It has been asserted by many authors, that all monsters produced by a mixture of different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals, such as mules, are barren; but this does not hold universally, even with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, which is the instance most generally adduced. Sterility in women sometimes happens from a miscarriage, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> violent labour injuring some of the genital parts; but one of the most frequent causes is the suppression of the menstrual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a>.—There are other causes arising from various diseases incident to those parts, by which the uterus may be unfit to receive or retain the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> seed;—from the tubes fallopianæ being too short, or having lost their erectile power; in either of which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> can take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>;—from universal debility and relaxation; or a local debility of the genital system; by which means, the parts having lost their tone or contractile power, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is thrown off immediately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> coitum;—from imperforation of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a>, the uterus, or the tubes, or from diseased ova, &c. Hence medical treatment can only avail in cases arising from topical or universal debility; in correcting irregularities of the menstrual flux, or in removing tumors, cicatrices, or constrictions of the passage, by the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>.

STERIS

Pages 331-331

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class pentandria. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STERLING

Pages 331-331

an epithet by which genuine English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is distinguished. It is unnecessary to mention the various conjectures of antiquaries about the origin and meaning of this appellation. The most probable Henry's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> seems to be this, that some artists from Ger. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of many, who were called Efflerings, from the situation of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, had been employed in fabricating our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Eastain, vol. iii. money, which consisted chiefly of silver pennies; and that from them the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> was called an efflering, and our money efflering <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sterling money.

STERN

Pages 331-331

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a ship; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which is represented to the view of a spectator, placed on the continuation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> behind. The stern is terminated above by the taffrail, and below by the counters; it is limited on the sides by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-pieces, and the intermediate spaces comprehends the galleries and windows of the different cabins. See Quarter of a Ship, Ship, and Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>.

STERN-FAST

Pages 331-331

a rope used to confine the stern of a ship <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> to any wharf or jetty head, &c.

STERN-MAST

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, usually denotes that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a fleet of ships which is in the rear, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> farther aft-stern, as opposed to head-most.

STERNA

Pages 332-332

the TERN; a genus of birds arranged under the order of palmipeds. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STERNE

Pages 332-332

Laurence, an English writer of a very peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, was born at Clowmwell, in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, on 24th November 1713. His father Roger Sterne was the grandson of Sterne archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, who has been supposed, we know not upon what grounds, to have been the author of the excellent book entitled "The Whole Duty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>." Laurence inherited nothing of his ancestor's manner of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, but rather resembled Rabelais, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> he carried with him even into the pulpit. In 1722 he was sent to school at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till 1732, when he was removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. How <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> he resided in college, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> what progress he made in literature or science, is not known: his works display rather native genius than profound erudition. Upon quitting the university he went to York, and being in orders was presented to the living of Sutton by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his uncle Dr Sterne, a prebendary of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In 1741 he married, and was soon afterwards made a prebendary of York, by the interest also of his uncle, who was then upon very good terms with him; but "quickly quarrelled with him (he says), and became his bitterest enemy, because he would not be a party man, and write paragraphs in the newspapers." By his wife's means he got the living of Stillington, but remained near 20 years at Sutton, doing duty at both places. He was then in very good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, which, however, soon after forsook him; and books, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, fiddling, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a>, were, as he tells us, his amusements. In 1760, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to publish his two first volumes of "Tristram Shandy;" and was that year presented to the curacy of Coxwold. In 1762 he went to France, and two years after to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of his health; but his health never was recovered. He languished under a consumption of the lungs, without the slightest depreration of spirits, till 1768, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his terrestrial existence. The works of Sterne are very generally read. They consist of, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> and Opinions of Tristram Shandy; 2. Sermons; 3. A Sentimental Journey; 4. Letters, published since his death. In every serious page, and in many of much levity, the author writes in praise of benevolence, and declares that no one who knew him could suppose him one of those wretches who heap misfortune upon misfortune: But we have heard anecdotes of him extremely well authenticated, which proved that it was easier for him to praise this virtue than to practise it. His wit is universally allowed; but many readers have persuaded themselves that they found wit in his blank <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, while it is probable that he intended nothing but to amuse himself with the idea of the sage conjectures to which these pages would give occasion. Even his originality is not such as is generally supposed by those fond admirers of the Shandean manner, who have presumed to compare him with Swift, Arbuthnot, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a>. He has borrowed both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and manner from various authors, and in particular from an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, "The Anatomy of Melancholy by Burton," as every reader may be convinced by the learned, elegant, and candid comments on his works published by Dr Ferrier, in the fourth volume of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Literary and Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>.

STERNE-POST

Pages 331-332

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> straight piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> erected on the extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, to sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> and terminate the ship behind. This piece ought to be well secured and supported; because the ends of all the lower planks of the ship's bottom are fixed in a channel, cut on its surface; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the rudder is sustained by it. STERNE-Sheets, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> which is contained between the stern and the aftmost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hindmost seat of the rowers. It is generally furnished with benches to accommodate the passengers. See BOAT.

STERNO-COSTALES

Pages 332-332
commonly called the musculi triangulares sterni, in Anatomy, are five pairs of fleshly planes, disposed more or less obliquely on each side the sternum, on the insides of the cartilages of the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth true ribs.

STERNO-HYOIDUS

Pages 332-332

in Anatomy. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles, under the article ANATOMY.

STERNOMANTIS

Pages 332-332

in antiquity, a designation given to the Delphian priests, more usually called PYTHIA.—Sternomantis is also used for any one that had a prophesying demon within him. STERNOMASTOID/EUS, a muscle. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles, under ANATOMY.

STERNOTHYROIDEUS

Pages 332-332

a muscle. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles, under ANATOMY. STERNUM. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STERNUTATIVE

Pages 332-332
or STERNUTATORY, a medicine proper to produce sneezing. See SNEEZING.

STETIN

Pages 332-332
or STETTIN, a sea-port town of Germany, in the circle of Upper Saxony, and capital of Hither Pomerania, with the title of a duchy, and a castle. It had long a famous school, which the wars of Germany never disturbed. The ancient dukes of Pomerania resided here; and it was taken by the elector of Brandenburg in 1676, but given to Sweden by the treaty of Nimeguen. In 1713 it submitted to the allies; and then the said elector was put in possession again of this important place, which is a bulwark to the marche of Brandenburg; and the fortifications have been greatly improved. It is now a flourishing place, and carries on a considerable trade. It is seated on the river Oder, 72 miles north of Franconia, and 70 north by east of Berlin. E. Long. 14° 38'. N. Lat. 53° 35'. The duchy is 125 miles in length, and borders upon Mecklenburg, and partly upon Brandenburg. The breadth is from 17 to 25 miles, and it is divided by the river Oder into two parts.

STEW

Pages 332-332

those places which were permitted in England to women of professed incontinency; so called, because dissolute persons are wont to prepare themselves for venereal acts by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>; and hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> were by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> reckoned among the effeminate sort of pleasures. These laws were suppressed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. about the year 1546.

STEWARD

Pages 332-335

an officer appointed in another's stead <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and always taken for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officer within his jurisdiction. Of these there are various kinds. The greatest officer under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-steward of England, an office that was anciently the inheritance of the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, till forfeited by Simon de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry III. But the power of this officer is so very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that it has not been judged safe to trust it any longer in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a subject, excepting only pro hac vice, occasionally: as to officiate at a coronation, at the arraignment of a nobleman for high-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, or the like. During his office, the steward bears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, &c. ended, he breaks the staff, and with it his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> expires. There is likewise a lord-steward of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, who is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officer of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, has the care of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and authority over all the officers and servants of the household, except such as belong to the chapel, chamber, and stable. Steward, an officer in a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, appointed by the purser to distribute the different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> to the officers and crew; for which purpose he is furnished with a mate and proper assistants. Court of the Lord High Steward of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is a court instituted for the trial of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> indicted for treason or felony, or for misprision of either. The office of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and was formerly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>, or at least held for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, or dum bene se gerit: but now it is usually, and hath been for many centuries past, granted pro hac vice only; and it hath been the constant practice (and therefore seems now to have become necessary) to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> it to a lord of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, else he is incapable to dry such delinquent peer. When such an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> is therefore found by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of freeholders in the King's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, or at the assizes before the justices of eyre and terminer, it is to be removed by a writ of certiorari into the court of the lord high-steward, which has the only power to determine it. A peer may plead a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> before the court of King's bench, and the judges have power to allow it, in order to prevent the trouble of appointing an high-steward merely for the purpose of receiving such <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>: but he may not plead in that inferior court any other plea, as guilty or not guilty of the indictment, but only in this court; because, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such plea, it is possible that judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> might be awarded against him. The king, therefore, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a peer be indicted of treason, felony, or misprision, creates a lord high-steward pro hac vice by commission under the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; which recites the indictment so found, and gives his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a> power to receive and try it secundum legem et consuetudinem Anglie. Then when the indictment is regularly removed by writ of certiorari, commanding the inferior court to certify it up to him, the lord high-steward directs a precept to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> at arms, to summon the lords to attend and try the indicted peer. This precept was formerly issued to summon only 18 or 20 selected from the body of the peers; then the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> came to be indefinite; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was for the lord-high-steward to summon as many as he thought proper (but of late years not less than 23); and that those lords only should sit upon the trial; which threw a monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of power into the hands of the crown, and this its great officer, of selecting only such peers as the then predominant party should most approve of. And accordingly, when the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Clarendon fell into disgrace with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., there was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> formed to prorogue the parliament, in order to try him by a select number of peers; it being doubted whether the whole house could be induced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in with the views of the court. But now, by statute 7 W. III. c. 3., upon all trials of peers for treason or misprision, all the peers who have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to sit and vote in parliament shall be summoned at least 20 days before such trial, to appear and vote therein; and every lord appearing shall vote in the trial of such peer, first taking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy, and subscribing the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>. During the session of parliament, the trial of an indicted peer is not properly in the court of the lord high-steward, but before the court last mentioned of our lord the king in parliament. It is true, a lord high-steward is always appointed in that case to regulate and add weight to the proceedings: but he is rather in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a speaker pro tempore, or chairman of the court, than the judge of it; for the collective body of the peers are therein the judges both of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and fact, and the high-steward has a vote with the rest in right of his peerage. But in the court of the lord high-steward, which is held in the recess of parliament, he is the sole judge of matters of law, as the lords triors are in matters of fact; and as they may not interfere with him in regulating the proceedings of the court, so he has no right to intermix with them in giving any vote upon the trial. Therefore, upon the conviction and attainer of a peer for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> in full parliament, it hath been holden by the judges, that in case the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> appointed in the judgement for execution should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> before execution done, a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of execution may be appointed by either the high court of parliament during its sitting, though no high-steward be existing, or, in the recess of parliament, by the court of King's bench, the record being removed into that court. It has been a point of some controversy, whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> have now a right to sit in the court of the lord-high-steward to try indictments of treason and misprision. Some incline to imagine them included under the general words of the statute of King William "all peers who have a right to sit and vote in parliament;" but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> had been much clearer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had been "all lords," and not "all peers;" for though bishops, on account of the baronies annexed to their bishoprics, are clearly lords of parliament, yet their blood not being ennobled, they are not universally allowed to be peers with the temporal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>: and perhaps this word might be inserted purposely with a view to exclude them. However, there is no instance of their sitting on trials for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offences, even upon impeachments or indictments in full parliament, much less in the court we are now treating of; for indeed they usually withdraw voluntarily, but enter a protest, declaring their right to stay. It is observable, that in the 11th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the constitutions of Clarendon, made in parliament 11th Henry II., they are expressly excused, rather than excluded, from fitting and voting in trials, which concern life or limb: episcopi, sicut ceteri barones, debent interficere judicium cum baronibus, quoque perenniat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> diminutionem membrorum vel ad mortem. And Becket's quartel with the king hereupon was not on account of the exception (which was agreeable to the canon law), but of the general rule, that compelled the bishops to attend at all. And the determination of the house of lords Steward, lords in the earl of Danby's case, which hath ever since been adhered to, is consonant to these constitutions; "that the lords spiritual have a right to stay and fit in court in capital <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, till the court proceeds to the vote of guilty or not guilty." It must be noted, that this revolution extends only to trials in full parliament; for to the court of the lord high-steward (in which no vote can be given, but merely that of guilty or not guilty), no bishop, as such, ever was or could be summoned: and though the statute of King William regulates the proceedings in that court, as well as in the court of parliament, yet it never intended to new-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> or alter its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and consequently does not give the lords spiritual any right, in cases of blood, which they had not before. And what makes their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> more reasonable is, that they have no right to be tried themselves in the court of the lord high-steward, and therefore surely ought not to be judges there. For the privilege of being thus tried depends upon nobility of blood rather than a seat in the house, as appears from the trials of the popish lords, of lords under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and (since the union) of the Scotch nobility, though not in the number of the fifteen; and from the trials of females, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> consort or dowager, and of all peersesses by birth; and peersesses by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> also, unless they have, when dowagers, disparaged themselves by taking a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a> to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> husband. STEWARD of the Chiltern <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">Hundreds</a>. See CHILTERN Hundreds. STEWART; Dr MATTHEW, an eminent mathematician, was in 1717 born at Rothsay in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Bute, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> his father was minister. Being intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he went through the usual course of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and was in 1734 received as a student into the university of Glasgow. There he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of having for his preceptors in moral science and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> the celebrated professors Hutcheson and Simson; by the latter of whom he was instructed in what may not improperly be called the arcana of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>. Mr Stewart's views making it necessary for him to remove to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, he was introduced by Dr Simson to Mr Maclaurin, that his mathematical studies might in the Edinburgh Philosophical Transactions, vol. i., by Mr Playfair. Account of Dr Stewart in the Edinburgh Philosophical Transactions, vol. i., by Mr Playfair. not suffer no interruption; and he attended the lectures of that great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> with such advantage as might be expected from eminent abilities, directed by the judgement of him who made the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and geometry of Newton intelligible to ordinary capacities. Mr Stewart, however, had acquired, from his intimacy with Dr Simson, such a predilection for the ancient geometry, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, however powerfully recommended, could not lessen; and he kept up a regular correspondence with his old master, giving him an account of his progress and his discoveries in geometry, and receiving in return many curious communications respecting the Loci Plani and the porisms of Euclid. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORISM">PORISM</a> and SIMSON. While the second <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of porisms, to which more genius was perhaps required than to the first discovery of them, employed Dr Simson, Mr Stewart pursued the same subject in a different and new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. In doing so, he was led to the discovery of those curious and interesting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> which were published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of General Theorems in 1746. They were given without the demonstrations; but did not fail to place their discoverer at once among the geometers of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. They are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> porisms, though Mr Stewart, careful not to anticipate the discoveries of his friend, gave them no other name than that of theorems. Our author had before this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> entered into the church; and obtained, through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle and the earl of Bute, the living of Rosneath, a retired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> parish in the west of Scotland: but in 1747 he was elected to the mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the university of Edinburgh, which had become vacant the year before by the death of Mr Maclaurin. The duties of this office gave a turn somewhat different to his pursuits, and led him to think of the most simple and elegant means of explaining those difficult propositions which were hitherto only accessible to men deeply versed in the modern analysis. In doing this, he was pursuing the object which of all others he most ardently wished to attain, viz. the application of geometry to such problems as the algebraic <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a> alone had been thought able to resolve. His solution of Kepler's problem was the first specimen of this kind which he gave to the world; and it was impossible to have produced one more to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the method he followed, or of the abilities with which he applied it. On this problem the utmost resources of the integral calculus had been employed. But though many excellent solutions had been given, there was none of them at once <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> in its method and simple in its principles. Mr Stewart was so happy as to attain both these objects; and his solution appeared in the second volume of the Essays of the Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Edinburgh for the year 1756. In the first volume of the same collection there are some other propositions of Mr Stewart's, which are an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of a curious theorem in the fourth book of Pappus. They have a relation to the subject of porisms, and one of them forms the gist of Dr Simson's Retortation. They are besides very beautiful propositions, and are demonstrated with all the elegance and simplicity of the ancient analysis. The prosecution of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which he had formed of introducing into the higher parts of mixed mathematics the strict and simple form of ancient demonstration, produced the Treatise Physical and Mathematical, which were published in 1761, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>'s Distance, which was published in 1763. In this last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it is acknowledged that he employed geometry on a task which geometry cannot perform; but while it is granted that his determination of the sun's distance is by no means free from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, it may safely be asserted that it contains a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> always <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> geometers, and will always be admired by them. Few errors in science are redeemed by the display of so much ingenuity, and what is more singular, of so much <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> reasoning. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> is everywhere elegant, and will probably be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> regarded as a specimen of the most arduous inquiry which has been attempted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> geometry. The Sun's Distance was the last work which Dr Stewart published; and though he lived to see several animadversions on it made public, he declined entering into any controversy. His disposition was far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a>; and he knew the value of that quiet which a literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should rarely suffer his antagonists to interrupt. He used to say, that the decision of the point Stewart, in question was now before the public; that if his investigation was right it would never be overturned, and that if it was wrong it ought not to be defended. A few months before he published the essay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, he gave to the world another work, intitled Propositiones Geometricae More Veterum Demonstratae. This title, it is said, was given to it by Dr Simson, who rejoiced in the publication of a work so well calculated to promote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the ancient geometry. It consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of geometrical theorems for the most part new; investigated first by an analysis, and afterwards synthetically demonstrated by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> of the same analysis. Dr Stewart's constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the geometrical analysis had put him in possession of many valuable propositions which did not enter into the plan of any of the works that have been enumerated. Of these not a few have found a place in the writings of Dr Simson, where they will forever remain to mark the friendship of these two mathematicians, and to evince the esteem which Dr Simson entertained for the abilities of his pupil. Soon after the publication of the Sun's Distance, Dr Stewart's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> began to decline, and the duties of his office became burdensome to him. In the year 1772 he retired to the country, where he afterwards spent the greater part of his life, and never resumed his labours in the university. But though mathematics had now ceased to be his business, they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be his amusement till a very few years before his death, which happened on the 23rd of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1785, at the age of 68. The habits of study, in a man of original genius, are objects of curiosity, and deserve to be remembered. Concerning those of Dr Stewart, his writings have made it unnecessary to remark, that from his youth he had been accustomed to the most intense and continued application. In consequence of this application, added to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> vigour of his mind, he retained the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his discoveries in a manner that will hardly be believed. He rarely wrote <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> any of his investigations till it became necessary to do so for the purpose of publication. When he discovered any proposition, he would put down the enunciation with great accuracy, and on the same piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> would construct very neatly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> to which it referred. To these he trusted for recalling to his mind at any future period the demonstration or the analysis, however complicated it might be. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> had taught him, that he might place this confidence in himself without any danger of disappointment; and for this singular power he was probably more indebted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of his invention than the mere tenacity of his memory. Though he was extremely studious, he read few books, and verified the observation of M. D'Alembert, that of all the men of letters, mathematicians read least of the writings of one another. His own investigations occupied him sufficiently; and indeed the world would have had reason to regret the misapplication of his talents, had he employed in the mere acquisition of knowledge that time which he could dedicate to works of invention.
