a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 37th order, Columniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Stibadium <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STIBADIUM

Pages 335-335

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a low kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> couch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of a circular form, which succeeded to the triclinia, and was of different sizes, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of guests for which it was designed. Tables of this kind were called hexactina, octactina, or enneactina, according as they held six, eight, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> guests, and so of any other number.

STICHOS

Pages 335-335

a name given by the old writers to a pectoral confection, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient of which was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> Marrubium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> horseradish.

STICKLEBACK

Pages 335-335

a genus of fishes. See GASTRORHINUS, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Foot-Sticks, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>, slips of wood that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between the foot of the page and the chefs, to which they are wedged fast by the quoins, to keep the form firm, in conjunction with the side-sticks, which are placed at the side of the page, and fixed in the same manner by means of quoins.

STIFFLE

Pages 335-335
or GREAT MUSCLE, in the manege, is the part of the hind leg of a horse which advances towards its belly. This is a most dangerous part to receive a blow upon.

STIGMA

Pages 335-335

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the summit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> top of the style, accounted by the sexualists the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> organ of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which receives the fecundating dust of the tops of the flamina, and transmits its vapour or effluvia through the style into the heart of the seed-bud, for the purpose of impregnating the seeds.

STIGMATA

Pages 335-335

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> introduced by the Franciscans, to express the marks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of our Saviour's wounds, said to have been miraculously impressed by him on the body of their ferapic father St Francis.

STIGMATIZING

Pages 335-336

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was inflicted upon slaves as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, but more frequently as a mark to know them by: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it was done by applying a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> marked with certain letters to their foreheads, till a fair <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> was made; and then pouring <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a> into their furrows, that the inscription might be the more conspicuous. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a> were branded in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> with the name <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> character of their general. After the same manner, it was customary to stigmatize the worshippers and votaries of some of the gods. The marks used on these occasions were various; sometimes they contained the name of the god, sometimes his particular ensign, as the thunderbolt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, the ivy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, &c.; or they marked themselves with some mythical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, whereby the god's name was described. To these three ways of stigmatizing St John is supposed to refer (Rev. chap. xiii. ver. 16, 17). Theodoret is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the Jews Jews were forbidden to brand themselves with figmata, because the idolaters, by that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, used to consecrate themselves to their false gods. Among some nations, figmatizing was considered as a distinguishing mark of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. In Thrace, as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> tells us *, it was practised by none but persons of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, nor omitted by any but persons of the meanest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons are also said to have imprinted on the bodies of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> the figures of animals, and other marks, with hot irons.

STILBE

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clas polygamia, and order of dioecia. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STILBITE

Pages 336-336

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mineral, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> variety of zeolite. See Zeolite, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. STILE. See Style.

STILL

Pages 336-336

the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> for various purposes, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of ardent spirits. STILL-Bottoms, in the distillery, a name given by the traders to what remains in the still after working the wash into low wines. These bottoms are procured in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> from the malt-wash, and are of so much value to the distiller in the fattening of hogs, &c., that he often finds them one of the most valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the business.

STILL DE GRAIN

Pages 336-336

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> trade, the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and is made of a decoction of the lychum or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a> berry, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>-water, which is mixed with whitening into a paste, and formed into twisted sticks. It ought to be chosen of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, very fine, tender, and friable, and free from dirt.

STILLAGO

Pages 336-336

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to clas gyandria. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STILLINGFLEET

Pages 336-337

EDWARD, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, was the son of Samuel Stillingfleet, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, and was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRANBORNE">Cranborne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in 1635. He was educated at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; and having received holy orders, was, in 1657, presented to the rectory of Sutton in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>. By publishing his Origines Sacrae, one of the ablest defences of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> that has ever been written, he soon acquired such reputation, that was appointed preacher of the Rolls Chapel; and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1665 was presented to the rectory of St Andrew's, Holborn. He was afterwards chosen lecturer at the Temple, and appointed chaplain in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. In 1668 he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and was soon after engaged in a dispute with those of the Roman religion, by publishing his discourse concerning the idolatry and fanaticism of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, which he afterwards defended against several antagonists. In 1680 he preached at Guildhall chapel a sermon on Phil. iii. 26, which he published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The Mischief of Separation; and this being immediately attacked by several writers, he in 1683 published his Unreasonableness of Separation. In 1685 appeared his Origines Britannicae, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Antiquities of the British Church, in folio. During the reign of King James II. he wrote several tracts against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, and was procurator of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, as he had likewise been under Charles II. After the Revolution he was advanced to the bishopric of Worcester, and was engaged in a dispute with the Socinians, and also with Mr Locke; in which last contest he is generally thought to have been unsuccessful. He died at Westminster in 1699, and Stillingfleet was interred in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Worcester, where a monument was erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> by his son. Dr Stillingfleet wrote other works besides those here mentioned, which, with the above, have been reprinted in 6 vols. folio. Stillingfleet, Benjamin, an ingenious naturalist, was grandson of the preceding. His father Edward was fellow of St John's College in Cambridge, F.R.S. M.D. and Greatham professor of physic; but marrying in 1692, he lost his lucrative offices and his father's favour; a misfortune that affected both himself and his posterity. However, going into orders, he obtained, by his father's means, the living of Newington-Butts, which he immediately exchanged for that of Wood-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a> and Swanton in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>. He died in 1708. Benjamin, his only son, was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a> school, which he left in 1720, with the character of an excellent scholar. He then went to Trinity-College in Cambridge, at the request of Dr Bentley, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, who had been private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to his father, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain to his grandfather, and much indebted to the family. Here he was a candidate for a fellowship, but was rejected by the master's influence. This was a severe and unexpected disappointment, and but little alleviated afterwards by the Doctor's apology, that it was a pity that a gentleman of Mr Stillingfleet's parts should be buried within the walls of a college. Perhaps, however, this ingratitude of Dr Bentley was not of any real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> to Mr Stillingfleet. By being thrown into the world, he formed many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and valuable connections. He dedicated some translations of Linnaeus to the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Lyttleton, partly, he says, from motives of private respect and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. Lord Barrington gave him, in a very polite manner, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the master of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KENNINGTON">Kennington</a>; a favour to which Mr Stillingfleet, in the dedication of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">Calendar</a> of Flora to that nobleman, alludes with equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, as well as with the warmest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. His Calendar of Flora was formed at Stratton in Norfolk in the year 1755, at the hospitable seat of his very worthy and ingenious friend Mr Marsham, who had made several observations of that kind, and had communicated to the public his curious observations on the growth of trees. But it was to Mr Wyndham of Felbrigg in Norfolk that he appears to have had the greatest obligations: he travelled abroad with him, spent much of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and was appointed one of his executors (Mr Garrick was another), with a considerable addition to an annuity which that gentleman had settled upon him in his lifetime. Mr Stillingfleet's genius seems, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may judge from his works, to have led him principally to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; which he prosecuted as an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, an useful citizen, and a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. In this walk of learning he mentions, as his friends, Dr Watson, Mr (afterwards Dr) Solander, Mr Hudson, Mr Price of Foxley, and some others; to whom may be added the ingenious Mr Pennant. Nor can we omit the flattering mention which Mr Gray makes of him in one of his letters, dated from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1761: "I have lately made an acquaintance with this philosopher, who lives in a garret here in the winter, that he may support some near relations who depend upon him. He is always employed, consequently (according to my old maxim)" maxim) always happy, always cheerful, and seems to me a very worthy honest man. His present scheme is to send some persons, properly qualified, to reside a year or two in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, to make themselves acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, productions, and natural history of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, that we may understand <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, &c. who have been heathen Greek to us for so many ages; and this he has got proposed to Lord Bute, no unlikely person to put it in execution, as he is himself a botanist." Mr Stillingfleet published a volume of miscellaneous tracts, which is in much esteem, and does <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> honour to his head and heart. They are chiefly translations of some essays in the *Amantissae Academicae*, published by Linnaeus, interspersed with some observations and additions of his own. In this volume he shows also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for classical learning, and entertains us with some elegant poetical effusions of his own. But his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Conversation, published in the first volume of Doddley's Collection of Poems, entitles him to a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among our English poets. This poem is addressed to Mr Wyndham, with all that warmth of friendship which distinguishes Mr Stillingfleet. As it is chiefly didactic, it does not admit of so many ornaments as some compositions of other kinds. However, it contains much good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, shows a considerable knowledge of mankind, and has several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> that in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and easy versification would not disgrace the writings of our most admired poets. Here more than once Mr Stillingfleet shows himself still sore for Dr Bentley's cruel treatment of him; and towards the beautiful and moral side of it (where it is supposed he gives us a sketch of himself) seems to hint at a mortification of a more delicate <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which he is said to have suffered from the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. To these disappointments it was perhaps owing that Mr Stillingfleet neither married nor went into orders. His London residence was at a faddler's in Piccadilly; where he died in 1771, aged above 70, leaving several valuable papers behind him. He was buried in St James's church, without the slightest monument to his memory.

See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **STILYARD.** See <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">STEEL</a>-Yard.

STILOBATUM

Pages 337-337

STILPO

Pages 337-337

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, flourished under the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Evergetes. In his youth he had been addicted to licentious pleasures, from which he religiously refrained from the moment that he ranked himself among philosophers. When Ptolemy Soter, at the taking of Megara, offered him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and requested that he would accompany him into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, he accepted but a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the offer, and retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ægina, whence, on Ptolemy's departure, he returned to Megara. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> being again taken by Demetrius the son of Antigonus, and the philosopher required to give an account of any effects which he had lost during the hurry of the plunder, he replied, that he had lost nothing; for no one could take from him his learning and eloquence. So <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> was the fame of Stilpo, that the most eminent philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in attending upon his discourses. His peculiar doctrines were, that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> universals have no real existence, and that one thing cannot be predicated of another. With respect to the former of these opinions, he seems to have taught the same doctrine with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> afterwards known by the appellation of Nominalists. To prove that one thing cannot be predicated of another, he said, that *goodness* and *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>*, for instance, are different things, which cannot be confounded by afflicting the one to be the other; he argued farther, that *goodness* is an universal, and universals have no real existence; consequently since nothing cannot be predicated of any thing, *goodness* cannot be predicated of man. Thus, whilst this subtle logician was, through his whole argument, precluding one thing of another, he denied that any one thing could be the accident or predicate of another. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> Stilpo was serious in this reasoning; if he meant any thing more than to expose the sophistry of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, he must be confessed to have been an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the art of wrangling; and it was not wholly without reason that Glycera, a celebrated courtezan, when she was reproved by him as a corrupter of youth, replied, that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> might be justly retorted upon himself, who spent his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in filling their heads with sophistical quibbles and useless subtleties. In ethics he seems to have been a Stoic, and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> he had a public and a private doctrine, the former for the multitude, and the latter for his friends. He admitted the existence of a supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, but had no reverence for the Grecian superstitions.

STILTON

Pages 337-337

a town of England, in Huntingdonshire, 7½ miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, south-west of Yaxley, on the Roman highway from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAISTOR">Caistor</a> to Huntingdon, called Ermine Street, some parts of which, in this neighbourhood, appear still paved with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is famous for cheese called English Parmesan, which is generally kept till it is old before it is brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of decay is accelerated by various means, to render it agreeable to a vitiated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. For making Stilton cheese, the following receipt is given in the first volume of the *Repository of Arts and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a>*: "Take the night's cream, and put it to the morning's new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, with the rennet; when the curd is come, it is not to be broken, as is done with other cheeses, but take it out with a foil-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> altogether, and place it in a sieve to drain gradually; and as it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>, keep gradually pressing it till it becomes firm and dry; then place it in a wooden hoop; afterwards to be kept dry on boards, turned frequently, with cloth binders round it, which are to be tightened as occasion requires, and changed every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> until the cheese become firm enough to support itself; after the cloth is taken off, the cheese is rubbed every day all over, for two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three months, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be damp or moist twice a-day; and even before the cloth is taken off, the top and bottom are well rubbed every day."

STIMULANTS

Pages 337-337

in Medicine, substances which increase the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of certain parts of the body. In particular, they quicken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the blood, increase the action of the muscular fibres, and affect the nervous system.

STIMULI

Pages 337-338

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of armature <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> offensive weapon, with which some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, as nettle, cattail, etc., STING da, acalypa, and tragia, are furnished. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, says Linnaeus, is by their venomous punctures to keep off naked animals that would approach to hurt them.

STING

Pages 338-338

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> in the bodies of certain insects, in form of a little spear, serving them as a weapon of offence. STING-Ray. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-RAIA">RAIA</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STINK-POT

Pages 338-338

an earthen jar <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shell, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with powder, grenades, and other materials of an offensive and suffocating smell. It is frequently used by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>, in the western ocean, in the attack of an enemy whom he designs to board; for which purpose it is furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> at the opening or touch-hole. See BOARDING.

STIPA

Pages 338-338

Feather Grass, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class triandria, and order of digynia; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging under the 4th order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STIPEND

Pages 338-338

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, signifies the same with tribute; and hence stipendarii were the same with tributarii.

STIPULA

Pages 338-338

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, one of the fulcra <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> props of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, defined by Linnaeus to be a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, or small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, stationed on each side the base of the footstalks of the flower and leaves, at their first appearance, for the purpose of support. Elmgren restricts it to the footstalks of the leaves only.

STIPULATION

Pages 338-338

in the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of stipulating, that is, of treating and concluding terms and conditions to be inserted in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. Stipulations were anciently performed at Rome, with abundance of ceremonies; the first whereof was, that one party should interrogate, and the other answer, to give his consent, and oblige himself. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman law, nobody could stipulate but for himself; but as the tabelliones were public servants, they were allowed to stipulate for their matters; and the notaries succeeding the tabelliones have inherited the same privilege.

STIRIA

Pages 338-338

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Germany, in the circle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the archduchy of Austria, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>, and on the west by Carinthia and the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>; it is 125 miles in length and 17 in breadth, and is said to contain 22 cities, 95 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 338 castles, 15 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, and 200,000 inhabitants. Though it is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, yet there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> fit for tillage, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is so good, that the inhabitants never were in want of corn. It contains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of very good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; whence the arms made there are in great esteem. The women differ greatly from the Austrians, and are very plain and ingenious. They have all swellings on their throats, called bronchaeles. The men are also very simple, and are rather disposed to indulge in indolence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATZ">Gratz</a>.

STIRLING

Pages 338-340

a town of Scotland, situated on the river Forth, 35 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 50' N. Lat. 56° 6'. It is also called <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a> and Striveling; from the former of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> falsely derives the name Sterling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; because, says he, Olfelt, a Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, after the overthrow of the Scots, established a mint there. The name of Striveling is said to have been derived from the frequency of skirmishes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conflicts in the neighbourhood. The town contains about 4000 inhabitants. It has a manufacture of tartans and thalboons, and employs about 30 looms in that of carpets. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> street is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. In it is the tolbooth, where is kept the standard for the wet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of Scotland. The other streets are narrow and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>.—Stirling is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> a resemblance of Edinburgh; being built on a rock of the same form, with a fortres on the summit. The origin of the castle is unknown. The rock of Stirling was strongly fortified by the Piets, amongst whom <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and several other useful arts had made a considerable progress. As it lay in the extremities of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, the possession of it was the occasion of frequent contests betwixt them and their neighbours the Scots and Northumbrians; each of whose dominions did, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, terminate near it. When the Scots, under Kenneth II., overthrew the Pictish empire near the middle of the ninth century, they endeavoured to obliterate every memorial of that people. They not only gave new names to provinces and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, but, with all the rage of barbarians, demolished many magnificent and useful edifices which had been reared up by them, and this fortres among the rest. It was, however, soon rebuilt, though upon an occasion not very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to the Scots. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Kenneth II., in 855, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Donald V. mounted the throne of Scotland. In the beginning of his reign the kingdom was invaded by Olbrecht and Ella, two Northumbrian princes, who, uniting their forces with the Cumbrian Britons, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Piets, who upon their expulsion from their native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> had taken refuge in England, advanced to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEDBURGH">Jedburgh</a>, where Donald encountered them; and, after a fierce and bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, obtained a complete victory: but, having taken up his station in Berwick, in supine security, the Northumbrians, informed of the carelefs posture in which the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> lay, surprized them by a hasty <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, dispersed them, and made a prisoner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. Pursuing the advantage they had gained, they marched northward, and subdued all before them to the frith of Forth and the town of Stirling. But the forlorn situation of the Scots, without a king and without an army, obliging them to sue for peace, they obtained it, upon condition that they should pay a sum of money for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of the king, and yield up all their dominions upon the south side of the Forth to the conquerors. The Northumbrians taking possession of the territories ceded to them by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, rebuilt the castle of Stirling, and planted it with a strong garrison, in order to preserve their new conquests, upon the frontiers of which it was situated. Our authorities also inform us, that they erected a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Forth, upon the summit of which a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> was raised, with the following inscription in monkifh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>. Anglos a Scotia separat crux ista remotis; Armis hic stant Brutis, Scotti stant hic, cruce tuti. Which is thus translated by Bellenden. I am free marche, as passengeris may ken, To Scottis, to Britonis, and to Inglistmen. None of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English historians mentions this conquest. The whole story, as well as the inscription, wears much of a monkish garb; yet its authenticity is not a little confirmed by the arms of the town of Stirling, upon which is a bridge, with a cross, and the last line of the above Latin ditich is the motto round it. We must not, however, imagine, that in those times that fortresses bore any resemblance to the present structure, which is adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of firearms. Its size and form probably resembled those castles which, under the feudal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, the English and Scottish barons used to erect upon their estates for dwelling-houses; and which, in those barbarous ages, they found necessary to fortify for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, not only against foreign invaders, but often against the attacks of their own neighbours. It is directly such a Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> as this which represents the Castrum Strivelense upon the arms of Stirling. This fortress, after it had <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the possession of the Northumbrian Saxons about 20 years, was, together with the whole country upon the south side of the Forth, restored to the Scots, upon condition of their afflicting the Saxons against their turbulent invaders the Danes. Upon the arms of Stirling are two branches of a tree, to represent the Nensis Strivelense; but the situation and boundaries of that fortress, which was probably a wing of the Caledonian, cannot be ascertained. Upon the south of Stirling, vestiges of a forest are still discernible for several miles. Banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> still remain in the castle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>, at Murray's wood, and near Nether <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANNOCKBURN">Bannockburn</a>; and stumps of trees, with much brughwood, are to be seen in all the adjacent fields. When Kenneth III received intelligence of the Danes having invaded his dominions, he appointed the castle of Stirling to be the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of rendezvous for his army; and he marched from thence to the battle of Loncarty, where he obtained a victory over those rovers, in the end of the 10th century. In the 12th century, this castle is spoken of as a place of great importance, and one of the strongest fortresses in the kingdom. In 1174, a calamity, not unusual amongst the Scottish monarchs, befell William, who at that time occupied the throne. He was taken prisoner in an unsuccessful expedition which he made into England; and, after having been detained 12 months in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, was released, upon stipulating to pay a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of money for his ransom; and, until payment thereof, delivering into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fortresses in the kingdom, which in those days were Stirling, Edinburgh, Roxburgh, and Berwick. This was the first great advantage that England obtained over Scotland; and indeed the most important transaction which had passed between these kingdoms from the Norman conquest. Though the Scottish monarchs, in their frequent perambulations through the kingdom, often visited Stirling, and held their courts for some time in the castle; yet it did not become a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence till the family of Stuart mounted the throne, and it was from different princes of this family that it received its present form. It was the place of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> of James II.; and, when raised to the throne, he frequently kept his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in it. It is well known to have been the place where that prince perpetrated an atrocious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Douglas, whom he stabbed with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The royal apartments were at that time in the north-west corner of the castle, and are now the residence of the Stirling fort-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>. The room where the murder was committed still goes by the name of Douglas's room. James III., contracting fondness for the castle on account of its pleasant situation, made it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> place of his residence, and added several embellishments to it. He built within it a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, which in those days was deemed a noble structure, and is still entire. It now goes by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, having been designed for the accommodation of that supreme court. It was covered with an oaken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of exquisite workmanship, which, though very little decayed, was a few years ago removed to make way for one of more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> structure. James also erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> priests in the castle, which he called the chapel royal, and which proved one cause of his own ruin. As the expenses necessary for maintaining the numerous officers of such an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> were considerable, he annexed to it the revenues of the rich priory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLDINGHAM">Coldingham</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERSE">Merse</a>, which at that time happened to become vacant. This priory had for a long time been held by persons connected with the family of Hume; and that family, considering it as belonging to them, strongly opposed the annexation. The dispute seems to have lasted several years; for one parliament had passed a vote, annexing the priory to the chapel-royal, and a subsequent one enacted a statute prohibiting every attempt that was contrary or prejudicial to that annexation. James V. was crowned in the castle of Stirling; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which is the chief ornament of it, was the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of that prince. This is a stately and commodious structure, all of hewn stone, with much statuary work upon it. It is built in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, with a small court in the middle, in which the king's lions are said to have been kept; and hence it still goes by the name of the lions den. The palace contains many large and elegant apartments; the ground-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is now converted into barrack-rooms for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the garrison; the upper affords a house for the governor, with lodgings for some of the subaltern officers. Opposite to the palace, upon the north, stands an elegant chapel, which was built by James VI. for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> of his son, Prince Henry, in 1594. In this chapel is preserved the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">hulk</a> of a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, which that whimsical monarch caused to be built and placed upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, in order to convey into the castle the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> for that solemnity. A strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, with a tier of guns pointing to the bridge over the Forth, was erected during the regency of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of Lorraine, mother to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Mary. It is called the French battery, probably because constructed by engineers of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. The last addition was made to the fortifications in the reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. Formerly they reached no farther than the old gate, upon which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> now stands; but in that reign they were considerably enlarged upon the side towards the town; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, with several other conveniences for a siege, were erected. Upon the south side of the castle lies a park inclosed with a stone-wall, called the king's park, and near to the foot of the rock on which the castle stands, lay the royal gardens; vestiges of the walks and parterres, with a few stumps of fruit-trees, are still visible; but by long neglect, and the natural wetness of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, the place is now now little better than a marsh. In the gardens is a mount of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, with benches of earth around it, where, according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, the court sometimes held feasts-champetres. In the castle-hill is an hollow, comprehending about an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of ground, and having all the appearance of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> work, which was used for jousts, tournaments, and other feats of chivalry. Northward of the castle lies the Govan, or perhaps more properly the Gowling hill (A); in the middle of which is a small mound called Hurly Haaky, upon which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Murdoch and his two sons were executed for treasonable practices in the reign of James I. The prospect from the castle is most delightful, as well as extensive, being greatly beautified, especially upon the east, by the windings of the Forth; which are so numerous, that though the distance by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> from Stirling to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLOA">Alloa</a> is, in a straight line, not quite six miles, it is said to be 24 by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. As this river generally runs upon plain ground, it rolls its stream in so slow and silent a manner, that what Silius Italicus <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of the Ticinus is applicable to it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, instead of lucens in that poet, we should read luens; for the clay-banks, together with the tide, which flows above Stirling, render the Forth perpetually muddy: Vix credas labi, ripis tam mitis opacis Somniferam ducit luolo gurgite lympham. The lordship and castle of Stirling were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the usual dowry of the queens of Scotland, at least after the family of Stuart came to the throne, in which they were invested at their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Robert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Erskine was appointed governor of the castle by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> II. and the office continued in that family till 1715. This fortress hath been the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of many transactions. Being by its situation considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> to the northern parts of the kingdom, the possession of it hath been always esteemed of great importance to those who sought to be masters of Scotland. It was undoubtedly a place of strength when the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> by ordnance was in its infancy; but though it resisted the utmost efforts of the rebels in 1746, it could not now hold out three days if besieged by an army of a few thousand men, conducted by an engineer of knowledge and integrity.

STIRLINGSHIRE

Pages 340-340

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, of which Stirling is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It extends 20 miles in length and 12 in breadth; being bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Lennox and Clydesdale; on the east, by <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol6.html#article-CLACKMANNANSHIRE">Clackmannanshire</a>, the river Forth, and part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>; on the south-east, by Lothian; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is open and agreeable, diversified by hill and dale, well watered with streams and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is the Forth, rising in the neighbourhood of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain called Ben-Lomond, and, running eastward, forms the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The southern part is hilly, affording plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and pasturage for sheep, horses, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. The eastern part is fertile, producing plentiful harvests of corn, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance of coal. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a>-ore is found in different parts of the county; and the rivers abound with pike, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, and salmon. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this county at two different periods, and according to the different parishes, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a> | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790—1798 | |-----------------|--------------------|-------------------------| | Airth | 2316 | 2350 | | Alva | 436 | 612 | | Balernoak | 621 | 620 | | Balfron | 755 | 1381 | | Bothkennar | 529 | 600 | | Buchanan | 1699 | 1111 | | Campsie | 1399 | 2517 | | Denny | 1392 | 1400 | | Drymen | 2789 | 1667 | | <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALKIRK">Falkirk</a> | 3932 | 8020 | | Fintry | 891 | 543 | | Gargunnock | 956 | 830 | | Killearn | 959 | 973 | | Kilfly | 1395 | 2450 | | Kippen | 1799 | 1777 | | Larbert and Dunipace | 1864 | 4000 | | Muiravonside | 1539 | 1065 | | Polmont | 1094 | 1400 | | St Ninians | 6491 | 7079 | | Slamannan | 1269 | 1010 | | Stirling | 3951 | 4668 | | Strathblane | 797 | 620 | | | 38,813 | 46,663 | | | | 38,813 | Increase, 7850* *Stat. Hist. of Scotland.

STIRRUP

Pages 340-341

in the manege, a rest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> support for the horseman's foot, for enabling him to mount, and for keeping him firm in his seat. Stirrups were unknown to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The want of them in getting upon horseback was supplied by agility or art. Some horses were taught to stoop to take their riders upon; but the riders often leapt up by the help of their spears, or were assisted by their slaves, or made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of ladders for the purpose. Græcchus filled the highways with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which were intended to answer the same end. The same was also required of the surveyors of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their duty. Menage observes, that St Jerome is the first author who mentions them. But the passage alluded to is not to be found in his epistles; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were there, it would prove nothing, because St Jerome lived at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when stirrups are supposed to have been invented, and after the use of saddles. Monfacon denies the authenticity of this passage; and, in order to account for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the ancients with regard to an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> so useful and so easy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, he observes, that while cloths and housings only were laid upon the horses backs, on which the riders were to fit, stirrups could not have been used, because they could not have been fastened with the same security as upon a saddle. But it is more (A) So called from the wailings and lamentations (in Scotch, gowlings) that were made for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> Murdoch. more probable, that in this instance, as in many others, the progress of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> genius and invention is uncertain and slow, depending frequently upon accidental causes. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STIRUP">STIRUP</a> of a Ship**, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> put upon a ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, when some of her keel happens to be beaten off; and they cannot come conveniently to put or fit in a new piece; then they patch in a piece of timber, and bind it on with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which goes under the ship's keel, and comes up on each side of the ship, where it is nailed strongly with spikes; and this they call a stirrup.

STOBAEUS

Pages 341-341

JOHN**, a laborious Greek writer, who lived at the end of the fourth century, composed many works, of which there are only his Collections remaining, and even these are not as he composed them; many things being inserted by later authors. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> contains many important sentiments collected from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, poets, and philosophers.

STOCK
