in trade. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">Capital</a> Stock. **STOCK-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROKER">Broker</a>.** See Broker and Stocks. **STOCK-Dove.** See Columba, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **STOCK-Jobbing**, the art <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mystery of trafficking in the public stocks or funds. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">Fund</a> and Stock-Jobbing. **STOCK Gilly-flower.** See Cheiranthus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

STOCKHOLM

Pages 341-342

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, is situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Upland, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 30' and N. Lat. 59° 23'. Its foundation is by the best Swedish writers generally attributed to Birger Jarl, regent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> about the middle of the 13th century during the minority of his son Waldemar, who had been raised to the throne by the states of the kingdom; but it was not before the 18th century that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence was transferred from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UPSALA">Upsala</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. This capital, which is very long and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, occupies, beside two peninsulas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> small rocky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, scattered in the Mälaren, in the streams which issue from that lake, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Bothnia. A variety of contrasted and enchanting views are formed by numberless rocks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> rising boldly from the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, partly bare and craggy, partly dotted with houses, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> feathered with wood. The harbour is an inlet of the Baltic: the water is clear as crystal, and of such depth that ships of the largest burthen can approach the quay, which is of considerable breadth, and Core's Tra- lined with spacious buildings and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> houses. At the extremity of the harbour several streets rise one above another in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, crowns the summit. Towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, about two or three miles from the town, the harbour is contracted into a narrow strait, and, winding among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rocks, disappears from the sight; and the prospect is terminated by distant hills, overspread with forest. It is far beyond the power of words, or of the Stockholm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, to delineate these singular views. The central <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, from which the city derives its name, and the Ritterholm, are the handsomest parts of the town. Excepting in the suburbs, where the houses are of wood painted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, the generality of the buildings are of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or brick fluecoated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. The royal palace, which stands in the centre of Stockholm, and upon the highest spot of ground, was begun by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XI.; it is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quadrangular stone edifice, and the style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is both elegant and magnificent. It is the habitation not only of the royal family, but also of the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the officers belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. It likewise comprehends the national or supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the colleges of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; a chapel, armory, library, and office for the public records; but the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inferior officers and servants belonging to the court, are, with the foot-guards, quartered on the burghe rs. The cattle, and all the flatly edifices in the kingdom, are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. The palace of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, in which this order sits during the session of the diet, is an elegant building adorned on the outside with marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and columns, and on the inside with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>. This and three other palaces stand on the banks of the lake, and are built on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, so as to compose an uniform piece of architecture. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, built at the expense of the city, is a noble edifice, and joins with many sumptuous houses belonging to the nobility in exhibiting a splendid appearance. The houses of the burghe rs are generally built of brick in the city; but in the suburbs they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made up of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and therefore very subject to conflagrations. These houses are often framed in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> and dimensions prescribed: whence they are transported in pieces to Stockholm by water, and there set up by the carpenters. These wooden habitations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> kept in proper repair, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> last 30 or 40 years, and are deemed warmer, neater, and more healthy, than those of brick or stone. To prevent the danger of conflagrations, the city is divided into 12 wards. In each of these there is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and four assistants, who forthwith repair to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the fire breaks out; and all porters and labourers are obliged to range themselves under the master of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> to which they belong. A fire-watch patrols the streets by night, to give warning or assistance as it may be wanted; and a centinell is maintained in the steeple of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, to toll the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a> on the first appearance of any such accident. The <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> of Stockholm is entirely subjected to the regulations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> governor, assisted by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> of the castle. This city is the emporium of Sweden, to which all the commodities of the kingdom are brought for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, and where almost all the imports from abroad are deposited. The port or haven formed by the lake Mälaren is large enough to contain 1000 sail of shipping; and furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> or wharf about an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, to which the vessels may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> with their broadsides. The greatest inconveniences attending this situation are, the distance from the sea, which is not within less than 10 miles of the town; the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>; and the winding of the river, which is remarkably crooked. It opens into the Baltic; and the entrance, which is dangerous and rocky, the Swedes have secured with two small forts: within, it is perfectly safe and commodious. Stockholm, dious. The northern suburbs are remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s gardens, and for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of artisans who have chosen their habitations in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. In the southern suburbs the Muscovite commodities are sold; and here is a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> daily assemble. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 80,000.

STOCKING

Pages 342-342

that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the clothing of the leg and foot which immediately covers and preserves them from the rigour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. Anciently, the only stockings in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> were made of cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of milled stuffs sewed together; but since the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of knitting and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> stockings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cotton, thread, &c., the use of cloth stockings is quite discontinued. Dr Howel, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the World (vol. ii. p. 222.) relates, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, in 1501, was presented with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> knit silk stockings by her silk-woman, and thenceforth she never wore cloth ones any more. The same author adds, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. ordinarily wore cloth hose, except there came from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chance, a pair of silk stockings. His son, King Edward VI., was presented with a pair of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> Spanish silk stockings by Sir Thomas Greham, and the present was then much taken notice of. Hence it should seem, that the invention of silk knit stockings originally came from Spain. Others relate, that one William Hider, an apprentice on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, seeing at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of an Italian merchant a pair of knit worsted stockings from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, took the hint, and made a pair exactly like them, which he presented to William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, and that they were the first of that kind worn in England, anno 1564. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> stockings, whether woven or knit, are formed of an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little knots, called stitches, loops, or meshes, intermingled in one another. Knit stockings are wrought with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> made of polished <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> wire, which interlace the threads and form the meshes the stocking consists of. At what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the art of knitting was invented it is perhaps impossible to determine, though it has usually been attributed to the Scots, as it is said that the first works of this kind came from Scotland. It is added, that it was on this account that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of stocking-knitters, established at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1527, took for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> St Fiacre, who is said to have been the son of a king of Scotland. But it is most probable that the method of knitting stockings by wires or needles was first brought from Spain. Woven stockings are generally very fine; they are manufactured on a frame, or machine made of polished iron, the structure of which it is needless to describe, as it may be seen in almost every considerable town in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The invention of this machine is, by Mr Anderson, attributed to William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>, M.A. of St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> so early as 1589. Others have given the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of this invention to a student of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> at a much later period, who, it is said by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> Hill*, was driven to it by dire <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. This young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, falling in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with an innkeeper's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, married her though he had not a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, and he by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> lost a fellowship. They soon fell into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> poverty; and their marriage producing the consequences naturally to be expected from it, the amorous pair became miserable, not so much on account of their sufferings, as from the melancholy dread of what would become of their yet unborn infant. Their only means of support were the knitting of stockings, at which the woman was very expert: "But fixing constantly together from morning to night, and the scholar often fixing his eyes, with steadfast observation, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of his wife's fingers in the dexterous management of her needles, he took it into his imagination, that it was not impossible to contrive a little loom which might do the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with much more expedition. This thought he communicated to his wife, and joining his head to her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, the endeavour succeeded to their wish. Thus the ingenious stocking-loom, which is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> now, was first invented; by which he did not only make himself and his family happy, but has left his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> indebted to him for a benefit which enables us to export silk stockings in great quantities, and to a vast advantage, to those very countries from whence before we used to bring them at considerable loss in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of our traffic."

STOCKS

Pages 343-343

a wooden machine to put the legs of offenders in, for securing disorderly persons, and by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, ordained by statute, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKTON">STOCKTON</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEES">Tees</a>, a handsome town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, about 16 miles south of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Durham. It is now a port of considerable trade; though, at the restoration, it was a despicable village, the best <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in which could hardly boast of anything better than clay-walls and a thatched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. About 40 years ago it sent out in one year 75 vessels for the port of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and the trade is much increased since.

STOEBE

Pages 343-343
BASTARD AETHIOPIAN, a genus of plants belonging to the clas syngenesia; and in the natural system ranging under the 49th order compositae. See BOTANY Index.

STOICS

Pages 343-343

the name given to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Grecian philosophers, from στοά, "the porch in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>," which the founder of the sect chose for his school. For the peculiar tenets of this sect, see <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, Chap. iv. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> 3. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">MORAL <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">PHILOSOPHY</a>, no 8. and ZENO.

STOKESIA

Pages 343-343

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the syngenesia clas, and order of polygama aequalis. The corollas in the ray are disposed in the shape of a funnel, and are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> is four-bristled, and the receptacle is naked. One <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> only is known, which is a herbaceous plant, and a native of South Carolina.

STOLBERG

Pages 343-343

a small town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and territory of Thuringia, of which it is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It is situated between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, 50 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Leipzig. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 8. N. Lat. 51. 42.

STOLE

Pages 343-343

a sacred ornamental worn by the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> priests above their surplice, as a mark of superiority in their respective churches; and by other priests over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALB">alb</a>, at celebrating of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it goes across the stomack; and by deacons, over the left shoulder, scarf-wise: when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> reads the gospel for any one, he lays the bottom of his stole on his head. The stole is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> swath, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> slip of stuff, hanging from the neck to the feet, with three croffles thereon. Croom of the STOLE, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of his Majesty's bedchamber, whose office it is to present and put on his Majesty's first garment, or shirt, every morning, and to order the things in the chamber.

STOMACH

Pages 343-343

in Anatomy. See ANATOMY, no 91. STOMACHIC MEDICINES are such as strengthen the stomack and promote digestion, &c. Stomachic corroboratives are such as strengthen the tone of the stomack and intestines; among which are carminatives, as the roots of galangals, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> gentian, zedoary, pimpinella, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALAMUS">calamus</a> aromaticus, and arum. Of barks and rhinds, those of canella <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">alba</a>, falafiras, citrons, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> oranges, &c. Of spices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, Stomoxys, ginger, cloves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, cardamums, and mace.

STOMOXYS

Pages 343-343

a genus of insects belonging to the order of diptera. See ENTOMOLOGY, p. 214.

STONE

Pages 361-361

in merchandize, denotes a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> for weighing commodities. A stone of beef at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of eight pounds: in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> 12 pounds: in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> 16 pounds. A stone of glass is five pounds; of wax eight pounds. A stone of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> (according to the statute of 11 Hen. VII.) is to weigh 14 pounds; yet in some places it is more, in others less; as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> 15 pounds; in Herefordshire 12 pounds. Among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-couriers a stone is the weight of 14 pounds. The reason of the name is evident. Weights at first were generally made of stone. See Deut. xxv. 13, where the word translated weight, properly signifies a stone. STONE-CHATTER. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOTACILLA">MOTACILLA</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STONEHENGE

Pages 361-362

a celebrated monument of antiquity, stands in the middle of a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> near the summit of a hill six miles distant from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. It is inclosed by a circular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> and ditch near 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, after crossing which we ascend 30 yards before we reach the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The whole fabric consists of two circles and two ovals. The outer circle is about 108 feet diameter, consisting when entire of 60 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, 30 uprights and 30 imposts, of which remain only 24 uprights, 17 standing and 7 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, 3½ feet slumber, and 8 imposts. Eleven uprights have their 5 imposts on them by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> entrance. These stones are from 13 to 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The lesser circle is somewhat more than 8 feet from the inside of the outer one, and consisted of 40 lesser stones (the highest 6 feet), of which only 19 remain, and only 11 standing: the walk between these two circles is 300 feet in circumference. The Adytum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">Cell</a> is an oval formed of 10 stones (from 16 to 22 feet high), in pairs, with imposts, which Dr Stukeley calls trilithons, and above 30 feet high, rising in height as they go round, and each <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> separate, and not connected as the outer pair; the highest 8 feet. Within these are 10 more smaller flint stones, of which only 6 are standing. At the upper end of the Adytum is the altar, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> slab of blue coarse marble, 26 inches thick, 16 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 4 broad; pressed down by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the vast stones that have fallen upon it. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stones, uprights, imposts, and altar, is exactly 140. The stones are far from being <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, but were most probably brought from those called the Grey Weathers on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>, 15 or 16 miles off; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> tried with a tool they appear of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, grain, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, generally reddish. The heads of oxen, deer, and other beasts, have been found on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> in and about Stonehenge; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> in the circumjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROWS">barrows</a>. There are three entrances from the plain to this structure, the most considerable of which is from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east, and at each of them were raised on the outside of the trench two huge stones with two smaller within <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to them. It has been long a dispute among the learned, by what <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and for what purpose, these enormous stones were collected and arranged. The first account of this structure we meet with is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GEOFFROY_OF_MONMOUTH">Geoffroy of Monmouth</a>, who, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Stephen, wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Britons in Latin. He tells us, that it was erected by the counsel of Merlin the British enchanter, at the command of Aurelius Ambrosius the last British king, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of 460 Britons who were murdered by Hengist the Saxon. The next account is that of Polydore <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, who says that the Britons erected this as a sepulchral monument of Aurelius Ambrosius. Others suppose it to have been a sepulchral monument of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOADICEA">Boadicea</a> the famous British <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. Inigo Jones is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that it was a Roman temple; from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> 16 feet long, and four broad, placed in an exact position to the eastward altar-fashion. Mr Charlton attributed it to the Danes, who were two years masters of Wiltshire. A tin tablet, on which were some unknown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, supposed to be Punic, was dug up near it in the reign of Henry VIII. but is lost; probably that might have given some information respecting its founders. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name, Stonehenge, is Saxon, and signifies a "stone gallows," to which those stones, having transverse imposts, bear some resemblance. It is also called in Welsh choir gour, or "the giants dance." Mr Grofe thinks that Dr Stukeley has completely proved this structure to have been a British temple in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a> officiated. He supposes it to have been the metropolitan temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and translates the words choir gour "the great choir or temple." The learned Mr Bryant is of opinion that it was erected by a colony of Cuthites probably before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Druids; because it was usual with them to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> one vast stone upon another for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> memorial; and these they often placed so equably, that even a breath of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> would sometimes make them vibrate. Of such stones one remains at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the pile of Stonehenge. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> distinguished stones erected with a religious view, by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>; by which was signified any thing solar and divine. The Grecians called them ἀμβρόσια πέτραι, petrae ambrosiae. Stonehenge, according to Mr Bryant, is composed of these amber stones: hence the next town is denominated Ambrosbury; not from a Roman Ambrofus, for no such person ever existed, but from the ambrosiac petrae, in whose vicinity it stood. Some of these were rocking stones; and there was a wonderful monument of this sort near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a> in Cornwall, which still retains the name of main-amber, or the sacred stones. Such a one is mentioned by Apollonius Rhodius, supposed to have been raised in the time of the Argonauts, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Tinos, as the monument of the two-winged sons of Boreas, slain by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; and there are others in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and other countries.

STONEHIVE

Pages 344-345

STONEHIVE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STONEHAVEN">STONEHAVEN</a>, a small town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINCARDINE">Kincardine</a>, Scotland, 15 miles south from Aberdeen. It was built in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, and stands at the foot of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cliffs, in a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, with a rocky bottom, opening a little in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, so that small vessels may find admittance, but only at high <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. A pier runs out from the harbour on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side to secure them after their entrance. The town contains about 800 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are fail-cloths and osnaburghs, knit worsted and thread stockings.

STONES

Pages 345-345

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, have been defined bodies which are insipid, not ductile, nor inflammable, nor soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. For a view of the classification of stones and of their distribution, see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a>. Here we shall make a few observations on some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> discussions relative to their natural history. As philosophers have perplexed themselves much about the origin and formation of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> (a subject certainly far beyond the ken of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> intellect, at least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we believe that it was made by the Almighty power of God), so they have also proposed theories to explain the origin of stones. When philosophers limit their inquiries within the boundaries of science, where they are led by the sober and safe conduct of observation and experiment, their conclusions may be <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and may be useful; but when, throwing experiment and observation aside, they rear a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> upon an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> nothing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> upon a single detached fact, their theories <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> vanish before the touch of true <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> as a romantic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> before the rod of the enchanter. Sometimes from whim, or caprice, or vanity, they attempt to confound every thing: they wish to prove that the foul is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> are animals, and that fossils are plants, and thus would banish two substances, spirit and dead matter, entirely from the world; as if the Author of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> were actuated by fordish views of parsimony in the works of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, though we evidently see that a generous profusion is one of the characteristic marks of these works. We leave the talk of confounding the different classes of being to those philosophers whose minds are too contracted to comprehend a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of being at one view, or who prefer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> to every thing else. We content ourselves with the old <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the foul is a spiritual substance; that plants are plants, and that stones are stones. We have been led into these remarks by finding that some philosophers say that stones are vegetables; that they grow and increase in size like a plant. This theory, we believe, was first offered to the world by M. Tournefort, in the year 1702, after returning from his travels in the east. It was founded on a curious fact. In surveying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, he observed that the names which visitors had engraved upon the rock were not formed of hollow but of prominent letters like basaltic reliefs. He supposes that these letters were at first hollowed out by knives; that the hollows have since been filled up by the growth of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and hence he concludes that stones vegetate. We wish we were fully assured of the fact that the letters were at first hollowed, before we attempt to account for their prominence. But even allowing the supposition to be true that they were at first hollow, we reply it is only a single fact, and that it is altogether unphilosophical to deduce a general system from a single fact. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, this protuberance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> is very improperly called vegetation, for it is not produced by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in any respect like the vegetation of a plant. Vegetation supposes vessels containing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> and growth by expansion; but who ever heard of vessels in a stone, of fluids moving in them, or of the different parts expanding and swelling like the branch or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree? Even the fact which Tournefort mentions proves nothing. He does not pretend to say, that the rock itself is increasing, but only that a few small hollows are filled with new stony matter, which rises a little above the surrounding surface of the rock. This matter evidently has been once liquid, and at length has congealed in the channel into which it had run. But is not this easily explained by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> process, the formation of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALACTITES">stalactites</a>? When water <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with calcareous matter is exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, the water evaporates, and leaves the calcareous earth behind, which hardens and becomes like a stone. Having thus examined the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fact upon which M. Tournefort founds his theory, it is unnecessary to follow him minutely through the rest of his subject. He compares the accretion of matter in the labyrinth to the consolidation of a bone when broken, by a callus formed of the extravasated nutritious juice. This observation is thought to be confirmed, by finding that the projecting matter of the letters is whitish and the rock itself greyish. But it is easy to find comparisons. The difficulty, as Pope says, is to apply them. The resemblance between the filling up of the hollow of a stone, and the consolidation of a broken bone by a callus, we confess ourselves not philosophers enough to see. Were we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> in bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, perhaps it might appear. The circumstance, that the prominent matter of the letters is whitish, while the rock is greyish, we flatter ourselves strengthens our supposition that it consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of calcareous matter. Upon the whole, we conclude, we hope logically, that no such theory as this, that stones are vegetables, can be drawn from the supposed fact respecting the labyrinth. We have to regret, that the account which we have seen of the subject is so imperfect, that we have not sufficient materials for a proper <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. Tournefort has not even told us of what kind of stone or earth the accretion consists; yet this single information would probably have decided the question (A). Vol. XIX. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> II. --- (A) To give a more distinct notion of Tournefort's theory, we shall subjoin his conclusions: From these observations (he says) it follows, that there are stones which grow in the quarries, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> that are fed; that the same juice which nourishes them serves to rejoin their parts when broken; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of animals, and the branches of trees, when kept up by bandages; and, in a word, that they vegetate. There is, then (he says), no room to doubt but that they are organized; or that they draw their nutritious juice from the

STONES AND EARTHS

Pages 345-346
Analysis of. At the close of our article Mineralogy, we referred to this place for an account of the method of examining the chemical constitution of earths and stones. In the article Ores, we have given a pretty full detail of the methods of analyzing that class of minerals. In this place we propose briefly to point out the most improved processes for the analysis of the other three classes of mineral bodies, viz., earths and stones, salts, and combustibles; to which we shall add some account of the method of examining soils. But before proceeding to the immediate object of this treatise, it may be useful to make some observations on some preliminary processes connected with the subject under consideration. In the first place, it is necessary that the mineral to be examined be reduced to a fine powder. To effect this with very hard stones, they are made red hot, and in this state thrown into cold water. By the sudden change of temperature in the different parts of the stone, it cracks, and falls to pieces. If the pieces be not sufficiently small, the same process is to be repeated. The fragments are then to be reduced to smaller pieces in a polished steel mortar, and the cavity of this mortar ought to be cylindrical. A pestle of the same metal should be made to fit it exactly, that no part of the stone may escape during the operation of pounding. The stone being in this way reduced to powder, a determinate quantity is taken, 100 or 200 grains, for example, and this is to be reduced to as fine a powder as possible; or, as it is called, to an impalpable powder. This operation is most successfully performed in an agate mortar, with a pestle of the same mineral; a mortar of about four inches in diameter, and rather more than one inch deep, is found to answer the purpose very well. It is found most convenient to operate on small quantities only at a time; not more than five or six grains. When the powder feels soft, adheres, and appears under the pestle in the form of a cake, it is then as fine as possible. It is now to be accurately weighed, and it is usually found to have acquired some additional weight, arising from part of the mortar being worn off during the pounding. This additional weight must be attended to, and after the analysis is completed, a part of the substance of the mortar must be subtracted. In the case of an agate or flint mortar being used, the portion rubbed off, which increases the weight, may be regarded as pure filaceous earth. The chemical vessels necessary for the analysis of minerals are crucibles for exposing the substances to heat, preliminary glazes and shallow dishes for solutions and evaporations. Processes. The crucibles should be of platinum or pure silver, and of such a capacity as to hold from seven to eight cubic inches of water. The vessels in which the solutions, evaporations, and other processes are performed, should be of glass or porcelain; the glass vessels, as being more brittle, and therefore more apt to break, are found to be less economical than those of porcelain. Some chemists employ porcelain vessels which are in the form of sections of spheres, and are glazed both in the inside and outside, excepting part of the bottom, which comes into immediate contact with the fire. Wedgwood's glazed vessels for evaporations, are found to answer very well; the glaze is thin, and the vessels are not very apt to crack; but it is supposed by some chemists, that it is occasionally acted on by strong acids. It is scarcely necessary to add, that an accurate balance is a necessary instrument in the hands of the analyst. I. Of the Analysis of Earths and Stones.

STOPPERS

Pages 362-372

in a ship, certain short pieces of rope, which are usually knotted at one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> both ends, according to the purpose for which they are designed. They are either used to suspend any heavy body, or to retain a cable, shroud, &c., in a fixed position. Thus, the anchors, when first hoisted up from the ground, are hung to the cat head by a stopper attached to the latter, which passing through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, is afterwards fastened to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-head; and the same rope serves to fasten it on the bow at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; or to suspend it by the ring which is to be sunk from the ship to the bottom. The stoppers of the cable have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> knot and a laniard at one end, and are fastened to a ring-bolt in the deck by the other. They are attached to the cable by the laniard, which is fastened securely round both by several turns passed behind the knot, or about the neck of the stopper; by which means the cable is restrained from running out of the ship when the rides at anchor. The stoppers of the shroud have a knot and a laniard at each end. They are only used when the shrouds are cut adunder in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, or disabled by tempestuous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they are lashed, in the same manner as those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, to the separated parts of the shroud, which are thereby reunited, so as to be fit for immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. This, however, is only a temporary expedient. STOPS. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCTUATION">Punctuation</a>; and Scripture, No. 136. STORAX. See STYRAX, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. STORK. See ARDEA, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOVE">STOVE</a> for heating apartments, greenhouses, hot-houses, fruit-walls, &c. When treating of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> properties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, we explained in sufficient detail the manner in which the expansion produced in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of air by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> produces that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> up our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a> which is called the draught of the chimney; and, in the article SMOKER, we considered the circumstances which tend to check, to promote, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> this current, so as to free us from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> and vitiated air which necessarily accompanies the consumption of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">PNEUMATICS</a> we also attended to the manner in which our fires immediately operate in warming our apartments. At present, when about to describe a method of warming intrinsically different, we must pay some more <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the distinguishing circumstance. Without pretending to explain the physical connection of heat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it may suffice to observe, that heat, as well as light, is communicated to distant bodies in an instant by radiation. A person passing hastily by the door of a glass-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> feels the glow of heat in the very moment he sees the dazzling light of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> mouth, and it is interrupted by merely screening his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. In this way is an apartment partly warmed by an open fire; and we avoid the oppressive heat by fitting where the fire is not seen, or by interposing a screen. We are apt to connect this so strongly in the imagination with the light emitted by the fire, that we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the heat to the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the light. But this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is shown to be gratuitous by a curious experiment made before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> by Dr Hooke, and afterwards, with more care and accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, by Mr Scheele. They found, that by bringing a plate of the most transparent glass briskly between the fire and one's face, the heat is immediately intercepted without any sensible diminution of the light. Scheele, by a very pretty <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, discovered that the glass made the separation, and did it both in refraction and reflection; for he found, that when the light of the same fire was collected into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> by means of a polished metal concave speculum, a thermometer placed there was infinitely affected. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we employ a glass speculum foiled in the usual manner with quicksilver, of the same diameter and focal distance, and of equally brilliant reflection, there is hardly any sensible heat produced in the focus, and the thermometer must remain there for a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> while before it is sensibly affected. When we repeated this curious experiment, we found, that after the glass has remained a long while in this position, whether transmitting or reflecting the light, it loses in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> its power of intercepting the heat. By varying this observation in many of its circumstances, we think ourselves entitled to conclude, that the glass absorbs the heat which it intercepts, and is very quickly heated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a>. While it rises in its own temperature, it intercepts the heat powerfully; but when it is, as it were, saturated, attracting no more than what it immediately imparts to the air in corporeal contact with it, the heat passes freely through along with the light. If the glass be held so near the fire that the surrounding air is very much heated, no sensible interruption of heat is perceived after the glass is thus saturated. We found the cheek more quickly sensible than the thermometer of this instantaneous radiation of the heat which accompanies the light, or is separated from it in this experiment. It is a very instructive experiment in the physiology of heat. We cannot say how far this radiation of heat may extend, nor whether the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPANIMENT">accompaniment</a> of light is absolutely necessary. The mathematician proceeds on the supposition that it extends as far as the radiation of light, and that, being also rectilineal, the density of the heat is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to that of the light. But these notions are somewhat gratuitous; and there are appearances which render them doubtful. When with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENS">lens</a> of an inch in diameter we form a focus on a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> unpolished marble of an inch diameter, the mathematician must allow that no more rays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the marble than if the lens were away; therefore the marble should be equally warmed in either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. But it is by no means so, as we have repeatedly found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> it during equal times, and then dropping it into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The water which is heated by the marble on which the focus has been formed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found to have acquired from it much more heat than from the other. The tops of lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which are never shaded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, but enjoy perpetual sunshine and fertility, instead of being warmer than the valleys below, are covered with never-melting snow; and we have some grounds to suspect that the genial influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> requires the cooperation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and to doubt whether there is any warmth at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, on which no atmosphere like ours can be observed. Perhaps the heat which cheers us, and fertilizes our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, is chemically separated from our atmosphere by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> for the light of the sun. Our successors in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">meteorology</a> need not fear that the subject of their research will be soon deprived of scientific allurements. We know but little of it after all the progress we have made during this last century, and it still presents an ample field of discussion. We said that the accompaniment of light is not demonstrably necessary. We are certain that heat may be imparted without any sensible light, in a manner which we can hardly suppose anything but radiation. If a piece of very hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> be placed a little without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> focus of a metallic concave speculum, and a very sensible air-thermometer be placed in its conjugate focus, it will instantly show an elevation of temperature, although the iron is quite imperceptible to an eye which has even been a long while in the dark. No such rise of temperature is observed if the thermometer be placed a little to one side of the focus of the speculum; therefore the phenomenon is precisely similar to the radiation of light. We are obliged therefore to acknowledge that the heat is radiated in this experiment in the same way that light is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> optical experiments. Although this is the most usual way that we in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> employ fuel for warming our apartments, it is by no means the only way in which the heat diffused from this fuel may be imparted to distant bodies. It is not even the most effectual method; it is diffused also by immediate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> to bodies in contact. The air in immediate contact with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> fuel is heated, and imparts some of its heat to the air lying beyond it, and this is partly shared with the air which is still farther off; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a>, by communication in contact, goes on till the remote air contiguous to the walls, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, the ceiling, the furniture, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, all get a share of it in proportion to their attractions and their capacities. And as the air is thus continually supplied, and continually gives out heat, the walls, &c., become gradually warmer, and the room becomes comfortable and pleasant. But we apprehend that no great proportion of the heat actually acquired by the room is communicated in this way. This diffusion by contact is but slow, especially in air which is very dry; so slow indeed, that the air in the immediate neighbourhood of the fuel is hurried up the chimney before it has time to impart any of the heat received in contact. We know that the time employed in diffusing itself in this way through stagnant air to any moderate distance is very considerable. We imagine therefore that the heat communicated to our rooms by an open fire is chiefly by radiation, but in a way something different from what we mentioned before. We imagine, that as the piece of glass in Dr Hooke's experiment absorbs the heat, so the whole mass of air which fills the room intercepts the radiated heat in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the room where the fire is seen, and is as it were saturated with it throughout, and ready to impart it to every body immersed in it. We cannot otherwise account for the equality of the heat in the different parts of the room. More radiation on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies would warm them in the inverse duplicate ratio of their distances from the fire; and diffusion by contact, if compatible with the rapid current up the chimney, would heat the room still more unequally. Recollect how slowly, and with what rapid diminution of intensity, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of blue vitriol is communicated to water even to a very small distance. But because all parts of the air of the room absorb radiated heat, what is saturated at a higher temperature, being nearer to the fire, rises to the ceiling, spreads outwards along the ceiling, and has its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> supplied by the air, which is thus pushed towards the fire from the places which are not directly illuminated. Far different is the method of warming the room by a stove. Here the radiation, if any, is very feeble or scanty; and if a passage were allowed up the chimney for the warmed air, it would be quickly carried off. This is well known to the English who reside in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> climates of St Petersburg, Archangel, &c. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> the exhilarating flutter of an open fire, and often have one in their parlour; but this, so far from warming the room during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> cold weather, obliges them to heat their stoves more frequently, and even abstracts the heat from a whole suite of apartments. But all passage this way is shut up when we warm a room by stoves. The air immediately contiguous to the stove is heated by contact, and this heat is gradually, though slowly, diffused through the whole room. The diffusion would however be very slow indeed, were it not for the great expansibility of air by heat. But the air surrounding the stove quickly expands and rises to the ceiling, while the neighbouring air slides in to supply the place, nay is even pushed in by the air which goes outwards aloft. Thus the whole air is soon mixed, and the room acquires almost an equal temperature throughout. The warming by stoves must therefore be managed upon very different principles from those adopted in the employment of open fires. The general principle is, 1st, To employ the fuel in the most effectual manner for heating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> part of the stove, which is immediately efficient in warming the contiguous air; and, 2nd, To keep in the room the air already warmed, at least as much as is consistent with wholesomeness and cleanliness. The first purpose is accomplished by conducting the fire of the furnace round its external parts, or, in short, by making every part of the flue external. Of all forms, that of a long pipe, returned backwards and forwards, up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> (provided only that the place of its last discharge be considerably higher than its entry from the fire-place), would be the most effectual. We have seen a very small stove constructed in this way, the whole being inclosed in a handsome case of polished iron plate, pierced and cut into elegant foliage like the cock of a watch, so that the odd looking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> were completely concealed. Though only three feet long, one foot thick, and five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, it warmed a very lofty room of 24 feet by 18, and consumed less than half the fuel of a stove of the more usual make, which did not so fully warm a smaller chamber. It would occupy a volume to describe the immense variety of stoves which ingenuity or architectural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> has constructed. We shall content ourselves with giving a specimen of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> classes into which they may be distinguished. The air of a room may be equally warmed, either by applying it to the surface of a small stove made very hot, or to the surface of a much larger stove more moderately heated. The first kind is chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and the milder climates of Germany and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. The last are universally used in the frozen climates of Russia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. The first are generally made of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-iron, and the last of brick-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> covered with glazed tiles or flueco. Fig. 1 represents a small German stove fully sufficient for warming a room of 24 feet by 18. The base is about three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and 14 inches deep, that is, from back to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet high. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> is in the fashion of that country; but the operative structure of it will admit of any style of ornament. A, is the fire-place, and the wood or charred coal is laid on the bottom, which has no bars. Bars would admit the air too freely among the fuel, and would both confine it too fast and raise too great a heat. That no heat may be uselessly expended, the sole of the fire-place and the whole bottom of the stove is raised an inch or two above the floor of the room, and the air is therefore warmed by it in succession, and rises upwards. For the same reason the back of the stove is not in contact with the wall of the room, or of the niche in which it is placed. The fire-place is shut up by a door which fits closely to its case, and has a small wicket at the bottom, whose aperture is regulated by a sliding plate, so as to admit no more air than what suffices for slowly consuming the fuel. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> and heated air rise to the top of the fire-place three or four inches above the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> or mantle-piece, and get out laterally by two narrow <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> B, B, immediately below the top-plate of the base. The current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> downward on each side, passes at C, C, under the partition plates which divide the two side chambers, and then rises upwards through the outer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of each, and passes through narrow slits D, D, in the top plate, and from thence along the two hollow piers E, E. The two lateral currents unite at the top of the arch, and go through the single passage F into the larger hollow behind the escutcheon G. From this place it either goes straight upwards into the vent in the wall by a pipe on the top of the stove, or it goes into the wall behind by a pipe inserted in the back of the stove. The propriety of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> is very obvious. The current of hot air is applied to exterior parts of the stove everywhere except in the two side chambers of the base, where the partition-plates form one side of the canal. Even this might be avoided by making each of these side-chambers a detached hollow pillar. But this would greatly increase the trouble of construction and joining together, and is by no means necessary. The arch H has a graceful appearance, and affords a very warm situation for any thing that requires it, such as a drink in a sick person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber, &c. Perches of a certain class <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this place for keeping a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> warm; nay, the lower part of the arch is frequently occupied by an inclosed chamber, where the heat rises high enough even for dressing victuals, as will be easily imagined when we reflect that the sole of it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the fire-place. The stove now described is supplied with fuel and with air by the front door opening into the room. That there may be room for fuel, this middle part projects a few inches before the two side-chambers. These last, with the whole upper part of the stove, are not more than ten inches deep. The passages, therefore, from the fire-place are towards the back of it; so that if we have a mind to see the fire (which is always cheerful), the door may be thrown open, and there is no danger of the smoke coming out after the current has once warmed the upper part of the stove. When the stove is of such dimensions that the base is about two feet and a half or three feet high, the fire-place may be furnished with a small grate in the British style. If the door is so hung that it can not only be thrown back, but lifted off its hinges, we have a stove grate of the completest kind, fully adequate, in our mild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, to warm a handsome apartment, even with an open fire; and when we hang on the door, and shut up the fire-place, a stove of the dimensions already given is almost too much for a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>-room. We have frequently remarked, that one side of these stoves grows much warmer than the other, and that it was difficult to prevent or remedy this; and we imagine that this is an unavoidable defect in all stoves with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> flue. It is scarcely possible to make the fire so equable in the fire-place, that one side shall not be a little warmer than the other, and a brisker current will then be produced in it. This must increase the consumption of the fuel on this side, which will increase the current, will heat this side still more, and thus go on continually till the fuel on this side is expended; after which the other side will obtain and increase the superiority. The flue is made double, that the fire-place may occupy the middle of the front; and it will be difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> this point of symmetry with one flue. The inconvenience may, however, be corrected by damping valves placed in some part of the upright funnels E, E. In the colder winters on the continent, it is thought necessary to increase the effect by making the fire-place open to the back of the stove. Its mouth or door communicates with or is joined to an opening of the same dimensions formed in the wall, and the door is on the other side in an antechamber or lobby. In Westphalia, and other places of Germany, the apartments are disposed round a spacious lobby, into which all their fire-places open, and are there supplied with fuel. By this construction it is plain that the air of the room, already warmed by the stove, is not carried off, and the room is more heated. But this method is very unfavourable to cheerfulness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The same air, confined, and repeatedly breathed and compounded with all the volatile emanations of the room, quickly loses that refreshing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that is so desirable, and even so necessary for health. It is never renewed except by very partial admixtures when the room doors are thrown open, and becomes disagreeable to any person coming in from the open air; and in the houses of the less opulent becomes really offensive and nauseous. Something of this is unavoidable in all rooms heated by stoves. Even in our apartments in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, persons of delicate nerves are hurt by what they call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> air of a room; and it is long before the smell of dinner is quite removed from a dining-room, notwithstanding the copious current up the chimney. This must be incomparably more sensible in a room heated by a stove; and this inconvenience is peculiarly sensible with respect to the stove which we are considering at present, where we employ a small surface heated to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Such stoves are seldom made of anything else than cast-iron. This (in those parts at least which are in immediate contact with the fuel) is in a state of continual calcination, and even throwing off scales. This indeed is not seen, because it is the bottom or sole of the fire-place which is so heated; but the effect on the air of the room is the same. The calcination of the iron is occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of pure vital air with the iron. This is abstracted from the general mass of atmospheric air in the room, of which it usually constitutes about two-fifths. By this abstraction the remainder becomes less fit for supporting animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or flame, and may even become highly deleterious. In every degree the remainder becomes less refreshing, and grows dull and oppressive. This is always accompanied by a peculiar smell, which, though not disgusting, is unpleasant. It resembles the smell of burnt feathers, or more exactly the smell we feel if we rub violently for some time the palms of our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> together when perfectly dry. For similar reasons these iron stoves occasion a sickly smell, by burning every particle of dust which falls on the hot parts; and if they be wiped with a woollen cloth, or any cloth not perfectly free from every kind of greasy or oily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, a smell is produced for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or days afterwards; so that without the most scrupulous attention we suffer by our very cleanliness. For such reasons we think that the stoves of brick-work covered with stucco or with glazed tiles are vastly preferable. These are much used in the gentler houses in Flanders and Holland, where they are made in the most elegant forms, and decorated with beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> or enamel; but it is plain that they cannot be so effectual, nor equally warm a room with the same expense of fuel. Earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, especially when covered with porous stucco, is far inferior to metal in its power of conducting heat. If built of bricks, they must be vastly more bulky when the fire-place and flues are of the same dimensions. The most perfect way of constructing them would certainly be to make them of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a>, in parts exactly fitted to each other, and joined by a proper cement. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of constructing would admit of every elegance of form or richness of ornament, and would not be so bulky as those which are built of bricks. The great difficulty is to prevent their cracking by the heat. Different parts of the stove being of very different heats, they expand unequally, and there is no cement which can withstand this, especially when we recollect that the same heat which expands the baked earth causes the clay or cement, with which the parts of the stove are put together or covered, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. Accordingly those earthen ware stoves seldom stand a winter or two without cracking in some place or other, even when strengthened by iron hoops and cramps judiciously disposed within them. Even hooping them them externally, which would be very unsightly, will not prevent this; for nothing can resist the expansion and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> by heat and cold. When a crack happens in a stove, it is not only unsightly, but highly dangerous; because it may be so situated, that it will discharge into the room the air vitiated by the fire. For these and other reasons, we can scarcely hope to make stoves of brick-work or pottery which shall bear the necessary heat without cracking; and their use must therefore be confined to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where very moderate heat is sufficient. We need not describe their construction. It is evident that it should be more simple than that of iron stoves; and we imagine that in the very few cases in which they are likely to be employed in this country, a single fire-place and an arch over it, divided, if we please, by a partition or two of thin tile to lengthen the flue, will be quite enough. If the stove is made in whole or in part of potters ware, a base for the fireplace, with an urn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, obelisk, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> above it, for increasing the surface, will also be sufficient. The failure <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> happens at the joinings, where the different pieces of a different heat, and perhaps of a different <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, are apt to expand unequally, and by working on each other one of them must give way. Therefore, instead of making the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> close and using any cement, the upper piece should stand in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> formed in the undermost, having a little powdered chalk or clay sprinkled over it, which will effectually prevent the passage of any air; and room being thus given for the unequal expansion, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> remains entire. This may be considered as a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> for all furnace-work, where it is in vain to attempt to hinder the mutual working of the parts. We have seen stoves in small apartments at St Petersburg, which were made internally of potters ware, in a great variety of forms, and then covered with a thick coat of stucco, finished externally with the utmost elegance of ornament, and we were informed that they were very rarely subject to crack. They did not give much heat, on account of the very low conducting power of the porous stucco; but we imagine that they would be abundantly warm for a moderate room in this country. When fitted up in these situations, and with these precautions, the brick or pottery stoves are incomparably more sweet and pleasant than the iron ones. But in the intense colds of Russia and Sweden, or even for very large rooms in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, stoves of these small dimensions are not sufficiently powerful, and we must follow the practice of those countries where they are made of great size, and very moderately heated. It is needless to describe their external form, which may be varied at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Their internal structure is the same in all, and is distinctly described in PNEUMATICS, No. 364. We shall only enlarge a little on the peculiarities connected with the general principle of their construction. The stove is intended as a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, in which a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of heat may be quickly accumulated, to be afterwards slowly communicated to the air of the room. The stove is therefore built extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a>; and it is found that they are more powerful when coated with clay as wet as can be made to hang together. We imagine the reason of this to be, that very wet clay, and more particularly flucco, must be exceedingly porous when dry, and therefore a very slow conductor of heat. Instead of sticking on the glazed tiles with no more clay or flucco than is sufficient to attach them, each tile has at its back a sort of box baked in one piece about two or three inches deep. It is represented in Fig. 2. This is filled with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and then stuck on the brick-work of the stove, which has a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of iron pins or hooks driven into the joints, which may sink into this clay and keep it firmly attached when dry. This coating, with the massive brick-work, forms a great mass of matter to be heated by the fuel. The lowest chamber, which is the fire-place, is somewhat wider, and considerably thicker than the stories above, which are merely flues.
