When the fire-place is finished and about to be arched over, a flat iron <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of small thickness is laid along the top of the side-wall on both sides, a set of finishing bricks being moulded on purpose with a notch to receive the iron bar. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a> bars are laid over these, one at each end and one or two between, having a bit turned down at the ends, which takes hold of the longitudinal bars, and keeps them from being thrust outwards either by the pressure of the arch or by the swelling in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the heat. In Fig. 3, A is the cross <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of one of the long bars, and BC is part of one of the cross bars, and CD is the clench which confines the bar A. This precaution is chiefly necessary, because the contraction of the stove upwards obliges the walls of the other stories to bear a little on the arch of the fire-place. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> above is kept together in like manner by other courses of iron bars at every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> return of the flue. The top of the stove is finished by a pretty thick covering of brick-work. The last passage for the air at H (see PNEUMATICS, Fig. 62.) has a ring lining its upper extremity, and projecting an inch or two above it. The flat round it is covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. When we would stop this passage, a covered shape like a basin or cover for dishes at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> is whelmed over it. The rim of this, resting on the lead, effectually prevents all air from coming through and getting up the vent. Access is had to this damper by a door which can be shut tight enough to prevent the heated air of the room from wafting itself up the vent. When the room is too warm, it may be very rapidly cooled by opening this door. The warm air rushes up with great rapidity, and is replaced by cool air from without. The management of the stove is as follows. About eight o'clock in the morning the pietchnick, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> who has the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the stoves, takes off the cover, shuts the damper-door, and opens the fire-place door. He then puts in a handful of wood shavings or straw, and kindles it. This warms the stove and vent, and begins a current of air through it. He then lays a few chips on the sole of the fire-place, immediately within the door; and behind this he arranges the billets of birchwood, with their ends inwards. Then he lays on more wood in the front, till he thinks there is enough. He sets fire to the chips, shuts the door, and opens the small wicket at its bottom. The air blows the flame of the chips upon the billets behind them, and thus kindles them. They consume slowly, while the billets in front remain untouched by the fire. The servant, having made his first round of the rooms, returns to this stove, and opens the door above to admit air into the vent. This is to supply its draught, and thus to check the draught in the body of the stove, which is generally too strong at this time, and would consume the fuel too fast. By this time the billets in the front are burning, first at the bottom, and the rest in succession as they sink down on the embers and come opposite to the wicket. The room does not yet feel any effect from the fire, the heat of which has not yet reached its external surface; but in about half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> this grows warm. The upper door is shut again, that no heat may now be wasted. The pietchnick by and by spreads the embers and ashes over the whole bottom of the fire-place with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a>, by which the bottom is greatly heated, and heats the air contiguous to it externally (for it stands on little pillars) very powerfully. He takes care to bring up to the top of the ashes every bit of wood or coal that is not yet consumed, that all may be completely expended. He does this as briskly as possible, that the room may not lose much warmed air by keeping open the fire-place door. At his last visit, when he observes no more glowing embers, he shuts the fire-place door and wicket, and puts the damper on the passage above, and shuts its door.—All this is over in about an hour and a half after kindling the fire. All current of air is now at an end within the stove, and it is now a great mass of brick-work, heated to a great degree within, but only about blood-warm externally. The heat gradually spreads outwards, and the external surface of the stove acquires its greatest heat about three o'clock in the afternoon; after which it gradually cools till next morning. This heat seldom is so great that one cannot bear to touch the stove with his cheek, and to keep it there. In consequence of this it can burn none of the dust which unavoidably falls on the stove, and we are never troubled with the sickening smells that are unavoidable when we employ the small cast-iron stoves much heated. The great expense of heat in a room arises from the glass windows. The pane is so thin that the external air keeps it continually cold, and thus the windows are continually robbing the air of the room of its heat. This expense of heat is reduced to less than one-third by double casements. The inner casement is about as much colder than the room as the outer casement is warmer. warmer than the air of the fields; and we have the singular advantage of having no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> formed on the glaases. But to ensure this last advantage, the seams of the inner casement must be pasted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and those of the outer casement must be left ungasketed. If we do the contrary, we shall certainly have ice on the outer casement; the reason of which is easily seen. We have been thus particular in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the management, because the reasons of some particulars are not very obvious, and the practice would not readily occur to us in this country; so that a person who, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of our recommendation, should prefer one of these stoves to the German stove, whose management is simple and obvious, might be greatly disappointed. But by following this method, we are confident that the Russian stove will be found much superior both in warmth and agreeable air. The spreading out of the embers, and waiting till all is reduced to ashes before the doors are shut, is also absolutely necessary, and a neglect of it would expose us to imminent danger of suffocation by fixed air; and this is the only inconvenience of the Russian stove, from which the other stove is free. The fixed air has no smell; and the first indication of its presence is a slight giddiness and lassitude, which disposes us to sit down and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. This would be fatal; and we must immediately open the upper passage and the fireplace door, so as to produce a strong current to carry the vitiated air of the room up the chimney. Throwing up the sashes, or at least opening all the doors, is proper on such an occasion. If we burn pit-coal, either raw or charred, this precaution is still more necessary; because the cinder is not so easily or so soon completely consumed. This fuel will require a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the management from wood fuel, but which is easily seen by any person of reflection. The safe way would be to rake out all half-burnt coal before shutting up the doors. If we use raw pit-coal, great care is necessary to prevent the accumulation of heat in the upper part of the stove. It is an inaccessible place for the chimney-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a>; and if we attempt to burn it out, we run a great risk of splitting that part of the stove which is the most slightly constructed. It is advisable therefore to burn it away every day, by giving a brisk draught with an open door for five minutes. With wood or coak there is no danger. It will not be improper in this place to give some instructions for the construction of stoves for warming several floors in a great manufactory, such as a cotton-mill, or a public library or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>. In such situations we think cleanliness, wholesomeness, and sweetness of air, no less necessary than in the drawing-room of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of opulence. We therefore recommend the brick-stove in preference to the iron one; and though it would not be the best or most economical practice to heat it but once a-day, and we should rather prefer the German practice of constant feeding, we still think it highly proper to limit the heat to a very moderate degree, and employ a large surface. If the disposition of the rooms allows us the convenience of a thick party-wall, we would place the stove in the middle of this wall, in an arch which pierces through the wall. Immediately above this arch we would carry up a very wide chimney through the whole height. This chimney must have a passage opening into each floor on both sides, which may be very accurately shut up by a door. The stove being set up under the arch, it must have a pipe communicating with its flue, and rising up through this chimney. Could an earthen pipe be properly supported, and secured from splitting by hoops, we should prefer it for the reasons already given. But as this is perhaps expecting too much, we must admit the use of a cast-iron pipe. This is the real chimney or flue of the stove, and must be of as great diameter as possible, that it may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, by an extensive surface, all the way up. The stove stands under the arch in the wall; but the air that is warmed by its surface would escape on both sides, and would be expended in that single floor. To prevent this, the stove must be inclosed in a cage; this may be of brick-work, at the distance of two or three inches from the stove all round. It must be well shut in above, and at the foundation must have a row of small holes to admit the air all around it. This air will then be warmed over the whole space between the stove and the cage, past up the chimney, and there receive additional heat from the flue-pipe which is in the middle. Great care must be taken that the fire-place door have no communication with the space between the stove and its cage, but be inclosed in a mouth-piece which comes through the cage, and opens into the feeding-room. Thus all the air which goes up to the rooms will be pure and wholesome, provided we take care that everything be kept clean and sweet about the air-holes below. Observe that those air-holes which are near the furnace door must be inclosed in a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> which takes in its air at some distance from this door; for since the current between the stove and cage may be almost as great as the current within the stove (nay, when a puff of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> beats down the chimney, it may even exceed it), there is a risk of some vitiated air and smoke being drawn into the cage. If the stove cannot be placed in the arch of a party-wall, it may be set adjoining to a side or outer wall, and furnished with a cage, a large chimney, and a flue-pipe, in the same manner. But in this case a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of heat is wasted on this outer wall, and carried off by the external air. In this situation we would recommend to line that part of the wall which is behind the stove (at two or three inches distance), and the whole of the chimney, with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> on laths. These should be nailed on battens properly fastened on the wall, leaving a space of an inch between the laths and the wall. The plaster should be of the most spungy kind, having in it a quantity of clay in powder instead of the full proportion of sand. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>-dung, washed with water and strained through coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a>, leaves a great portion of unaffiliated vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a>, which will mix very intimately in the plaster, and make it a substance very unfit for conducting heat. There is no danger of catching fire by this lining. We have seen a most tremendous fire rage for three hours, in contact with a partition of lath and plaster (on the plaster-side however), without discolouring the thin laths on the other side. We once <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a cottage chimney on fire, and burn till the foot was consumed. This chimney was nothing but a pipe of a foot wide, made of laths, and plastered on the inside and outside; and it passed through a thatched roof. We therefore recommend this in place of the brick-cage for inclosing the stove. It would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> heat; and as it might be made in pieces on detached frames, which could be joined by iron straps and hinges, any part of the stove could be laid open for repairs at pleasure. We have no hesitation in saying that a stove constructed in this manner would be greatly superior in power to any we have seen, and would be free from many of their disgusting defects. We beg leave therefore to introduce here the description of one which was to have been erected in one of the churches of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. Fig. 4. is a sketch of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> contained in the parallelogram AFED. P marks the place of the pulpit, and LMNO the front of the galleries. These are carried back to the side-walls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> and DC. But at the end opposite to the pulpit they do not reach so far, but leave a space BFEC about 12 feet wide. Below the back of the galleries, on each side, there is a passage ABGH, KICD, separated from the heated part of the church by partitions which reach from the floor to the galleries, so that the space HGIK is completely shut in. The church is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Gothic building, of a light and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> structure, having two rows of large windows above the arcades, and a spacious window in the east end above the pulpit. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> complain of a cold air, which they feel pouring down upon their heads. This is more particularly felt by those sitting in the fronts of the galleries. We imagine that this arises chiefly from the extensive surface of the upper row of windows, and of the cold <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-walls above, which rob the air of its heat as it glides up along the sides of the church. It becomes heavier by collapsing, and in this state defends in the middle of the church. The stove S is placed against the middle of the west wall at the distance of a few inches, and is completely inclosed in a case of lath and plaster. The vent, which is to carry off the smoke and burnt air, is conveyed up or along the wall, and through the roof or side-wall, but without any communication with the case. In like manner the fire-place door is open to the passage, without communicating with the case; and care is taken that the holes which admit the air into the case are so disposed that they shall run no risk of drawing in any air from the fire-place door. From the top of this case proceed two trunks Q, R, each of which is two feet broad and six inches deep, coated within and without with the most flouncy plaster that can be composed. For this purpose we should recommend a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of powdered <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> and as much clay and quicklime as will give it a very slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a>. We know that a piece of this may be held in the hand, without inconvenience, within an inch of where it is of a glowing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> heat.—These trunks open into another trunk XVTYZ, which ranges along the partition immediately under the galleries, and may be formed externally into a corniche, a little massive indeed, but not unsightly in a building of this style. This trunk is coated in the same manner. It has several openings a, a, &c., which have sliders that can be drawn aside by means of handles accessible from the outer passage.—At the extremities X and Z of this trunk are two perpendicular trunks which come up through the galleries, and are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to a considerable height. At their junction with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> trunk are two doors large enough to admit a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>. Each perpendicular trunk has also a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALVE">valve</a> by which it can be completely flopped. The stove is managed as follows: Early in the morning the superintendent shuts all the sliders, and sets a lamp (burning) in each of the trunks X and Z, and shuts the doors. He then puts on and kindles the fire in the stove, and manages it either in the Russian or German method. Perhaps the latter is preferable, as being liable to fewer accidents from mistake or neglect. The lamps set in the lower ends of the upright trunks presently warm them, and produce a current of air upwards. This must be supplied by the horizontal trunk, which must take it from the case round the stove. Thus a current is begun in the direction we wish. By and by the air in the case acquires heat from the stove, and the current becomes extremely brisk. When the manager perceives this, he removes the lamps, shuts the valves, and opens the holes a, a, &c., beginning with the most remote, and proceeding slowly towards the stove from each extremity of the horizontal branches. The heated air now issues by these holes, glides along the ceiling below the galleries, and escapes, by rising up along the fronts of the galleries, and will be sensibly felt by those sitting there, coming on their faces with a gentle warmth. It will then rise (in great part) straight up, while some of it will glide backwards, to the comfort of those who sit behind. The propriety of shutting the valves of the upright trunks is evident. If they were left open, no air would come out by the holes a, a, &c.; but, on the contrary, the air would go in at these holes to supply the current, and the stove be rendered useless. The air delivered by these holes will keep close to the ceiling, and will not, as we imagine, inconvenience those who sit below the galleries. But if it should be found to render these parts too warm, holes may be pierced through the ceiling, by which it will rise among the people above, and must be very comfortable. It will require the careful attention of some intelligent person to bring all this into a proper train at first, by finding the proper apertures of the different holes, so as to render the heat equable through the whole space. But this being once ascertained the difficulty is over. The air trunks must be very capacious, but may be contracted towards the extremities as their lateral discharges diminish; and the row of holes which admit the air to the case round the stove must be fully able to supply them. It must be observed, that in this construction the ascensional force is but small. It is only the height of a short column of warm air from the ground to the galleries. At first indeed it is great, having the unlimited height of the perpendicular trunks at X and Z; but during the use of the stove it is reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten feet. It is necessary, therefore, that the stove be highly heated, perhaps considerably beyond the Russian practice, but yet inferior to the heat of the German iron stoves. But still we strongly recommend the brick or pottery stoves, on account of the wholesome sweetness of the air which they furnish; and we are certain that a stove of moderate dimensions, eight feet long, for instance, by eight feet high, will be sufficient for warming a church holding 1200 or 1500 people. If the stove could be placed lower, which in many situations is very practicable, its effect would be proportionally greater, because all depends on the rapidity of the current. When we are limited in height, we must extend the stove so much the more in length, and make the air trunks more capacious. These and many other circumstances of local modification must be attended to by the erecter of the stove; and without the judicious attention of an intelligent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, we may expect nothing but disappointment. It is hardly possible to give instructions suited to every situation; but a careful attention to the general principle which determines the accidental force will free the artist from any great risk of failure. We may say the same thing of stoves for conservatories, hot-houses, hot walls, &c., and can hardly add anything of consequence to what we have already said on these heads in the article PNEUMATICS. We must not, however, dismiss the subject without taking notice of the very ingenious projects which have been frequently offered for drying malt by stoves. Many of these are to be seen in the publications of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">Academies</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>, Upsal, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>; and some have been erected in this kingdom, but they have not been found to answer. We apprehend that they cannot answer. To dry malt, and make it fit for the ales and beers for which this island is so famous, it is by no means enough that we give it a proper and an equable supply of heat.—This alone would bake it and make it flinty, causing the moisture to penetrate the mealy particles of the grain; and, by completely dissolving the soluble parts, would render each kernel an uniform mass, which would dry into a flinty grain, breaking like a piece of glass.—A grain of malt is not an inert pulp. It is a seed, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> state, growing, and of an organized structure. We wish to stop it in this state, and kill it, not by heating it, but by abstracting its moisture. We thus leave it in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a> or organized form, springy, and fit for imbibing water in the mash tub, without running into a paste. To accomplish these purposes, the construction of our malt kilns seems very well adapted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a> is the only flue of the furnace, and a copious current of air is formed through among the grains, carrying off with it the water which is evaporating by the heat. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, being chiefly in consequence of the vapour being immediately dissolved by the passing air, will stop as soon as the current of air stops. This current has to make its way through moist grain, laid in a pretty thick bed, and matted together. Some force, therefore, is necessary to drive it through. This is furnished by the draught of the kiln. Substituting a stove, immediately applied to the malt, will not have this effect. The only way in which we think this can be done different from the present, is to have a horizontal flue, as has been proposed in these projects, spread out at a small distance below the grate on which the malt is laid, and to cover the whole with a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a>, like a glass-house dome. This being filled with a tall column of hot air, and having no passage into it but through the malt, would produce the current which we want. We are convinced that this will make much less fuel serve; but we are by no means certain that the sulphurous and carbonic acid which accompanies the air in our common kiln is not a necessary or a useful ingredient in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. It is well known that different coals, cinders, or charcoal, impart different qualities to the malts, and are preferred each for its own purpose. A stove constructed on similar principles, but composed of very different materials, has been lately erected in several of the churches in Edinburgh. This stove, which is formed entirely of cast iron, may be considered as a double stove, an outer case, and a furnace or inner stove. The fuel is burnt in the inner stove; and the smoke produced during the process of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a>, is carried off by a chimney, which passes through the top of the outer stove, and is conveyed to the outside of the building. The outer case includes not only the furnace or inner stove, but also a considerable space, occupied by the air of the atmosphere, which is freely admitted through a number of openings placed around it; and when any current of air is produced, it passes off from the space between the outer case and inner stove, and is conveyed by tubes through the body of the apartment. But we shall first describe the different parts of which the stove is composed, after which we shall be better able to understand its mode of operation. Fig. 5. exhibits a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> view of this stove. AB is the body, which is about three feet high, and of a circular form. BC is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> pedestal on which the stove is placed, and which contains the ash pit DD. The height of the pedestal is about a foot, and it is nearly insulated by resting on the spherical supports <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">aa</a>, also of cast iron. EEE are openings in front of the ash pit through which the air enters to support the combustion. These openings can be enlarged or diminished, or opened and shut at pleasure. FF is the door of the furnace through which the fuel is introduced. This door is attached to the inner furnace, and is double. It is one foot broad, and 11 inches high. GG is the chimney, which passes from the furnace within, through the outer case, and conveys the smoke out of the building. HH are openings in the outer case, and are eight in number, through which the air enters, and being heated, is greatly rarified, and passes off through the funnel or pipe IIII. This pipe communicates only with the outer stove, and being shut at the end K, the air rushes out from the small tubes LL, inserted into the side of the pipe IIII, and thus mixes with the cold air of the church. The diameter of the outer case at the bottom is about two feet, and the diameter of the furnace within is about 16 inches. Fig. 6. is a section of the stove. AB is the outer case, from which passes off the pipe or funnel CCC, by which the heated air is conveyed through the church. DD is the furnace in the inside, in which the fuel is burnt, and EEE is the chimney or funnel which conveys the smoke from the inner furnace out of the building. It passes through the outer stove AB at F. Fig. 7. is a plan of this stove. AB is the pedestal on which it rests, and which contains the ash pit. CC is the outer case, and DD is the furnace within, in which are seen the transverse bars which support the fuel. The length of the body of the church, in which two stoves of the form and dimensions now described are erected, is about 60 feet, and the breadth is about 45 feet. The tubes IIII are conveyed along the lower edge of the gallery, about half the length of the church. The fires are lighted up about four or five o'clock on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> morning, during the earlier part of the cold season; but as the season advances, it is usual to light them up the night before. From this time till the congregation assemble for the afternoon service, the furnaces are are kept constantly supplied with fuel. By this management the air in the church is kept comfortably warm during the coldest season of the year. These stoves, it appears to us, are susceptible of some improvement, both in their construction and in the places in which they are erected. With regard to the first circumstance, an external coating of plaster work, or of the same kind of materials as are used for coating the inside of chemical furnaces, would be of some use in preventing an unnecessary waste of heat, as well as the disagreeable smell which is sometimes complained of, and which is supposed to arise from the combustion of light bodies floating in the air and drawn by the current to the heated metal; and with regard to the last, viz., the places in which they are erected, it is perfectly obvious that they ought to be as completely insulated as possible, and particularly ought not to communicate with any body which is a good conductor of heat. Some of the stoves erected in the churches of Edinburgh, which we have examined, are faulty in this respect. One in particular is placed in close contact with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GABLE">gable</a> wall. The quantity of coals consumed in two of these stoves in one of the churches of Edinburgh during the course of a season, we have been informed, amounts to about five carts of 12 cwt. each; so that at the Edinburgh prices of coal, the expense for fuel for heating one of the churches is about 50 shillings. This being added to the expenses of attendance, includes the whole expenditure, besides some occasional repairs which are required in heating a church of the above dimensions. The following is the description of an improved stove by Mr Field of Newman Street <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in which, it is stated by the author, the various advantages of heating, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, steaming, evaporating, drying, ventilating, &c., are united; some of which we shall detail in his own words. "Fig. 8 represents a longitudinal section of the stove, showing the course of the air from its entrance into the flues of the stove at A, to its entrance into the upper chamber of the stove at B; and also the course of the smoke from the fire-place at C, till it escapes from the stove at D. E, E, are the doors or openings of the fire-place and ash-hole. "Fig. 9. is a similar section at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> with the above, exhibiting the course of the air through the chambers of the stove, from its entrance into the chamber No. 1, at B to its entrance beneath the fire-place at F. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> also shows sections of the flues, with the divisions through which the air and smoke <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> separately, the smoke-flue in the centre, and the air-flues on each side. G, G, are doors and openings through which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> to be dried are introduced into the chambers. "When the fire is lighted, and the doors of the chambers, ash hole, and fire-place, closed, the air by which the fire is supplied enters at A, fig. 8, passes through the air-flues a, a, a, enters the upper chamber at B, traverses and descends through the chambers No. 1, 2, 3, and arrives beneath the fire at F, fig. 9. Having supplied the fire with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a>, it passes through the flue with the smoke, and escapes at D, heating in its protracted course the chambers and air-flues. "As the cold air enters the stove at A, immediately above a plate forming the top of the fire-place, and pursues a similar route with the fire-flue, it enters the chambers very much heated and rarefied. Hence any moist substance placed in the chambers evaporates in consequence, not only of the heated flues circulating round them, but of a stream of warm rarefied air, which, while it continually raises evaporation, as continually bears away the exhaled moisture in its passage to the fire, thus imitating the gradual and efficacious plan of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in drying by the sun and air. While these effects are taking place within the stove, part of the air which enters at A, fig. 8, and 9, passes through air-flues on the other side of the fire-flue, pursues a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> course with the first, and gives out a current of warm air to the room at an aperture H. This effect may be obtained in a much higher degree, if the doors of the chambers and ash-hole are opened: should the hand or face be then brought near, they would be fanned with a stream of warm air, especially from the upper chamber. "By means of this stove I have evaporated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> to dryness, without burning or discolouring it; and have dried cherries, plums, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, so as to imitate those which are received from abroad. I have repeatedly dried colours and the most delicate substances without the slightest injury, even though the operation proceeded quickly. "The height of the stove is about five feet and a half; its diameter two feet and a half, and that of the flues four inches. The external part is constructed of brick, and the internal parts of thin Rye gate or fire-stone, except the top of the fire-place, which is a plate of cast iron. Were it to be wholly formed of iron, its effects would necessarily be more powerful. "Fig. 10. represents an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the plan, in which stoves of this kind may be advantageously connected with one or more furnaces for chemical or other uses. The fire-place, brought out, either in front or on one side, by the present positions of its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> 1, forms a reverberatory furnace, or will make a sand-bath by reverberating it. "The space occupied by the fire-place in fig. 8, may in this be converted into apartments for evaporating substances, or occasionally for cooling them by an opening at K to admit cold air, while the warm air of the stove is excluded by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> or door. The dotted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> show the manner in which a second furnace may be connected by an opening into the flue at L. "In addition to the uses already pointed out, this stove would probably be found extremely serviceable in drying japanners' goods, and containing the noxious fumes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">gas</a> which arise from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> used in this business. "Since the stove is not limited to any certain dimensions, it might be adapted to the drying of malt and hops, perhaps of herbs, corn, and seeds generally. It might also be accommodated to the purposes of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>, connected with the great fires they employ for their boilers. It has been shown to be useful in the confectioners' art, and probably it may be equally so in baking biscuits for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>; nor less so in drying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> for the laundress, dyer, calico-printer, and bleacher. I have myself found it well accommodated for a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a>."

STOURBRIDGE

Pages 372-373
or STURBRIDGE, the name of a field near Cambridge, noted for its famous fair kept annually on the 7th of September, and which continues for a fortnight. The commodities are, horses, hops, iron, wool, leather, cheese, &c. This place is also noted noted for an excellent species of clay capable of resisting intense heat. It is used in making pots for glass-houses, fire-bricks, &c.; and is sold at a high price.

STOW

Pages 373-373

John, the industrious historian, son of Thomas Stow merchant-taylor of St Michael's, Cornhill, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was born about the year 1525. Of the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> we know very little, except that he was bred to his father's business, which in the year 1560 he relinquished, devoting himself entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians, chronicles, annals, charters, registers, and records. Of these he made a considerable collection, travelling for that purpose to different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and transcribing such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> as he could not purchase. But this profession of an antiquary being attended with no present emolument, he was obliged for subsistence to return to his trade.—It happened, however, that his talents and necessities were made known to Dr Parker archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>; who being himself an antiquary, encouraged and enabled Mr Stow to prosecute his darling study. In those times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> was then upon the throne, honest John Stow did not escape danger. His collection of Popish records was deemed cause of suspicion. His younger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Thomas preferred no less than 140 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> against him before the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> being insufficient, he was acquitted. In 1565 he first published his Summary of the Chronicles of England. About the year 1581 he began his Survey of London. In 1583 he was one of the two collectors for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> mutter of Limehouse <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a>: in the same year he petitioned the corporation of London to befallow on him the benefit of two freemen, to enable him to publish his survey; and in 1589 he petitioned again for a pension. Whether he succeeded, is not known. He was principally concerned in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of Holinshed's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a>, published in 1587. He also corrected, and twice augmented, Chaucer's works, published in 1561 and in 1597. His survey of London was first published in 1598. To these laborious works he would have added his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Chronicle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England; but he lived only to publish an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of it, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Flores Historiarum. The folio volume, which was printed after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, with the title of Stow's Chronicle, was taken from his papers by Edmund Howes. Having thus spent his life and fortune in these laborious pursuits, he was at last obliged to solicit the charitable and well disposed for relief. For this purpose, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James I granted him, in 1603, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>, which was renewed in 1604, authorizing him to collect in churches the benefactions of his fellow-citizens. He died in April 1605, aged 80; and was buried in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Andrew's, Underhaft, where his widow erected a decent monument to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. John Stow was a most indefatigable antiquarian, a faithful historian, and an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>.

STOWAGE

Pages 373-373

the general disposition of the several materials contained in a ship's hold, with regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, magnitude, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> solidity. In the stowage of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, as ballast, casks, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, bales, and boxes, there are several general rules to be observed, according to the circumstances or qualities of those materials. The casks which contain any liquid are, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> phrase, to be hung-up and bilge-free, i.e. closely wedged up in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, and resting on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>: so that the bilges where they are thickest being entirely free all round, cannot rub against each other by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the vessel. Dry goods, or such as may be damaged by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, are to be carefully inclosed in casks, bales, cases, or wrappers; and wedged off from the bottom and sides of the ship, as well as from the bow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and compass-well. Due <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> must likewise be had to their disposition with regard to each other, and to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIM">trim</a> and centre of gravity of the ship; so that the heaviest may always be nearest the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and the lightest gradually above them.

STOWMARKET

Pages 373-373

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, in England, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 6' N. Lat. 52° 16'. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, situated between the branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Gipping and Orwell, and is remarkable for having the best cherries in England.

STRABO

Pages 373-374

a celebrated Greek geographer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and historian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMASIA">Amasia</a>, and was descended from a family settled at Gnoissus in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Xenarchus, a Peripatetic philosopher, and at length attached himself to the Stoics. He contracted a strict friendship with Cornelius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLUS">Gallus</a>, governor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and travelled into several countries to observe the situation of places, and the customs of nations. He flourished under Augustus, and died under Tiberius about the year 23, in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.—He composed several works, all of which are lost except his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a> in 17 books; which are justly esteemed very precious remains of antiquity. The two first books are employed in showing, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of geography is not only worthy of, but even necessary to, a philosopher; the third describes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; the fourth, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> and the Britannic isles; the fifth and sixth, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the adjacent isles; the seventh, which is imperfect at the end, Germany; the countries of the Getæ and Illyrii, Taurica Chersonesus, and Epirus; the eighth, ninth, and tenth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> with the neighbouring isles; the four following, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> within Mount Taurus; the fifteenth and sixteenth, Asia without Taurus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; and the seventeenth, Egypt, Æthiopia, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and other places of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was published with a Latin version by Xylander, and notes by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Casaubon (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather by Henry Scrimzeer, from whom Casaubon chiefly stole them), at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1620, in folio. But the best edition is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1707, in two volumes folio, by the learned Theodore Janlonius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> Almelooeven, with the entire notes of Xylander, Casaubon, Meursius, Cluver, Holstenius, Salmasius, Bochart, Ex. Spanheim, Cellarius, and others. To this edition is subjoined the Chremomathie, or epitome of Strabo; which according to Mr Dodwell, who has written a very elaborate and learned dissertation about it, was made by some unknown person between the years of Christ 676 and 996. It has been found of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, not only in helping to correct the original, but in supplying in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the defect in the seventh book. Mr Dodwell's dissertation is prefixed to this edition.

STRADA

Pages 374-374

FAMIANUS, a very ingenious and learned Jesuit, was born at Rome in the latter end of the 16th century, and taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> there, in a public manner, for fifteen years. He wrote several pieces upon the art of oratory, and published some orations with a view of illustrating by example what he had inculcated by precept. But his Prolytiones Academicae and his Historia de Bello Belgico are the works which raised his reputation, and have preserved his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> was published at Rome; the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECADE">decade</a> in 1642, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1647; the whole extending from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., which happened in 1558, to the year 1590. It is written in good Latin, as all allow; but its merit in other respects has been variously determined. His Prolytiones Academicae show <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ingenuity, and a masterly skill in classical literature; that proliferation especially in which he introduces Lucan, Lucretius, Claudian, Ovid, Statius, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, each of them verifying according to his own strain. They have been often printed. We know not the year of Strada's birth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of his death.

STRAHAN

Pages 374-375

WILLIAM, an eminent printer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> in the year 1715. His father, who had a small appointment in the customs, gave his son the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> which every one of decent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> then received in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where the avenues to learning were easy, and open to men of the most moderate circumstances. After having passed through the tuition of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, he was put apprentice to a printer; and when a very young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, removed to a wider sphere in that line of business, and went to follow his trade in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Sober, diligent, and attentive, while his emoluments were for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very scanty, he contrived to live rather within than beyond his income; and though he married early, and without such a provision as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> might have looked for in the establishment of a family, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to thrive, and to better his circumstances. This he would often mention as an encouragement to early matrimony; and used to say, that he never had a child born that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> did not send some increase of income to provide for the increase of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. With sufficient vigour of mind, he had that happy flow of animal spirits that is not easily discouraged by unpromising appearances. His abilities in his profession, accompanied with perfect integrity and unabating diligence, enabled him, after the first difficulties were overcome, to advance with rapid success. And he was one of the most flourishing men of the trade, when, in the year 1770, he purchased a share of the patent for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s printer of Mr Eyre, with whom he maintained the most cordial intimacy during the rest of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Beside the emoluments arising from this appointment, as well as from a very extensive private business, he now drew largely from a field which required some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> sagacity to cultivate on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> literary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which he acquired by purchasing the copy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the most celebrated authors of the time. In this his liberality kept pace with his prudence, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> went perhaps rather beyond it. Never had such rewards been given to the labours of literary men as now were received from him and his associates in those purchases of copy-rights from authors. Having now attained the first great object of business, wealth, Mr Strahan looked with a very allowable ambition on the stations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> rank and eminence. Politics had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> occupied his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> mind, which he had for many years pursued as his favourite amusement, by corresponding on that subject with some of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Mr Strahan's queries to Dr Franklin in the year 1769, reflecting the discontentments of the Americans, published in the London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a> of 28th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1778, show the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> he entertained of the important consequences of that dispute, and his anxiety as a good subject to investigate, at that early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the proper means by which their grievances might be removed, and a permanent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> restored between the two countries. In the year 1775 he was elected a member of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for the borough of Malmesbury in Wiltshire, with a very illustrious colleague, the Hon. C. J. Fox; and in the succeeding parliament, for Wootton Bassett, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. In this station, applying himself with that industry which was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to him, he was a useful member, and attended the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with scrupulous punctuality. His talents for business acquired the consideration to which they were entitled, and were not unnoticed by the minister. In his political connection he was constant to the friends to whom he had first been attached. He was a steady supporter of that party who were turned out of administration in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> 1784, and lost his seat in the house of commons by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of parliament with which that change was followed: a situation which he did not shew any desire to resume on the return of the new parliament; arising from a feeling of some decline in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, which had rather suffered from the long fittings and late hours with which the political warfare in the preceding had been attended. Without any fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, his strength visibly declined; and though his spirits survived his strength, yet the vigour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of his mind were considerably impaired. Both continued gradually to decline till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened on the 9th of July 1785 in the 71st year of his age. Endued with much natural sagacity, and an attentive observation of life, he owed his rise to that station of opulence and respect which he attained, rather to his own talents and exertion, than to any accidental occurrence of favourable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fortunate circumstances. His mind was not unformed by letters; and from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to style, he acquired a considerable portion of critical acuteness in the discernment of its beauties and defects. In one branch of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> he particularly excelled—the epistolary; in which he not only showed the precision and clearness of business, but possessed a neatness as well as a fluency of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>-writers have been known to surpass. Letter-writing was one of his favourite amusements; and among his correspondents were men of such eminence and talents as well repaid his endeavours to entertain them. Among these, as before mentioned, was the justly celebrated Dr Franklin, originally a printer like Mr Strahan, whose friendship and correspondence, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of their sentiments in political matters, he continued to enjoy till his death. One of the latest letters which he received from his illustrious and venerable friend contained a humorous allegory of the state of politics in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, drawn from the profession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>; of which, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> had quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, he had not forgotten the terms. The judicious disposition which Mr Strahan made of his property, affords an evident <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and propriety. After providing sufficiently for his widow and children, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> seems to have been to mitigate the affliction of those (and many there were) who would more immediately have felt his loss, by bequeathing them liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> for their lives; and (recalling that all of a profession are not equally provident) he left £1000. to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of Stationers, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to be divided among inform old printers. As the virtuous connections of the life and the heart are always pleasing to trace,—of Mr Strahan it may briefly be said, that his capacity, diligence, and probity, raised him to the head of his profession. The good humour and obliging disposition which he owed to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, he cultivated with care, and confirmed by habit. His sympathetic heart <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> time to the joy and sorrow of his friends. His advice was always ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> youth, and his purse open to relieve indigence. Living in times not the purest in the English annals, he escaped unfulfilled through the artifices of trade and the corruption of politics. In him a strong natural figuracy, improved by an extensive knowledge of the world, served only to render respectable his unaffected simplicity of manners, and to make his Christian philanthropy more discerning and useful. The uninterrupted health and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> which accompanied him for half a century in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, proves honesty to be the best policy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, and the essential duties of life its most agreeable amusement. In his elevated fortune, none of his former acquaintance ever accused him of neglect. He attained prosperity without envy, enjoyed wealth without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, and dispensed bounty without ostentation.

STRAIKS

Pages 375-375

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, are strong plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, fixed in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, fixed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nails called straik-naits, on the circumference of a cannon-wheel, over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the fellows; both to strengthen the wheel, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the fellows from wearing on hard ways <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> streets.

STRAIN

Pages 375-375

Stress, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, are terms indiscriminately used to express the force which is excited in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a machine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> structure of any kind tending to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> it in that part. Thus every part of a rope is equally strained by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> which it suspends. Every part of a pillar is equally strained by the load which it supports. A mill axle is equally twisted and strained in every part which lies between the part of the wheel actuated by the moving power and the part which is resisted by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to be performed. Every part of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> is differently strained by a force acting on a distant part. It is evident that we cannot make the structure fit for its purpose, unless the strength at every part be at least equal to the stress laid on, or the strain excited in that part. It is no less plain, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we are ignorant of the principles which determine this strain, both in intensity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, in relation to the magnitude and the situation of its remote cause, the only security we have for success is to give to every part of the assemblage such solidity that we can leave no doubt of its sufficiency. But daily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> shows us that this vague security is in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> uncertain, if we are thus ignorant. In all cases it is slovenly, unlike an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, attended with useless expense, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> is attended with a loss of power which is wasted in changing the motions of a needless load of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. It must therefore greatly tend to the improvement of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> occupied in the erection or employment of such structures, to have a distinct notion of the strains to which these parts are exposed. Frequently, nay generally, these strains are not immediate, but arise from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of forces on distant parts, by which the assemblage is strained, and there is a tendency to rupture in every part. This strain is induced on every part, and is there modified by fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> laws. There it is our business to learn; but our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> object in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> is to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRENGTH_OF_MATERIALS">strength of materials</a> which it is necessary to oppose in every part to this strain; and how to oppose this strength in such a manner that it shall be exerted to the best advantage. The notions of strain and strength therefore hardly admit of separation; for it is even by means of the strength of the intermediate parts that the strain is propagated to, or excited in, the part under consideration. It is proper therefore to consider the whole together under the article STRENGTH of Materials in mechanics.

STRAINING

Pages 375-375

is the clarification of a liquor, by passing it through a sieve <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> filter. The word is derived from the French, effreindre; which is formed from ex, "out of," and stringere, "to press."

STRAIT

Pages 375-375

a narrow channel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, shut up between lands on either side, and affording a passage out of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sea into another. There are three kinds of straits. 1. Such as join one ocean to another. Of this kind are the straits of Magellan and Le Maire. 2. Those which join the ocean to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>: the straits of Gibraltar and Babelmandel are of this kind, the Mediterranean and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> sea being only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> gulfs. 3. Those which join one gulf to another; as the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a>, which join the Palus Maeotis to the Euxine or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea. The passage of straits is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> dangerous, on account of the rapidity and opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of currents. The most celebrated strait in the world is that of Gibraltar, which is about from 24 to 36 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and from 15 to 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, joining the Mediterranean sea with the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. The straits of Magellan, discovered in 1520 by F. Magellan, were used some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as a passage out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> into the South sea; but since the year 1616, that the strait of Le Maire has been discovered, the former has been disused; both because of its length, which is full three hundred miles, and because the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> thereof is very dangerous, from the waves of the North and South seas meeting in it and clashing. The strait at the entrance of the Baltic is called the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>; that between England and France, Le pas de <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, or the Channel. There are also the straits of Weigats, of Jeffo, of Anian, of Davis, and Hudson, &c.

STRAKES

Pages 375-376
or STREAKS, in a ship, the uniform ranges of planks on the bottom and sides of a ship, or the continuation of planks joined to the ends of each other. other, and reaching from the stem to the stern-post and fashion-pieces; the lowest of these, which is called the garboard-streak, is let into the keel below, and into the stem and stern-post. They lay also a ship heels a stake, that is, hangs or inclines to one side the quantity of a whole plank's breadth. Stakes, or frets, in mining, are frames of boards fixed on or in the ground, where they wash and dress the small ore in a little stream of water, hence called streaked ore.

STRALSUND

Pages 376-376

a strong and rich <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of Germany, in Hither Pomerania, formerly an important trading-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In 1678 it was forced to surrender to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, after 1800 houses had been burnt to ashes in one night's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. After this the Swedes defended it to the last extremity; and Chas. XII., in 1714, came hither after his return out of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>. But the throne of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> not being able to hold out against five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> powers, it was forced to submit in 1715. In 1720 it was rendered back to Sweden, but in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> condition. It is almost surrounded by the sea and the lake Francen, and has a harbour separated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Rugen by a narrow strait. It is 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Gripsholm, and 40 north-east of Gudrow. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 28'. N. Lat. 54° 17'.

STRAND

Pages 376-376

any shore <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river. Hence the street in the west suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, which lay next the shore or bank of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, was called the Strand. An immunity from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, and all impositions upon goods or vessels by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, was usually expressed by strand or fireman.

STRANDED

Pages 376-376

is when a ship is by tempest, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by ill steerage, run on ground, and so perishes. Where a vessel is stranded, justices of the peace, &c. shall command constables near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coasts to call assistance for the preservation of the ship; and officers of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> are to be aiding and assisting thereto.

STRANGE

Pages 376-377

Sir Robert, an eminent engraver, who carried the art to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and was distinguished not only as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, but highly respected and beloved on account of his private virtues and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> habits. Modest as he was ingenious, he used to say that the works of an artist should serve for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and monument. His works no doubt <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perpetuate his name whilst any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for the fine arts remains. Sir Robert Strange was born in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Pomona in Orkney, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> the 14th 1721; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> July the 5th 1792. He was lineally descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Strange <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Strang, a younger son of the family of the Stranges or Strangs of Balcaisky, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fife, who settled in Orkney at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Reformation. But as there were no males remaining of the elder branch of the Stranges of Balcaisky, Sir Robert became the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> representative of it, and was found by a legal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> to have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the armorial bearings and every other mark of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> belonging to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family. He received his classical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KIRKWALL">Kirkwall</a> in Orkney, under the care of a learned, worthy, and much respected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, Mr Macdonald Mackenzie, who has rendered infinite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to his country by the accurate surveys and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a> he has given of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Orkney, Shetland, and of the British and Irish coasts. Originally intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, Mr Strange soon became tired of that profession, and perceived that his genius decisively led him to the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and engraving. For this purpose he was introduced to the late Mr Richard <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">Cooper</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, the only person there who had then any taste in that line of the fine arts. He was bound with him as an apprentice for six years; during which time he made such progress in his new profession, that his friends entertained the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of his success; nor were they disappointed. In the year 1747 he married Isabella, only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of William Lumiden, son of Bishop Lumiden; and soon after his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> he went to France, where with the most ardent application he prosecuted his studies, chiefly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the celebrated Le Bas, who engraved many excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> from the Dutch painters. It was from Le Bas he had the first hint of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the dry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>; but which he afterwards greatly improved by his own genius, and which has added such superior beauties to his engravings. In the year 1751 Mr Strange removed with his family from Edinburgh and settled at London, where he engraved several fine historical prints, which justly acquired to him great reputation. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> historical engraving had made little progress in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and he may be properly considered as its father. The admiration he always had for the works of the great Italian painters made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> desire to visit <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the seat of the fine arts; and the farther he advanced in life, he became the more persuaded that a journey to that country was essential to an artist who had the laudable ambition to excel in his profession. He therefore undertook this journey in the year 1760. In Italy he made many admirable drawings, several of which he afterwards engraved. These drawings are now in the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Dundas. Everywhere in Italy singular marks of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> were bestowed on Mr Strange; not only by great personages, but by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> of the fine arts in that country. He was made a member of the academies of Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, and professor in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy at Parma. To show the estimation in which his talents were held at Rome, we cannot but record the following anecdote. The ceiling of the room of the Vatican library, in which the collection of engravings is kept, is elegantly painted by Signor Rotarielli. It represents the portraits of engravers; and the portraits of the most eminent artists in that line are there introduced, among which is that of our artist. Under his arm he holds a portfolio, on which his name is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>. He is the only British artist on whom this honour has been conferred. In France, where he resided many years at different periods, his talents likewise received every mark of attention that could be bestowed on a foreigner. He was made a member of the royal academy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> at Paris. His majesty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> George III., ever attentive to the progress of the fine arts in Britain, and sensible of the advantages of which engraving particularly has been to Strange. this country, even in a commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; and desirous to give a mark of his royal approbation of the merit of Mr Strange, whom he considered as at the head of his profession and the great improver of it—was graciously pleased to confer the honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> on him the 5th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1787. Such was Sir Robert Strange as an artist; nor was he less distinguished by his truly amiable moral qualities, which endeared him to all who had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to know him. With regard to his works, he left fifty <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> plates, still in good condition, which are carefully preserved in his family. They are engraved from pictures by the most celebrated painters of the Roman, Florentine, Lombard, Venetian, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. They are historical, both sacred and profane, poetical, allegorical. From his earliest establishment in life, Sir Robert carefully preserved about eighty copies of the finest and most choice impressions of each plate he engraved; which, from length of time, have acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, mellowness, and brilliancy, easier seen than described.
