When for any of the foregoing purposes of pointing, building, &c., such a cement is required much cheaper and coarser-grained, then much coarser clean land than the foregoing coarse land, or well-washed fine rubble, is to be provided. Of this coarse land or rubble take 56 pounds, of the foregoing coarse land 28 pounds, and of the fine land 14 pounds; and after mixing these, and wetting them with the cementing liquor in the foregoing manner, add 14 pounds, or somewhat less, of the (v) purified lime, and then 14 pounds or somewhat less. used after it is drawn limpid from the butt into open vessels, it will grow turbid again, and deposit the lime changed to whitening by the gas absorbed from the air. The calcareous matter which subsides in the butt resembles whitening the more nearly as the lime has been more sparingly employed; in the contrary circumstances, it approaches to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of lime; and in the intermediate state, it is fit for the common composition of the plasterers for inside stucco. (1) "At the time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> this specification, I preferred this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> before that of lime-water, on grounds which I had not sufficiently examined. (i) "The vapour which arises in the flaking of lime contributes greatly to the flaking of these pieces which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in its way; and an unnecessary waste of the liquor is prevented, by applying it to the lime heaped in a pit or in a vessel, which may restrain the issue of the vapour, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> it through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. If more of the liquor be used than is necessary to flake the lime, it will create <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in weighing the flaked powder, and will prevent a part of it from passing freely through the sieve. The liquid is therefore to be used sparingly, and the lime which has escaped its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is to be sprinkled apart with fresh liquor. (ii) "When the aggregation of the lumps of lime is thus broken, it is impaired much sooner than it is in the former state, because the air more freely pervades it. (iii) "Because it consists of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matter or of ill-burnt lime; which last will flake and pass through the sieve, if the lime be not immediately fitted after the flaking, agreeable to the text. (iv) "These proportions are intended for a cement made with sharp sand, for incrustation in exposed situations, where it is necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the effects of hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and rain. In general, half this quantity of bone-ashes will be found sufficient; and although the incrustation in this latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> will not harden deeply so soon, it will be ultimately stronger, provided the weather be favourable. (v) "The injuries which lime and mortar sustain by exposure to the air, before the cement is finally placed in a quiescent state, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; and therefore our cement is the worse for being long beaten, but the better as it is quickly beaten until the mixture is effected, and no longer. (o) "The quantity of bone-ashes is not to be increased with that of the lime; but it is to be lessened as the exposure and purposes of the work will admit. (p) "Because less lime is necessary, as the sand is coarser." less of the bone-ash, mixing them together in the manner already described. When my cement is required to be white, white sand, white lime; and the whitest bone-ashes are to be chosen. Gray sand, and gray bone-ashes formed of half-burnt bones, are to be chosen to make the cement gray; and any other colour of the cement is obtained, either by choosing coloured sand, or by the admixture of the necessary quantity of coloured talc in powder, or of coloured, vitreous, or metallic powders, or other durable colouring ingredients commonly used in paint. "To the end that such a water-cement as I have described may be made as useful as it is possible in all circumstances; and that no person may imagine that my claim and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> under these letters-patent may be eluded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> variations, which may be made in the foregoing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> without producing any notable defect in the cement; and to the end that the principles of this art, as well as the art itself, of making my cement, may be gathered from this specification and perpetuated to the public; I shall add the following observations: "This my water-cement, whether the coarse or fine grained, is applicable in forming <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> stone, by making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> layers of the cement and of flint, hard stone, or brick, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the intended stone, and by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the masses so formed to the open air to harden. "When such cement is required for water fences, two-thirds of the prescribed quantity of bone-ashes are to be omitted; and in the place thereof an equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of powdered terras is to be used; and if the sand employed be not of the coarsest sort, more terras must be added, so that the terras shall be by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> one-sixth part of the weight of the sand. "When such a cement is required of the finest grain (s) or in a fluid form, so that it may be applied with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, flint powder, or the powder of any quartofe or hard earthy substance, may be used in the place of terras; but in a quantity smaller, as the flint or other powder is finer; so that the flint-powder, or other such powder, shall not be more than five times the weight of the lime, nor less than four times its weight. The greater the quantity of lime within these limits, the more will the cement be liable to crack by quick drying, and vice versa. "Where such sand as I prefer cannot be conveniently procured, or where the sand cannot be conveniently washed and sorted, that sand which most resembles the mixture of coarse and fine sand above prescribed, may be used as I have directed, provided due <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to the quantity of the lime, which is to be greater (t) as the quantity is finer, and vice versa. "Where sand cannot be easily procured, any durable stony body, or baked earth grossly powdered (u), and sorted nearly to the sizes above prescribed for sand, may be used in the place of sand, measure for measure, but not weight for weight, unless such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> powder be as heavy specifically as sand. "Sand may be cleansed from every softer, lighter, and less durable matter, and from that part of the sand which is too fine, by various methods preferable (x), in certain circumstances, to that which I have described. "Water may be found naturally free from fixable gas, feline, or clay; such water may, without any notable inconveniences, be used in the place of the cementing liquor; and water approaching this state will not require so much lime as I have ordered to make the cementing liquor; and a cementing liquor sufficiently useful may be made by various methods of mixing lime and water in the described proportions, or nearly so. "When stone-lime cannot be procured, chalk-lime, or shell-lime, which best resembles stone-lime, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> above written of lime, may be used in the manner (Q) "But they must not be exposed to the rain until they are almost as strong as fresh Portland stone; and even then they ought to be sheltered from it as much as the circumstances will admit. These stones may be made very hard and beautiful, with a small expense of bone-ash, by soaking them, after they have dried thoroughly and hardened, in the lime liquor, and repeating this process twice or thrice, at distant intervals of time. The like effect was experienced in incrustations. (R) "In my experiments, mortar made with terras-powder, in the usual method, does not appear to form so strong a cement for water-fences as that made, according to the specification, with coarse sand; and I see no more reason for avoiding the use of sand in terras-mortar, than there would be for rejecting stone from the embankment. The bone-ashes present in this place are the dark gray or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> sort. I am not yet fully satisfied about the operation of them in this instance. (S) "The qualities and uses of such fine calcareous cement are recommended chiefly for the purpose of smoothing and finishing the stronger <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFORM">cruciform</a> works, or for washing walls to a lively and uniform colour. For this last intention, the mixture must be as thin as new cream, and laid on briskly with a brush, in dry weather; and a thick and durable coat is to be made by repeated washing; but is not to be attempted by using a thicker liquor; for the coat made with this last is apt to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, whilst the former endures the weather much longer than any other thin calcareous covering that has been applied in this way. Fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>-ochre is the cheapest colouring ingredient for such wash, when it is required to imitate Bath-stone, or the warm-white stones. (T) "If <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-sand be well washed in fresh water, it is as good as any other round sand. (U) "The cement made with these and the proper quantities of purified lime and lime-water, are inferior to the best, as the grains of these powders are more perishable and brittle than those of sand. They will not therefore be employed, unless for the sake of evasion, or for want of sand: in this latter case, the finer powder ought to be washed away. (X) "This and the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a> is inserted with a view to evasions, as well as to suggest the easier and cheaper methods which may be adopted in certain circumstances, by artists who understand the principles which I endeavour to teach." manner described, except that fourteen pounds and a half of chalk-lime will be required in the place of fourteen pounds of lime. The proportion of lime which I have preferred above may be increased without inconvenience, when the cement or stucco is to be applied where it is not liable to dry quickly; and in the contrary circumstance, this proportion may be diminished; and the defect of lime in quantity or quality may be very advantageously supplied (Y), by causing a considerable quantity of the cementing liquor to soak into the work, in successive portions, and at distant intervals of time, so that the calcareous matter of the cementing liquor, and the matter attracted from the open air, may fill and strengthen the work. "The powder of almost every well-dried or burnt animal substance may be used instead of bone-ash; and several earthy powders, especially the micaceous and the metallic; and the eloxated ashes of divers vegetables whose earth will not burn to lime; and the ashes of mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, which are of the calcareous kind, but will not burn to lime, will answer the ends of bone-ash in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. "The quantity of bone-ash described may be lessened without injuring the cement, in those circumstances especially which admit the quantity of lime to be lessened, and in those wherein the cement is not liable to dry quickly. And the art of remedying the defects of lime may be advantageously practised to supply the deficiency of bone ash, especially in building, and in making artificial stone with this cement."

STUDDING-SAILS

Pages 428-428

certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> sails extended, in moderate and steady breezes, beyond the skirts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sails, where they appear as wings upon the yard-arms.

STUFF

Pages 428-428

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a general name for all kinds of fabrics of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thread, manufactured on the loom; of which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are velvets, brocades, mohairs, satins, taffetas, cloths, ferges, &c.

STUKELY

Pages 428-428

Dr William, a celebrated antiquarian, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, was born at Holbech in 1687, and educated in Bennet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. While an undergraduate, he often indulged a strong propensity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>; but made physic his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and first began to practise at Bolton in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In 1717 he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where, on the recommendation of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a>, he was soon after elected a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; he was one of the first who revived that of the antiquarians in 1718, and was their secretary for many years during his residence in town. In 1729 he took holy orders by the encouragement of Archbishop Wake; and was soon after presented by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> with the living of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALL_SAINTS">All-Saints</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a>. In 1741 he became one of the founders of the Egyptian society, which brought him acquainted with the benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Montague, one of the members; who prevailed on him to leave Stamford, and presented him to the living of St George the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>. He died of a stroke of the palsy in 1765. In his physical capacity, his Dissertation on the Spleen was well received; and his Itinerarium Curium, the first fruit of his juvenile excursions, was a good specimen of what was to be expected from his riper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and profound researches into the dark remains of antiquity, enabled him to publish many elaborate and curious works; his friends used to call him the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-druid of his age. His discourses, intitled Paleographia Sacra, on the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, bespeak him a botanist, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and divine.

STUM

Pages 428-428

in the wine-trade, denotes the unfermented juice of the grape after it has been several times racked off and separated from its sediment. The casks are for this purpose well matched <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fumigated with brimstone every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to prevent the liquor from fermenting, as it would otherwise readily do, and become wine. See Must. STUPIDITY. The Greek word μωρότης corresponds most with our English word stupidity or foolishness, when used to express that state of mind in which the intellects are defective. The immediate causes are said to be, a deficiency of vital <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, or a defect in the brain. Stupid children sometimes become sprightly youths; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> stupidity continues to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of puberty, it is hardly ever removed. If stupidity follows upon a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, an injury done to the head, or other evident cause, and if it continues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, it becomes incurable. But the stupidity which consists in a loss of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and succeeds a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a>, spontaneously ceases when the lethargy is cured.

STUPOR

Pages 428-428

a numbness in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, whether occasioned by ligatures obstructing the blood's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, by the palsy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like.

STUPPA

Pages 428-428
or STUPE, in Medicine, is a piece of cloth dipped in some proper liquor, and applied to an affected part.

STURDY

Pages 428-428

a distemper to which cattle are subject, called also the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> evil. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. STURGEON. See ACIFENSER, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index.

STURMIUS

Pages 428-429

John, a learned philologer and rhetorician, was born at Sleida in Estel near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1507. He studied at first in his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with the sons of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Mandercheid, whose receiver his father was. He afterwards pursued his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St Jerom; and then went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a> in 1524. Five years he spent there, three in learning and two in teaching. He set up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-press with Rugger Recius professor of the Greek tongue, and printed several Greek authors. He went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1529, where he was highly esteemed, and read public lectures on the Greek and Latin writers, and on logic. He married there, and kept a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of boarders; but as he liked what were called the new opinions, he was more than once in danger; and this undoubtedly was the reason why he removed to Straiburg in 1537, in order to take possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> offered him by the magistrates. The year following he opened a school, which became (y) "This practice is noticed, as the remedy which may be used for the defects arising from evasive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and as the method of giving spongy incrustations containing bone-ashes the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>." became famous, and by his means obtained of Maximilian II. the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of an university in 1566. He was very well skilled in polite literature, wrote Latin with great purity, and was a good teacher. His talents were not confined to the school; for he was frequently intrusted with deputations in Germany and foreign countries, and discharged these employments with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and diligence. He showed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to the refugees on account of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>: He not only laboured to assist them by his advice and recommendations; but he even impoverished himself for them. He died in his 82nd year, after he had been for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>. He published many books; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Partitiones Dialectice. 2. De Educatione Principum. 3. De Nobilitate Anglicana. 4. Lingua Latina resolvente Ratio. 5. Excellent Notes on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERMOGENES">Hermogenes</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, &c. He ought not to be confounded with John Sturmius, a native of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MECHLIN">Mechlin</a>, and physician and professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> at Louvain, who also wrote several works.

STURNUS

Pages 429-429

the Starling; a genus of birds belonging to the order of passerines. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STYLE

Pages 429-429

in Music, denotes a peculiar manner of singing, playing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> composing; being properly the manner that each person has of playing, singing, or teaching; which is very different both in respect of different geniuses, of countries, nations, and of the different matters, places, times, subjects, passions, expressions, &c. Thus we say, the style of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTRINA">Palestrina</a>, of Lully, of Corelli, of Handel, &c.; the style of the Italians, French, Spaniards, &c. Old STYLE, the Julian method of computing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as the New STYLE is the Gregorian method of computation. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDAR">Kalendar</a>.

STYLEPHORUS CHORDATUS

Pages 429-429

a genus of fishes belonging to the order of apodes. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Transactions of the Linnean <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, vol. i.

STYLET

Pages 429-429

a small dangerous kind of poniard which may be concealed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, chiefly used in treacherous affixations. The blade is usually triangular, and so small that the wound it makes is almost imperceptible.

STYLITES

Pages 429-429

Pillar Saints, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an appellation given to a kind of solitaries, who stood motionless upon the tops of pillars, raised for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, and remained there for several years, amidst the admiration and applause of the stupid populace. Of these we find several mentioned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, and even as low as the twelfth century, when they were totally suppressed. The founder of the order was St Simeon Stylites, a famous anchorite in the fifth century, who first took up his abode on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> six cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; then on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of twelve cubits, a third of twenty-two, a fourth of thirty-five, and on another of forty cubits, where he thus passed thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The tops of these columns were only three feet in diameter, and were defended by a rail that reached almost to the girdle, somewhat resembling a pulpit. There was no lying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in it. The Syrians, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> devout people of the East, imitate this extraordinary kind of life to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>.

STYLOCERALOIDES

Pages 429-429

STYLO-GLOSSUS, STYLO-Hyoideus, STYLO-Pharyngeus, STYLOIDES, STYLOSANTHES, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 32d order, Papilionaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STYPTIC

Pages 429-429

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a medicine which by its astringency stops haemorrhages, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STYRAX

Pages 429-430

the Storax-tree, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the clefs decandra, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> system ranging ranging under the 18th order, bicornes. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

STYX

Pages 430-430

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a celebrated river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>; round which it flows <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> times. The gods held the waters of the Styx in such veneration, that to swear by them was reckoned an oath altogether inviolable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any of the gods had perjured themselves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> obliged them to drink the waters of the Styx, which lulled them for one whole year into a senseless stupidity, for the nine following years they were deprived of the ambrosia and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a> of the gods, and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of the years of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, they were restored to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the deities, and to all their original privileges. It is said that this veneration was shown to the Styx, because it received its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Styx, who with her three daughters assisted Jupiter in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a>. Styx was a river which it was necessary for departed shades to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> before they could enter the infernal regions; and it was the office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> to ferry them over in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> which was kept for that purpose. The ghosts of those who had not been honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of sepulture were obliged to wander an hundred years before Charon could admit them into his boat to convey them before the judges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADES">Hades</a>. What could have given rise to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Charon and his boat, it is not very material to inquire. Mythological writers have said, that the Greeks learned it from the Egyptians, which is indeed probable enough; that the Egyptians framed both this, and some other fables relating to the dead, from certain customs peculiar to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; that in particular there was, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>, a famous burying-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to which the dead bodies were conveyed in a boat across the lake Acherusia; and that Charon was a boatman who had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> officiated in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The learned Dr Blackwell says, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, that, in the old Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, Charon signified "ferryman."

SUABIA

Pages 430-430

a circle of Germany, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the circle of Franconia and that of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; on the west by the circle of the Lower Rhine and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALSACE">Alsace</a>; on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; and on the east by the circle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. Of all the circles of the empire, Suabia is the most divided; it contains four ecclesiastic and thirteen lay principalities, nineteen independent prelacies and abbeys, twenty-five earldoms and lordships, and thirty-one free cities. The prime directors of the circle, as they are termed, were formerly the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>. But this circle has suffered similar changes with neighbouring states. The mixture of the various forms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sects; the oppression exercised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> constantly played by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, who possesses many pieces of detached <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in Suabia, which depend not on the circle, and can, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his privileges as archduke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, extend his possessions in it by various ways; are circumstances (says Baron Riebeck) which give the cultivation of the country, and the character of the inhabitants, a most extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. In several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> where you stop, you see the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of cultivation in the midst of the most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> wilderness; a great degree of knowledge and polish of manners, mixed with the grossest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; traces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, under the deepest oppression; national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, together with the contempt and neglect of the native country; in short, all the social qualities in striking <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> and opposition to each other. Those parts of Suabia which belong to the great potentates, such as Wurtemberg, Austria, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, are certainly the most improved. The whole of Suabia may comprehend about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> hundred German <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and two millions of people. More than half of these are subjects of the three above mentioned princes, though they are not proprietors of near one half of the lands.

SUAES

Pages 430-430

Francis, a Jesuit, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1548. He was a professor of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> at Alcala, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, Rome, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> in 1617 with the greatest resignation; "I never thought (said he) that it was so easy to die." His <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was astonishing; he could repeat the whole of his voluminous works by heart. His writings fill 23 folio volumes, and are mostly on theological and moral subjects. His Treatise of Laws has been reprinted in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a> against the Errors of England was written at the request of Pope Paul V. This book was publicly burnt at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by order of James I. When Suares heard it, he is said to have exclaimed, "O that I too could feel with my blood the truths which I have defended with my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>!"

SUBAH

Pages 430-430

the general name of the viceroysthips, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> greater governments, into which the Mogul empire was divided, consisting of several provinces. The jurisdiction of a subahdar, the same as subahhip, subadaree, or nizamut.

SUBAHDAR

Pages 430-430

the viceroy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governor, holding a subah; the same as nabob or nazim. Also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> commander of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of feapoys.

SUBALTERN

Pages 430-430

a subordinate officer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one who discharges his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> under the command and subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of another; such are lieutenants, sublieutenants, cornets, and ensigns, who serve under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>.

SUBCLAVIAN

Pages 430-430

in Anatomy, is applied to anything under the armpit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shoulder, whether artery, nerve, vein, or muscle.

SUBDEACON

Pages 430-430

an inferior minister, who anciently attended at the altar, prepared the sacred vessels, delivered them to the deacons in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, attended the doors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>-service, went on the bishop's embassies with his letters <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> messages to foreign churches, and was invested with the first of the holy orders. They were so subordinate to the superior rulers of the church, that, by a canon of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Laodicea, they were forbidden to sit in the presence of a deacon without his leave. According to the canons, a person must be twenty-two years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> to be promoted to the order of subdeacon. See Deacon.

SUBDUPE RATIO

Pages 430-430

is when any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is contained in another twice. Thus 3 is said to be subduple of 6, as 6 is duple of 3. See Ratio.

SUBDUPLICATE

Pages 430-431

SUBDUPLICATE ratio of any two quantities, is the ratio of their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> roots.

SUBINFEUDATION

Pages 431-431

was where the inferior lords, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of their superiors, began to carve out and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> estates than their own, to be held of themselves; and were so proceeding downwards in infinitum, till the superior lords observed, that by this method of subinfeudation they lost all their feudal profits, of wardships, marriages, and ejectments, which fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> middle lords, who were the immediate superiors of the terre-tenant, or him who occupied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. This occasioned the stat. of Westm. 3. or quia emptores, 18. Edw. I. to be made; which directs, that, upon all sales or feoffments of lands, the feoffee shall hold the same, not of his immediate feoffee, but of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee of whom such feoffee himself held it. And from hence it is held, that all manors existing at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> must have existed by immemorial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>; or at least ever since the 18 Edw. I., when the statute of quia emptores was made.

SUBITO

Pages 431-431

in the Italian muse, is used to signify that a thing is to be performed quickly and hastily: thus we meet with volti subito, turn over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> quickly.

SUBJECT

Pages 431-431

a person under the rule and dominion of a sovereign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state. SUBJECT is also used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of an art or science, or that which it considers, or whereon it is employed; thus the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body is the subject of medicine.

SUBLIMATE

Pages 431-431

a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, consisting of quicksilver united with muriatic acid. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

SUBLIMATION

Pages 431-431

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the condensing and collecting, in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form, by means of vessels aptly constructed, the fumes of bodies raised from them by the application of a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>.

SUBLIME

Pages 431-431
or Sublimity. See the article Grandeur and Sublimity. SUBLINGUAL ARTERY. See Anatomy. SUBLINGUAL Glands, in Anatomy, two glands under the tongue, placed one on each side thereof.

SUBMULTIPLE

Pages 431-431

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, &c. A submultiple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, is that which is contained a certain number of times in another, and which, therefore, repeated a certain number of times, becomes exactly equal thereto. Thus 3 is a submultiple of 21. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> a submultiple coincides with an aliquot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>. SUBMULTIPLE Ratio, is that between the quantity contained and the quantity containing. Thus the ratio of 3 to 21 is submultiple. In both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> submultiple is the reverse of multiple: 21, e.g. being a multiple of 3, and the ratio of 21 to 3 a multiple ratio. SUBORDINARIES. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, Chap. III., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. II.

SUBORDINATION

Pages 431-431

a relative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, expressing an inferiority betwixt one person and another.

SUBORNATION

Pages 431-431

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a secret, underhand, preparing, instructing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bringing in a false witness; and from hence subornation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a> is the preparing or corrupt alluring to perjury. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for this crime was formerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, then banishment or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> out the tongue, afterwards forfeitures of goods; and it is now a fine and imprisonment, and never more to be received as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. The statute 2 Geo. II. c. 25. further added a power for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to order the offender to be sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of correction for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> not exceeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, or be transported for the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>.

SUBPOENA

Pages 431-431

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">Equity</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in equity, calling on a defendant to appear and answer to the complainant's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. See statute 5th Geo. II. c. 25. which enacts, that where the party cannot be found to be served with a subpoena, and abandons (as is believed) to avoid being served, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> shall be appointed him to appear to the bill of the plaintiff; which is to be inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> Gazette, read in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> where the defendant last lived, and fixed up at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">Exchange</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the defendant doth not appear upon that day, the bill shall be taken pro confesso.

SUBROGATION

Pages 431-431
or Surrogation, in the civil law, the act of substituting a person in the place, and intitling him to the rights, of another. In its general sense, surrogation implies a succession of any kind, whether of a person to a person, or of a person to a thing. There are two kinds of surrogation: the one conventional, the other legal. Conventional surrogation is a contract whereby a creditor transfers his debt, with all appurtenances thereof, to the profit of a third person. Legal surrogation is that which the law makes in favour of a person who discharges an antecedent creditor; in which case there is a legal translation of all rights of the ancient creditor to the person of the new one.

SUBSCRIPTION

Pages 431-434

in general, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> put at the bottom of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, it is used for the share or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> which particular persons take in a public stock or a trading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, by writing their names, and the shares they require, in the books or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> thereof. Subscription to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> is required of the clergy of every established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and of some churches not established. Whether such subscription serves any good purpose, in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> or theological view, is a very doubtful question. It may be necessary in an establishment, as a test of loyalty to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>, but it cannot produce produce uniformity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. As all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is more or less ambiguous, it becomes difficult, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not impossible, to determine in what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the words of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> established creeds are to be interpreted; and we believe that the clergy of the churches of England and Scotland seldom consider themselves as fettered by the Thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> Articles, or the Confession of Faith, when composing instructions either for their respective parishes or for the public at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>. Subscription, in the commerce of books, signifies an engagement to take a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of copies of a book, intended to be printed, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> obligation of the bookeller or publisher to deliver the said copies, on certain terms. These subscriptions, which had their rise in England about the middle of the 17th century, were lately very frequent in France and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and are now very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among ourselves. Subsequent, something that comes after another, particularly with regard to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Subsidy, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies an aid or tax granted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, for the necessary occasions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and is to be levied on every subject of ability, according to the rate or value of his lands or goods: but this word, in some of our statutes, is confounded with that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. See Tax. Substance, the subjects to which we suppose qualities belong. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> is the substance to which the qualities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a>, yellowness, density, &c., belong. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, No. 145. Substantial, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, something belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of substance. Substantive, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>. See Grammar. Substitute, a person who officiates for another in his absence. Substitution, in the Civil Law, a disposition of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>, whereby the testator substitutes one heir for another, who has only the usufruct, and not the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> or the thing, left him. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUBTRACTION">Subtraction</a>, or Subtraction, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> rule, or rather operation, in arithmetic, whereby we deduct a less number from a greater, to learn their precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. See Arithmetic and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>. Subtangent of a Curve, the line that determines the intersection of a tangent with the axis; or that determines the point wherein the tangent cuts the axis prolonged. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUBTENSE">Subtense</a>, formed from sub "under," and tendo "I stretch," in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line which is opposite to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, and drawn between the two extremities of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> that angle. Subterraneous, whatever is under ground: thus naturalists speak of subterraneous fires, subterraneous damps, &c. Subterraneous Cavern. See Quarries. Subtile, in Physics, an appellation given to whatever is extremely small, fine, and delicate; such as the animal spirits, the effluvia of odorous bodies, &c., are supposed to be. Subularia, Rough-leaved Alyssum, or Aulwort, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the class tetradynamia, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order ranging under the 39th order, Filicofce. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Subulated, something shaped like an awl. Succedaneum, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, denotes a drug substituted in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of another. Succession, in Metaphysics, the idea which we get by reflecting on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> that follow one another in our mind; and from the succession of ideas we get the idea of time. See Metaphysics, No. 93, and 209. Succession, in Law. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">Descent</a>. Succession to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">Hereditary</a> Right.—From the days of Egbert, the first folk monarch of England, even to the present, the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> maxims mentioned in that article have ever been held constitutional canons of succession. It is true, as Sir William Blackstone observes, this succession, through fraud or force, or sometimes through <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, when in hostile times the crown descended on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> or the like, has been very frequently suspended; but has generally at last returned back into the old hereditary channel, though sometimes a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> has intervened. And even in those instances where this succession has been violated, the crown has ever been looked upon as hereditary in the wearer of it. Of which the usurpers themselves were so sensible, that they for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> endeavoured to vamp up some feeble show of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> by descent, in order to amuse the people, while they gained the possession of the kingdom. And, when possession was once gained, they considered it as the purchase or acquisition of a new estate of inheritance, and transmitted, or endeavoured to transmit it, to their own posterity by a kind of hereditary right of usurpation. (See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>. Com. vol. i. 197—217.) From the historical view there given, it appears that the title to the crown is at present hereditary, though not quite so absolutely hereditary as formerly: and the common flock or ancestor, from whom the descent must be derived, is also different. Formerly the common flock was King Egbert; then William the Conqueror; afterwards, in James I.'s time, the two common flocks united; and so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the vacancy of the throne in 1688: now it is the Prince's Sophia in whom the inheritance was vested by the new king and parliament. Formerly, the descent was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, and the crown went to the heir without any restriction: but now, upon the new settlement, the inheritance is conditional: being limited to such heirs only, of the body of the Prince's Sophia, as are Protestant members of the church of England, and are married to none but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. And in this due medium consists the true constitutional notion of the right of succession to the imperial crown of these kingdoms. The extremes between which it fleers are each of them equally destructive of those ends for which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> were formed and kept on foot. Where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, upon every succession, is elected by the people, and may by the express provision of the laws be deposed (if not punished) by his subjects, this may found like the perfection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and look well enough when delineated on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; but in practice <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be ever productive of tumult, contention, and anarchy. And, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, divine indefeasible hereditary right, when coupled with the doctrine of unlimited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> obedience, is surely of all constitutions the most thoroughly flavished and dreadful. But when such an hereditary right as our laws have created and vested in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> stock, is closely interwoven with those liberties which are equally the inheritances of the subject; this union union will form a constitution, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> the most beautiful of any, in practice the most approved, and, we trust, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> the most permanent. In France the succession to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> was limited to heirs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> (see Salic); but in Navarre the crown was inherited by the heir of line, whether male or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> stands thus: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> the Fourth, king of France, surnamed the Fair, in the year 1285 espoused Jane <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Navarre in her own right; and as king consort of this latter kingdom added the title of Navarre to his former one of France. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> X. son and heir of Philip and Jane (surnamed Hutin or the Boilereous), succeeded to both crowns. By Margaret his first wife, who had been crowned queen of Navarre, he left one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, Joan or Jane. His second wife Clementina was pregnant at the time of his decease, and was delivered of a posthumous son, whom most of the French annalists recognize as John I. of France, though he lived no longer than three weeks. On his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the kingdom of France passed to Philip V. (surnamed the Long), and that of Navarre (to which the Salic law could by no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> extend) to Joanna the only child and heir of Louis and Margaret. From Joanna, in lineal succession, the kingdom of Navarre passed to Jane d'Albret, mother of Henry IV. of France, and wife of Anthony of Vendome, who as king consort wore the crown of Navarre. On the accession of Henry to the kingdom of France, the two monarchies were united, and the four succeeding princes assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> titles. Succinic acid, an acid extracted from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> by sublimation in a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and which rises in a concrete form into the neck of the subliming vessel. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. Succinum, Amber, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of bitumen classified under the inflammable substances. See Mineralogy Index. Succory. See Cichorium, Botany Index. Succoth, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town which lay between the brook Jabbok and the river Jordan, where <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> fixed his tents. There was another Succoth, where the Israelites first encamped after their departure from Ramees towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Succoth signifies tents. Sucubus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by some writers for a demon who assumes the shape of a woman, and as such lies with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; in which sense it stands opposed to incubus, which was a demon in form of a man, that lies with a woman. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the succubus is only a species of the nightmare. See Medicine, No. 329. Succula, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, an axis or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, with flaves in it to move it round; but without any tympanum or peritrochium. Succulent plants, among botanists, such whose leaves are thick and full of juice. Sucker. See Cyclopterus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. Suckers, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the same with Offsets. Sucking-fish. See Lachneis, Ichthyology Index. Suckling, Sir John, an English poet and dramatic writer, was the son of Sir John Suckling, comptroller of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> to King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and born at Witham in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in 1613. He discovered an uncommon propensity to the acquiring of languages, in so much that he is reported to have spoken Latin at five years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and to have written it at nine. When he grew Suckling up, he travelled; but seems to have affected nothing more than the character of a courtier and fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>; which he so far attained, that he was allowed to have the peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of making every thing he did become him. In his travels he made a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Gustavus Adolphus; and his loyalty, if not his valour, appeared in the beginning of our civil wars; for, after his return to England, he raised a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> for the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> entirely at his own <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>; and mounted them so completely and richly, that they are said to have cost him 12,000l. This troop, with Sir John at its head, behaved so ill in the engagement with the Scots, upon the English borders, in 1639, as to occasion the famous lampoon composed by Sir John Mennis; "Sir John he got him an ambling nag," &c. This ballad, which was set to a brisk tune, was much sung by the parliamentarians, and continues to be sung to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. This disastrous expedition, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> that attended it, was supposed to have hastened his death; being seized by a fever, of which he died, at 28 years of age. He was a frightfully <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and an easy versifier, but no great poet. His works, consisting of a few poems, letters, and plays, have nevertheless gone through several editions. Suction, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of sucking or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up a fluid, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, or the like, by means of the mouth and lungs; or, in a similar manner, by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> means. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUDATORY">Sudatory</a>, a name given by the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to their hot or sweating rooms; sometimes also called Laconica. Suderoe. See Ferro-Ilandi. Sudorific, an appellation given to any medicine that causes or promotes sweat. Suessiones, a branch of the Remi, a people of Gallia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELGICA">Belgica</a> (Pliny); called sometimes Sueiones, in the lower age Suebi; situated between the Remi to the east, the Nervii to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the Veromandui to the west, and the Medae to the south, in the tract now called le Saffronais.—Suefiones, Sueiones, and Sueiones, the name of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the lower age; thought to have been formerly called Noviodunum (Caesar), is now called Saffron. Suet, Sevum, or Selum, in Anatomy, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> fat found in several animals, as sheep, oxen, &c. but not in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> species. See the article Fat.—It is of the sevum that tallow is made. Suetonius Tranquillus, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a>, a famous Latin historian, was born at Rome, and became secretary to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, about the 118th year of the Christian era; but that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> was taken from him three years after, when several persons fell under that prince's displeasure for not showing the empress Sabina all the respect she deserved. During his disgrace he composed many works, which are lost. Those now extant are his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the XII first Emperors, and a part of his treatise of the Illustrious Grammarians and Rhetoricians. Pliny the Younger was his intimate friend, and persuaded him to publish his books. His History of the XII Roman Emperors has been much commended by most of our polite scholars. He represents, in a continued <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of curious and interesting particulars, without any digressions or reflections, the actions of the emperors, without omitting their vices, which he exposes with all their Suetonius their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, and with the same freedom mentions the good qualities of the very same persons; but the horrid dissoluteness and obscene actions he relates of Tibertius, Caligula, Nero, &c., have made some say, that he wrote the lives of the emperors with the same licentiousness with which they lived. The edition of this history procured by Graevius at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> in 1672, with the excellent Commentaries of Torrentius and Caffabon, and the notes of some other learned critics, is much esteemed. Burman also published an edition in 2 vols. 4to, with notes.

SUEVI

Pages 434-434

the Catti <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Chatti of Caesar (Strabo), placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>: the reason of Caesar's calling them thus does not appear, though considerably distant from the proper Suevi or Alemanni. Suevi, (Tacitus), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of the people situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>, distinguished otherwise by particular names; as in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, Suevi Angelici, Suevi Sennones.

SUEVUS

Pages 434-434

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a river of Germany, thought to be the same with the Viadrus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>, emptying itself at three mouths into the Baltic, the middlemost of which is called Swine or Swene; which last comes nearer the name Suevus.

SUEZ

Pages 434-435

a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town, situated near the northern extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Sea, and about 30 hours' journey east from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> around it is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain, without the smallest spot of verdure. The only <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which can be drunk is brought from El-Naba, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, at the distance of three hours' journey; and it is so brackish, that without a mixture of rum it is insupportable to Europeans. The town itself is a collection of miserable ruins, the khans being the only <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> buildings; yet from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, the season when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JIDDA">Jidda</a> and Yambo fleet arrives, the town becomes crowded; but after its departure nobody remains except the governor, who is a Mamlouk, 12 or 14 persons who form his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and the garrison. The fortres is a defenceless heap of ruins, which the Arabs consider as a citadel, because it contains six <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> four-pounders, and two Greek gunners, who turn their heads aside when they fire. The harbour is a wretched quay, where the smallest boats are unable to reach the shore, except at the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. There, however, the merchandise is embarked, to convey it over the banks of sand to the vessels which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. This road, situated a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the town, is separated from it by a flore which is left dry at low water; it has no works for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, so that the vessels which Mr. Volney tells us he has seen there, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 28 at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, might be attacked without opposition; for the ships themselves are incapable of resistance, none having any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> than four rusty swivels. Suez has always been, notwithstanding its local disadvantages, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, on account of its geographical situation. It was by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Suez that the commodities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> were formerly conveyed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, till the discovery of the passage by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope converted that trade into a new channel. As the isthmus of Suez, which separates the Red Sea from the Mediterranean, is not more than 57 miles, it has been frequently proposed to join these two seas together by a canal. As there are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> nor remarkable inequalities of surface, this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> would at first view appear easy to be executed. But though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of levels would not prevent a junction, the great difficulty arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the corresponding coasts of the Mediterranean and the Red sea, which are of a low and sandy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, where the waters form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, shoals, and marshes, so that vessels cannot approach within a considerable distance. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> therefore be found scarcely possible to dig a permanent canal amid these shifting sands: not to mention, that the shore is destitute of harbours, which must be entirely the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of art. The country besides has not a drop of fresh water, and to supply the inhabitants, it must be brought as far as from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. The best and only method therefore of effecting this junction, is that which has been already successfully practised at different times; which is, by making the river itself the medium of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, for which the ground is perfectly well calculated; for Mount Makatun suddenly terminating in the latitude of Cairo, forms only a low and semicircular mound, round which is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> plain from the banks of the Nile as far as the point of the Red sea. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who early understood the advantage to be derived from this situation, adopted the idea of joining the two seas by a canal connected with the river. Strabo * observes, that this was first executed under Seleucus, who reigned about the time of the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and this work was so formidable as to occasion it to be remarked, "that it was 100 cubits (or 170 feet) wide, and deep enough for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels." After the Greeks conquered the country, it was restored by the Ptolemies, and again renewed by Trajan. In short, even the Arabs themselves followed these examples. "In the time of Omar ibn-el-Kattab (says the historian El Makin), the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> and Medina suffering from famine, the caliph ordered Amrou governor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> to cut a canal from the Nile to Kolumzoum, that the contributions of corn and barley appointed for <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> might be conveyed that way." This canal is the same which runs at present to Cairo, and lies itself in the country to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of Berket-el-Hadj, or the Lake of the Pilgrims. The place on the west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the gulf of Suez, where the children of Israel are supposed to have entered it, is called Badea, about six miles to the north of Cape Korondel, on the other side of the gulf, as we are informed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the ingenious Edward Worley Montague, F.R.S. to Dr. Watson, containing an account of his journey from Cairo to the Written Mountains in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>. Opposite to Badea is a strong current which sets to the opposite shore, about south-east, with a whirlpool called Birque Pharaone, the well or pool of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>, being the place where his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> is said to have been destroyed. We are told by the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, that the Egyptian shore from Suez to Badea is so rocky and steep, that there was no entering upon the gulf but at one of these two places. The British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, we believe, never attempted to carry on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with any of the ports of the Red Sea beyond Jidda, till, on the suggestion of Mr. Bruce, in 1776, some British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> equipped two or three vessels for Suez, laden with piece-goods of Bengal and coast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The command of the vessels was committed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Greig, a meritorious seaman; and the management of the goods was entrusted to Mr. Straw, a gentleman distinguished for his mercantile knowledge. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> turned out to advantage; but such such great expenses were incurred in making presents to the bey of Cairo and Suez, as to consume the whole profits gained by the sale of the cargo. The great purpose of the expedition was, however, accomplished, as a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRMAN">firman</a> was obtained from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Cairo to trade by the way of Suez. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, three ships went to Suez the following year, and as many in 1778. The opening of this trade alarmed the jealousy of the East India <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>; they applied to our government, and orders were given to relinquish this promising commerce. These orders reached Egypt sooner than Bengal, and the consequence was fatal to the unfortunate adventurers who visited Suez that year (1779). By a plan concerted between the beys, a large body of Bedouin Arabs attacked the caravan passing from Suez to Cairo with goods valued at 12 lacks of rupees. The goods were plundered, the Europeans were stripped and left naked in the desert, exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, without a drop of water to quench their thirst, or food to support <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Most of them died, and some of their bodies were afterwards found mangled and disfigured by wolves. We have been favoured with a particular account of the sufferings of our countrymen by a correspondent, which, we are sorry, we have not room to insert. Those who wish to obtain a more full account may consult the Annual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a> for 1781 or 1782.

SUFFETULA

Pages 435-435
