The proprietor of the estate is generally a wealthy Dutchman, who has erected on it substantial mills, boiling and curing houses. He rents this estate to a Chinese, who resides on it as a superintendent; and this renter (supposing the estate to consist of 300 or more acres) relents it to free men in parcels of 50 or 60 on these conditions: 'That they shall plant it in canes, and receive so much per pecul of 133½ pounds for every pecul of sugar that the canes shall produce.' When crop time comes on, the superintendent collects a sufficient number of persons from the adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> or villages, and takes off his crop as follows. To any set of tradesmen who bring their carts and buffaloes he agrees to give such a price per pecul to cut all his crop of canes, carry them to the mill and grind them. A second to boil them per pecul. A third to clay them and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> them for market per pecul. So that by this method of conducting a sugar estate the renter knows to a certainty what the produce of it will cost him per pecul. He has not any permanent or unnecessary expense; for when the crop is taken off, the taskmen return to their several pursuits in the towns and villages they came from; and there only remain the cane planters who are preparing the next year's crop. This like all other complex arts, by being divided into several branches, renders the labour cheaper and the work more perfectly done. Only clayed sugars are made at Batavia; these are in quality equal to the best from the West Indies, and are sold so low from the sugar estates as eighteen shillings sterling per pecul of 133½ lbs. This is not the selling price to the trader at Batavia, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> there is arbitrary, and sugar subject to duties imposed at will. The Shabander exacts a dollar per pecul on all sugar exported. The price of common labour is from 9d. to 10d. per day. By the method of carrying on the sugar estates, the taskmen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> considerably more than this not only from working extraordinary hours, but from being considered artists in their several branches. They do not make spirits sugar on the sugar estates. The molasses is sent for sale to Batavia, where one distillery may purchase the produce of an hundred estates. Here is a vast saving and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the price of spirits; not as in the West Indies, a distillery, for each estate; many centre in one, and arrack is sold at Batavia from 21 to 25 rixdollars per leaguer of 160 gallons; say 8d. per gallon." The SUGAR MAPLE, (the acer saccharinum of Lin-Description), as well as the sugar-cane, produces a great quantity of sugar. This tree grows in great numbers in the western counties of all the middle states of the American union. Those which grow in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> yield the sugar in a greater quantity than those which grow on the waters of the Ohio.—These trees are generally found mixed with the beech, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a>, white and water ash, the cucumber tree, linden, aspen, butternut, and wild cherry trees. They sometimes appear in groves covering five or six acres in a body, but they are more commonly interspersed with some or all of the forest trees which have been mentioned. From 30 to 50 trees are generally found upon an acre of ground. They grow only in the richest American soils, and frequently in stony ground. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">Springs</a> of the purest water abound in their neighbourhood. They are, when fully grown, as tall as the white and black oaks, vol. iii., and from two to three feet in diameter. They put forth a beautiful white blossom in the spring before they show a single leaf. The colour of the blossom distinguishes them from the acer rubrum, or the common maple, which affords a blossom of a red colour. The wood of the sugar maple-tree is extremely inflammable, and is preferred upon that account by hunters and surveyors for fire-wood. Its small branches are so much impregnated with sugar as to afford support to the cattle, horses, and sheep of the first settlers, during the winter, before they are able to cultivate forage for that purpose. Its ashes afford a great quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, exceeded by few, or perhaps by none, of the trees that grow in the woods of the United States. The tree is supposed to arrive at its full growth in the woods in twenty years. It is not injured by tapping; on the contrary, the more often it is tapped, the more syrup is obtained from it. In this respect it follows a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of animal secretion. A single tree had not only survived, but flourished after syrup is obtained from the yearly discharge of sap from the tree, in improving and increasing the sap, are demonstrated from the superior excellence of those trees which have been perforated in an hundred places, by a small wood-pecker which feeds upon the sap. The trees, after having been wounded in this way, distil the remains of their juice on the ground, and afterwards acquire a black colour. The sap of these trees is much sweeter to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> than that which is obtained from trees which have not been previously wounded, and it affords more sugar. From twenty-three gallons and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of sap, procured in twenty-four hours from only two of these dark coloured trees, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> Noble, Esq. of the state of New York, obtained four pounds and thirteen ounces of good grained sugar. A tree of an ordinary size yields in a good season from twenty to thirty gallons of sap, from which are made from five to six pounds of sugar. To this there are sometimes times remarkable exceptions. Samuel Lowe, Esq., a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, in the state of New York, informed Arthur Noble, Esq., that he had made twenty pounds and one ounce of sugar between the 14th and 23rd of April, in the year 1789, from a single tree that had been tapped for several successive years before. From the influence which culture has upon forest and other trees, it has been supposed, that by transplanting the sugar maple-tree into a garden, or by destroying such other trees as shelter it from the rays of the sun, the quantity of the sap might be increased, and its quality much improved. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a> county, in the state of Pennsylvania, planted a number of these trees above twenty years ago in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, from three gallons of the sap of which he obtains every year a pound of sugar. It was observed formerly, that it required five or six gallons of the sap of the trees which grow in the woods to produce the same quantity of sugar. The sap diffuses from the wood in the spring months. Trees which have been cut down in the winter for the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals of the new settlers, yield a considerable quantity of sap as soon as their trunks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> feel the rays of the sun in the spring of the year. It is in consequence of the sap of these trees being equally diffused through every part of them, that they live three years after they are girdled, that is, after a circular incision is made through the bark into the substance of the tree for the purpose of destroying it. It is remarkable that grafts thrive better under this tree in a meadow, than in situations exposed to the constant action of the sun. The season for tapping the trees is in February, March, and April, according to the weather which occurs in these months. Warm days and frothy nights are most favourable to a plentiful discharge of sap. The quantity obtained in a day from a tree is from five gallons to a pint, according to the greater or less heat of the air. Mr. Lowe informed Arthur Noble, Esq., that he obtained near three and twenty gallons of sap in one day (April 14, 1789,) from the single tree which was before mentioned. Such instances of a profusion of sap in single trees are however not very common. There is always a suspension of the discharge of sap in the night if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> succeed a warm day. The perforation in the tree is made with an axe or an auger. The latter is preferred from experience of its advantages. The auger is introduced about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an inch, and in an ascending <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> (that the sap may not be frozen in a slow current in the mornings or evenings), and is afterwards deepened gradually to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of two inches. A spout is introduced about half an inch into the hole made by this auger, and projects from three to twelve inches from the tree. The spout is generally made of the hawthorn or elder, which usually grows in the neighbourhood of the sugar trees. The tree is first tapped on the south side; when the discharge of its sap begins to lessen, an opening is made on the north side, from which an increased discharge takes place. The sap flows from four to six weeks, according to the temperature of the weather. Troughs large enough to contain three or four gallons made of white pine, or white ash, or of dried water ash, aspen, linden, poplar, or common maple, are placed under the spout to receive the sap, which is carried every day to a large receiver, made of either of the trees before mentioned. From this receiver it is conveyed, after being strained, to the boiler. We understand that there are three modes of reducing the sap to sugar; by evaporation, by freezing, and by boiling; of which the latter is most general, as being the most expeditious. We are farther assured, that the profit of the maple tree is not confined to its sugar. It affords most agreeable melodies, and an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>. The sap which is suitable for these purposes is obtained after the sap which affords the sugar has ceased to flow, so that the manufacturers of these different products of the maple tree, by succeeding, do not interfere with each other. The melodies may be made to compose the basis of a pleasant summer beer. The sap of the maple is moreover capable of affording a spirit; but we hope this precious juice will never be prostituted to this ignoble purpose. Should the use of sugar in diet become more general in this country (says Dr. Rush) it may tend to lessen the inclination or supposed necessity for spirits, for I have observed a relish for sugar in diet to be seldom accompanied by a love for strong drink. There are several other vegetables raised in our own country which afford sugar; as beet-roots, skirrets, parsnips, potatoes, celery, red cabbage stalks, the young shoots of Indian wheat. The sugar is most readily obtained from these, by making a tincture of the subject in rectified spirit of wine; which, when saturated by heat, will deposit the sugar upon standing in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. Sugar of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">Milk</a>. See Milk, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Acid of Sugar. See Chemistry Index. Sugillation, in Medicine, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRAVASATION">extravasation</a> of blood in the coats of the eye, which at first appears of a reddish colour, and afterwards livid or black. If the disorder is great, bleeding and purging are proper, as are also diuretics.

SURDOMINANT

Pages 430-430

in Music, a name given by M. Rameau to the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the tone, which of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> is the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> from the tonic when descending as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a> in rising. This denomination arises from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> which this author finds by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of the subdominant and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> mode of the tonic.
